faqs.q: What is a healthy waist size for Indians?
faqs.a: For Asian Indians, a waist below about 90 cm for men and 80 cm for women is considered healthy. Higher values increase the risk of diabetes and heart disease.

faqs.q: Why is belly fat more dangerous than other fat?
faqs.a: Because it lies around organs and releases inflammatory substances that cause insulin resistance, fatty liver and high cholesterol. It strongly raises diabetes and heart risks.

faqs.q: Can I have belly fat with a normal BMI?
faqs.a: Yes. Many Indians have a normal BMI but a large waist and high visceral fat. This pattern still increases metabolic risk, so waist measurement is important.

faqs.q: How fast can I lose belly fat?
faqs.a: Visceral fat often responds early to weight loss and exercise. A loss of 5 to 10 percent of body weight can reduce it noticeably. Aim for gradual, steady change.

faqs.q: Do crunches reduce belly fat?
faqs.a: No. Crunches strengthen muscles but do not burn fat from the belly alone. A combination of diet, aerobic activity and strength training reduces overall and visceral fat.

faqs.q: Does belly fat increase the risk of diabetes?
faqs.a: Yes. Visceral fat is a major driver of insulin resistance, which leads to prediabetes and type 2 diabetes. Reducing waist size lowers this risk.

Belly Fat, Diabetes and Metabolic Health: Why Waist Matters
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 12 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
Belly fat, also called visceral or abdominal fat, surrounds organs such as the liver and pancreas and releases substances that cause inflammation and insulin resistance. A larger waist raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, fatty liver, high blood pressure and heart disease, even when BMI looks normal. For Asian Indians, waist targets are lower: below about 90 cm for men and 80 cm for women.
Two people can weigh the same and have very different health risks. The difference is often where the fat sits. Fat around the belly is more dangerous than fat on the hips or thighs, and it is especially common in Indians.
What is visceral fat?
There are two main types of body fat:
Subcutaneous fat: Sits under the skin. It is the pinchable fat.
Visceral fat: Lies deep inside the abdomen, around organs. It is metabolically active and harmful.
Many Indians have more visceral fat at a lower BMI, a pattern sometimes called "thin-fat" or "normal weight obesity".
Why is belly fat harmful?
It releases inflammatory chemicals.
It drains fatty acids directly into the liver, causing fatty liver and insulin resistance.
It raises triglycerides and lowers HDL (good) cholesterol.
It increases blood pressure.
It raises the risk of heart disease and stroke.
It is linked to sleep apnoea and some cancers.
How do you measure it?
Waist circumference
Measure with a tape around the abdomen at the level of the navel, after a normal breath out. For Asian Indians, a value above about 90 cm in men and 80 cm in women is considered high.
Waist-to-height ratio
Divide waist by height. A ratio above about 0.5 suggests increased risk.
Other tests
Ultrasound, DEXA or CT scans can estimate visceral fat, but they are rarely needed for routine care.
Why is BMI not enough?
BMI does not tell you where fat is stored. A person with a normal BMI but a large waist may have a high risk. Using both BMI and waist gives a better picture.
How can you reduce belly fat?
Eat for metabolic health
Cut sugary drinks, sweets and refined flour.
Choose pulses, vegetables, nuts and whole grains.
Include protein at every meal.
Avoid late, heavy dinners and frequent snacking.
Be active
Walk briskly for 30 minutes most days.
Add strength exercises two to three times a week.
Break up long periods of sitting.
Sleep and stress
Poor sleep and chronic stress increase belly fat through hormones such as cortisol. Aim for seven to eight hours of sleep and learn simple stress management.
Limit alcohol
Alcohol adds calories and encourages fat storage in the abdomen and liver.
Medical help
In people with obesity or diabetes, medicines such as GLP-1 medicines or metabolic surgery may help reduce visceral fat when lifestyle is not enough.
Does spot reduction work?
No. Sit-ups alone do not remove belly fat. Fat is lost from the whole body, and visceral fat often reduces early when you lose weight.
When should you see a doctor?
Get checked if your waist is above the targets, you have a family history of diabetes, or you have high blood pressure, cholesterol or fatty liver. A blood sugar, HbA1c and lipid test are good starting points.
Points to keep
Visceral belly fat is more harmful than fat elsewhere.
Waist size is a simple but powerful health measure.
Indian targets are lower than international ones.
Diet, exercise, sleep and weight loss reduce belly fat.
Early testing can prevent diabetes and heart disease.
Your tape measure tells you more than your weighing scale. Small, regular steps can shrink your waist and lower your risk. For a personalised assessment and plan, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.

Frequently asked questions
What is a healthy waist size for Indians?
For Asian Indians, a waist below about 90 cm for men and 80 cm for women is considered healthy. Higher values increase the risk of diabetes and heart disease.
Why is belly fat more dangerous than other fat?
Because it lies around organs and releases inflammatory substances that cause insulin resistance, fatty liver and high cholesterol. It strongly raises diabetes and heart risks.
Can I have belly fat with a normal BMI?
Yes. Many Indians have a normal BMI but a large waist and high visceral fat. This pattern still increases metabolic risk, so waist measurement is important.
How fast can I lose belly fat?
Visceral fat often responds early to weight loss and exercise. A loss of 5 to 10 percent of body weight can reduce it noticeably. Aim for gradual, steady change.
Do crunches reduce belly fat?
No. Crunches strengthen muscles but do not burn fat from the belly alone. A combination of diet, aerobic activity and strength training reduces overall and visceral fat.
Does belly fat increase the risk of diabetes?
Yes. Visceral fat is a major driver of insulin resistance, which leads to prediabetes and type 2 diabetes. Reducing waist size lowers this risk.

faqs.q: What is the best Indian breakfast for diabetes?
faqs.a: Breakfasts with protein and fibre work well, such as moong dal chilla, egg bhurji with whole wheat roti, vegetable daliya, sprouts chaat or idli with plenty of sambar. Portion control is important.

faqs.q: Is poha good for diabetics?
faqs.a: Poha can be eaten in moderation if you add vegetables and protein such as peanuts or sprouts and keep the portion small. Plain poha alone may raise blood sugar quickly.

faqs.q: Can diabetics eat idli for breakfast?
faqs.a: Yes, in controlled portions with a generous serving of vegetable sambar. Ragi or oats idli adds fibre. Avoid eating many idlis with only coconut chutney.

faqs.q: Should diabetics skip breakfast?
faqs.a: Skipping breakfast is not usually recommended, especially if you take certain diabetes medicines, as it can lead to low sugar or overeating later. A balanced breakfast helps keep sugar steady.

faqs.q: Is tea okay for diabetics in the morning?
faqs.a: Tea without sugar or with minimal sugar is fine for most people. Avoid sweetened tea and pair it with a protein-rich breakfast rather than biscuits.

Best Indian Breakfast for Diabetes: Options and Mistakes
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 5 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
A diabetes-friendly Indian breakfast combines protein, fibre and moderate carbohydrates. Good options include moong dal or besan chilla, vegetable oats or daliya, egg bhurji with whole wheat roti, vegetable upma with sprouts, idli with sambar in controlled portions and paneer stuffed rotis. Avoid sugary cereals, white bread with jam, fried snacks and sweetened tea or juice.
Breakfast sets the tone for blood sugar through the morning. For people with diabetes, a breakfast with enough protein and fibre and a controlled amount of carbohydrate helps prevent spikes and mid-morning hunger. Many traditional Indian breakfasts can be adapted to suit diabetes.
What makes a good diabetes breakfast?
Protein, such as eggs, dal, paneer, curd or sprouts
Fibre from vegetables, whole grains or millets
Moderate portions of carbohydrates
Little or no added sugar
Healthy fats in small amounts
Practical Indian breakfast ideas
Moong dal or besan chilla
Packed with protein and can include grated vegetables. Serve with mint chutney or curd.
Vegetable daliya or oats
Broken wheat or oats cooked with vegetables give fibre. Avoid instant flavoured oats with added sugar.
Egg bhurji or omelette
Add onions, tomatoes and spinach, and pair with one whole wheat or millet roti.
Vegetable upma or poha with sprouts
Add plenty of vegetables and peanuts or sprouts to boost protein, and keep portions moderate.
Idli with sambar
Two idlis with a generous bowl of vegetable sambar provide a balanced meal. Ragi or oats idli adds fibre.
Paneer or vegetable stuffed roti
Whole wheat or multigrain roti stuffed with paneer, methi or mixed vegetables, with curd.
Sprouts chaat
Moong sprouts with onion, tomato, lemon and spices make a high-protein option.
What are common breakfast mistakes?
Skipping breakfast, which can lead to overeating later
White bread with jam or butter alone
Sugary breakfast cereals and packaged juices
Fried items such as puri, vada or samosa
Large portions of poha or upma without protein
Sweetened tea or coffee
Eating only fruit for breakfast
Is fruit okay at breakfast?
Whole fruit can be part of breakfast in a moderate portion alongside protein, such as an apple with eggs or curd. Avoid fruit juice.
How do you know if your breakfast works?
Checking blood sugar about two hours after breakfast, as advised by your doctor, helps you see which options suit you best.
The quick version
Include protein and fibre at breakfast.
Many Indian breakfasts can be adapted for diabetes.
Control portions of rice and wheat-based dishes.
Avoid sugary cereals, juices and fried foods.
Check post-breakfast sugar to personalise.
A thoughtful breakfast can make blood sugar easier to manage for the rest of the day. Familiar Indian dishes, adjusted with more protein and vegetables, work well. Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur helps patients plan diabetes-friendly meals.
When to seek urgent care
Seek urgent care for vomiting, confusion, unusual drowsiness or symptoms of very high or very low sugar, especially if you take insulin or tablets that can cause low sugar.
Sources and further reading
WHO: Healthy diet
NIDDK: Diabetes diet, eating and physical activity
Frequently asked questions
What is the best Indian breakfast for diabetes?
Breakfasts with protein and fibre work well, such as moong dal chilla, egg bhurji with whole wheat roti, vegetable daliya, sprouts chaat or idli with plenty of sambar. Portion control is important.
Is poha good for diabetics?
Poha can be eaten in moderation if you add vegetables and protein such as peanuts or sprouts and keep the portion small. Plain poha alone may raise blood sugar quickly.
Can diabetics eat idli for breakfast?
Yes, in controlled portions with a generous serving of vegetable sambar. Ragi or oats idli adds fibre. Avoid eating many idlis with only coconut chutney.
Should diabetics skip breakfast?
Skipping breakfast is not usually recommended, especially if you take certain diabetes medicines, as it can lead to low sugar or overeating later. A balanced breakfast helps keep sugar steady.
Is tea okay for diabetics in the morning?
Tea without sugar or with minimal sugar is fine for most people. Avoid sweetened tea and pair it with a protein-rich breakfast rather than biscuits.

faqs.q: Can diabetics eat white rice?
faqs.a: Yes, in controlled portions and paired with dal, vegetables and protein. White rice raises sugar faster than higher-fibre options, so smaller portions and balanced meals help.

faqs.q: Is brown rice better for diabetes?
faqs.a: Brown rice has more fibre and nutrients and may raise blood sugar more slowly than white rice. Portion size still matters, so do not overeat brown rice.

faqs.q: How much rice should a diabetic eat?
faqs.a: Many people do well keeping cooked rice to about a quarter of their plate, often half to one cup per meal. Your doctor or dietitian can personalise portions based on your sugar readings.

faqs.q: Is it better to eat roti or rice for diabetes?
faqs.a: Both contain carbohydrates. Whole wheat or millet rotis usually have more fibre than white rice, but portion size and pairing matter most. Many people include both in moderation.

faqs.q: Does eating vegetables first help with rice?
faqs.a: Yes. Eating vegetables and protein before rice can slow sugar absorption and reduce post-meal spikes. A short walk after meals also helps.

Can People With Diabetes Eat Rice? Practical Tips
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 5 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
Yes, people with diabetes can usually eat rice in controlled portions. Keep rice to about a quarter of your plate, pair it with dal, vegetables and protein, choose less polished or brown rice or mix with millets, and avoid having rice alone or in large amounts. Check your blood sugar after meals to see how you respond.
Rice is a staple in many Indian homes, and many people with diabetes worry they must give it up. Rice is a carbohydrate that raises blood sugar, but with the right portion, type and pairing, many people with diabetes can include rice in their meals.
Why does rice raise blood sugar?
White rice is mostly starch, which breaks down into glucose. Polished white rice has less fibre and can raise blood sugar quickly, especially in large portions. The total amount of carbohydrate you eat matters most.
Which types of rice are better?
Brown rice
Contains more fibre and nutrients than white rice and may raise blood sugar more slowly.
Parboiled rice
Partly processed in a way that can lower its effect on blood sugar compared with polished white rice.
Hand-pounded or less polished rice
Retains more of the outer layers and fibre.
Mixing with millets
Combining rice with jowar, bajra, foxtail millet or other millets increases fibre.
Portion still matters for every type.
How much rice can you eat?
Portions depend on your body size, activity level and blood sugar control. A practical approach is to keep cooked rice to roughly a quarter of the plate, often about half to one cup per meal, as advised by your doctor or dietitian. Monitoring your sugar helps you personalise this.
How can you reduce blood sugar spikes?
Eat vegetables and protein first, then rice
Pair rice with dal, sambar, rajma, paneer, fish, egg or chicken
Add a large salad or vegetable side
Avoid rice with only potato or other starchy dishes
Choose cooled and reheated rice occasionally, which may have more resistant starch
Take a 10 to 15 minute walk after meals
Should you have rice at dinner?
Many people find a lighter dinner helps sugar control. If you eat rice at dinner, keep the portion small and pair it well. Avoid eating late at night.
What about rice-based foods?
Idli, dosa, poha, upma and pulao can fit in moderation. Add vegetables and protein, such as sambar, chutney with peanuts or sprouts, and watch portions.
In short
Rice can fit into a diabetes diet with portion control.
Brown, parboiled or millet mixes add fibre.
Pair rice with protein and vegetables.
Eat vegetables and protein first.
Check sugar after meals to personalise portions.
You do not have to give up rice to manage diabetes. Smart portions and pairings can keep blood sugar steady while you enjoy familiar meals. Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur helps patients build practical Indian meal plans.
When to seek urgent care
Seek urgent care for vomiting, confusion, unusual drowsiness or symptoms of very high or very low sugar, especially if you take insulin or tablets that can cause low sugar.
Sources and further reading
WHO: Healthy diet
NIDDK: Diabetes diet, eating and physical activity
Frequently asked questions
Can diabetics eat white rice?
Yes, in controlled portions and paired with dal, vegetables and protein. White rice raises sugar faster than higher-fibre options, so smaller portions and balanced meals help.
Is brown rice better for diabetes?
Brown rice has more fibre and nutrients and may raise blood sugar more slowly than white rice. Portion size still matters, so do not overeat brown rice.
How much rice should a diabetic eat?
Many people do well keeping cooked rice to about a quarter of their plate, often half to one cup per meal. Your doctor or dietitian can personalise portions based on your sugar readings.
Is it better to eat roti or rice for diabetes?
Both contain carbohydrates. Whole wheat or millet rotis usually have more fibre than white rice, but portion size and pairing matter most. Many people include both in moderation.
Does eating vegetables first help with rice?
Yes. Eating vegetables and protein before rice can slow sugar absorption and reduce post-meal spikes. A short walk after meals also helps.

faqs.a: Some changes appear within weeks, but HbA1c usually shows improvement after about three months. Most people need several months of consistent changes to return to the normal range.

faqs.q: How much weight should I lose with prediabetes?
faqs.a: Losing about 5 to 7 percent of body weight can lower diabetes risk significantly. For someone weighing 80 kg, that is about 4 to 6 kg. Your doctor can set a personal target.

faqs.q: Is walking enough to reverse prediabetes?
faqs.a: Regular brisk walking helps a lot, especially combined with healthy eating and weight loss. Adding strength training further improves insulin sensitivity.

faqs.q: Do I need medicine for prediabetes?
faqs.a: Most people start with lifestyle changes. Doctors may add metformin for some high-risk people. Discuss options with your doctor.

Can Prediabetes Go Away? How to Lower Your Risk
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 3 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
Yes, prediabetes can often go back to normal blood sugar levels, especially when caught early. Losing about 5 to 7 percent of body weight, doing about 150 minutes of moderate activity each week, eating fewer refined carbohydrates and sugary foods, sleeping well and managing stress can lower the risk of type 2 diabetes. Regular testing tracks progress.
Prediabetes means your blood sugar is higher than normal but not yet in the diabetes range. It is common and often silent. The encouraging news is that prediabetes can often return to normal, and many people prevent or delay type 2 diabetes through lifestyle changes.
Why does prediabetes happen?
Prediabetes usually develops because cells become less responsive to insulin, a state called insulin resistance. Excess weight, especially around the waist, inactivity, poor sleep, family history and age all contribute. In Indians, insulin resistance can develop at a lower body weight.
Which changes make the biggest difference?
Weight loss
Even modest weight loss improves insulin sensitivity. Studies show that losing about 5 to 7 percent of body weight can significantly reduce the chance of developing diabetes.
Physical activity
Brisk walking, cycling or swimming for about 150 minutes a week, spread over most days, helps muscles use glucose. Strength training two to three times a week adds benefit.
Healthier eating
Reduce sugary drinks, sweets and refined flour products
Choose whole grains, millets, pulses and vegetables
Include protein at meals
Watch portion sizes of rice and rotis
Limit fried and processed foods
Sleep and stress
Poor sleep and chronic stress raise blood sugar. Aim for regular, adequate sleep and practical stress relief.
Stop smoking and limit alcohol
Both affect blood sugar and overall health.
How long does it take?
Some people see improvement in fasting sugar within weeks, while HbA1c usually reflects changes after about three months. Consistency over months matters more than quick fixes.
Can medicines help?
For some high-risk people, doctors may prescribe metformin alongside lifestyle changes. Medicines do not replace healthy habits.
Does prediabetes always become diabetes?
No. Without changes, many people progress over time, but lifestyle measures can prevent or delay this. Even if diabetes develops later, the habits you build will improve control.
How often should you test?
Usually at least once a year, or more often while making changes. Your doctor will guide timing based on your risk.
In short
Prediabetes can often return to normal.
Losing 5 to 7 percent of body weight lowers risk.
Aim for 150 minutes of activity weekly.
Cut refined carbohydrates and sugary drinks.
Test regularly to track progress.
Prediabetes is a chance to change course before diabetes develops. Small, sustained steps can make a big difference. Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur helps patients build practical, personalised prevention plans.
When to seek urgent care
Seek urgent care for extreme thirst with vomiting, confusion, deep rapid breathing or unusual drowsiness, which can signal very high sugar.
Sources and further reading
ADA: Prediabetes
NIDDK: Preventing type 2 diabetes
Frequently asked questions
Can prediabetes be reversed?
Yes, many people return to normal blood sugar levels with weight loss, regular exercise and healthier eating. Results vary, and continued healthy habits are needed to keep sugar levels in range.
How long does it take to reverse prediabetes?
Some changes appear within weeks, but HbA1c usually shows improvement after about three months. Most people need several months of consistent changes to return to the normal range.
How much weight should I lose with prediabetes?
Losing about 5 to 7 percent of body weight can lower diabetes risk significantly. For someone weighing 80 kg, that is about 4 to 6 kg. Your doctor can set a personal target.
Is walking enough to reverse prediabetes?
Regular brisk walking helps a lot, especially combined with healthy eating and weight loss. Adding strength training further improves insulin sensitivity.
Do I need medicine for prediabetes?
Most people start with lifestyle changes. Doctors may add metformin for some high-risk people. Discuss options with your doctor.

faqs.q: Can type 2 diabetes be cured permanently?
faqs.a: Type 2 diabetes is not usually considered curable, but it can go into remission, meaning blood sugar stays normal without medicines. The tendency remains, so diabetes can return if weight is regained.

faqs.q: What is the definition of diabetes remission?
faqs.a: Remission is commonly defined as HbA1c below 6.5 percent for at least three months after stopping glucose-lowering medicines. Your doctor confirms remission with tests.

faqs.q: How much weight loss is needed for diabetes remission?
faqs.a: Greater weight loss increases the chance of remission, and losing a meaningful percentage of body weight early after diagnosis gives the best chance. Your doctor can set a safe, realistic target.

faqs.q: Can I stop my diabetes medicines if my sugar becomes normal?
faqs.a: Do not stop medicines on your own. Your doctor will reduce or stop them gradually while monitoring sugar levels to avoid problems.

faqs.q: Does remission mean I no longer need check-ups?
faqs.a: No. You still need regular HbA1c tests and checks for eyes, kidneys, feet and heart, because diabetes can return and some complications may already be present.

Quick answer

It is most likely with significant weight loss, especially soon after diagnosis, through structured diet changes, physical activity, medicines that aid weight loss or metabolic surgery. Diabetes can return, so monitoring and healthy habits must continue.
Many people with type 2 diabetes ask whether their diabetes can be reversed. Doctors prefer the term remission, which means blood sugar returns to the non-diabetic range without diabetes medicines for a sustained period. Remission is possible for some people, but it is not the same as a permanent cure.
What does remission mean?
Remission means your blood sugar is in a healthy range without medicines. The underlying tendency to diabetes remains, so blood sugar can rise again if weight is regained or other risk factors return. Regular check-ups, including HbA1c, eye, kidney and foot checks, should continue.
Who is more likely to achieve remission?
People diagnosed recently, often within the first few years
Those who lose a significant amount of weight
People who are not yet on insulin or many medicines
Those with good remaining insulin production
Remission is less likely after many years of diabetes, but improving control still brings major health benefits.
How can remission be achieved?
Weight loss
Losing excess weight, particularly fat around the liver and pancreas, can improve insulin function. Many studies show that greater weight loss increases the chance of remission.
Structured eating plans
Doctor-supervised plans, including low-calorie programmes, reduced refined carbohydrates and balanced Indian meals, can support weight loss. Crash diets without supervision are not advised.
Physical activity
Regular aerobic and strength exercise improves insulin sensitivity and supports weight maintenance.
Medicines that support weight loss
Some medicines, such as GLP-1-based therapies, can aid weight loss and sugar control under medical supervision.
Metabolic surgery
For selected people with obesity, bariatric or metabolic surgery can lead to remission in many cases.
Is it safe to stop diabetes medicines?
Never stop medicines on your own. Your doctor will reduce or stop them gradually as blood sugar improves, while monitoring to avoid both high and low sugar.
What happens if diabetes returns?
If weight is regained or sugar rises again, medicines may need to restart. This is not a failure. It reflects the nature of the condition. Continuing healthy habits lowers the risk.
What if remission is not possible?
Even without remission, losing weight, eating well, staying active and taking the right medicines can greatly reduce the risk of heart, kidney, eye and nerve complications.
In short
Remission means healthy sugar levels without medicines.
It is most likely with significant weight loss soon after diagnosis.
Diet, exercise, medicines and surgery can help.
Never stop medicines without medical guidance.
Monitoring continues because diabetes can return.
Remission is a realistic goal for some people with type 2 diabetes and a strong motivator for healthy change. A diabetologist can create a safe, personalised plan and adjust medicines as you improve. Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur supports patients aiming for better control and remission.
When to seek urgent care
Seek urgent care for extreme thirst with vomiting, confusion, deep rapid breathing, unusual drowsiness, or signs of very low sugar such as sweating, shaking and confusion.

WHO: Diabetes fact sheet
NIDDK: What is diabetes
Frequently asked questions
Can type 2 diabetes be cured permanently?
Type 2 diabetes is not usually considered curable, but it can go into remission, meaning blood sugar stays normal without medicines. The tendency remains, so diabetes can return if weight is regained.
What is the definition of diabetes remission?
Remission is commonly defined as HbA1c below 6.5 percent for at least three months after stopping glucose-lowering medicines. Your doctor confirms remission with tests.
How much weight loss is needed for diabetes remission?
Greater weight loss increases the chance of remission, and losing a meaningful percentage of body weight early after diagnosis gives the best chance. Your doctor can set a safe, realistic target.
Can I stop my diabetes medicines if my sugar becomes normal?
Do not stop medicines on your own. Your doctor will reduce or stop them gradually while monitoring sugar levels to avoid problems.
Does remission mean I no longer need check-ups?
No. You still need regular HbA1c tests and checks for eyes, kidneys, feet and heart, because diabetes can return and some complications may already be present.

faqs.q: Is CGM safe during pregnancy?
faqs.a: CGM is generally considered safe in pregnancy and is used in diabetic pregnancies. Sensor adhesives can irritate the skin, and some devices are validated for pregnancy while others are not. Ask your doctor which one to use.

faqs.q: What is the glucose target in pregnancy on CGM?
faqs.a: For type 1 diabetes, the common target is more than 70 percent of time between 63 and 140 mg/dL, with less than 4 percent below 63 mg/dL. Your team may set different targets.

faqs.q: Do I still need finger-pricks if I use CGM?
faqs.a: Sometimes. You may need them to confirm unusual readings, during rapid changes or when symptoms do not match the CGM. Your team will advise.

faqs.q: Can women with gestational diabetes use CGM?
faqs.a: Some do, especially if sugars are unstable or if on insulin. Many women are managed with a glucometer alone. Discuss with your doctor.

faqs.q: Does CGM reduce the risk of complications in pregnancy?
faqs.a: In type 1 diabetes pregnancies, CGM has been linked with better glucose control and fewer neonatal complications such as low blood sugar in newborns. Evidence in other groups is still growing.

faqs.q: How often should my CGM data be reviewed?
faqs.a: Often every one to two weeks during pregnancy, because insulin needs change quickly. Your team will set the schedule.

CGM in Pregnancy: When It Helps and What to Know
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 16 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
CGM can help pregnant women with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, and may be useful in some with gestational diabetes, by showing glucose patterns day and night. Pregnancy targets are tighter than usual, about 63 to 140 mg/dL with more than 70 percent time in range. CGM supports but does not completely replace finger-pricks, and should be used with advice from the diabetes and obstetric team.
Blood sugar control matters a great deal in pregnancy. Tight, stable sugars protect both the mother and baby. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) can give a fuller picture than finger-pricks alone, and is increasingly used in diabetic pregnancies.
Why does blood sugar control matter in pregnancy?
High blood sugar can increase the risk of a large baby, premature birth, birth injuries, low blood sugar in the newborn, high blood pressure in pregnancy and caesarean delivery. In early pregnancy, uncontrolled sugars can raise the risk of birth defects. Low sugars also need to be avoided, especially in women on insulin.
How can CGM help?
It shows patterns that finger-pricks miss, such as post-meal peaks and night-time lows.
It supports precise insulin dose changes, which are frequent in pregnancy.
It can alert you to dangerous lows.
It gives your doctor a clear 14-day report.
Studies in type 1 diabetes in pregnancy show that CGM can improve time in range and may reduce complications for babies.
What are the pregnancy targets?
Typical targets for CGM in pregnancy with type 1 diabetes are:
Time in range (63 to 140 mg/dL): more than 70 percent
Time below 63 mg/dL: less than 4 percent
Time below 54 mg/dL: less than 1 percent
Time above 140 mg/dL: less than 25 percent
Targets in type 2 and gestational diabetes may be similar, but your team will individualise them.
Who may benefit most?
Pregnant women with type 1 diabetes
Women with type 2 diabetes using insulin
Women with gestational diabetes who have unclear or unstable sugars, or are on insulin
Women with frequent or unnoticed low blood sugar
Women who find it hard to do multiple finger-pricks
What are the limits?
A small lag compared with blood readings
Possible errors in the first day of a sensor or with pressure on it
Skin irritation from adhesives
Cost and availability in India
Not all brands are approved or validated for pregnancy use
Need to confirm unusual readings with a finger-prick
How should you use CGM safely in pregnancy?
Start with your doctor's advice, preferably before or in early pregnancy.
Choose a sensor that is suitable for pregnancy.
Wear it as continuously as possible.
Keep a food and insulin diary.
Check with a glucometer when a reading does not match your symptoms.
Review the report with your doctor or diabetes educator every one to two weeks.
Do not change insulin doses on your own.
What about gestational diabetes?
Many women with gestational diabetes manage with diet and a glucometer. A CGM may be useful for a short period to understand patterns, particularly when sugars are hard to control. Its role is still being studied, and practices differ.
When should you see a doctor?
Contact your team if you have repeated lows or highs, a sensor that gives suspicious readings, skin reactions, or symptoms such as extreme thirst, vomiting or reduced baby movements.
Points to keep
CGM can improve safety and control in diabetic pregnancies.
Pregnancy targets are tighter than usual.
It is most helpful for type 1 or insulin-treated diabetes.
Finger-pricks are still needed when readings are doubtful.
Use it under the guidance of your diabetes and obstetric team.
A steady sugar level gives your baby the best start. CGM is a helpful tool, not a replacement for care and follow-up. For guidance during pregnancy, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
Sources and further reading
NIDDK: Continuous glucose monitoring
WHO: Diabetes fact sheet
Frequently asked questions
Is CGM safe during pregnancy?
CGM is generally considered safe in pregnancy and is used in diabetic pregnancies. Sensor adhesives can irritate the skin, and some devices are validated for pregnancy while others are not. Ask your doctor which one to use.
What is the glucose target in pregnancy on CGM?
For type 1 diabetes, the common target is more than 70 percent of time between 63 and 140 mg/dL, with less than 4 percent below 63 mg/dL. Your team may set different targets.
Do I still need finger-pricks if I use CGM?
Sometimes. You may need them to confirm unusual readings, during rapid changes or when symptoms do not match the CGM. Your team will advise.
Can women with gestational diabetes use CGM?
Some do, especially if sugars are unstable or if on insulin. Many women are managed with a glucometer alone. Discuss with your doctor.
Does CGM reduce the risk of complications in pregnancy?
In type 1 diabetes pregnancies, CGM has been linked with better glucose control and fewer neonatal complications such as low blood sugar in newborns. Evidence in other groups is still growing.
How often should my CGM data be reviewed?
Often every one to two weeks during pregnancy, because insulin needs change quickly. Your team will set the schedule.

faqs.q: Is CGM better than a glucometer?
faqs.a: A CGM gives more information, including trends and alarms, and is especially useful for people on insulin. A glucometer is still accurate, cheaper and enough for many people. The better option depends on your needs.

faqs.q: Do I still need finger-pricks with a CGM?
faqs.a: Often fewer. Many modern CGMs do not need routine finger-pricks, but you may check with a glucometer if symptoms do not match the reading or when advised.

faqs.q: How long does a CGM sensor last?
faqs.a: Most sensors last about 10 to 15 days, depending on the device. You then replace it with a new one.

faqs.q: Is CGM accurate?
faqs.a: Modern CGMs are generally accurate, but they measure fluid under the skin, so readings lag slightly behind blood. During rapid changes, differences can be larger.

faqs.q: Can type 2 diabetics without insulin use CGM?
faqs.a: Yes. It can help them understand food and activity effects, even in short-term use, though evidence of benefit is strongest in insulin users. Discuss with your doctor.

faqs.q: Is CGM expensive in India?
faqs.a: Cost varies by brand and duration. Ask your doctor for current options, including short-term use, which can be cheaper.

CGM vs Glucometer: Which Is Better for Type 2 Diabetes?
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 16 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
A glucometer measures your blood sugar at one moment, using a drop of blood from a finger-prick. A CGM uses a small sensor on the arm or abdomen to measure sugar in the fluid under the skin every few minutes, showing trends and patterns. A CGM is more informative and convenient, especially for people on insulin, but costs more. A glucometer is still reliable, affordable and useful for many people.
For decades, a finger-prick glucometer was the only way to check blood sugar at home. Now continuous glucose monitors (CGMs) show sugar levels all day and night. Both have a place. Understanding the difference helps you choose well.
How does a glucometer work?
You prick your finger, place a drop of blood on a test strip and the meter shows a number. It gives a precise reading for that moment. Most people test fasting, before meals or two hours after meals, as advised.
How does a CGM work?
A tiny sensor filament sits just under the skin, held by a patch. It measures glucose in the interstitial fluid every one to five minutes. A reader or phone displays the current level, the trend arrow and a graph. Sensors usually last 10 to 15 days and then need replacing.
What are the differences?

Glucometer

What are the benefits of a CGM?
You see how food, exercise, stress and sleep affect your sugar.
It can warn you about low blood sugar, which is especially valuable if you use insulin or sulfonylureas.
It reveals night-time lows and early-morning highs.
It reduces the number of finger-pricks.
Reports help your doctor adjust treatment more precisely.
It can motivate behaviour change.
What are the limitations?
Higher cost, and in some cases limited availability
A small lag compared with blood readings
Occasional sensor errors, skin irritation or sensor falling off
Readings should be checked with a finger-prick when symptoms do not match
Data overload can cause anxiety in some people
Who benefits most from a CGM?
People on multiple daily insulin injections
People with frequent or unrecognised low blood sugar
Those with unpredictable sugar levels
Pregnant women with diabetes
People wanting to understand food and activity effects, in consultation with the doctor
When is a glucometer enough?
For many people with stable type 2 diabetes on tablets, a glucometer used at planned times is enough. A CGM can also be used for short periods, such as 10 to 14 days, to review patterns and adjust treatment.
Can you use both?
Yes. Many people with a CGM still keep a glucometer for checking symptoms, confirming unusual readings or when a sensor fails.
When should you see a doctor?
See your doctor if your readings are often above target, you have low sugar symptoms, or you want to know whether a CGM suits you.
In short
A glucometer gives a single reading. A CGM gives continuous readings and trends.
CGM is especially helpful for people on insulin or with low sugar episodes.
A glucometer is affordable and enough for many people with stable diabetes.
Short-term CGM use can guide treatment.
Your doctor can help you decide.
The best tool is the one that helps you control your sugar safely and fits your life and budget. To choose the right monitoring plan, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.

WHO: Diabetes fact sheet
Frequently asked questions
Is CGM better than a glucometer?
A CGM gives more information, including trends and alarms, and is especially useful for people on insulin. A glucometer is still accurate, cheaper and enough for many people. The better option depends on your needs.
Do I still need finger-pricks with a CGM?
Often fewer. Many modern CGMs do not need routine finger-pricks, but you may check with a glucometer if symptoms do not match the reading or when advised.
How long does a CGM sensor last?
Most sensors last about 10 to 15 days, depending on the device. You then replace it with a new one.
Is CGM accurate?
Modern CGMs are generally accurate, but they measure fluid under the skin, so readings lag slightly behind blood. During rapid changes, differences can be larger.
Can type 2 diabetics without insulin use CGM?
Yes. It can help them understand food and activity effects, even in short-term use, though evidence of benefit is strongest in insulin users. Discuss with your doctor.
Is CGM expensive in India?
Cost varies by brand and duration. Ask your doctor for current options, including short-term use, which can be cheaper.

faqs.q: How long does a CGM sensor last?
faqs.a: Most sensors are worn for about 10 to 15 days, depending on the system, and then replaced with a new one, ideally on a different spot to give the skin a rest. Clinic-based professional CGMs are usually worn for a fixed two-week period. Afterwards, the doctor downloads the recorded data and goes through the patterns with you.

faqs.q: What is a good time in range for someone with diabetes?
faqs.a: For most adults with Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes, the usual goal is more than 70% of the day between 70 and 180 mg/dL, roughly 17 hours. Time below 70 mg/dL should ideally stay under 4%. Older adults and people prone to lows often have gentler targets, because avoiding hypoglycaemia comes first. Your doctor will set goals that suit you.

faqs.q: Is a CGM more accurate than a glucometer?
faqs.a: Not quite. A glucometer tests blood directly and is very accurate for a single moment. A CGM reads the fluid under the skin, so it can lag several minutes behind, especially when sugar is changing fast. What a CGM offers is continuous data and direction of change. Most people who use a CGM keep a glucometer for backup checks.

faqs.q: Can a CGM pick up low sugar at night?
faqs.a: Yes, and this is one of its most useful features. Because the sensor records continuously, it catches overnight lows that people often sleep through without noticing. Real-time systems can sound an alarm when glucose falls below a set level. Doctors reviewing CGM reports frequently find night-time lows that lead to safer changes in medicine or insulin timing.

faqs.q: Do I need a CGM if I have Type 2 diabetes and don't take insulin?
faqs.a: Not necessarily, though it can help. Current international guidance supports CGM for people with Type 2 diabetes on non-insulin medicines when it improves management. Even two weeks of data can show how your meals, activity and tablets affect your sugar. Whether ongoing use makes sense depends on how stable your control is, your treatment plan and cost.

faqs.q: Can I shower, swim or work out with a CGM?
faqs.a: Most sensors are water-resistant, so bathing, showering and exercise are usually fine. Water depth and time limits differ between devices, so check your instructions before swimming. Heavy sweating can loosen the adhesive, and some people add an overpatch to keep it secure. In contact sports, a sensor can occasionally get knocked off, so a little extra care helps.

faqs.q: What is an AGP report?
faqs.a: The Ambulatory Glucose Profile is a standard one-page CGM summary, usually covering 14 days. It shows your time in range, average glucose and glucose management indicator, along with a graph that overlays all the days as though they were one. That makes repeating patterns, like post-breakfast spikes or overnight lows, much easier for your doctor to spot.

faqs.q: Does putting on a CGM hurt?
faqs.a: Most people feel a quick pinch, and some feel nothing at all, when the sensor is applied. After that, the thin filament under the skin is rarely noticed during normal activity. A few people get mild itching or irritation from the adhesive. If you notice pain, swelling, spreading redness or discharge around the site, have a doctor take a look.

Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM): How It Works, Who Needs It & How to Read the Data
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 15 October 2026 · 14 minutes
Quick answer
Continuous glucose monitoring uses a wearable sensor to measure glucose in the fluid under the skin every few minutes, day and night. It shows trends, highs, lows and "time in range," the share of the day your glucose stays between 70 and 180 mg/dL. People with Type 1 diabetes, people with Type 2 diabetes on insulin or other medicines, pregnant women with diabetes, and anyone with frequent or unnoticed lows are most likely to benefit. The data should be reviewed with a doctor before any treatment changes.
A continuous glucose monitor, or CGM, is a small sensor you wear on your arm or abdomen that checks your glucose every few minutes, around the clock, for up to two weeks. You get a moving picture of your sugar levels rather than one reading taken whenever you remember to prick your finger.
That difference matters more than it sounds. A fasting sugar of 118 mg/dL tells you about one moment on one morning. It says nothing about the 2 a.m. low you slept through or the spike that followed Sunday's lunch.
This guide covers how CGM works, who tends to get real value from it, how to read the report your doctor hands you, and where the technology falls short.
What is continuous glucose monitoring?
A CGM system has a sensor, something that sends the data, and a screen to see it on.
The sensor is a very thin, flexible filament that sits just under the skin. It is usually worn on the back of the upper arm, sometimes on the abdomen. A transmitter, either built in or clipped on, sends readings to a phone app or a small handheld reader. In some setups the readings go straight to an insulin pump.
Depending on the device, a new reading comes in every one to fifteen minutes. Across a day that adds up to hundreds of values. Most people using a glucometer manage three or four.
Sensors are generally worn for 10 to 15 days and then replaced.
How does a CGM work?
Here is the part that surprises many patients: a CGM does not measure the glucose in your blood. It measures glucose in the interstitial fluid, the thin layer of fluid that bathes the cells just beneath your skin.
The sensor filament is coated with an enzyme that reacts with glucose and produces a tiny electrical signal. The device turns that signal into a number.
Why doesn't my CGM match my finger-prick reading?
Glucose reaches the interstitial fluid a little after it appears in the blood, usually somewhere between 5 and 15 minutes later. When your sugar is steady, the two readings sit close together. When it is moving fast, after a meal, during a brisk walk, or while you are treating a low, the sensor will trail behind.
So if your glucometer says 82 and your CGM says 101 twenty minutes after you drank juice for a low, neither device is broken. They are measuring different places at slightly different times.
What do the arrows next to the number mean?
Most apps show an arrow beside the current reading. A flat arrow means glucose is holding steady. An angled one means it is drifting up or down. A straight up or straight down arrow means it is changing quickly.
In practice, the arrow can matter as much as the number. A reading of 110 heading sharply downward before bedtime calls for a different response than 110 sitting flat. If you take insulin, ask your doctor to walk you through how to respond to each arrow.

CGM or glucometer: which do you need?
Think of a glucometer as a photograph and a CGM as a video.
A glucometer measures glucose in a drop of blood from your fingertip. It is accurate, cheap per test, and tells you exactly where you stand at that moment. What it can't do is show direction, fill in the hours you didn't test, or wake you when your sugar drops at 3 a.m.
A CGM fills those gaps. It records through the night, shows whether glucose is rising or falling, and in many systems raises an alarm when you cross a set limit. You'll rarely need to prick your finger, though that depends on the device.

Even with a CGM, keep your glucometer. It is your backup when the sensor fails, when a reading looks wrong, or when your symptoms don't match the screen.
What does a CGM show that HbA1c misses?
HbA1c reflects your average blood sugar over roughly the last two to three months. It's a reliable long-term marker, and it isn't going anywhere. But averages hide things.
Picture two people, both with an HbA1c of 7%. One stays fairly steady all day. The other dips below 70 overnight and climbs past 250 after most meals. Their lab reports look the same. Their risks, and what their doctors should do next, are very different.
A CGM separates these two people. It can show night lows you never felt, which foods send your sugar up and for how long, and whether your morning highs start at 4 a.m. (the dawn phenomenon, a natural hormone-driven rise before waking). It shows what a walk after dinner actually does. It also shows whether your medicine or insulin is peaking at the right time of day.
There are situations where HbA1c itself becomes less trustworthy, such as anaemia, some inherited haemoglobin variants, pregnancy, kidney disease or recent blood loss. In those cases, CGM data can help explain why the lab number and daily readings don't agree.
Who may benefit from a CGM?
The guidance here has shifted a lot. In its 2026 Standards of Care, the American Diabetes Association moved to recommending CGM from the time of diagnosis onward for anyone with diabetes who could benefit from it. It is no longer something reserved for insulin users or people with frequent lows.
That doesn't mean everyone needs to wear one permanently. It means the decision now rests on what would actually help you.
Type 1 diabetes. In many clinics, CGM has become a routine part of Type 1 care. Insulin doses shift with food, exercise and illness, and continuous data makes those adjustments safer.
Type 2 diabetes on insulin. Any insulin brings some risk of low sugar. CGM catches lows early and guides dose changes. The 2026 ADA update specifically added older adults with Type 2 diabetes on insulin to its CGM recommendations.
Type 2 diabetes on tablets or other medicines. Even without insulin, a couple of weeks on a CGM can show exactly how your meals, walks and medicines affect your sugar. Sometimes that confirms things are fine. Sometimes it shows why the HbA1c won't come down.
People who don't feel their lows. After years of diabetes, some people lose the usual warning signs: the sweating, trembling, pounding heart. Doctors call this hypoglycaemia unawareness. A CGM alert can step in where the body's signals no longer do.
Pregnancy. Targets in pregnancy are tighter and can change week to week. More on this below.
Children and teenagers. Fewer finger pricks, and parents can often follow readings on their own phones, which helps at night and during school hours.
When HbA1c and home readings don't line up. A CGM period can settle the question.
Does every person with diabetes need a CGM?
No. Someone with stable Type 2 diabetes on simple treatment may do perfectly well with regular HbA1c tests and the occasional glucometer check. A two-week CGM once or twice a year can be enough to confirm nothing is slipping.
The decision usually comes down to your type of diabetes and treatment, how likely you are to have lows, how steady your control has been, whether pregnancy is involved, cost, and your comfort with using a phone app.
There's also a simpler question. Will anyone actually look at the data? The ADA's own technology section points out that checking glucose, by itself, does nothing to lower it. The readings only help once they shape treatment and daily habits. A CGM that nobody reviews is an expensive sticker.
How to read CGM data
Most CGM reports summarise 14 days. For that summary to be trustworthy, the sensor needs to have been recording for most of the period, generally at least 70% of the time. If yours fell off on day five, the report may not tell the full story.
What is time in range?
Time in range (TIR) is the percentage of time your glucose stays between 70 and 180 mg/dL.
A TIR of 70% means you spent roughly 17 hours a day in that band. Many patients find this easier to relate to than HbA1c, because it maps onto an actual day. "You were in range from breakfast until late evening, then drifted high overnight" is a more useful conversation than "your A1c is 7.4."
Time below and time above range
Time below range is split into two levels: below 70 mg/dL, and below 54 mg/dL. The second is treated more seriously, as clinically significant hypoglycaemia.
Time above range works the same way, with one level above 180 mg/dL and a second above 250 mg/dL.

GMI: the cGM's estimate of HbA1c
The glucose management indicator (GMI) takes your average CGM glucose and converts it into a figure that looks like an HbA1c percentage.
GMI and your lab HbA1c are often close. Sometimes they aren't, and that doesn't automatically mean one of them is wrong. People differ in how glucose sticks to their red blood cells. Doctors look at both side by side.
Glucose variability
Coefficient of variation (CV) measures how much your glucose swings around its average. A CV of 36% or lower is generally considered stable. Higher numbers tend to go with more frequent lows, even when the average looks fine.
How to read an AGP report
The Ambulatory Glucose Profile, or AGP, is the one-page summary most CGM software produces. Its trick is to take all 14 days and lay them on top of each other, as if they all happened on a single day. Anything that repeats at the same time of day jumps out.
At the top you'll see a stacked coloured bar. Green in the middle is time in range. Yellow and orange above it are the highs. Red at the bottom is the lows. Ideally the green is large and the red is barely visible.
Below that is the main graph. The dark line through the middle is your median glucose, your typical level at each hour. Around it is a darker shaded band showing where your readings fall on most days, and a lighter, wider band showing the less common highs and lows.
When you look at your own AGP, a few things are worth noticing:
A narrow band close to the target zone means your days are fairly predictable.
A wide band at a particular hour means that part of the day varies a lot.
A curve sinking toward 70 overnight suggests possible night lows.
A hump an hour or two after breakfast or lunch points to post-meal spikes.
A slow climb from about 3 a.m. to 8 a.m. may be the dawn phenomenon.
Most reports also include a strip of individual daily graphs underneath. These are useful for matching a bad day to what happened: a wedding dinner, a missed dose, a long drive, a night of poor sleep.
Patterns doctors commonly look for
Some patterns come up again and again in CGM reports.
A sharp rise an hour or two after certain meals usually reflects the carbohydrate in that meal, the portion, or medicine timing. For many Indian households, breakfast is a common culprit: poha, upma, bread or tea with biscuits can push sugar up faster than people expect.
Lows between roughly 2 and 4 a.m. can mean an evening insulin dose or certain tablets are too strong for that person. High fasting readings with normal bedtime readings might be the dawn phenomenon. Occasionally they are a rebound after an unnoticed night low, which is why doctors check the overnight trace before increasing any dose.
Glucose that falls during exercise, or several hours later, reflects the body becoming more sensitive to insulin after activity. Readings that stay high through most of the day usually mean treatment needs another look. Wide swings from one day to the next often trace back to irregular meal times, sleep or medicine timing.
One odd day doesn't make a pattern. Doctors generally want to see something repeat over several days before acting on it.
And please don't adjust insulin or diabetes tablets on your own because of what you see on your CGM. Bring the report to your doctor first.
How accurate is a CGM?
Accurate enough to manage diabetes day to day. Many current systems are approved for treatment decisions without routine finger-prick confirmation. They are not flawless, though.
Readings tend to be less reliable in the first 12 to 24 hours after a new sensor goes in, and when glucose is changing quickly. Lying on the sensor during sleep can squeeze the tissue and produce a false low, sometimes called a compression low. Dehydration can throw readings off, and certain medicines or supplements affect some devices. High-dose vitamin C is a known example for some systems.
Check with a glucometer whenever you feel low but the screen says you're fine, when your symptoms and the number simply don't agree, when the device shows an error or no arrow, or whenever your CGM's instructions ask you to confirm before acting.
If in doubt, trust how you feel and check.
What's it like to wear one?
Easier than most people expect.
The sensor goes on with a spring-loaded applicator, and most people describe a quick pinch or feel almost nothing. Once it's on, you usually stop noticing it within a day. You can bathe and exercise with it, though water limits vary between devices, so check yours before swimming.
Some people get mild itching or redness from the adhesive. Rotating the site and keeping the skin clean and dry helps. Pain, swelling, spreading redness or any discharge around the sensor should be shown to a doctor.
Sensors generally need to come off before an MRI, CT scan or certain X-rays, so tell the radiology staff you're wearing one. If you're travelling, pack a spare sensor and your glucometer.
Is CGM useful during pregnancy?
Pregnancy with diabetes needs tighter glucose control, because higher sugar levels can affect both mother and baby. Levels can also shift quickly as the weeks go on.
For women with Type 1 diabetes, CGM is widely used in pregnancy, and the consensus target is stricter: more than 70% of the time between 63 and 140 mg/dL, with very little time below that. For Type 2 diabetes in pregnancy and for gestational diabetes, the evidence on CGM-specific targets is still being built, and finger-prick testing remains a central part of care.
Targets in pregnancy should always come from your treating team, and CGM data should be reviewed regularly by both your diabetologist and your obstetrician.
Should people without diabetes use a CGM?
CGMs are now sold as wellness gadgets, and plenty of people without diabetes are curious. For someone with prediabetes or obesity, a short trial can be eye-opening about how food, sleep and activity move their numbers.
A few words of caution, though. Glucose naturally rises after eating in everyone, and watching that happen on your phone can cause needless worry or push people toward overly strict diets. Normal CGM ranges for people without diabetes are also less clearly defined. And a CGM cannot diagnose diabetes or prediabetes. That still takes a fasting glucose, an HbA1c or an oral glucose tolerance test.
If you're worried about prediabetes or insulin resistance, start with a proper medical assessment rather than a sensor.
What does a CGM cost in India?
Cost depends on the system, how long each sensor lasts, and whether you wear one continuously or just now and then. The sensors are the main ongoing expense, since each is replaced every 10 to 15 days.
Brands and prices in India change often enough that it's best to ask your doctor or a verified supplier what's currently available. It's also worth talking through whether you need continuous use or periodic two-week checks, whether alerts matter for your safety, whether a phone-based system or separate reader suits you, and whether your insurance or employer covers any of it.
For many people with Type 2 diabetes, a two-week CGM every few months, reviewed properly with the doctor, gives much of the benefit at a far lower cost than wearing one all year.
How Niramay Clinics uses CGM data
The report itself is only half the value. The other half is the conversation you have about it.
At Niramay Clinics in Dhantoli, Nagpur, diabetes care looks beyond blood sugar to the heart, kidneys, eyes and nerves, with the aim of preventing long-term complications. CGM data fits into that picture by answering practical questions. Are there hidden lows making treatment unsafe? Which meals or times of day need work? Is a new medicine or insulin dose doing what it should? Is sugar steady enough during pregnancy?

At the clinic, CGM is used alongside HbA1c, clinical examination, complication screening and a lifestyle plan that fits how the patient actually lives.
When to get urgent medical help
A CGM alert is useful, but some situations need medical attention whatever the screen says.
Get urgent help for signs of a severe low: confusion, strange behaviour, being unable to eat or drink, a seizure, or passing out. If someone can't swallow safely, don't put food or drink in their mouth; call for emergency help. Seek care too for lows that keep coming back after treatment with fast-acting sugar.
Very high glucose together with vomiting, stomach pain, fast or deep breathing, drowsiness or a fruity smell on the breath can signal diabetic ketoacidosis, especially in Type 1 diabetes. This needs emergency treatment. So do signs of severe dehydration with persistently high sugar, and any chest pain, breathlessness, sudden weakness, slurred speech or drooping of the face.
If your CGM and your body disagree, go with your body and check with a glucometer.
Common misconceptions about CGM
Some people assume a CGM means fewer doctor visits. It gives you more information, but deciding what to do with it still needs a clinician.
Others think CGM is only for people on insulin. Current guidance covers a much wider group, including people with Type 2 diabetes on other medicines.
Seeing your sugar rise after a meal can feel alarming at first. Some rise is normal. What matters is how high it goes, how long it stays there, and whether it happens every day.
Many people expect the CGM and glucometer to match exactly. Small differences are normal, because they measure different fluids with a short time gap.
A good HbA1c doesn't make CGM pointless either. It can still hide frequent lows or big swings.
And the insertion is not the ordeal people imagine. Most feel a brief pinch, if anything.
A quick recap
A CGM measures glucose every few minutes through a small sensor usually worn for 10 to 15 days.
It picks up patterns that HbA1c and occasional finger pricks miss, particularly night lows and post-meal spikes.
Time in range (70 to 180 mg/dL) is the headline number, with a general target of over 70% for most adults with diabetes.
The AGP report stacks two weeks onto one page so repeating patterns are easy to spot.
Current international guidance supports CGM for a much wider group of people with diabetes, based on individual need.
Sensor readings trail blood glucose slightly, so keep a glucometer as backup.
Any change to medicine or insulin should be made with your doctor.
For years, diabetes care relied on a handful of readings and a lab test every few months, with a lot of guesswork in between. CGM fills in those gaps. Patients and doctors can finally see what glucose does through ordinary days of work, meals, sleep and exercise.
It isn't a treatment, and not everyone needs one all the time. But for many people, even a couple of weeks with a sensor makes their diabetes easier to understand and their treatment safer to adjust. The sensible first step is to talk with your doctor about whether it fits your situation, and how the data will actually be used.

Frequently asked questions
How long does a CGM sensor last?
Most sensors are worn for about 10 to 15 days, depending on the system, and then replaced with a new one, ideally on a different spot to give the skin a rest. Clinic-based professional CGMs are usually worn for a fixed two-week period. Afterwards, the doctor downloads the recorded data and goes through the patterns with you.
What is a good time in range for someone with diabetes?
For most adults with Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes, the usual goal is more than 70% of the day between 70 and 180 mg/dL, roughly 17 hours. Time below 70 mg/dL should ideally stay under 4%. Older adults and people prone to lows often have gentler targets, because avoiding hypoglycaemia comes first. Your doctor will set goals that suit you.
Is a CGM more accurate than a glucometer?
Not quite. A glucometer tests blood directly and is very accurate for a single moment. A CGM reads the fluid under the skin, so it can lag several minutes behind, especially when sugar is changing fast. What a CGM offers is continuous data and direction of change. Most people who use a CGM keep a glucometer for backup checks.
Can a CGM pick up low sugar at night?
Yes, and this is one of its most useful features. Because the sensor records continuously, it catches overnight lows that people often sleep through without noticing. Real-time systems can sound an alarm when glucose falls below a set level. Doctors reviewing CGM reports frequently find night-time lows that lead to safer changes in medicine or insulin timing.
Do I need a CGM if I have Type 2 diabetes and don't take insulin?
Not necessarily, though it can help. Current international guidance supports CGM for people with Type 2 diabetes on non-insulin medicines when it improves management. Even two weeks of data can show how your meals, activity and tablets affect your sugar. Whether ongoing use makes sense depends on how stable your control is, your treatment plan and cost.
Can I shower, swim or work out with a CGM?
Most sensors are water-resistant, so bathing, showering and exercise are usually fine. Water depth and time limits differ between devices, so check your instructions before swimming. Heavy sweating can loosen the adhesive, and some people add an overpatch to keep it secure. In contact sports, a sensor can occasionally get knocked off, so a little extra care helps.
What is an AGP report?
The Ambulatory Glucose Profile is a standard one-page CGM summary, usually covering 14 days. It shows your time in range, average glucose and glucose management indicator, along with a graph that overlays all the days as though they were one. That makes repeating patterns, like post-breakfast spikes or overnight lows, much easier for your doctor to spot.
Does putting on a CGM hurt?
Most people feel a quick pinch, and some feel nothing at all, when the sensor is applied. After that, the thin filament under the skin is rarely noticed during normal activity. A few people get mild itching or irritation from the adhesive. If you notice pain, swelling, spreading redness or discharge around the site, have a doctor take a look.

A sharp rise an hour or two after certain meals usually reflects the carbohydrate in that meal, the portion, or medicine timing. For many Indian households, breakfast is a common culprit: poha, upma, bread or tea with biscuits can push sugar up faster than people expect.

Lows between roughly 2 and 4 a.m. can mean an evening insulin dose or certain tablets are too strong for that person. High fasting readings with normal bedtime readings might be the dawn phenomenon. Occasionally they are a rebound after an unnoticed night low, which is why doctors check the overnight trace before increasing any dose.

Readings that stay high through most of the day usually mean treatment needs another look. Wide swings from one day to the next often trace back to irregular meal times, sleep or medicine timing.
One odd day doesn't make a pattern. Doctors generally want to see something repeat over several days before acting on it.

Readings tend to be less reliable in the first 12 to 24 hours after a new sensor goes in, and when glucose is changing quickly. If in doubt, trust how you feel and check.

The sensor goes on with a spring-loaded applicator, and most people describe a quick pinch or feel almost nothing. Once it's on, you usually stop noticing it within a day. You can bathe and exercise with it, though water limits vary between devices, so check yours before swimming.

For Type 2 diabetes in pregnancy and for gestational diabetes, the evidence on CGM-specific targets is still being built, and finger-prick testing remains a central part of care.
Targets in pregnancy should always come from your treating team, and CGM data should be reviewed regularly by both your diabetologist and your obstetrician.

CGMs are now sold as wellness gadgets, and plenty of people without diabetes are curious. For someone with prediabetes or obesity, a short trial can be eye-opening about how food, sleep and activity move their numbers.

A few words of caution, though. Glucose naturally rises after eating in everyone, and watching that happen on your phone can cause needless worry or push people toward overly strict diets. If you're worried about prediabetes or insulin resistance, start with a proper medical assessment rather than a sensor.

Cost depends on the system, how long each sensor lasts, and whether you wear one continuously or just now and then. The sensors are the main ongoing expense, since each is replaced every 10 to 15 days.

Brands and prices in India change often enough that it's best to ask your doctor or a verified supplier what's currently available. It's also worth talking through whether you need continuous use or periodic two-week checks, whether alerts matter for your safety, whether a phone-based system or separate reader suits you, and whether your insurance or employer covers any of it.
For many people with Type 2 diabetes, a two-week CGM every few months, reviewed properly with the doctor, gives much of the benefit at a far lower cost than wearing one all year.
The report itself is only half the value. The other half is the conversation you have about it.

Published 15 October 2026 · 14 minutes
Quick answer

Continuous glucose monitoring uses a wearable sensor to measure glucose in the fluid under the skin every few minutes, day and night. It shows trends, highs, lows and "time in range," the share of the day your glucose stays between 70 and 180 mg/dL. People with Type 1 diabetes, people with Type 2 diabetes on insulin or other medicines, pregnant women with diabetes, and anyone with frequent or unnoticed lows are most likely to benefit. The data should be reviewed with a doctor before any treatment changes.

A continuous glucose monitor, or CGM, is a small sensor you wear on your arm or abdomen that checks your glucose every few minutes, around the clock, for up to two weeks. You get a moving picture of your sugar levels rather than one reading taken whenever you remember to prick your finger.

That difference matters more than it sounds. A fasting sugar of 118 mg/dL tells you about one moment on one morning. It says nothing about the 2 a.m. low you slept through or the spike that followed Sunday's lunch.
This guide covers how CGM works, who tends to get real value from it, how to read the report your doctor hands you, and where the technology falls short.
A CGM system has a sensor, something that sends the data, and a screen to see it on.

The sensor is a very thin, flexible filament that sits just under the skin. It is usually worn on the back of the upper arm, sometimes on the abdomen. A transmitter, either built in or clipped on, sends readings to a phone app or a small handheld reader. In some setups the readings go straight to an insulin pump.
Depending on the device, a new reading comes in every one to fifteen minutes. Across a day that adds up to hundreds of values. Most people using a glucometer manage three or four.
Sensors are generally worn for 10 to 15 days and then replaced.

Here is the part that surprises many patients: a CGM does not measure the glucose in your blood. It measures glucose in the interstitial fluid, the thin layer of fluid that bathes the cells just beneath your skin.
The sensor filament is coated with an enzyme that reacts with glucose and produces a tiny electrical signal. The device turns that signal into a number.

Glucose reaches the interstitial fluid a little after it appears in the blood, usually somewhere between 5 and 15 minutes later. When your sugar is steady, the two readings sit close together. When it is moving fast, after a meal, during a brisk walk, or while you are treating a low, the sensor will trail behind.
So if your glucometer says 82 and your CGM says 101 twenty minutes after you drank juice for a low, neither device is broken. They are measuring different places at slightly different times.

Most apps show an arrow beside the current reading. A flat arrow means glucose is holding steady. An angled one means it is drifting up or down. A straight up or straight down arrow means it is changing quickly.

In practice, the arrow can matter as much as the number. A reading of 110 heading sharply downward before bedtime calls for a different response than 110 sitting flat. If you take insulin, ask your doctor to walk you through how to respond to each arrow.
There are three broad kinds, and they suit different people.
Which devices are available, and at what price, changes fairly often in India. Your doctor can tell you what is practical right now.
Think of a glucometer as a photograph and a CGM as a video.

A glucometer measures glucose in a drop of blood from your fingertip. It is accurate, cheap per test, and tells you exactly where you stand at that moment. What it can't do is show direction, fill in the hours you didn't test, or wake you when your sugar drops at 3 a.m.

A CGM fills those gaps. It records through the night, shows whether glucose is rising or falling, and in many systems raises an alarm when you cross a set limit. You'll rarely need to prick your finger, though that depends on the device.
Even with a CGM, keep your glucometer. It is your backup when the sensor fails, when a reading looks wrong, or when your symptoms don't match the screen.
HbA1c reflects your average blood sugar over roughly the last two to three months. It's a reliable long-term marker, and it isn't going anywhere. But averages hide things.

Picture two people, both with an HbA1c of 7%. One stays fairly steady all day. The other dips below 70 overnight and climbs past 250 after most meals. Their lab reports look the same. Their risks, and what their doctors should do next, are very different.

A CGM separates these two people. It can show night lows you never felt, which foods send your sugar up and for how long, and whether your morning highs start at 4 a.m. (the dawn phenomenon, a natural hormone-driven rise before waking). It shows what a walk after dinner actually does. It also shows whether your medicine or insulin is peaking at the right time of day.

There are situations where HbA1c itself becomes less trustworthy, such as anaemia, some inherited haemoglobin variants, pregnancy, kidney disease or recent blood loss. In those cases, CGM data can help explain why the lab number and daily readings don't agree.

The guidance here has shifted a lot. In its 2026 Standards of Care, the American Diabetes Association moved to recommending CGM from the time of diagnosis onward for anyone with diabetes who could benefit from it. It is no longer something reserved for insulin users or people with frequent lows.
That doesn't mean everyone needs to wear one permanently. It means the decision now rests on what would actually help you.
Type 1 diabetes. In many clinics, CGM has become a routine part of Type 1 care. Insulin doses shift with food, exercise and illness, and continuous data makes those adjustments safer.

Type 2 diabetes on insulin. Any insulin brings some risk of low sugar. CGM catches lows early and guides dose changes. The 2026 ADA update specifically added older adults with Type 2 diabetes on insulin to its CGM recommendations.

Type 2 diabetes on tablets or other medicines. Even without insulin, a couple of weeks on a CGM can show exactly how your meals, walks and medicines affect your sugar. Sometimes that confirms things are fine. Sometimes it shows why the HbA1c won't come down.

People who don't feel their lows. After years of diabetes, some people lose the usual warning signs: the sweating, trembling, pounding heart. Doctors call this hypoglycaemia unawareness. A CGM alert can step in where the body's signals no longer do.
Pregnancy. Targets in pregnancy are tighter and can change week to week. More on this below.
Children and teenagers. Fewer finger pricks, and parents can often follow readings on their own phones, which helps at night and during school hours.
When HbA1c and home readings don't line up. A CGM period can settle the question.

No. Someone with stable Type 2 diabetes on simple treatment may do perfectly well with regular HbA1c tests and the occasional glucometer check. A two-week CGM once or twice a year can be enough to confirm nothing is slipping.

The decision usually comes down to your type of diabetes and treatment, how likely you are to have lows, how steady your control has been, whether pregnancy is involved, cost, and your comfort with using a phone app.

Time below range is split into two levels: below 70 mg/dL, and below 54 mg/dL. The second is treated more seriously, as clinically significant hypoglycaemia.
Time above range works the same way, with one level above 180 mg/dL and a second above 250 mg/dL.

faqs.q: Does walking help blood sugar?
faqs.a: Yes. Regular walking improves insulin sensitivity.

faqs.q: Is fasting a good way to lower sugar?
faqs.a: Extreme fasting can be unsafe, especially with medicines.

faqs.q: How quickly can lifestyle changes lower sugar?
faqs.a: Some improvement can appear within weeks.

faqs.q: Should I skip meals?
faqs.a: No. Skipping meals can cause swings in sugar.
