How to Control Blood Sugar Naturally: What Works and What Does Not
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 1 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
Regular physical activity, a balanced diet with controlled portions, weight loss if you are overweight, good sleep and stress control can all lower blood sugar. Supplements and "miracle cures" are not proven replacements for treatment. Never stop prescribed medicines without your doctor's advice.
Many people with diabetes want to manage blood sugar through lifestyle first. Healthy habits are powerful, but they work best with medical guidance.
What works
Eat in a balanced way
Fill half the plate with vegetables
Choose whole grains, millets and pulses
Include protein with each meal
Limit sweets, sugary drinks and refined flour
Move regularly
Brisk walking on most days
A short walk after meals
Strength exercise twice a week
Lose excess weight
Even modest weight loss improves insulin response.
Sleep and stress
Poor sleep and chronic stress can raise blood sugar.
What does not replace treatment
Herbal powders, juices and supplements sold as cures
Extreme fasting or crash diets
Stopping medicines because sugar looks better
Monitor your progress
Regular blood sugar checks and HbA1c show whether your plan is working.
When medicines are needed
If lifestyle alone does not reach your target, medicines are a normal and safe next step.
Points to keep
Lifestyle is the foundation of diabetes care.
Food, activity, weight and sleep all matter.
Miracle cures are not proven.
Do not stop medicines on your own.
Monitor and review with your doctor.
Small, steady habits make the biggest difference. For a personalised plan, you can consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
When to seek urgent care
Seek urgent care for extreme thirst with vomiting, confusion, deep rapid breathing, unusual drowsiness, or signs of very low sugar such as sweating, shaking and confusion.
Sources and further reading
WHO: Diabetes fact sheet
NIDDK: What is diabetes
Frequently asked questions
Can diabetes be controlled without medicine?
Some people can, especially early on, but this depends on the individual.
Are bitter gourd or fenugreek enough?
They are not proven to replace treatment. Discuss any supplement with your doctor.
Does walking help blood sugar?
Yes. Regular walking improves insulin sensitivity.
Is fasting a good way to lower sugar?
Extreme fasting can be unsafe, especially with medicines.
How quickly can lifestyle changes lower sugar?
Some improvement can appear within weeks.
Should I skip meals?
No. Skipping meals can cause swings in sugar.

faqs.q: Why does diabetes increase the risk of heart disease?
faqs.a: High sugar damages blood vessels, and diabetes often comes with high blood pressure, abnormal cholesterol, belly fat and inflammation, all of which promote heart disease.

faqs.q: Can a person with diabetes have a silent heart attack?
faqs.a: Yes. Nerve damage can reduce pain, so symptoms may be mild, such as unusual tiredness, sweating or breathlessness. Get checked for any new symptoms.

faqs.q: What cholesterol level should a diabetic aim for?
faqs.a: Targets are individual, but LDL is often kept below 70 mg/dL, and lower for those with heart disease. Your doctor will set your target.

faqs.q: Do all diabetics need a statin?
faqs.a: Many adults with diabetes benefit from a statin, particularly those over 40 or with other risk factors. Your doctor will decide based on your risk.

faqs.q: Which diabetes medicines protect the heart?
faqs.a: Certain GLP-1 medicines and SGLT2 inhibitors have been shown to reduce heart events or heart failure in selected patients. Metformin also has a long track record. Your doctor will choose.

faqs.q: How often should a diabetic person have heart checks?
faqs.a: At least once a year, including blood pressure, cholesterol and symptom review. More tests such as ECG or stress tests are done if you have symptoms or high risk.

Diabetes and Heart Disease: The Metabolic Risk Link
Metabolic Syndrome and Cardiometabolic Health
Diabetes and Heart Disease: The Metabolic Risk Link
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 20 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
People with diabetes are about two times more likely to develop heart disease and stroke than people without it, and often at a younger age in India. High blood sugar damages blood vessels, and diabetes usually comes with other risks such as high blood pressure, abnormal cholesterol, belly fat and kidney disease. Controlling all of these together, not only sugar, lowers the risk.
Most people with diabetes know about the risk to eyes and kidneys. Fewer realise that heart disease is the biggest threat. Understanding how diabetes and the heart are linked puts you in a stronger position to protect both.
How does diabetes harm the heart?
Damaged blood vessels: High sugar injures the inner lining of arteries, making fatty plaques form faster.
Inflammation and clotting: Diabetes increases inflammation and the tendency to form clots.
High blood pressure: Common in diabetes and strains the heart.
Abnormal cholesterol: High triglycerides, low HDL and small dense LDL particles are typical.
Insulin resistance and belly fat: Which drive many of these changes.
Kidney disease: Raises heart risk further.
Nerve damage: Diabetes can affect the nerves of the heart, so a heart attack may cause little or no chest pain.
What heart conditions are more common?
Coronary artery disease and heart attack
Stroke
Heart failure
Peripheral artery disease (poor blood flow to the legs)
Abnormal heart rhythms such as atrial fibrillation
What are the warning signs?
Chest pain, pressure or tightness, especially with effort
Breathlessness, tiredness or reduced stamina
Swelling of the legs
Pain in the calves while walking
Palpitations or dizziness
In diabetes, symptoms may be subtle: unusual tiredness, indigestion-like discomfort, sweating or jaw and arm pain
Call emergency services for sudden chest pain, severe breathlessness, weakness of one side of the body or trouble speaking.
Which numbers matter?
Besides HbA1c, discuss targets for:
Blood pressure: Generally below 130/80 mm Hg.
LDL cholesterol: Often below 70 mg/dL, and lower in those with heart disease. Your doctor will set it.
Triglycerides: Below 150 mg/dL.
Waist: Below 90 cm in men and 80 cm in women.
Kidney tests: uACR and eGFR.
Weight and BMI.
How can you protect your heart?
Control sugar, but safely
Aim for the HbA1c target your doctor sets, which is usually around 7 percent for many adults, but individualised.
Control blood pressure
Reduce salt, stay active, lose excess weight and take medicines as prescribed.
Treat cholesterol
Most adults with diabetes benefit from a statin. Take it regularly and do not stop without advice.
Choose medicines with heart benefits
Some diabetes medicines reduce heart attacks, strokes or heart failure in selected patients. Examples include certain GLP-1 medicines and SGLT2 inhibitors. Your doctor will choose based on your risk.
Eat well and stay active
Choose vegetables, pulses, whole grains, nuts and fish. Limit sugar, refined foods, fried snacks and processed meat. Exercise for 150 minutes a week, with strength training twice a week.
Quit tobacco and limit alcohol
Smoking greatly multiplies the risk of heart attack in diabetes.
Sleep and stress
Treat sleep apnoea and manage stress.
Regular checks
Have an annual review of blood pressure, cholesterol, kidney tests, eyes and feet. Your doctor may advise an ECG or other heart tests.
Should you take aspirin?
Not automatically. Aspirin is advised for those with established heart disease. In others, the bleeding risk may outweigh the benefit. Ask your doctor.
When should you see a doctor?
See your doctor if you have chest discomfort, breathlessness, swollen legs, calf pain on walking or if your blood pressure or cholesterol is above target.
Points to keep
Diabetes doubles the risk of heart disease and stroke.
Blood sugar, blood pressure, cholesterol and belly fat all matter.
Symptoms may be subtle in people with diabetes.
Statins, blood pressure control, healthy habits and heart-protective diabetes medicines help.
Regular check-ups catch problems early.
Protecting your heart is part of managing diabetes. Small improvements across several numbers add up to a big reduction in risk. To review your heart risk, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
Sources and further reading
NHLBI: Metabolic syndrome
NIDDK: Insulin resistance and prediabetes
Frequently asked questions
Why does diabetes increase the risk of heart disease?
High sugar damages blood vessels, and diabetes often comes with high blood pressure, abnormal cholesterol, belly fat and inflammation, all of which promote heart disease.
Can a person with diabetes have a silent heart attack?
Yes. Nerve damage can reduce pain, so symptoms may be mild, such as unusual tiredness, sweating or breathlessness. Get checked for any new symptoms.
What cholesterol level should a diabetic aim for?
Targets are individual, but LDL is often kept below 70 mg/dL, and lower for those with heart disease. Your doctor will set your target.
Do all diabetics need a statin?
Many adults with diabetes benefit from a statin, particularly those over 40 or with other risk factors. Your doctor will decide based on your risk.
Which diabetes medicines protect the heart?
Certain GLP-1 medicines and SGLT2 inhibitors have been shown to reduce heart events or heart failure in selected patients. Metformin also has a long track record. Your doctor will choose.
How often should a diabetic person have heart checks?
At least once a year, including blood pressure, cholesterol and symptom review. More tests such as ECG or stress tests are done if you have symptoms or high risk.

Diabetes and Kidney Disease: Which Tests You Need
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 20 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
People with diabetes should have two tests at least once a year: a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR) to detect protein leak, and a blood test for creatinine to calculate eGFR, which estimates kidney function. Type 2 diabetes screening starts at diagnosis. Early detection allows treatment that can slow or prevent kidney failure.
Diabetes is one of the leading causes of kidney disease worldwide. The danger is that damage starts quietly, with no pain or swelling, and by the time symptoms appear, a lot of kidney function may be lost. Two simple tests can catch it early.
How does diabetes damage the kidneys?
High blood sugar and high blood pressure harm the tiny filters in the kidneys (glomeruli). Over years, the filters leak protein into the urine and gradually lose their ability to clean the blood. This is called diabetic kidney disease. It often develops after 5 to 10 years of diabetes, but in type 2 diabetes it may already be present at diagnosis.
What are the warning signs?
Early kidney disease usually has no symptoms. Later signs include:
Foamy urine
Swelling of the feet, legs or face
Tiredness and weakness
Poor appetite or nausea
Itching
High blood pressure that is hard to control
Reduced urine output
Do not wait for symptoms to be tested.
Which tests should you have?
1. urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR)
A spot urine sample (ideally the first morning sample) measures the amount of albumin, a protein, relative to creatinine.
Below 30 mg/g: Normal
30 to 300 mg/g: Moderately increased (formerly microalbuminuria)
Above 300 mg/g: Severely increased
An abnormal result should be confirmed on two of three samples over three to six months, as fever, exercise, urine infection or high sugar can cause temporary rises.
2. eGFR (estimated glomerular filtration rate)
Calculated from serum creatinine, age and sex. It estimates how well the kidneys filter blood.
90 or above: Normal
60 to 89: Mildly reduced
45 to 59: Mild to moderate reduction
30 to 44: Moderate to severe reduction
15 to 29: Severely reduced
Below 15: Kidney failure
Some guidelines also use cystatin C for more precise estimates in selected people.
3. other tests
Blood pressure at every visit
Urine routine and microscopy
Kidney ultrasound if needed
Blood tests for potassium, haemoglobin and electrolytes
How often should you test?
At diagnosis of type 2 diabetes
At least once a year if results are normal
More often, every 3 to 6 months, if kidney disease is present or progressing
How can you protect your kidneys?
Keep HbA1c in your target range.
Control blood pressure, usually below 130/80 mm Hg.
Take kidney-protecting medicines if advised. ACE inhibitors or ARBs, SGLT2 inhibitors, finerenone in some patients and certain GLP-1 medicines have shown kidney benefits.
Reduce salt and avoid excess protein supplements.
Avoid painkillers such as ibuprofen, diclofenac and other NSAIDs unless prescribed.
Stop smoking.
Stay hydrated, unless told to limit fluids.
Ask your doctor before using contrast dye, herbal products or new medicines.
When should you see a doctor?
See your doctor promptly if you notice swelling, foamy urine, reduced urine output, new high blood pressure or if your reports show a falling eGFR or rising uACR. You may need a kidney specialist (nephrologist) if eGFR is low or falling fast, or if protein loss is high.
What to remember
Diabetic kidney disease is silent in its early stages.
Test uACR and eGFR at least once a year.
Good control of sugar and blood pressure protects the kidneys.
Some medicines offer extra kidney protection.
Avoid NSAID painkillers and check with your doctor before new medicines.
Two simple yearly tests can save your kidneys. Early action slows damage, and often keeps you away from dialysis. To get your kidney checks done, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
Sources and further reading
NHLBI: Metabolic syndrome
NIDDK: Insulin resistance and prediabetes
Frequently asked questions
Which tests check kidney health in diabetes?
The urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR) and the blood creatinine test with eGFR. They should be done at least once a year.
How often should a diabetic person check kidney function?
At diagnosis and then at least yearly if normal. If there is kidney disease, testing may be every 3 to 6 months.
What is a normal uACR?
Below 30 mg/g is normal. Values between 30 and 300 suggest moderately increased albumin, and above 300 suggests severe leak. Abnormal results should be repeated for confirmation.
Can diabetic kidney disease be reversed?
Early damage can be slowed or sometimes improved with good control of sugar and blood pressure and protective medicines. Advanced damage is harder to reverse.
Are painkillers harmful to the kidneys in diabetes?
NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and diclofenac can harm the kidneys, particularly with diabetes, dehydration or existing kidney disease. Use them only if your doctor advises.
When should I see a nephrologist?
If your eGFR is low or falling quickly, you have significant protein leak, or kidney disease is advanced or unexplained. Your diabetologist will advise a referral.

faqs.q: What is diabesity?
faqs.a: Diabesity is a term for type 2 diabetes occurring together with overweight or obesity. It isn't a separate disease. It's used because the two conditions are so closely connected: fat stored around the abdomen increases insulin resistance, which pushes blood sugar up. Treating weight and sugar together generally works better than focusing on sugar readings alone.

faqs.q: How does obesity cause type 2 diabetes?
faqs.a: Excess fat, especially visceral fat inside the abdomen, makes cells respond less well to insulin. The pancreas produces extra insulin to compensate, and for a while that keeps sugar near normal. Over time the pancreas can't keep up, and blood sugar rises into the prediabetes and then diabetes range. Family history, age and activity levels also affect who develops it.

faqs.q: How much weight should I lose to improve my diabetes?
faqs.a: Many people see better blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol after losing about 5% of their body weight. For someone weighing 80 kg, that's around 4 kg. Larger losses of 10 to 15% or more, kept off over time, usually bring bigger benefits and may allow some medicines to be reduced. Your doctor can help set a target that suits you.

faqs.q: Can losing weight reverse type 2 diabetes?
faqs.a: In some people, particularly those diagnosed recently, significant weight loss brings blood sugar back to the non-diabetic range. Doctors call this remission when HbA1c stays below 6.5% for at least three months without diabetes medicines. It isn't a permanent cure. Sugar can rise again, especially with weight regain, so regular testing should continue.

faqs.q: Why do Indians get diabetes at a lower weight?
faqs.a: Many Indians carry more fat around the abdomen and internal organs, and less muscle, than people of the same weight from some other populations. This raises insulin resistance even when BMI looks normal or only slightly high. Indian guidelines therefore use lower BMI and waist cut-offs to identify people at higher metabolic risk.

faqs.q: Are GLP-1 injections safe for weight loss in people with diabetes?
faqs.a: For suitable people, GLP-1 medicines can improve both blood sugar and weight. They're prescription medicines, though, and need a doctor's assessment first. Nausea, vomiting and constipation are common early side effects, and they aren't appropriate for people with certain medical histories. They work best alongside dietary changes and regular exercise, with ongoing medical follow-up.

faqs.q: Does insulin cause weight gain?
faqs.a: Insulin can lead to some weight gain in certain people, partly because the body stops losing glucose in urine once sugar is better controlled. That isn't a reason to avoid or stop it. Doctors can often limit the effect through dose adjustments, meal planning, or combining insulin with medicines that help with weight.

faqs.q: What waist size is considered risky for diabetes in India?
faqs.a: For Indian adults, a waist of 90 cm or more in men and 80 cm or more in women is commonly used as a marker of higher metabolic risk. Waist size reflects abdominal fat, which is closely tied to insulin resistance. It's most useful read together with BMI, blood reports and blood pressure.

Diabetes and Obesity (Diabesity): Weight Management, Insulin Resistance and Metabolic Health
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 11 October 2026 · 15 minutes
Quick answer
Diabesity refers to type 2 diabetes occurring together with overweight or obesity. Fat stored deep in the abdomen (visceral fat) drives insulin resistance, which makes blood glucose harder to control. Treatment usually combines changes in eating, regular activity, attention to sleep, and medicines that help both blood sugar and weight. Losing even around 5% of body weight can improve blood sugar in many people.
When type 2 diabetes and obesity occur in the same person, doctors sometimes call it diabesity. The two are tied together mainly through insulin resistance: extra body fat, particularly fat stored around the abdomen, makes the body less responsive to insulin, and blood sugar gradually climbs. That's why weight management is usually part of diabetes treatment itself.
A lot of people hear "you need to lose weight" at the same appointment where they're told their sugar is high. It can feel like a lecture. It shouldn't be. This article explains what's going on in the body, why weight loss is often harder for people with diabetes, what treatment options exist today, and what kind of progress is realistic.
What is diabesity?
Diabesity isn't a separate diagnosis. It's shorthand for a very common combination: type 2 diabetes plus excess body weight.
The term exists because the two conditions keep pushing on each other. Carrying extra fat raises the chance of developing diabetes. Once diabetes is present, some of its effects, and some of the medicines used to treat it, can make weight harder to shift. If only the sugar readings get attention, results are often disappointing.
Is obesity a disease?
Yes. Most major medical bodies now classify obesity as a chronic medical condition. Body weight is shaped by genes, hormones, appetite signalling, sleep, stress, medicines, working hours, cost of food and plenty more. Nobody decides to develop obesity, and treating it with the same seriousness as high blood pressure tends to lead to better care and less shame.
How are diabetes and obesity connected?
Start with insulin. It's a hormone made by the pancreas, and after a meal it helps glucose move out of the blood and into muscle, liver and fat cells.
Excess fat, especially fat packed inside the abdomen and around the liver, interferes with this. Cells respond less well to insulin, so the pancreas makes more to get the same job done. For a few years that extra effort can keep blood sugar close to normal, and nothing seems wrong. Eventually the insulin-producing cells can't keep pace. Glucose starts to rise, first into the prediabetes range, then into diabetes.
The traffic runs both ways. High insulin levels encourage the body to store fat. Insulin and sulfonylureas can cause weight gain in some people. And fatigue, joint pain or low mood make it harder to stay active.
So when someone with diabetes says they're trying hard and the scale isn't moving, they're usually telling the truth. There's biology working against them.
What is insulin resistance?
Insulin resistance means the body's cells don't respond to insulin as well as they should, so glucose has trouble getting from the blood into the cells. The pancreas compensates by producing more insulin, which can mask the problem for a long time.
On its own, insulin resistance usually causes no clear symptoms. Some people notice their waist getting bigger, or feel heavy and sleepy after meals. Others develop dark, velvety skin at the back of the neck or in the armpits (acanthosis nigricans), or skin tags. None of these proves anything by itself. Fasting glucose, HbA1c, a lipid profile, blood pressure and a waist measurement together tell a doctor much more.
Why does belly fat matter more than body weight?
Fat under the skin, on the hips and thighs for example, is called subcutaneous fat. Fat stored deep inside the abdomen, wrapped around the liver, pancreas and intestines, is visceral fat.
Visceral fat is the more troublesome of the two. It's metabolically active and closely linked with insulin resistance, fatty liver, high triglycerides, raised blood pressure and heart disease. Two people who weigh exactly the same can have quite different risk depending on where that weight sits, which is why your doctor may reach for a measuring tape as well as the weighing scale.
Why are Indians at higher risk at a lower weight?
Studies have repeatedly found that many South Asians, Indians included, carry more abdominal and visceral fat and less muscle than some other populations at the same body weight. You'll sometimes hear this described as the "thin-fat" body type.
In practice, it means type 2 diabetes often shows up earlier and at a lower weight in Indians. Someone who looks only slightly overweight may already have marked insulin resistance. Indian guidelines use lower BMI and waist cut-offs for exactly this reason.
How is obesity measured in diabetes?
Doctors look at a few numbers together rather than relying on one.
Measure
What it tells you
Cut-offs commonly used for Indian adults
Body Mass Index (BMI)
Weight in relation to height
Normal 18.5 to 22.9; overweight 23 to 24.9; obesity 25 and above
Waist circumference
Fat around the abdomen
Higher risk at 90 cm or more (men), 80 cm or more (women)
Waist-to-height ratio
Abdominal fat relative to height
A waist more than half your height suggests higher risk
BMI is a screening number. It can't tell fat from muscle and says nothing about where fat is stored. Where available, body composition analysis adds detail. Your doctor will read all of this alongside your blood reports, blood pressure and medical history.
What are the signs that diabetes and excess weight are affecting your health?
Early on, many people feel perfectly fine. That's part of the problem.
When symptoms do appear, the usual ones are thirst, passing urine more often, tiredness, blurred vision, cuts that take longer to heal, and repeated infections. Excess weight adds its own set: snoring, broken sleep, daytime sleepiness, getting breathless on stairs, and aching knees or back. Some people just notice their waist creeping up even though they haven't changed what they eat.
Because so much of this develops quietly, regular blood tests are more reliable than waiting to feel unwell.
Who is at higher risk of diabesity?
Your risk is higher if diabetes runs in your family, or if you've already been told you have prediabetes. A history of gestational diabetes or PCOS raises it too. So do high blood pressure, abnormal cholesterol, fatty liver and a waist above the cut-offs mentioned earlier. A desk-bound job, short or poor sleep, sleep apnoea and long-term use of certain medicines (steroids and some psychiatric drugs, for instance) all play a part.
Having one or more of these doesn't mean diabetes is inevitable. It does mean testing earlier and more regularly makes sense.
How is diabesity diagnosed and assessed?
Type 2 diabetes is confirmed with blood tests. Assessing diabesity goes a step further, looking at what the combination of high sugar and extra weight is doing elsewhere in the body.
What tests are commonly used?
Fasting plasma glucose: blood sugar after an overnight fast
HbA1c: a reflection of average blood sugar over roughly the last two to three months
Post-meal glucose or an oral glucose tolerance test: how well the body copes with a glucose load
Lipid profile: cholesterol and triglycerides
Liver function tests, and an ultrasound if fatty liver is suspected
Kidney function and urine albumin, to pick up early kidney changes
Blood pressure
Thyroid tests, if symptoms or history point that way
A sleep assessment, if there's heavy snoring, pauses in breathing or daytime sleepiness
Why look for underlying causes of weight gain?
Weight gain sometimes has a contributing medical cause: a hormonal problem, a sleep disorder, a medicine side effect. Finding it can change the whole plan. At Niramay Clinics, obesity care begins by looking for these possible causes before deciding on treatment.
How much weight loss improves Type 2 diabetes?
Less than most people expect, at least to start seeing benefits.
Diabetes guidelines generally say that losing about 5% of body weight can improve blood glucose, blood pressure and cholesterol in many people. Bigger losses that are kept off, often in the 10 to 15% range or beyond, usually bring larger improvements and sometimes allow medicines to be reduced.
If you weigh 90 kg, 5% is roughly 4.5 kg. That's a goal you can actually picture.
Can type 2 diabetes go into remission with weight loss?
For some people, yes, particularly if diabetes was diagnosed fairly recently. After substantial weight loss, blood sugar can return to the non-diabetic range. When HbA1c stays under 6.5% for at least three months without diabetes medicines, doctors call this remission.
Remission isn't a cure. Sugar can rise again, especially if weight comes back, so checks continue. And it isn't possible for everyone. People who don't reach remission still benefit a great deal from losing weight.
What are the treatment options for diabesity?
The plan should deal with blood sugar and weight at the same time, and it will change as you go.
Nutrition
No single diet suits everybody. The one that works is the one that brings your sugar down and that you can keep following on an ordinary Tuesday.
For most Indian households, a few things help. Try filling about half the plate with vegetables or salad, a quarter with protein such as dal, chana, rajma, paneer, curd, eggs, fish or chicken, and the remaining quarter with roti, rice or millets. Go easy on white rice, maida, biscuits, namkeen and sweet drinks, since these push sugar up quickly. Fruit juice counts as a sweet drink; whole fruit is a better choice. Having some protein at each meal helps with hunger and protects muscle while you lose weight. Fibre from whole grains, pulses and vegetables slows down how fast glucose enters the blood.
Festivals, weddings and restaurant meals are part of life. Planning a smaller portion usually works better than trying to avoid them altogether.
One caution. If you take insulin, or tablets that can cause low sugar, don't make big changes to your meals without talking to your doctor first.
Physical activity
Moving your muscles helps them take up glucose, and this happens even before any weight comes off.
For many adults with type 2 diabetes, the usual guidance is at least 150 minutes a week of moderate activity like brisk walking, spread over most days, plus strength exercise two or three times a week. That can be as simple as bodyweight squats, resistance bands or light weights. Breaking up long sitting spells with a few minutes of walking helps. So does a short walk after meals, which can blunt the post-meal sugar spike.
Start where you are and build slowly. If you have heart disease, foot problems or eye complications, or you're on insulin or sulfonylureas, ask your doctor what's safe for you and how to avoid low sugar during exercise.
Sleep and stress
Sleep gets overlooked. Short or poor sleep raises appetite, disturbs hunger hormones and worsens insulin resistance. Most adults do better with seven hours or more.
Loud snoring, stopping breathing at night or feeling drowsy through the day can point to obstructive sleep apnoea. It's common with obesity and makes both blood pressure and blood sugar harder to control, so mention it at your next visit.
Ongoing stress affects what and when people eat, and it can nudge blood sugar up. Dealing with it is a genuine part of treatment.
Medicines
Which medicine suits you depends on your sugar levels, weight, heart and kidney health, other conditions, cost and what you prefer. Diabetes medicines don't all affect weight in the same way.
Medicine group
Usual effect on weight
Notes
Metformin
Neutral or slight loss
Often the first medicine used
SGLT2 inhibitors
Modest loss
Heart and kidney benefits in suitable patients
GLP-1 receptor agonists
Often meaningful loss
Reduce appetite, improve sugar
Dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist (tirzepatide)
Often meaningful loss
Acts on two hormone pathways
DPP-4 inhibitors
Neutral
Generally well tolerated
Sulfonylureas
Possible gain
Can cause low blood sugar
Pioglitazone
Possible gain
Improves insulin sensitivity
Insulin
Possible gain
Essential for many people; don't stop it yourself
This is a broad overview, not a guide to choosing. Please don't start, stop or change any diabetes medicine without speaking to your doctor.
GLP-1 and newer weight-management medicines
GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide, and tirzepatide, which acts on both GIP and GLP-1 pathways, have changed how doctors approach diabesity. They copy the action of gut hormones that regulate blood sugar, slow down stomach emptying and reduce appetite.
In many people they produce weight loss and sugar control that lifestyle changes alone couldn't achieve. They also come with trade-offs. Nausea, vomiting, constipation and loose motions are common in the first weeks. They aren't suitable for people with certain personal or family medical histories. Weight tends to come back if they're stopped without a plan for what comes next. They work better alongside good nutrition and strength exercise, and the cost adds up over months.
These are prescription medicines. They need a doctor's assessment and follow-up, and buying them from unreliable sources is risky.
Insulin
Many people with diabesity need insulin at some point to keep sugar safely under control. It isn't a punishment, and it doesn't mean diabetes has reached some final stage. If weight gain on insulin worries you, say so. Your doctor can often rework the plan, for example by pairing insulin with a medicine that supports weight loss. Don't cut down or stop insulin on your own.
Metabolic and bariatric surgery
For some people with severe obesity and type 2 diabetes, especially when other treatments haven't worked well enough, surgery may be an option. It can lead to large, lasting weight loss and big improvements in blood sugar. It's a serious step that needs careful evaluation beforehand and follow-up for life afterwards.
Monitoring and follow-up
Diabesity is long-term, so review visits are part of the treatment. Typically that means HbA1c every three to six months depending on how well controlled things are, along with weight, waist and blood pressure at each visit. Cholesterol and triglycerides get checked periodically. Kidney function and urine albumin are checked at least once a year, as are the eyes and feet. Liver tests are added if fatty liver is a concern.
Catching a drift early is much easier than dealing with a complication later.
Why is it so hard to lose weight with Type 2 diabetes?
This is probably the most common frustration we hear. "I've cut down on food and I'm still not losing weight."
Several things are usually going on at once. Insulin resistance and high insulin levels favour fat storage. Certain medicines raise appetite or add weight. When weight does come off, the body pushes back: hunger hormones rise and it burns a little less energy, which is why regain is so common. Low sugar episodes can lead to eating extra to correct them. Muscle declines with age and inactivity, lowering daily energy use. Then there's sleep, stress and long working hours, all of which affect appetite.
If you've been genuinely trying and nothing is changing, that's a reason to review the treatment. It isn't evidence that you've failed.
What happens if diabesity is not managed?
Years of high sugar, excess weight and the problems that travel with them raise the risk of complications. The main ones are heart attack and stroke, heart failure, kidney disease, damage to the retina (diabetic retinopathy), and nerve damage that causes numbness, tingling or pain in the feet. Fatty liver can progress to inflammation and scarring in some people. Sleep apnoea and knee arthritis are also more common.
None of these is guaranteed. Keeping sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol in range, not smoking and managing weight all lower the odds considerably.
How can complications be prevented?
It helps to think of prevention as several small levers pulled together rather than one big one.
Keep your blood sugar within the targets you've agreed with your doctor. Treat blood pressure and cholesterol, with medicines if needed. Aim for gradual weight loss and pay as much attention to keeping it off as to losing it. Stay active, and include strength work. Avoid tobacco in any form, including gutkha and kharra. Go for your yearly eye, kidney and foot checks even when you feel fine. And if a medicine is giving you side effects, tell your doctor rather than quietly stopping it.
Long-term diabetes care at Niramay Clinics in Dhantoli, Nagpur, looks at the heart, kidneys, eyes, liver and nerves alongside blood sugar for this reason.
When should you seek urgent medical help?
Go to a hospital or seek urgent care if there is:
Chest pain, pressure or tightness, particularly with breathlessness or sweating
Sudden weakness or numbness on one side, a drooping face or slurred speech
Confusion, unusual drowsiness or loss of consciousness
Low sugar symptoms (shaking, sweating, confusion) that don't settle after taking sugar, or a seizure
Repeated vomiting, especially with very high sugar readings or signs of dehydration
Severe abdominal pain that won't go away, particularly after starting a GLP-1 medicine
A foot wound that is red, swollen, warm, oozing or not healing
These can have more than one cause, and some are serious. They need to be seen quickly.
Common myths about diabetes and obesity
"It's just overeating." Food matters, but so do genes, hormones, sleep, medicines, stress and surroundings. Blame tends to delay care rather than improve it.
"There's no point unless I reach my ideal weight." Around 5% can already make a measurable difference.
"Starting insulin means it's all downhill." Insulin is safe and effective. Plenty of people use it for years while living full, active lives.
"Thin people don't get insulin resistance." Many Indians develop it, and diabetes too, at a normal-looking BMI because of abdominal fat.
"The injection will do the work." GLP-1 medicines do best with changes in diet and activity, and weight often returns when they're stopped without a plan.
"Skipping meals is the quickest way." On insulin or sulfonylureas, it's a quick way to a dangerous low. Supervised changes are much safer.
What to remember
Diabesity means type 2 diabetes and obesity together, linked mainly by insulin resistance.
Where fat sits matters. Abdominal fat carries more risk, and many Indians develop diabetes at lower weights.
About 5% weight loss can improve blood sugar; larger losses that are maintained help more and occasionally lead to remission.
Treatment brings together food, activity, sleep and medicines chosen for both sugar and weight, with a doctor guiding changes.
Regular checks of the heart, kidneys, eyes, liver and feet catch problems early.
Having diabetes and struggling with weight at the same time is tiring, and plenty of people have been told to "just lose weight" without any real help doing it. Treatment has moved on. There are more options now than there were even five years ago, and modest, steady progress counts for more than most people realise.
What works depends on your reports, your weight history, your other health conditions, your medicines and the life you actually live. A frank conversation with your doctor is a good place to start.

Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
MD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)

When type 2 diabetes and obesity occur in the same person, doctors sometimes call it diabesity. The two are tied together mainly through insulin resistance: extra body fat, particularly fat stored around the abdomen, makes the body less responsive to insulin, and blood sugar gradually climbs. That's why weight management is usually part of diabetes treatment itself.

A lot of people hear "you need to lose weight" at the same appointment where they're told their sugar is high. It can feel like a lecture. It shouldn't be. This article explains what's going on in the body, why weight loss is often harder for people with diabetes, what treatment options exist today, and what kind of progress is realistic.
Diabesity isn't a separate diagnosis. It's shorthand for a very common combination: type 2 diabetes plus excess body weight.

The term exists because the two conditions keep pushing on each other. Carrying extra fat raises the chance of developing diabetes. Once diabetes is present, some of its effects, and some of the medicines used to treat it, can make weight harder to shift. If only the sugar readings get attention, results are often disappointing.

Yes. Most major medical bodies now classify obesity as a chronic medical condition. Body weight is shaped by genes, hormones, appetite signalling, sleep, stress, medicines, working hours, cost of food and plenty more. Nobody decides to develop obesity, and treating it with the same seriousness as high blood pressure tends to lead to better care and less shame.
Start with insulin. It's a hormone made by the pancreas, and after a meal it helps glucose move out of the blood and into muscle, liver and fat cells.

Excess fat, especially fat packed inside the abdomen and around the liver, interferes with this. Cells respond less well to insulin, so the pancreas makes more to get the same job done. For a few years that extra effort can keep blood sugar close to normal, and nothing seems wrong. Eventually the insulin-producing cells can't keep pace. Glucose starts to rise, first into the prediabetes range, then into diabetes.

The traffic runs both ways. High insulin levels encourage the body to store fat. Insulin and sulfonylureas can cause weight gain in some people. And fatigue, joint pain or low mood make it harder to stay active.
So when someone with diabetes says they're trying hard and the scale isn't moving, they're usually telling the truth. There's biology working against them.

Insulin resistance means the body's cells don't respond to insulin as well as they should, so glucose has trouble getting from the blood into the cells. The pancreas compensates by producing more insulin, which can mask the problem for a long time.

On its own, insulin resistance usually causes no clear symptoms. Some people notice their waist getting bigger, or feel heavy and sleepy after meals. Others develop dark, velvety skin at the back of the neck or in the armpits (acanthosis nigricans), or skin tags. None of these proves anything by itself. Fasting glucose, HbA1c, a lipid profile, blood pressure and a waist measurement together tell a doctor much more.
Fat under the skin, on the hips and thighs for example, is called subcutaneous fat. Fat stored deep inside the abdomen, wrapped around the liver, pancreas and intestines, is visceral fat.

Visceral fat is the more troublesome of the two. It's metabolically active and closely linked with insulin resistance, fatty liver, high triglycerides, raised blood pressure and heart disease. Two people who weigh exactly the same can have quite different risk depending on where that weight sits, which is why your doctor may reach for a measuring tape as well as the weighing scale.

Studies have repeatedly found that many South Asians, Indians included, carry more abdominal and visceral fat and less muscle than some other populations at the same body weight. You'll sometimes hear this described as the "thin-fat" body type.

In practice, it means type 2 diabetes often shows up earlier and at a lower weight in Indians. Someone who looks only slightly overweight may already have marked insulin resistance. Indian guidelines use lower BMI and waist cut-offs for exactly this reason.
Doctors look at a few numbers together rather than relying on one.

BMI is a screening number. It can't tell fat from muscle and says nothing about where fat is stored. Where available, body composition analysis adds detail. Your doctor will read all of this alongside your blood reports, blood pressure and medical history.
Early on, many people feel perfectly fine. That's part of the problem.

When symptoms do appear, the usual ones are thirst, passing urine more often, tiredness, blurred vision, cuts that take longer to heal, and repeated infections. Excess weight adds its own set: snoring, broken sleep, daytime sleepiness, getting breathless on stairs, and aching knees or back. Some people just notice their waist creeping up even though they haven't changed what they eat.
Because so much of this develops quietly, regular blood tests are more reliable than waiting to feel unwell.

Your risk is higher if diabetes runs in your family, or if you've already been told you have prediabetes. A history of gestational diabetes or PCOS raises it too. So do high blood pressure, abnormal cholesterol, fatty liver and a waist above the cut-offs mentioned earlier. A desk-bound job, short or poor sleep, sleep apnoea and long-term use of certain medicines (steroids and some psychiatric drugs, for instance) all play a part.
Having one or more of these doesn't mean diabetes is inevitable. It does mean testing earlier and more regularly makes sense.
Type 2 diabetes is confirmed with blood tests. Assessing diabesity goes a step further, looking at what the combination of high sugar and extra weight is doing elsewhere in the body.
Fasting plasma glucose: blood sugar after an overnight fast
Fasting plasma glucose: blood sugar after an overnight fast
HbA1c: a reflection of average blood sugar over roughly the last two to three months
HbA1c: a reflection of average blood sugar over roughly the last two to three months
Post-meal glucose or an oral glucose tolerance test: how well the body copes with a glucose load
Post-meal glucose or an oral glucose tolerance test: how well the body copes with a glucose load
Lipid profile: cholesterol and triglycerides
Lipid profile: cholesterol and triglycerides
Liver function tests, and an ultrasound if fatty liver is suspected
Liver function tests, and an ultrasound if fatty liver is suspected
Kidney function and urine albumin, to pick up early kidney changes

Thyroid tests, if symptoms or history point that way
Thyroid tests, if symptoms or history point that way
A sleep assessment, if there's heavy snoring, pauses in breathing or daytime sleepiness
A sleep assessment, if there's heavy snoring, pauses in breathing or daytime sleepiness

Weight gain sometimes has a contributing medical cause: a hormonal problem, a sleep disorder, a medicine side effect. Finding it can change the whole plan. At Niramay Clinics, obesity care begins by looking for these possible causes before deciding on treatment.
Less than most people expect, at least to start seeing benefits.

Diabetes guidelines generally say that losing about 5% of body weight can improve blood glucose, blood pressure and cholesterol in many people. Bigger losses that are kept off, often in the 10 to 15% range or beyond, usually bring larger improvements and sometimes allow medicines to be reduced.
If you weigh 90 kg, 5% is roughly 4.5 kg. That's a goal you can actually picture.

For some people, yes, particularly if diabetes was diagnosed fairly recently. After substantial weight loss, blood sugar can return to the non-diabetic range. When HbA1c stays under 6.5% for at least three months without diabetes medicines, doctors call this remission.

Remission isn't a cure. Sugar can rise again, especially if weight comes back, so checks continue. And it isn't possible for everyone. People who don't reach remission still benefit a great deal from losing weight.
The plan should deal with blood sugar and weight at the same time, and it will change as you go.
No single diet suits everybody. The one that works is the one that brings your sugar down and that you can keep following on an ordinary Tuesday.

For most Indian households, a few things help. Try filling about half the plate with vegetables or salad, a quarter with protein such as dal, chana, rajma, paneer, curd, eggs, fish or chicken, and the remaining quarter with roti, rice or millets. Go easy on white rice, maida, biscuits, namkeen and sweet drinks, since these push sugar up quickly. Fruit juice counts as a sweet drink; whole fruit is a better choice. Having some protein at each meal helps with hunger and protects muscle while you lose weight. Fibre from whole grains, pulses and vegetables slows down how fast glucose enters the blood.
Festivals, weddings and restaurant meals are part of life. Planning a smaller portion usually works better than trying to avoid them altogether.
One caution. If you take insulin, or tablets that can cause low sugar, don't make big changes to your meals without talking to your doctor first.
Moving your muscles helps them take up glucose, and this happens even before any weight comes off.

For many adults with type 2 diabetes, the usual guidance is at least 150 minutes a week of moderate activity like brisk walking, spread over most days, plus strength exercise two or three times a week. That can be as simple as bodyweight squats, resistance bands or light weights. Breaking up long sitting spells with a few minutes of walking helps. So does a short walk after meals, which can blunt the post-meal sugar spike.

Start where you are and build slowly. If you have heart disease, foot problems or eye complications, or you're on insulin or sulfonylureas, ask your doctor what's safe for you and how to avoid low sugar during exercise.
Sleep gets overlooked. Short or poor sleep raises appetite, disturbs hunger hormones and worsens insulin resistance. Most adults do better with seven hours or more.

Loud snoring, stopping breathing at night or feeling drowsy through the day can point to obstructive sleep apnoea. It's common with obesity and makes both blood pressure and blood sugar harder to control, so mention it at your next visit.
Ongoing stress affects what and when people eat, and it can nudge blood sugar up. Dealing with it is a genuine part of treatment.
Which medicine suits you depends on your sugar levels, weight, heart and kidney health, other conditions, cost and what you prefer. Diabetes medicines don't all affect weight in the same way.
This is a broad overview, not a guide to choosing. Please don't start, stop or change any diabetes medicine without speaking to your doctor.

GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide, and tirzepatide, which acts on both GIP and GLP-1 pathways, have changed how doctors approach diabesity. They copy the action of gut hormones that regulate blood sugar, slow down stomach emptying and reduce appetite.

In many people they produce weight loss and sugar control that lifestyle changes alone couldn't achieve. They also come with trade-offs. Nausea, vomiting, constipation and loose motions are common in the first weeks. They aren't suitable for people with certain personal or family medical histories. Weight tends to come back if they're stopped without a plan for what comes next. They work better alongside good nutrition and strength exercise, and the cost adds up over months.
These are prescription medicines. They need a doctor's assessment and follow-up, and buying them from unreliable sources is risky.

Many people with diabesity need insulin at some point to keep sugar safely under control. It isn't a punishment, and it doesn't mean diabetes has reached some final stage. If weight gain on insulin worries you, say so. Your doctor can often rework the plan, for example by pairing insulin with a medicine that supports weight loss. Don't cut down or stop insulin on your own.

For some people with severe obesity and type 2 diabetes, especially when other treatments haven't worked well enough, surgery may be an option. It can lead to large, lasting weight loss and big improvements in blood sugar. It's a serious step that needs careful evaluation beforehand and follow-up for life afterwards.

Diabesity is long-term, so review visits are part of the treatment. Typically that means HbA1c every three to six months depending on how well controlled things are, along with weight, waist and blood pressure at each visit. Cholesterol and triglycerides get checked periodically. Kidney function and urine albumin are checked at least once a year, as are the eyes and feet. Liver tests are added if fatty liver is a concern.
Catching a drift early is much easier than dealing with a complication later.
This is probably the most common frustration we hear. "I've cut down on food and I'm still not losing weight."

Several things are usually going on at once. Insulin resistance and high insulin levels favour fat storage. Certain medicines raise appetite or add weight. When weight does come off, the body pushes back: hunger hormones rise and it burns a little less energy, which is why regain is so common. Low sugar episodes can lead to eating extra to correct them. Muscle declines with age and inactivity, lowering daily energy use. Then there's sleep, stress and long working hours, all of which affect appetite.
If you've been genuinely trying and nothing is changing, that's a reason to review the treatment. It isn't evidence that you've failed.

Years of high sugar, excess weight and the problems that travel with them raise the risk of complications. The main ones are heart attack and stroke, heart failure, kidney disease, damage to the retina (diabetic retinopathy), and nerve damage that causes numbness, tingling or pain in the feet. Fatty liver can progress to inflammation and scarring in some people. Sleep apnoea and knee arthritis are also more common.
None of these is guaranteed. Keeping sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol in range, not smoking and managing weight all lower the odds considerably.
It helps to think of prevention as several small levers pulled together rather than one big one.

Keep your blood sugar within the targets you've agreed with your doctor. Treat blood pressure and cholesterol, with medicines if needed. Aim for gradual weight loss and pay as much attention to keeping it off as to losing it. Stay active, and include strength work. Avoid tobacco in any form, including gutkha and kharra. Go for your yearly eye, kidney and foot checks even when you feel fine. And if a medicine is giving you side effects, tell your doctor rather than quietly stopping it.
Long-term diabetes care at Niramay Clinics in Dhantoli, Nagpur, looks at the heart, kidneys, eyes, liver and nerves alongside blood sugar for this reason.

These can have more than one cause, and some are serious. They need to be seen quickly.
"It's just overeating." Food matters, but so do genes, hormones, sleep, medicines, stress and surroundings. Blame tends to delay care rather than improve it.
"There's no point unless I reach my ideal weight." Around 5% can already make a measurable difference.
"Starting insulin means it's all downhill." Insulin is safe and effective. Plenty of people use it for years while living full, active lives.
"Thin people don't get insulin resistance." Many Indians develop it, and diabetes too, at a normal-looking BMI because of abdominal fat.
"The injection will do the work." GLP-1 medicines do best with changes in diet and activity, and weight often returns when they're stopped without a plan.
"Skipping meals is the quickest way." On insulin or sulfonylureas, it's a quick way to a dangerous low. Supervised changes are much safer.

Having diabetes and struggling with weight at the same time is tiring, and plenty of people have been told to "just lose weight" without any real help doing it. Treatment has moved on. There are more options now than there were even five years ago, and modest, steady progress counts for more than most people realise.
What works depends on your reports, your weight history, your other health conditions, your medicines and the life you actually live. A frank conversation with your doctor is a good place to start.
NIDDK: Health risks of overweight and obesity

Diabesity is a term for type 2 diabetes occurring together with overweight or obesity. It isn't a separate disease. It's used because the two conditions are so closely connected: fat stored around the abdomen increases insulin resistance, which pushes blood sugar up. Treating weight and sugar together generally works better than focusing on sugar readings alone.

Excess fat, especially visceral fat inside the abdomen, makes cells respond less well to insulin. The pancreas produces extra insulin to compensate, and for a while that keeps sugar near normal. Over time the pancreas can't keep up, and blood sugar rises into the prediabetes and then diabetes range. Family history, age and activity levels also affect who develops it.

Many people see better blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol after losing about 5% of their body weight. For someone weighing 80 kg, that's around 4 kg. Larger losses of 10 to 15% or more, kept off over time, usually bring bigger benefits and may allow some medicines to be reduced. Your doctor can help set a target that suits you.

In some people, particularly those diagnosed recently, significant weight loss brings blood sugar back to the non-diabetic range. Doctors call this remission when HbA1c stays below 6.5% for at least three months without diabetes medicines. It isn't a permanent cure. Sugar can rise again, especially with weight regain, so regular testing should continue.

Many Indians carry more fat around the abdomen and internal organs, and less muscle, than people of the same weight from some other populations. This raises insulin resistance even when BMI looks normal or only slightly high. Indian guidelines therefore use lower BMI and waist cut-offs to identify people at higher metabolic risk.

For suitable people, GLP-1 medicines can improve both blood sugar and weight. They're prescription medicines, though, and need a doctor's assessment first. Nausea, vomiting and constipation are common early side effects, and they aren't appropriate for people with certain medical histories. They work best alongside dietary changes and regular exercise, with ongoing medical follow-up.

Insulin can lead to some weight gain in certain people, partly because the body stops losing glucose in urine once sugar is better controlled. That isn't a reason to avoid or stop it. Doctors can often limit the effect through dose adjustments, meal planning, or combining insulin with medicines that help with weight.

For Indian adults, a waist of 90 cm or more in men and 80 cm or more in women is commonly used as a marker of higher metabolic risk. Waist size reflects abdominal fat, which is closely tied to insulin resistance. It's most useful read together with BMI, blood reports and blood pressure.

Liver tests are added if fatty liver is a concern.
Catching a drift early is much easier than dealing with a complication later.
This is probably the most common frustration we hear. "I've cut down on food and I'm still not losing weight."

Several things are usually going on at once. Insulin resistance and high insulin levels favour fat storage. Certain medicines raise appetite or add weight. When weight does come off, the body pushes back: hunger hormones rise and it burns a little less energy, which is why regain is so common. Low sugar episodes can lead to eating extra to correct them. Muscle declines with age and inactivity, lowering daily energy use. Then there's sleep, stress and long working hours, all of which affect appetite.
If you've been genuinely trying and nothing is changing, that's a reason to review the treatment. It isn't evidence that you've failed.

Years of high sugar, excess weight and the problems that travel with them raise the risk of complications. The main ones are heart attack and stroke, heart failure, kidney disease, damage to the retina (diabetic retinopathy), and nerve damage that causes numbness, tingling or pain in the feet. Fatty liver can progress to inflammation and scarring in some people. Sleep apnoea and knee arthritis are also more common.
None of these is guaranteed. Keeping sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol in range, not smoking and managing weight all lower the odds considerably.
It helps to think of prevention as several small levers pulled together rather than one big one.

Keep your blood sugar within the targets you've agreed with your doctor. Treat blood pressure and cholesterol, with medicines if needed. Aim for gradual weight loss and pay as much attention to keeping it off as to losing it. Stay active, and include strength work. Avoid tobacco in any form, including gutkha and kharra. Go for your yearly eye, kidney and foot checks even when you feel fine. And if a medicine is giving you side effects, tell your doctor rather than quietly stopping it.
Long-term diabetes care at Niramay Clinics in Dhantoli, Nagpur, looks at the heart, kidneys, eyes, liver and nerves alongside blood sugar for this reason.
When should you seek urgent medical help?
Go to a hospital or seek urgent care if there is:
These can have more than one cause, and some are serious. They need to be seen quickly.
"It's just overeating." Food matters, but so do genes, hormones, sleep, medicines, stress and surroundings. Blame tends to delay care rather than improve it.
"There's no point unless I reach my ideal weight." Around 5% can already make a measurable difference.
"Starting insulin means it's all downhill." Insulin is safe and effective. Plenty of people use it for years while living full, active lives.
"Thin people don't get insulin resistance." Many Indians develop it, and diabetes too, at a normal-looking BMI because of abdominal fat.
"The injection will do the work." GLP-1 medicines do best with changes in diet and activity, and weight often returns when they're stopped without a plan.
"Skipping meals is the quickest way." On insulin or sulfonylureas, it's a quick way to a dangerous low. Supervised changes are much safer.

Having diabetes and struggling with weight at the same time is tiring, and plenty of people have been told to "just lose weight" without any real help doing it. Treatment has moved on. There are more options now than there were even five years ago, and modest, steady progress counts for more than most people realise.
What works depends on your reports, your weight history, your other health conditions, your medicines and the life you actually live. A frank conversation with your doctor is a good place to start.

faqs.q: Can a diabetic person eat mithai?
faqs.a: Yes, in small portions and occasionally. Eat it after a balanced meal, avoid large amounts and adjust the rest of your meal. Check your blood sugar to see how you respond.

faqs.q: Which Indian sweet is best for diabetes?
faqs.a: No sweet is completely free of sugar impact, but small portions of nut-based sweets, or desserts made with less sugar, are better than syrup-based sweets. Portion size matters more than the type.

faqs.q: Are sugar-free sweets safe for diabetics?
faqs.a: Not always. Some sugar-free sweets still contain flour, dates, khoya or fats and can raise blood sugar. Check labels and keep the portion small.

faqs.q: How can I control blood sugar during Diwali?
faqs.a: Eat regular meals, keep sweets to a small portion after meals, avoid sweet drinks, stay active, and check your sugar more often. Avoid skipping meals and take medicines as prescribed.

faqs.q: Does jaggery or honey make sweets safer?
faqs.a: Not really. Jaggery and honey still raise blood sugar like sugar. They may have small amounts of minerals, but are not a safe substitute in large quantities.

faqs.q: How long after eating sweets should I check my sugar?
faqs.a: Check about two hours after the first bite. This shows your post-meal peak. If it is much above your target, reduce the portion or change the timing next time and discuss it with your doctor.

Diabetes and Sweets: Handling Mithai Without Spikes
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 6 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
People with diabetes can eat mithai occasionally in small portions, as part of a balanced meal, while keeping the total carbohydrates for the day in check. Avoid eating sweets on an empty stomach or in large amounts. Pair them with protein, fibre and a walk afterwards, and check your blood sugar to learn how your body responds.
Festivals, weddings and family visits all come with mithai. If you have diabetes, it can feel like everyone is enjoying something you must avoid. The truth is more kind. Most people with diabetes can enjoy a small portion of sweets now and then, if they plan well.
Why do sweets raise blood sugar?
Most mithai is made of sugar, refined flour, milk solids and ghee. The sugar and flour are digested fast and enter the blood quickly. Fat and milk slow this a little, but the overall carbohydrate load is high. A single piece of some sweets can carry as many carbohydrates as a full chapati or more.
Is a sugar-free sweet safe?
"Sugar-free" does not mean carbohydrate-free or calorie-free. Many such sweets contain dates, jaggery, refined flour, khoya or sugar alcohols, which can still raise blood sugar. Read the labels, and watch the portion. Artificial sweeteners in small amounts are usually acceptable, but they do not make a large portion safe.
How can you enjoy mithai safely?
1. keep the portion small
One small piece, about the size of a coin or a small cube, is a reasonable serving. Share a piece with someone, or cut it into halves and eat slowly.
2. do not eat it alone on an empty stomach
Eat it right after a balanced meal that contains vegetables, dal, curd or paneer. The fibre and protein slow the rise in blood sugar.
3. swap something else
Plan the day so that mithai replaces part of the carbohydrate in the meal, such as a roti or half the rice, rather than being added on top.
4. choose better options
Sweets made with nuts, such as a small piece of dry fruit burfi
Fruit-based desserts with no added sugar, such as a few strawberries or berries with curd
Homemade versions where you can reduce sugar and add nuts or seeds
Roasted makhana or chikki made with nuts in small servings
5. move after eating
A 10 to 15 minute walk after the meal helps lower the post-meal rise.
6. check your sugar
If you use a glucometer, check two hours after the sweet to learn your own response. If you take insulin or certain tablets, ask your doctor how to adjust.
What should you avoid?
Eating several pieces at once
Sweets with sugar syrup, such as jalebi, gulab jamun and rasgulla, in large portions
Sweet drinks, such as lassi with sugar and packaged juices
Snacking on sweets all day during festivals
Skipping meals to "save room" for dessert, which can cause low or very high sugar
How do you handle festivals and weddings?
Eat a healthy meal or snack before the event, so you are not very hungry.
Take a small plate and fill half with vegetables and salads.
Decide in advance which sweet you will have.
Say "no thank you" politely when hosts push you. You can say your doctor has advised moderation.
Keep your medicines and glucometer with you.
When should you talk to your doctor?
Your sugar is often above target even without sweets
You feel dizzy, shaky or sweaty after skipping meals
You are unsure how to adjust insulin or tablets for a festival
You have a very high reading with thirst, tiredness or blurred vision
Points to keep
Occasional mithai in a small portion is fine for most people with diabetes.
Eat it after a balanced meal, not on an empty stomach.
"Sugar-free" sweets are not always safe in large amounts.
A short walk after eating helps.
Plan ahead for festivals, and check your sugar to learn your response.
Diabetes care is about balance, not punishment. With a little planning, you can share in the joy of festivals while keeping your blood sugar steady. For a personalised food plan, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
Sources and further reading
WHO: Healthy diet
NIDDK: Diabetes diet, eating and physical activity
Frequently asked questions
Can a diabetic person eat mithai?
Yes, in small portions and occasionally. Eat it after a balanced meal, avoid large amounts and adjust the rest of your meal. Check your blood sugar to see how you respond.
Which Indian sweet is best for diabetes?
No sweet is completely free of sugar impact, but small portions of nut-based sweets, or desserts made with less sugar, are better than syrup-based sweets. Portion size matters more than the type.
Are sugar-free sweets safe for diabetics?
Not always. Some sugar-free sweets still contain flour, dates, khoya or fats and can raise blood sugar. Check labels and keep the portion small.
How can I control blood sugar during Diwali?
Eat regular meals, keep sweets to a small portion after meals, avoid sweet drinks, stay active, and check your sugar more often. Avoid skipping meals and take medicines as prescribed.
Does jaggery or honey make sweets safer?
Not really. Jaggery and honey still raise blood sugar like sugar. They may have small amounts of minerals, but are not a safe substitute in large quantities.
How long after eating sweets should I check my sugar?
Check about two hours after the first bite. This shows your post-meal peak. If it is much above your target, reduce the portion or change the timing next time and discuss it with your doctor.

Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur

Published 6 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer

People with diabetes can eat mithai occasionally in small portions, as part of a balanced meal, while keeping the total carbohydrates for the day in check. Avoid eating sweets on an empty stomach or in large amounts. Pair them with protein, fibre and a walk afterwards, and check your blood sugar to learn how your body responds.

Festivals, weddings and family visits all come with mithai. If you have diabetes, it can feel like everyone is enjoying something you must avoid. The truth is more kind. Most people with diabetes can enjoy a small portion of sweets now and then, if they plan well.

Most mithai is made of sugar, refined flour, milk solids and ghee. The sugar and flour are digested fast and enter the blood quickly. Fat and milk slow this a little, but the overall carbohydrate load is high. A single piece of some sweets can carry as many carbohydrates as a full chapati or more.

"Sugar-free" does not mean carbohydrate-free or calorie-free. Many such sweets contain dates, jaggery, refined flour, khoya or sugar alcohols, which can still raise blood sugar. Read the labels, and watch the portion. Artificial sweeteners in small amounts are usually acceptable, but they do not make a large portion safe.
One small piece, about the size of a coin or a small cube, is a reasonable serving. Share a piece with someone, or cut it into halves and eat slowly.
Eat it right after a balanced meal that contains vegetables, dal, curd or paneer. The fibre and protein slow the rise in blood sugar.
Plan the day so that mithai replaces part of the carbohydrate in the meal, such as a roti or half the rice, rather than being added on top.
A 10 to 15 minute walk after the meal helps lower the post-meal rise.
If you use a glucometer, check two hours after the sweet to learn your own response. If you take insulin or certain tablets, ask your doctor how to adjust.

faqs.q: Can I eat rice if I have diabetes?
faqs.a: Yes. Rice can be part of a diabetes meal plan. What matters is the portion, the type of rice, how frequently it is eaten and what accompanies it. Pairing an appropriate rice portion with vegetables and protein can make the overall meal more balanced.

faqs.q: Which Indian breakfast is good for diabetes?
faqs.a: Options can include vegetable poha, idli with sambar, moong or besan chilla, vegetable omelette and unsweetened oats with an appropriate protein source. Portion size and the overall composition of the breakfast are more important than finding one food that is labelled "diabetic."

faqs.q: Which fruits can I eat with diabetes?
faqs.a: Many whole fruits can be included, such as guava, apple, orange, pear and papaya. The appropriate portion depends on your overall eating pattern and carbohydrate needs. Whole fruit is generally preferable to fruit juice.

faqs.q: What foods should I avoid if I have diabetes?
faqs.a: There is no universal list of foods that every person must completely avoid. However, sugary drinks, frequent sweets, refined snacks, highly processed foods and frequent deep-fried foods are generally worth limiting.

faqs.q: Is roti healthier than rice for diabetes?
faqs.a: Neither is automatically better for everyone. Both provide carbohydrate. The portion, preparation, accompanying foods and your individual glucose response all matter.

faqs.q: Can I eat sweets if I have diabetes?
faqs.a: Small occasional portions may be possible for some people, particularly during celebrations, but sweets should not become a routine part of the diet. Your overall glucose control and treatment plan should be considered.

faqs.q: Can a diabetes diet help me lose weight?
faqs.a: It can. Reducing excessive portions, sugary drinks and highly processed foods while increasing vegetables, fibre and appropriate protein can support weight management. The appropriate approach varies between individuals.

faqs.q: Do I need a separate diabetes diet chart?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. A personalised plan using familiar foods can be easier to follow than a rigid chart. Your doctor or dietitian can help adjust portions and meal timing based on your medications, glucose levels, weight and other health conditions.
