Diabetes Diet for Indians: What to Eat, What to Limit & How to Build a Practical Meal Plan
Diabetes Diet for Indians
Diabetes Diet for Indians: What to Eat, What to Limit & How to Build a Practical Meal Plan
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 5 October 2026 · 20 min
Quick answer
A person with diabetes can generally eat a wide variety of foods, but meals should emphasise vegetables, suitable protein sources, fibre-rich foods and sensible portions of carbohydrate-rich foods such as rice, roti, poha, idli and dosa. Whole fruits can usually be included in appropriate portions. Sugary drinks, frequent sweets, refined snacks and heavily processed foods are better kept limited. People taking insulin or medicines that can cause low blood sugar may need individual advice about meal timing and carbohydrate intake. The important point is this: a diabetes diet is not simply a list of foods that are allowed and forbidden. It is a way of organising your everyday meals so that they support blood glucose control and remain realistic enough to follow over the long term.
Getting diagnosed with diabetes can make food feel unnecessarily complicated.
Suddenly, ordinary questions come up at almost every meal.
Can I still eat rice? Is roti better? What about mangoes? Should I stop eating sweets completely? Is poha okay for breakfast? What should I eat if I am also trying to lose weight?
Managing diabetes does not usually require throwing away the way you have always eaten.
For most people, the focus is on how much you eat, how often you eat it, what you combine it with, and how the overall diet fits into your treatment plan.
Indian food can absolutely be part of a diabetes-conscious eating pattern. Rice, roti, dal, vegetables, curd, fruit and many familiar home-cooked dishes can all have a place. The approach simply needs some thought around portions, preparation and balance.
This guide looks at how to make those changes without turning every meal into a complicated calculation.
What is a diabetes-friendly Indian diet?
There is no single meal plan that suits every person with diabetes.
Two people may both have Type 2 diabetes but have very different nutritional needs. One may need to lose weight, another may be underweight. One may exercise regularly, while another may spend most of the day sitting. Medication, insulin use, kidney health, age and other medical conditions can also change dietary requirements.
Still, some basic principles are useful for almost everyone.
A balanced eating pattern generally involves:
Keeping portions of carbohydrate-rich foods sensible
Eating more vegetables and other fibre-rich foods
Including an appropriate source of protein
Choosing minimally processed foods more often
Limiting added sugars
Reducing frequent fried and highly processed foods
Choosing whole fruit instead of relying on fruit juice
Paying attention to meal timing when medication requires it
Combining diet with appropriate physical activity
This does not mean you need to stop eating Indian food.
In fact, many traditional Indian meals already contain useful foods such as pulses, vegetables, curd, spices, whole grains, nuts and seeds.
The challenge is often the way the meal is put together and the quantity consumed.
How to build a balanced plate for diabetes
One of the easiest ways to think about a meal is to look at the plate rather than individual foods.
Instead of making rice or roti the centre of the meal, try building the meal around vegetables and protein, with a controlled amount of carbohydrate.
A simple structure looks like this:
Part of the meal
Examples
Vegetables
Bhindi, cabbage, cauliflower, beans, spinach, gourds, brinjal, cucumber, salad
Protein
Dal, beans, curd, eggs, paneer, tofu, fish or chicken
Carbohydrate
Roti, rice, millet, poha, idli, dosa or another grain-based food
The exact proportions will vary from person to person.
For example, someone who is physically active may have different requirements from someone who is trying to lose weight. A person with kidney disease may also need dietary adjustments that are not necessary for everyone else.
That is why the plate method is better viewed as a starting framework, rather than a rigid prescription.
Which Indian foods can be included in a diabetes diet?
A diabetes diagnosis does not suddenly make ordinary Indian foods unhealthy.
What matters is the overall pattern.
Vegetables
Non-starchy vegetables are useful additions to meals because they provide fibre, vitamins, minerals and volume without contributing the same amount of carbohydrate as foods such as rice, bread or potatoes.
You can rotate through foods such as:
Bhindi
Cabbage
Cauliflower
Beans
Capsicum
Brinjal
Spinach and other leafy vegetables
Bottle gourd
Ridge gourd
Bitter gourd
Cucumber
Tomato
Radish
Broccoli
Mushrooms
The cooking method matters too.
A vegetable dish prepared with a modest amount of oil is very different from a preparation that is heavily fried or made with large amounts of cream, butter or other calorie-dense ingredients.
Dal, pulses and beans
Dal and pulses are familiar staples in many Indian households and can be useful components of a balanced meal.
Examples include:
Moong dal
Masoor dal
Toor dal
Chana
Rajma
Chickpeas
Other beans and pulses
These foods provide protein and fibre, although they also contain carbohydrate.
That distinction is worth remembering. Calling dal a "protein food" does not mean it is carbohydrate-free.
A sensible portion alongside vegetables and an appropriate amount of rice or roti can work well for many people.
What about protein?
Protein is an important part of a satisfying meal.
Depending on your food preferences and medical requirements, sources may include:
Eggs
Fish
Chicken
Curd
Paneer
Tofu
Dal
Beans
Other pulses
For someone who also wants to lose weight, including an appropriate protein source may help make meals more filling.
However, more protein is not automatically better for everyone. People with kidney disease, for example, may require specific dietary advice.
Can you eat rice if you have diabetes?
Yes.
A diabetes diagnosis does not automatically mean rice has to disappear from your plate.
The more useful questions are:
How much rice are you eating?
What else is in the meal?
How often are you eating large portions?
Is there enough vegetables and protein?
How does your blood glucose respond?
A large serving of rice with little else in the meal is quite different from a moderate serving accompanied by vegetables, dal and an appropriate protein source.
You also do not need to assume that brown rice can be eaten without limits. Brown rice can contain more fibre than white rice, but it still contributes carbohydrate.
Simple ways to manage rice portions
You could try:
Serving a smaller amount of rice.
Increasing the vegetables on the plate.
Including dal or another suitable protein source.
Avoiding a meal where rice takes up almost the entire plate.
Monitoring your glucose when your healthcare professional has advised you to do so.
Some people find that they can comfortably include rice in their routine. Others may need to reduce the amount or change the way the meal is structured.
There is no universal portion that works for everyone.
Is roti better than rice for diabetes?
This is another question patients ask frequently.
There is no simple rule that says roti is always better than rice.
Roti and rice both contribute carbohydrate. The nutritional value and effect of a meal depend on the type, portion, preparation and what accompanies it.
Whole-wheat roti can be a useful option. But eating several large rotis can still provide a substantial amount of carbohydrate and calories.
Paratha deserves additional attention because the amount of oil or ghee used during preparation can increase its calorie content considerably.
Instead of asking which food is automatically "better," look at the complete meal.
For example:
Roti + vegetable sabzi + dal + curd
may be a very different meal from:
Several large parathas + little vegetable + a sugary drink.
The name of the food alone does not tell the whole story.
What should you eat for breakfast with diabetes?
Breakfast is often where Indian diets become heavily carbohydrate-based.
Poha, upma, idli, dosa and bread are common choices. These foods do not necessarily need to be eliminated, but the meal can often be improved by paying attention to portion and adding protein or fibre.
Some possible combinations include:
Vegetable poha
Keep the portion sensible and add vegetables. Pairing it with an appropriate protein source can make the meal more balanced.
Idli with sambar
Sambar can add pulses and vegetables to the meal. Portion still matters, particularly if several idlis are eaten.
Moong dal or besan chilla
These can be paired with vegetables and unsweetened curd.
Vegetable omelette
For people who eat eggs, an omelette with vegetables can provide protein. It can be paired with a controlled portion of whole-grain toast or roti if appropriate.
Oats with a protein source
Choose an unsweetened preparation rather than turning breakfast into a bowl of oats with sugar, flavoured syrups or sweetened toppings.
The goal is not to find one "perfect diabetic breakfast."
It is to avoid making breakfast almost entirely refined or rapidly digested carbohydrate.
Can people with diabetes eat fruit?
Yes.
Fruit is often unnecessarily restricted after a diabetes diagnosis.
Whole fruits provide carbohydrates, but they also provide fibre, vitamins, minerals and other nutrients. The practical issue is usually portion size and the total amount of carbohydrate being consumed, rather than avoiding fruit altogether.
Depending on your individual diet, fruits such as these can be included:
Guava
Apple
Orange
Pear
Papaya
Pomegranate
Melons
Berries
Other seasonal fruits
There is no need to label a fruit as "forbidden" simply because it tastes sweet.
At the same time, fruit is not carbohydrate-free. Eating very large portions can still affect blood glucose.
Whole fruit or fruit juice: which is better?
For most people with diabetes, whole fruit is the more practical choice.
When fruit is turned into juice, it becomes much easier to consume a large amount quickly. A glass may contain the juice of several pieces of fruit without providing the same level of fullness as eating the fruit itself.
Sweetened packaged fruit drinks are an even less suitable everyday choice.
So instead of:
Fruit blender juice
consider simply eating an appropriate portion of whole fruit.
What are better snack options for diabetes?
Snacking can quietly add a lot of carbohydrate, fat and calories to the day.
Biscuits with tea, namkeen, chips, bakery snacks and sweets are easy to eat without noticing how much has been consumed.
Depending on your individual needs, alternatives could include:
Roasted chana
A small serving of nuts
Unsweetened curd
Whole fruit
Sprouts
Boiled eggs
Vegetable-based snacks
And remember: not everyone needs snacks between meals.
Some people are perfectly comfortable with three main meals. Others may need snacks depending on their medication, activity, work schedule or other circumstances.
If you are eating because you are genuinely hungry, consider what is driving that hunger. If you are eating simply because snacks are always available, changing the routine may be more useful than searching for a "diabetic snack."
Which foods should be limited?
Rather than creating an enormous "foods to avoid" list, it is usually more useful to identify foods that are best kept occasional.
Sugary drinks
These include:
Soft drinks
Sweetened juices
Sweetened tea and coffee
Energy drinks
Other sugar-sweetened beverages
Liquid calories can add up quickly because they often provide little satiety.
Sweets and desserts
Indian sweets such as:
Gulab jamun
Jalebi
Ladoo
Barfi
Peda
Rasgulla
can contain considerable amounts of sugar and calories.
That does not mean every family celebration has to become stressful.
The bigger issue is making these foods an everyday habit.
Refined snacks
Keep foods such as biscuits, cakes, pastries, packaged snacks and other highly refined foods limited.
Deep-fried foods
Regularly eating samosas, pakoras, puris and other deep-fried foods can make weight management more difficult because they can be very energy-dense.
The occasional food is different from a daily routine.
Can you eat sweets during festivals?
Food is part of family life, celebrations and culture.
Diabetes management should leave room for that reality.
During festivals, rather than thinking:
"I have diabetes, so I cannot eat anything."
a more practical approach may be:
Have a smaller portion.
Avoid combining several sugary foods in one sitting.
Skip sugary drinks where possible.
Eat slowly.
Include vegetables and protein with the main meal.
Avoid arriving at a celebration extremely hungry.
Return to your normal routine afterward.
You do not need to "punish" yourself for having a small serving of mithai.
At the same time, a festival should not turn into several days of unrestricted sweets and sugary drinks.
The pattern over time matters.
Why do fibre and protein matter?
Two things that can make meals more satisfying are fibre and protein.
Fibre
Fibre is found in foods such as:
Vegetables
Whole fruits
Pulses
Beans
Whole grains
Nuts
Seeds
It contributes to digestive health and can help with fullness.
If your current diet is low in fibre, increase it gradually. Adequate fluid intake is also important unless you have been advised to restrict fluids.
Protein
Protein contributes to satiety and is important for maintaining body tissues and muscle.
Eggs, fish, chicken, curd, paneer, tofu, dal and beans are examples of foods that can contribute protein.
The amount needed varies from person to person.Again, this is one reason why copying someone else's diabetes meal plan is not always appropriate.
Can a diabetes diet help with weight loss?
It can, when the eating pattern helps create an appropriate reduction in overall calorie intake while still providing adequate nutrition.
For people who need to lose weight, useful changes may include:
Reducing oversized portions
Increasing vegetables
Choosing appropriate protein sources
Eating more fibre-rich foods
Cutting back on sugary drinks
Reducing frequent fried foods
Limiting highly processed snacks
Increasing physical activity where appropriate
There is no requirement to follow an extreme low-carbohydrate diet or survive on salads.
A diet that produces rapid weight loss but cannot be maintained is unlikely to be a useful long-term solution.
What about exercise after meals?
Physical activity is an important part of diabetes management.
For some people, a walk after a meal can be a convenient way to include activity in their daily routine.
However, exercise can affect blood glucose, particularly in people using insulin or certain medicines.
If you experience symptoms such as:
Shaking
Sweating
Dizziness
Confusion
Sudden weakness
Unusual hunger
during or after exercise, speak with your healthcare professional. These symptoms can sometimes occur with low blood glucose.
Your exercise routine and medication may need to be considered together.
Does diabetes medication affect meal timing?
Sometimes it does.
Different diabetes medicines work differently. Some need to be taken with meals, while insulin regimens can have specific relationships with food and activity.
This is why you should not make major changes to your meal pattern and independently change medication doses or timing.
If you take insulin or a medicine that can cause hypoglycaemia, ask your doctor how your meals, exercise and medication schedule should fit together.
Never change insulin or diabetes medication simply because you have changed your diet unless your treating clinician has advised you to do so.
How to create a practical Indian diabetes meal plan
A meal plan should fit your actual day.
It should account for your work schedule, family meals, food preferences, activity and medical treatment.
Here is a simple framework:
Time
Possible structure
Breakfast
Controlled carbohydrate + protein + vegetables/fibre
Mid-morning
Fruit or another suitable option if needed
Lunch
Vegetables + protein + controlled rice/roti portion
Evening
Nuts, roasted chana, curd or another suitable option if needed
Dinner
Vegetables + protein + controlled carbohydrate
Dessert
Occasional small portion
These are examples, not prescribed quantities.
A person's calorie and carbohydrate requirements can vary significantly.
Sample Indian meal combinations
Meal option 1
1 appropriate portion of roti
Mixed vegetable sabzi
Dal
Salad
Unsweetened curd
Meal option 2
Moderate portion of rice
Dal
Cooked vegetables
Suitable protein
Salad
Meal option 3
Moong chilla
Vegetable filling
Unsweetened curd
Meal option 4
Fish or chicken
Cooked vegetables
Salad
Appropriate carbohydrate portion
These examples are intended to demonstrate how to structure a meal, not to prescribe an identical diet to every patient.
What if you eat at restaurants?
You do not have to stop eating outside after being diagnosed with diabetes.
A few small decisions can make restaurant meals easier to manage.
Consider:
Grilled or roasted foods instead of deep-fried starters.
Vegetable dishes or salads alongside the main course.
Smaller portions when servings are large.
Water or unsweetened beverages instead of sugary drinks.
Sharing desserts.
Being cautious with creamy gravies and dishes containing large amounts of oil or butter.
Also remember that restaurant food may contain considerably more oil, salt and calories than you would use at home.
The occasional restaurant meal is not the problem. Frequency and overall eating habits matter.
Common diabetes diet myths
"I have diabetes, so i can never eat rice."
Not necessarily.
Rice can be included in a suitable meal plan. The amount and the rest of the meal are important.
"Fruit is basically sugar, so i should avoid it."
Whole fruit can generally be part of a balanced diet. It contains carbohydrate, but it also provides fibre and important nutrients.
The focus should be on appropriate portions rather than eliminating fruit without a medical reason.
"Brown rice is unlimited because it is healthy."
Brown rice may have nutritional advantages over refined white rice, but it still contains carbohydrate.
The serving still matters.
"Sugar-free means i can eat as much as i want."
No.
A product labelled sugar-free can still contain calories, fat or other sources of carbohydrate.
Look at the complete nutrition information and serving size rather than relying only on the front-of-pack claim.
"I need completely separate food from my family."
Not necessarily.
In many Indian households, the same meal can work for everyone.
The differences may simply be in portion sizes, preparation methods and what each person puts on their plate.
"I need expensive diabetic foods."
Not usually.
A balanced diabetes diet can be built around ordinary foods available in most Indian kitchens.
Vegetables, pulses, curd, eggs, fish, chicken, whole grains, nuts and fruit can all be part of a suitable eating pattern.
When should your diet be personalised?
General dietary advice is useful, but there are situations where individual guidance becomes particularly important.
Speak with your doctor or qualified dietitian if you have:
Frequent high blood glucose readings
Repeated episodes of low blood glucose
Insulin treatment
Kidney disease
Liver disease
Significant obesity
Unexplained weight loss
Pregnancy or gestational diabetes
Multiple diabetes medicines
Difficulty controlling blood glucose despite lifestyle changes
Your nutritional needs can also change over time.
A meal plan that suited you two years ago may no longer be appropriate if your weight, medication, activity level or health status has changed.
How to make a diabetes diet easier to follow
You do not need to change everything at once.
Start with a few changes that are realistic.
1. look at your carbohydrate portions
You may not need to remove rice or roti. Start by checking whether the portion is larger than you actually need.
2. Add vegetables
If your plate is mostly rice or roti, add more vegetables before adding another serving of carbohydrate.
3. Include protein
Dal, curd, eggs, paneer, tofu, fish, chicken and other suitable foods can make a meal more balanced.
4. Reduce liquid sugar
Cutting down on sugary tea, soft drinks and sweetened beverages can be one of the simpler dietary changes.
5. Eat fruit rather than drinking it
Choose whole fruit instead of regularly drinking fruit juice.
6. Keep sweets occasional
You do not need to turn every celebration into a restriction exercise, but sweets should not become an everyday habit.
7. Be careful with "healthy" labels
Multigrain, sugar-free and natural are not automatic guarantees that a product is appropriate in unlimited quantities.
8. Pay attention to your glucose pattern
If your healthcare professional has asked you to monitor blood glucose, the readings can provide useful information about how your meals are affecting you.
9. Keep moving
Regular physical activity is an important part of diabetes management when medically appropriate.
10. Review the plan when circumstances change
Medication changes, weight changes, pregnancy, kidney problems or significant changes in activity can all affect dietary requirements.
The bottom line
A diabetes diet does not have to mean giving up Indian food.
You can often continue eating familiar foods while making sensible changes to portions, cooking methods and meal composition.
Rice does not automatically have to disappear. Roti is not automatically a free food. Fruit does not have to be banned. And you do not need expensive products labelled specifically for diabetes.
Instead, build meals around vegetables, suitable protein, fibre and sensible portions of carbohydrate, while keeping sugary drinks, frequent sweets, refined snacks and heavily processed foods under control.
Most importantly, your diet should work in real life.
It should work when you are eating at home, when your family is having a celebration, when you go to a restaurant and when your daily routine gets busy.
If your blood glucose remains difficult to control despite making reasonable lifestyle changes, the answer may not simply be to make your diet stricter. Your medication, physical activity, weight, sleep and other aspects of diabetes management may also need to be reviewed.
When to seek urgent care
Seek urgent care for vomiting, confusion, unusual drowsiness or symptoms of very high or very low sugar, especially if you take insulin or tablets that can cause low sugar.

WHO: Healthy diet
NIDDK: Diabetes diet, eating and physical activity
Frequently asked questions
Can I eat rice if I have diabetes?
Yes. Rice can be part of a diabetes meal plan. What matters is the portion, the type of rice, how frequently it is eaten and what accompanies it. Pairing an appropriate rice portion with vegetables and protein can make the overall meal more balanced.
Which Indian breakfast is good for diabetes?
Options can include vegetable poha, idli with sambar, moong or besan chilla, vegetable omelette and unsweetened oats with an appropriate protein source. Portion size and the overall composition of the breakfast are more important than finding one food that is labelled "diabetic."
Which fruits can I eat with diabetes?
Many whole fruits can be included, such as guava, apple, orange, pear and papaya. The appropriate portion depends on your overall eating pattern and carbohydrate needs. Whole fruit is generally preferable to fruit juice.
What foods should I avoid if I have diabetes?
There is no universal list of foods that every person must completely avoid. However, sugary drinks, frequent sweets, refined snacks, highly processed foods and frequent deep-fried foods are generally worth limiting.
Is roti healthier than rice for diabetes?
Neither is automatically better for everyone. Both provide carbohydrate. The portion, preparation, accompanying foods and your individual glucose response all matter.
Can I eat sweets if I have diabetes?
Small occasional portions may be possible for some people, particularly during celebrations, but sweets should not become a routine part of the diet. Your overall glucose control and treatment plan should be considered.
Can a diabetes diet help me lose weight?
It can. Reducing excessive portions, sugary drinks and highly processed foods while increasing vegetables, fibre and appropriate protein can support weight management. The appropriate approach varies between individuals.
Do I need a separate diabetes diet chart?
Not necessarily. A personalised plan using familiar foods can be easier to follow than a rigid chart. Your doctor or dietitian can help adjust portions and meal timing based on your medications, glucose levels, weight and other health conditions.

A person with diabetes can generally eat a wide variety of foods, but meals should emphasise vegetables, suitable protein sources, fibre-rich foods and sensible portions of carbohydrate-rich foods such as rice, roti, poha, idli and dosa. Whole fruits can usually be included in appropriate portions. Sugary drinks, frequent sweets, refined snacks and heavily processed foods are better kept limited. People taking insulin or medicines that can cause low blood sugar may need individual advice about meal timing and carbohydrate intake. The important point is this: a diabetes diet is not simply a list of foods that are allowed and forbidden. It is a way of organising your everyday meals so that they support blood glucose control and remain realistic enough to follow over the long term.
Getting diagnosed with diabetes can make food feel unnecessarily complicated.
Suddenly, ordinary questions come up at almost every meal.
Can I still eat rice? Is roti better? What about mangoes? Should I stop eating sweets completely? Is poha okay for breakfast? What should I eat if I am also trying to lose weight?
Managing diabetes does not usually require throwing away the way you have always eaten.
For most people, the focus is on how much you eat, how often you eat it, what you combine it with, and how the overall diet fits into your treatment plan.

Indian food can absolutely be part of a diabetes-conscious eating pattern. Rice, roti, dal, vegetables, curd, fruit and many familiar home-cooked dishes can all have a place. The approach simply needs some thought around portions, preparation and balance.
This guide looks at how to make those changes without turning every meal into a complicated calculation.
There is no single meal plan that suits every person with diabetes.

Two people may both have Type 2 diabetes but have very different nutritional needs. One may need to lose weight, another may be underweight. One may exercise regularly, while another may spend most of the day sitting. Medication, insulin use, kidney health, age and other medical conditions can also change dietary requirements.
Still, some basic principles are useful for almost everyone.

Instead of making rice or roti the centre of the meal, try building the meal around vegetables and protein, with a controlled amount of carbohydrate.
The exact proportions will vary from person to person.

For example, someone who is physically active may have different requirements from someone who is trying to lose weight. A person with kidney disease may also need dietary adjustments that are not necessary for everyone else.
That is why the plate method is better viewed as a starting framework, rather than a rigid prescription.
A diabetes diagnosis does not suddenly make ordinary Indian foods unhealthy.

Non-starchy vegetables are useful additions to meals because they provide fibre, vitamins, minerals and volume without contributing the same amount of carbohydrate as foods such as rice, bread or potatoes.
A vegetable dish prepared with a modest amount of oil is very different from a preparation that is heavily fried or made with large amounts of cream, butter or other calorie-dense ingredients.
Dal and pulses are familiar staples in many Indian households and can be useful components of a balanced meal.

A sensible portion alongside vegetables and an appropriate amount of rice or roti can work well for many people.

pOnly: Diabetes Diet for Indians
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
MD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 5 October 2026 · 20 min
Quick answer

A person with diabetes can generally eat a wide variety of foods, but meals should emphasise vegetables, suitable protein sources, fibre-rich foods and sensible portions of carbohydrate-rich foods such as rice, roti, poha, idli and dosa. Whole fruits can usually be included in appropriate portions. Sugary drinks, frequent sweets, refined snacks and heavily processed foods are better kept limited. People taking insulin or medicines that can cause low blood sugar may need individual advice about meal timing and carbohydrate intake. The important point is this: a diabetes diet is not simply a list of foods that are allowed and forbidden. It is a way of organising your everyday meals so that they support blood glucose control and remain realistic enough to follow over the long term.
Getting diagnosed with diabetes can make food feel unnecessarily complicated.
Suddenly, ordinary questions come up at almost every meal.
Can I still eat rice? Is roti better? What about mangoes? Should I stop eating sweets completely? Is poha okay for breakfast? What should I eat if I am also trying to lose weight?
Managing diabetes does not usually require throwing away the way you have always eaten.
For most people, the focus is on how much you eat, how often you eat it, what you combine it with, and how the overall diet fits into your treatment plan.

Indian food can absolutely be part of a diabetes-conscious eating pattern. Rice, roti, dal, vegetables, curd, fruit and many familiar home-cooked dishes can all have a place. The approach simply needs some thought around portions, preparation and balance.
This guide looks at how to make those changes without turning every meal into a complicated calculation.
There is no single meal plan that suits every person with diabetes.

Two people may both have Type 2 diabetes but have very different nutritional needs. One may need to lose weight, another may be underweight. One may exercise regularly, while another may spend most of the day sitting. Medication, insulin use, kidney health, age and other medical conditions can also change dietary requirements.
Still, some basic principles are useful for almost everyone.
A balanced eating pattern generally involves:
This does not mean you need to stop eating Indian food.
In fact, many traditional Indian meals already contain useful foods such as pulses, vegetables, curd, spices, whole grains, nuts and seeds.
The challenge is often the way the meal is put together and the quantity consumed.
One of the easiest ways to think about a meal is to look at the plate rather than individual foods.
Instead of making rice or roti the centre of the meal, try building the meal around vegetables and protein, with a controlled amount of carbohydrate.
A simple structure looks like this:
The exact proportions will vary from person to person.

For example, someone who is physically active may have different requirements from someone who is trying to lose weight. A person with kidney disease may also need dietary adjustments that are not necessary for everyone else.
That is why the plate method is better viewed as a starting framework, rather than a rigid prescription.
A diabetes diagnosis does not suddenly make ordinary Indian foods unhealthy.
What matters is the overall pattern.

Non-starchy vegetables are useful additions to meals because they provide fibre, vitamins, minerals and volume without contributing the same amount of carbohydrate as foods such as rice, bread or potatoes.
You can rotate through foods such as:
The cooking method matters too.
A vegetable dish prepared with a modest amount of oil is very different from a preparation that is heavily fried or made with large amounts of cream, butter or other calorie-dense ingredients.
Dal and pulses are familiar staples in many Indian households and can be useful components of a balanced meal.
Examples include:
These foods provide protein and fibre, although they also contain carbohydrate.
That distinction is worth remembering. Calling dal a "protein food" does not mean it is carbohydrate-free.
A sensible portion alongside vegetables and an appropriate amount of rice or roti can work well for many people.
Protein is an important part of a satisfying meal.
Depending on your food preferences and medical requirements, sources may include:
For someone who also wants to lose weight, including an appropriate protein source may help make meals more filling.
However, more protein is not automatically better for everyone. People with kidney disease, for example, may require specific dietary advice.
Yes.
A diabetes diagnosis does not automatically mean rice has to disappear from your plate.
The more useful questions are:
A large serving of rice with little else in the meal is quite different from a moderate serving accompanied by vegetables, dal and an appropriate protein source.
You also do not need to assume that brown rice can be eaten without limits. Brown rice can contain more fibre than white rice, but it still contributes carbohydrate.
You could try:
Some people find that they can comfortably include rice in their routine. Others may need to reduce the amount or change the way the meal is structured.
There is no universal portion that works for everyone.
This is another question patients ask frequently.
There is no simple rule that says roti is always better than rice.
Roti and rice both contribute carbohydrate. The nutritional value and effect of a meal depend on the type, portion, preparation and what accompanies it.
Whole-wheat roti can be a useful option. But eating several large rotis can still provide a substantial amount of carbohydrate and calories.
Paratha deserves additional attention because the amount of oil or ghee used during preparation can increase its calorie content considerably.
Instead of asking which food is automatically "better," look at the complete meal.
For example:
Roti + vegetable sabzi + dal + curd
may be a very different meal from:
Several large parathas + little vegetable + a sugary drink.
The name of the food alone does not tell the whole story.
Breakfast is often where Indian diets become heavily carbohydrate-based.

Poha, upma, idli, dosa and bread are common choices. These foods do not necessarily need to be eliminated, but the meal can often be improved by paying attention to portion and adding protein or fibre.
Some possible combinations include:
Keep the portion sensible and add vegetables. Pairing it with an appropriate protein source can make the meal more balanced.
Sambar can add pulses and vegetables to the meal. Portion still matters, particularly if several idlis are eaten.
These can be paired with vegetables and unsweetened curd.
For people who eat eggs, an omelette with vegetables can provide protein. It can be paired with a controlled portion of whole-grain toast or roti if appropriate.
Choose an unsweetened preparation rather than turning breakfast into a bowl of oats with sugar, flavoured syrups or sweetened toppings.
The goal is not to find one "perfect diabetic breakfast."
It is to avoid making breakfast almost entirely refined or rapidly digested carbohydrate.
Yes.
Fruit is often unnecessarily restricted after a diabetes diagnosis.

Whole fruits provide carbohydrates, but they also provide fibre, vitamins, minerals and other nutrients. The practical issue is usually portion size and the total amount of carbohydrate being consumed, rather than avoiding fruit altogether.
Depending on your individual diet, fruits such as these can be included:
There is no need to label a fruit as "forbidden" simply because it tastes sweet.
At the same time, fruit is not carbohydrate-free. Eating very large portions can still affect blood glucose.
For most people with diabetes, whole fruit is the more practical choice.

When fruit is turned into juice, it becomes much easier to consume a large amount quickly. A glass may contain the juice of several pieces of fruit without providing the same level of fullness as eating the fruit itself.
Sweetened packaged fruit drinks are an even less suitable everyday choice.
So instead of:
Fruit blender juice
consider simply eating an appropriate portion of whole fruit.
Snacking can quietly add a lot of carbohydrate, fat and calories to the day.
Biscuits with tea, namkeen, chips, bakery snacks and sweets are easy to eat without noticing how much has been consumed.
Depending on your individual needs, alternatives could include:
And remember: not everyone needs snacks between meals.
Some people are perfectly comfortable with three main meals. Others may need snacks depending on their medication, activity, work schedule or other circumstances.

If you are eating because you are genuinely hungry, consider what is driving that hunger. If you are eating simply because snacks are always available, changing the routine may be more useful than searching for a "diabetic snack."
Rather than creating an enormous "foods to avoid" list, it is usually more useful to identify foods that are best kept occasional.
These include:
Liquid calories can add up quickly because they often provide little satiety.
Indian sweets such as:
can contain considerable amounts of sugar and calories.
That does not mean every family celebration has to become stressful.
The bigger issue is making these foods an everyday habit.
Keep foods such as biscuits, cakes, pastries, packaged snacks and other highly refined foods limited.
Regularly eating samosas, pakoras, puris and other deep-fried foods can make weight management more difficult because they can be very energy-dense.
The occasional food is different from a daily routine.
Food is part of family life, celebrations and culture.
Diabetes management should leave room for that reality.
During festivals, rather than thinking:
"I have diabetes, so I cannot eat anything."
a more practical approach may be:
You do not need to "punish" yourself for having a small serving of mithai.
At the same time, a festival should not turn into several days of unrestricted sweets and sugary drinks.
The pattern over time matters.
Two things that can make meals more satisfying are fibre and protein.
Fibre is found in foods such as:
It contributes to digestive health and can help with fullness.
If your current diet is low in fibre, increase it gradually. Adequate fluid intake is also important unless you have been advised to restrict fluids.
Protein contributes to satiety and is important for maintaining body tissues and muscle.
Eggs, fish, chicken, curd, paneer, tofu, dal and beans are examples of foods that can contribute protein.
The amount needed varies from person to person.Again, this is one reason why copying someone else's diabetes meal plan is not always appropriate.
It can, when the eating pattern helps create an appropriate reduction in overall calorie intake while still providing adequate nutrition.
For people who need to lose weight, useful changes may include:
There is no requirement to follow an extreme low-carbohydrate diet or survive on salads.
A diet that produces rapid weight loss but cannot be maintained is unlikely to be a useful long-term solution.
Physical activity is an important part of diabetes management.
For some people, a walk after a meal can be a convenient way to include activity in their daily routine.
However, exercise can affect blood glucose, particularly in people using insulin or certain medicines.
If you experience symptoms such as:
during or after exercise, speak with your healthcare professional. These symptoms can sometimes occur with low blood glucose.
Your exercise routine and medication may need to be considered together.
Sometimes it does.
Different diabetes medicines work differently. Some need to be taken with meals, while insulin regimens can have specific relationships with food and activity.
This is why you should not make major changes to your meal pattern and independently change medication doses or timing.
If you take insulin or a medicine that can cause hypoglycaemia, ask your doctor how your meals, exercise and medication schedule should fit together.
Never change insulin or diabetes medication simply because you have changed your diet unless your treating clinician has advised you to do so.
A meal plan should fit your actual day.
It should account for your work schedule, family meals, food preferences, activity and medical treatment.
Here is a simple framework:
These are examples, not prescribed quantities.
A person's calorie and carbohydrate requirements can vary significantly.
These examples are intended to demonstrate how to structure a meal, not to prescribe an identical diet to every patient.
You do not have to stop eating outside after being diagnosed with diabetes.
A few small decisions can make restaurant meals easier to manage.
Consider:
Also remember that restaurant food may contain considerably more oil, salt and calories than you would use at home.
The occasional restaurant meal is not the problem. Frequency and overall eating habits matter.
Not necessarily.
Rice can be included in a suitable meal plan. The amount and the rest of the meal are important.
Whole fruit can generally be part of a balanced diet. It contains carbohydrate, but it also provides fibre and important nutrients.
The focus should be on appropriate portions rather than eliminating fruit without a medical reason.
Brown rice may have nutritional advantages over refined white rice, but it still contains carbohydrate.
The serving still matters.
No.
A product labelled sugar-free can still contain calories, fat or other sources of carbohydrate.
Look at the complete nutrition information and serving size rather than relying only on the front-of-pack claim.
Not necessarily.
In many Indian households, the same meal can work for everyone.
The differences may simply be in portion sizes, preparation methods and what each person puts on their plate.
Not usually.
A balanced diabetes diet can be built around ordinary foods available in most Indian kitchens.
Vegetables, pulses, curd, eggs, fish, chicken, whole grains, nuts and fruit can all be part of a suitable eating pattern.
General dietary advice is useful, but there are situations where individual guidance becomes particularly important.
Speak with your doctor or qualified dietitian if you have:
Your nutritional needs can also change over time.
A meal plan that suited you two years ago may no longer be appropriate if your weight, medication, activity level or health status has changed.
You do not need to change everything at once.
Start with a few changes that are realistic.
You may not need to remove rice or roti. Start by checking whether the portion is larger than you actually need.
If your plate is mostly rice or roti, add more vegetables before adding another serving of carbohydrate.
Dal, curd, eggs, paneer, tofu, fish, chicken and other suitable foods can make a meal more balanced.
Cutting down on sugary tea, soft drinks and sweetened beverages can be one of the simpler dietary changes.
Choose whole fruit instead of regularly drinking fruit juice.
You do not need to turn every celebration into a restriction exercise, but sweets should not become an everyday habit.
Multigrain, sugar-free and natural are not automatic guarantees that a product is appropriate in unlimited quantities.
If your healthcare professional has asked you to monitor blood glucose, the readings can provide useful information about how your meals are affecting you.
Regular physical activity is an important part of diabetes management when medically appropriate.
Medication changes, weight changes, pregnancy, kidney problems or significant changes in activity can all affect dietary requirements.
A diabetes diet does not have to mean giving up Indian food.
You can often continue eating familiar foods while making sensible changes to portions, cooking methods and meal composition.
Rice does not automatically have to disappear. Roti is not automatically a free food. Fruit does not have to be banned. And you do not need expensive products labelled specifically for diabetes.

Instead, build meals around vegetables, suitable protein, fibre and sensible portions of carbohydrate, while keeping sugary drinks, frequent sweets, refined snacks and heavily processed foods under control.
Most importantly, your diet should work in real life.
It should work when you are eating at home, when your family is having a celebration, when you go to a restaurant and when your daily routine gets busy.

If your blood glucose remains difficult to control despite making reasonable lifestyle changes, the answer may not simply be to make your diet stricter. Your medication, physical activity, weight, sleep and other aspects of diabetes management may also need to be reviewed.
When to seek urgent care
Seek urgent care for vomiting, confusion, unusual drowsiness or symptoms of very high or very low sugar, especially if you take insulin or tablets that can cause low sugar.

faqs.q: Can I lose weight and still eat rice?
faqs.a: Yes, in controlled portions with vegetables and protein.

faqs.q: Are keto or very low carb diets safe with diabetes?
faqs.a: They can be risky with some medicines. Speak to your doctor first.

faqs.q: Is intermittent fasting safe?
faqs.a: It may not be safe with insulin or certain tablets. Get medical advice.

faqs.q: How much weight should I lose?
faqs.a: Even a modest loss helps. Your doctor can set a target.

faqs.q: Do I need to count calories?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Portion control and plate structure work well for many people.

faqs.q: Can I eat fruit?
faqs.a: Yes, in controlled portions, preferably whole fruit.

Diabetes Diet for Indians
Diabetes Diet for Weight Loss: An Indian Plate Guide
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 6 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
Aim for gradual weight loss using portion control, more vegetables and protein, fewer refined carbohydrates and sweets, and regular activity. Avoid crash diets and extreme fasting, especially if you take insulin or sugar-lowering medicines, as these can cause dangerously low sugar.
Weight loss can improve blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol. With diabetes, the way you lose weight matters as much as how much.
Build the plate
Half the plate: vegetables and salad
A quarter: protein such as dal, eggs, fish, paneer or chicken
A quarter: whole grains, millets or a controlled portion of rice or roti
Choices that help
Choose whole grains and millets over refined flour
Add fibre through vegetables, pulses and fruit in portions
Prefer baking, steaming and grilling over deep frying
Limit sweets, sugary drinks and packaged snacks
Eat at regular times and avoid long gaps
Portions and habits
Use a smaller plate
Eat slowly
Avoid eating in front of a screen
Keep healthy snacks like roasted chana or nuts in small amounts
Move more
Brisk walking, strength exercise and an active day support weight loss and sugar control.
Safety with medicines
If you take insulin or tablets that can cause low sugar, discuss diet changes with your doctor first, as doses may need adjusting.
Realistic pace
A steady loss over weeks to months is easier to sustain than rapid loss.
In short
Gradual loss is safest.

Cut refined carbohydrates and sweets.
Adjust medicines with medical advice.
Combine diet with activity.

faqs.q: At what age should I get my sugar tested?
faqs.a: From age 30, or earlier if you have a family history, a large waist, high blood pressure, PCOS, or had diabetes in pregnancy.

faqs.q: Which test is best for checking diabetes?
faqs.a: Fasting blood sugar and HbA1c are the most common. HbA1c shows your average sugar over about three months and does not need fasting. Your doctor may also advise a glucose tolerance test.

faqs.q: Can type 2 diabetes go away?
faqs.a: Some people, especially early in the condition, can bring their sugar back to normal without medicines after significant weight loss. Doctors call this remission, not cure, because sugar can rise again, so regular checks continue.

10 Common Myths About Diabetes, and the Facts
Diabetes
10 Common Myths About Diabetes, and the Facts
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 30 July 2026 · Updated 2 October 2026 · 5 min
In brief
Many people with type 2 diabetes have no symptoms for years, so testing matters even when you feel well.
Normal sugar readings on treatment mean the treatment is working, not that it can be stopped.
Insulin and modern diabetes medicines are tools, not signs of failure or harm.
Diabetes is one of the fastest-growing long-term conditions in India. In our clinic we regularly meet people whose diagnosis or treatment was delayed by something they had heard from a friend, a relative or a forwarded message. Knowing the facts helps you act early and avoid complications.
Diabetes and obesity: myth vs factMyth 1: "no one in my family has diabetes, so i cannot get it."
Fact: Family history raises the risk, but it is only one factor. Age, extra weight around the waist, inactivity, an unhealthy diet, stress, poor sleep and the "Asian Indian phenotype" (more abdominal and liver fat, less muscle) all contribute. Get your blood sugar checked from age 30, or earlier if you have risk factors.
Myth 2: "i have no symptoms, so i don't need a test."
Fact: Many people with type 2 diabetes feel completely well for years. A simple blood test (fasting sugar or HbA1c) can find diabetes long before symptoms or complications appear.
Myth 3: "i avoid sweets and i walk daily, so i don't need medicines."
Fact: Food and activity are the foundation of treatment. But type 2 diabetes involves both insulin resistance and a gradual fall in the body's own insulin, so many people also need medicines to reach their targets. Needing them is not a failure.
Myth 4: "diabetes means i am seriously ill."
Fact: Diabetes is a long-term condition that can be managed well. With good control of sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol, the risk of complications falls considerably.
Myth 5: "my sugar is normal now, so i can stop my medicines."
Fact: Normal readings usually mean the treatment is working. Stopping on your own often lets sugar rise again. Any change should be made by your doctor after reviewing your results.
Myth 6: "diabetes medicines damage the kidneys."
Fact: Uncontrolled diabetes is a leading cause of kidney damage. Medicines are chosen with your kidney function in mind, several of them protect the kidneys and the heart, and your kidney tests are checked regularly so treatment can be adjusted.
Myth 7: "insulin is the last stage of diabetes."
Fact: Insulin is life-saving in type 1 diabetes and is often needed at some point in type 2 diabetes, for example at diagnosis with very high readings, during illness, surgery or pregnancy. Starting insulin when it is needed is a step towards better control.
Myth 8: "i can stop my blood pressure and cholesterol medicines once sugar is controlled."
Fact: Diabetes care means looking after sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol together. Controlling all three lowers the risk of heart attack, stroke and kidney disease.
Myth 9: "i should stop my medicines when i am fasting or travelling."
Fact: Treatment should be adjusted, not stopped. Talk to your doctor at least two weeks before a planned fast or a long trip, and check your sugar more often during it.
Myth 10: "diabetes will spoil my child's marriage or career."
Fact: People with well-controlled diabetes study, work in almost every profession, marry and have healthy families.
Take-home messages
Get tested regularly if you are at risk, even if you feel well.
Eat a balanced diet, stay active and aim for a healthy waist size.
Take medicines exactly as prescribed, and never stop them on your own.
Check your sugar as advised and keep your follow-up visits.
Control blood pressure and cholesterol as well as sugar.
Trust your doctor over social media.
Frequently asked questions
At what age should I get my sugar tested?
From age 30, or earlier if you have a family history, a large waist, high blood pressure, PCOS, or had diabetes in pregnancy.
Which test is best for checking diabetes?
Fasting blood sugar and HbA1c are the most common. HbA1c shows your average sugar over about three months and does not need fasting. Your doctor may also advise a glucose tolerance test.
Can type 2 diabetes go away?
Some people, especially early in the condition, can bring their sugar back to normal without medicines after significant weight loss. Doctors call this remission, not cure, because sugar can rise again, so regular checks continue.

Fact: Insulin is life-saving in type 1 diabetes and is often needed at some point in type 2 diabetes, for example at diagnosis with very high readings, during illness, surgery or pregnancy. Starting insulin when it is needed is a step towards better control.
Fact: Diabetes care means looking after sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol together. Controlling all three lowers the risk of heart attack, stroke and kidney disease.
Fact: Treatment should be adjusted, not stopped. Talk to your doctor at least two weeks before a planned fast or a long trip, and check your sugar more often during it.
Fact: People with well-controlled diabetes study, work in almost every profession, marry and have healthy families.

Do GLP-1 Medicines Replace Metformin or Insulin?
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 14 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
In most cases GLP-1 medicines are added to metformin rather than replacing it. They may allow some people to reduce insulin doses, and a few may be able to stop insulin, but this depends on the person and must be decided by the doctor. Never stop metformin or insulin on your own.
GLP-1 medicines have changed diabetes care, but they do not simply swap out every older treatment.
How they fit with metformin
Metformin lowers sugar by reducing liver glucose output and improving insulin response. GLP-1 medicines work differently, so together they often give better control and may help weight.
How they fit with insulin
Some people on insulin add a GLP-1 medicine to improve control and reduce insulin needs
Insulin may be reduced gradually, with monitoring
People who need insulin because their own production is very low, such as type 1 diabetes, still need it
When changes might be made
Weight loss and improved sugar may lower medicine needs
Risk of low sugar may require dose reductions
Kidney or stomach issues may affect choices
Why doctors do not stop medicines casually
Stopping metformin or insulin too quickly can cause high sugar or ketones. Adjustments are made step by step with monitoring.
What you should do
Take medicines exactly as prescribed
Report nausea, vomiting, low sugar symptoms or stomach pain
Keep regular follow-up
Monitor sugar as advised
The quick version
GLP-1 medicines are usually added, not swapped.
Insulin doses may be reduced in some.
Never stop medicines on your own.
Monitoring guides changes.
Treatment is individual.
Newer medicines add options, but they work alongside good habits and monitoring. For guidance, you can consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
When to seek urgent care
Stop the medicine and seek urgent care for severe or persistent vomiting, severe upper stomach pain spreading to the back, fainting, or symptoms of very low sugar.
Sources and further reading
NIDDK: Prescription medicines for overweight and obesity
WHO: Diabetes fact sheet
Frequently asked questions
Can I stop metformin once I start a GLP-1 medicine?
Usually not. Your doctor decides.
Will I still need insulin?
Some people reduce or stop insulin, others still need it.
Are GLP-1 medicines safer than insulin?
They are different. Each has benefits and risks.
Can GLP-1 medicines be used in type 1 diabetes?
They are generally not a replacement for insulin in type 1 diabetes.
What if I get nausea?
Tell your doctor. Dose changes or eating habits can help.
How quickly do doses change?
Gradually, based on your readings.

faqs.a: It gives more information, but both are useful.

faqs.q: Can I use CGM for a short period?
faqs.a: Yes. Some people use it for a couple of weeks to learn patterns.

faqs.q: Does CGM replace HbA1c?
faqs.a: No. HbA1c is still used for long-term control.

faqs.q: Is it painful?
faqs.a: Most people feel only a brief sensation when applying the sensor.

faqs.q: Is CGM covered by insurance?
faqs.a: Coverage varies. Check with your insurer.

faqs.q: Can CGM help me lose weight?
faqs.a: It can show how foods affect sugar, but it is not a weight loss tool on its own.

Does Everyone With Type 2 Diabetes Need a CGM?
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 17 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
No. CGM is most useful for people on insulin, those with frequent low sugar, unpredictable readings or pregnancy, and anyone who needs detailed information to adjust treatment. Many people with stable type 2 diabetes on tablets do well with regular fingerstick checks and HbA1c. Your doctor can advise whether a CGM would help you.
A continuous glucose monitor (CGM) tracks sugar levels through the day and night using a small sensor worn on the body. It is a powerful tool, but not every person needs one.
Who benefits most
People on multiple daily insulin injections
Those with frequent or unnoticed low sugar
Pregnancy with diabetes
Unexplained swings in readings
People who want to understand how food and activity affect sugar, with medical guidance
Who may manage without
Stable type 2 diabetes on tablets with good HbA1c
Those who prefer simple monitoring
People for whom cost is a barrier
What a CGM shows
Trends through the day and night
Time spent in target range
Alerts for high and low sugar
Limits to know
Readings may lag slightly behind blood glucose
Sensors cost money and need replacing
Data needs interpretation, and more numbers can cause anxiety in some people
Fingerstick checks may still be needed
Getting value from a CGM
Review reports with your doctor
Focus on patterns, not single readings
Use it to guide meals, activity and medicines
A quick recap
CGM is helpful but not essential for everyone.
Insulin users benefit most.
Many stable patients manage with fingersticks.
Data needs interpretation.
Discuss with your doctor.
The best monitoring method is one that fits your treatment and lifestyle. For advice, you can consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
When to seek urgent care
Seek urgent care if a sensor or meter shows very high or very low readings with symptoms such as vomiting, confusion, unusual drowsiness, sweating, shaking or fainting.
Sources and further reading
NIDDK: Continuous glucose monitoring
WHO: Diabetes fact sheet
Frequently asked questions
Is CGM better than a glucometer?
It gives more information, but both are useful.
Can I use CGM for a short period?
Yes. Some people use it for a couple of weeks to learn patterns.
Does CGM replace HbA1c?
No. HbA1c is still used for long-term control.
Is it painful?
Most people feel only a brief sensation when applying the sensor.
Is CGM covered by insurance?
Coverage varies. Check with your insurer.
Can CGM help me lose weight?
It can show how foods affect sugar, but it is not a weight loss tool on its own.

faqs.q: Does gestational diabetes go away after delivery?
faqs.a: In most women, yes. Sugar levels return to normal within days after the placenta is delivered. But the risk of type 2 diabetes remains higher, and testing after birth is essential.

faqs.q: When should I get tested after delivery?
faqs.a: Get a glucose tolerance test 6 to 12 weeks after delivery. Then test every 1 to 3 years, or as your doctor advises.

faqs.q: Can I breastfeed with gestational diabetes?
faqs.a: Yes. Breastfeeding is encouraged. It benefits the baby and may help the mother's sugar metabolism and weight loss.

faqs.q: Will I get diabetes later if I had gestational diabetes?
faqs.a: Your risk is higher than average. Many women do not develop diabetes, especially with healthy weight, regular activity and good diet. Regular testing catches problems early.

Does Gestational Diabetes Go Away After Delivery?
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 18 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
In most women, gestational diabetes goes away within hours to days after delivery, once the placenta, which makes insulin-blocking hormones, is gone. However, some women continue to have high sugar, and all women who had it have a higher lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes. A blood sugar test at 6 to 12 weeks after delivery, and regular testing afterwards, are essential.
After months of watching your diet, checking sugars and attending visits, the big question is whether it ends with the birth. The short answer is that, for most women, blood sugar returns to normal soon after delivery. But the story does not end there.
Why does it usually settle?
During pregnancy, the placenta makes hormones that make the body more resistant to insulin. If the pancreas cannot make enough extra insulin to compensate, sugars rise. After delivery, these hormones drop quickly, and insulin sensitivity improves. Sugar levels in most women return to normal within days.
What happens in the first days after birth?
If you took insulin or tablets in pregnancy, they are usually stopped right after delivery.
Your sugar is checked in hospital, often fasting on the first day or two.
If sugars remain very high, you may have had diabetes before pregnancy, and treatment continues.
Your baby's sugar is also monitored, since babies of mothers with gestational diabetes can have low sugar after birth.
When should you be tested again?
6 to 12 weeks after delivery: A 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is recommended to see if diabetes or prediabetes persists. Fasting sugar and HbA1c may also be done, though OGTT is preferred in many guidelines.
Every 1 to 3 years: For life, even if the first test is normal, because the risk of type 2 diabetes remains elevated.
Before the next pregnancy: To check your sugar and plan.
How high is the risk of Type 2 diabetes?
Women who have had gestational diabetes have a much higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes later, with studies suggesting a risk several times greater than other women. In India, where the baseline risk is already high, this is especially important. The risk is highest in those who needed insulin, had high sugars early in pregnancy, were overweight or have a family history.
How can you lower your risk?
Return to a healthy weight gradually after delivery.
Follow a balanced diet with limited sweets and refined foods.
Exercise at least 150 minutes a week.
Breastfeed if possible, as it may help improve sugar metabolism.
Do not smoke.
Get sleep when you can.
Attend follow-up tests.
Discuss medicines such as metformin with your doctor if your risk is very high.
What about future pregnancies?
Gestational diabetes tends to recur in later pregnancies. Plan early testing and monitor sugars. Entering the next pregnancy at a healthy weight lowers the chance.
What about your baby?
Children of mothers with gestational diabetes may have a higher risk of obesity and diabetes later in life. Breastfeeding, a healthy diet and an active lifestyle for the child help.
When should you see a doctor?
See your doctor if after delivery you have excessive thirst, frequent urination, tiredness, blurred vision or repeated infections. Do not wait for the 6 to 12 week visit if you have symptoms.
A quick recap
Gestational diabetes usually resolves soon after delivery.
Test for diabetes 6 to 12 weeks after birth.
Lifelong screening every 1 to 3 years is needed.
Healthy weight, activity and breastfeeding lower your risk.
Plan for future pregnancies with early testing.
Your pregnancy gave you an early warning. Use it to protect your health for years to come. For a follow-up plan, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
Sources and further reading
WHO: Diabetes fact sheet
NIDDK: Gestational diabetes
Frequently asked questions
Does gestational diabetes go away after delivery?
In most women, yes. Sugar levels return to normal within days after the placenta is delivered. But the risk of type 2 diabetes remains higher, and testing after birth is essential.
When should I get tested after delivery?
Get a glucose tolerance test 6 to 12 weeks after delivery. Then test every 1 to 3 years, or as your doctor advises.
Can I breastfeed with gestational diabetes?
Yes. Breastfeeding is encouraged. It benefits the baby and may help the mother's sugar metabolism and weight loss.
Will I get diabetes later if I had gestational diabetes?
Your risk is higher than average. Many women do not develop diabetes, especially with healthy weight, regular activity and good diet. Regular testing catches problems early.
Do I need medicines after delivery?
Usually not. Insulin and tablets used during pregnancy are stopped. If sugars remain high, your doctor will decide on treatment.
Will gestational diabetes come back in my next pregnancy?
It can. The chance is higher if you gained weight or needed insulin before. Early testing and a healthy lifestyle before and during pregnancy help.

faqs.q: What is a dual agonist?
faqs.a: It is a medicine that activates two hormone receptors. Tirzepatide, for example, activates both GLP-1 and GIP receptors, which helps lower blood sugar and body weight.

faqs.q: What is a triple agonist?
faqs.a: A triple agonist activates three receptors, usually GLP-1, GIP and glucagon. Retatrutide is an example under study. Trials are ongoing, and it may not be approved in all countries.

faqs.q: Is tirzepatide better than semaglutide?
faqs.a: In several studies, tirzepatide produced greater average weight loss and HbA1c reduction than semaglutide. Individual response and tolerance differ, so your doctor will choose what suits you.

faqs.q: Are triple agonists available in India?
faqs.a: Availability depends on regulatory approval, which can change. Ask your doctor for current information, and never buy unapproved versions online.

faqs.q: Are newer GLP-1 medicines safer?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Newer medicines may have stronger effects, but long-term safety data take time. Approved medicines have established safety information.

faqs.q: What comes after triple agonists?
faqs.a: Researchers are studying combinations with amylin, longer-acting monthly injections, oral small molecules and drugs that protect muscle. These are still being tested.

Dual and Triple Agonists: What Comes After Semaglutide?
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 9 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
An agonist is a medicine that activates a receptor. Semaglutide is a single agonist that activates the GLP-1 receptor. Tirzepatide is a dual agonist acting on GLP-1 and GIP receptors. Triple agonists add a third target, usually glucagon. Early studies suggest bigger weight and metabolic effects, but long-term safety and availability are still being studied, and some are not approved.
Semaglutide changed how doctors treat diabetes and obesity. Tirzepatide then raised the bar. Now researchers are exploring medicines that act on even more hormones. Understanding the terms helps you follow the news without confusion.
What are the gut hormones involved?
GLP-1
Increases insulin release when sugar is high, lowers glucagon, slows stomach emptying and reduces appetite.
GIP
Another gut hormone that boosts insulin release after meals and may help with fat metabolism and appetite regulation.
Glucagon
Raises blood sugar in the fasting state but also increases energy use and fat burning in the liver. In combination with GLP-1, it may increase weight loss.
What is a dual agonist?
A dual agonist activates two receptors. Tirzepatide activates GLP-1 and GIP. In trials, it lowered blood sugar and weight more than semaglutide in several comparisons. Other dual agonists, such as GLP-1 and glucagon combinations, are being tested.
What is a triple agonist?
A triple agonist activates GLP-1, GIP and glucagon receptors. Retatrutide is one example in clinical trials. Early studies reported large average weight loss, along with improvements in fatty liver and other markers. However, these are trial results, and the drug is not yet approved for general use at the time of writing in most places. Check current status before making decisions.
What other approaches are being studied?
Amylin combinations, which add to the feeling of fullness
Once-monthly injections
Oral small-molecule GLP-1 medicines
Medicines that preserve muscle while reducing fat
Combination treatments with other weight-loss medicines
Why does targeting more hormones help?
Obesity and diabetes involve many signals from the gut, fat tissue, liver and brain. Medicines that act on several pathways can have broader effects on appetite, insulin release and energy use. However, more targets can also mean more side effects, and careful long-term studies are needed.
What are the possible concerns?
Stomach side effects such as nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea
Faster heart rate in some studies
Potential loss of muscle along with fat
Unknown long-term safety for newer agents
High cost when first launched
Misinformation and unregulated "research" products sold online
Do not buy unapproved products from the internet. They may be fake, unsafe or wrongly dosed.
What should patients do now?
Rely on approved medicines prescribed by your doctor.
Ask your doctor about new treatments as they are approved.
Stay informed using reliable sources.
Remember that diet, exercise and sleep stay important whatever the medicine.
When should you see a doctor?
Talk to a diabetologist if you are interested in the latest treatments, have not reached your targets with current medicines, or have side effects.
A quick recap
Semaglutide is a single agonist, tirzepatide a dual agonist, and triple agonists are in development.
Targeting more hormones may give greater benefits but needs long-term safety data.
Many new medicines are still being studied and are not available everywhere.
Never buy unapproved injectables online.
Medical guidance is essential.
The science is moving quickly, which is exciting. But the best treatment for you is the one that is approved, safe and suited to your health. To discuss current options, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.

NIDDK: Prescription medicines for overweight and obesity
WHO: Diabetes fact sheet
Frequently asked questions
What is a dual agonist?
It is a medicine that activates two hormone receptors. Tirzepatide, for example, activates both GLP-1 and GIP receptors, which helps lower blood sugar and body weight.
What is a triple agonist?
A triple agonist activates three receptors, usually GLP-1, GIP and glucagon. Retatrutide is an example under study. Trials are ongoing, and it may not be approved in all countries.
Is tirzepatide better than semaglutide?
In several studies, tirzepatide produced greater average weight loss and HbA1c reduction than semaglutide. Individual response and tolerance differ, so your doctor will choose what suits you.
Are triple agonists available in India?
Availability depends on regulatory approval, which can change. Ask your doctor for current information, and never buy unapproved versions online.
Are newer GLP-1 medicines safer?
Not necessarily. Newer medicines may have stronger effects, but long-term safety data take time. Approved medicines have established safety information.
What comes after triple agonists?
Researchers are studying combinations with amylin, longer-acting monthly injections, oral small molecules and drugs that protect muscle. These are still being tested.

faqs.q: Why do people with diabetes get fatty liver?
faqs.a: Insulin resistance and belly fat cause the liver to store fat. High sugar and triglycerides add to it. Fatty liver then makes diabetes harder to control.

faqs.q: Can fatty liver be reversed?
faqs.a: Early fatty liver can improve or disappear with weight loss, healthy eating, exercise and good diabetes control. Scarring is harder to reverse, so early action is important.

faqs.q: Is fatty liver dangerous?
faqs.a: It can be. Over time, it may lead to inflammation, scarring and cirrhosis. It also raises the risk of heart disease. Early treatment reduces these risks.

faqs.q: Which test checks for liver scarring in fatty liver?
faqs.a: FIB-4 score and FibroScan are commonly used. Ultrasound shows fat but not scarring. Your doctor will advise the right test.

faqs.q: Which diabetes medicines help fatty liver?
faqs.a: GLP-1 medicines and pioglitazone may reduce liver fat, and SGLT2 inhibitors may help modestly. The choice depends on your overall health and goals.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol with fatty liver and diabetes?
faqs.a: It is best to avoid alcohol or keep it minimal. Alcohol can worsen liver injury and affect blood sugar. Ask your doctor for personal advice.

Fatty Liver and Diabetes: Why They Occur Together
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 21 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
Fatty liver, now called metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), is a build-up of fat in the liver. It is very common in type 2 diabetes because both are driven by insulin resistance and excess belly fat. Left untreated, it can progress to inflammation, scarring (cirrhosis) and liver cancer. Weight loss, healthy food, activity and certain diabetes medicines can reduce it.
Many people with diabetes are told, often by chance on an ultrasound, that they have a fatty liver. It is easy to dismiss because it causes no symptoms. But fatty liver and diabetes feed each other, and ignoring it can lead to serious liver and heart problems.
What is fatty liver?
When fat makes up more than about 5 percent of the liver's weight, it is called fatty liver. Alcohol can cause it, but most fatty liver in people with diabetes is linked to metabolic causes, not alcohol. The newer term MASLD reflects this link to metabolic health. A more advanced form with inflammation is called MASH.
What are the symptoms?
Most people have no symptoms. Some feel tired or have discomfort in the upper right abdomen. Signs of advanced disease include yellow eyes, swelling of the legs or belly, easy bruising and confusion.
How is it detected?
Ultrasound: The most common test. It shows a bright liver but cannot show scarring.
Liver enzymes (SGPT/ALT, SGOT/AST): May be normal even when fatty liver exists.
FIB-4 score: A simple calculation using age, enzymes and platelet count that estimates the risk of scarring.
FibroScan (elastography): Measures liver stiffness and fat. It is useful for detecting scarring.
Blood tests: Cholesterol, triglycerides, HbA1c and others.
Liver biopsy: Rarely needed.
The 2026 diabetes guidance recommends that people with type 2 diabetes be screened for liver scarring risk, regardless of liver enzymes.
What does fatty liver lead to?
Liver inflammation (MASH)
Scarring (fibrosis) and cirrhosis
Liver failure and liver cancer in advanced stages
Increased risk of heart attack and stroke
Higher risk of kidney disease
In fact, heart disease is the commonest cause of death in people with fatty liver and diabetes.
How is it treated?
Lose weight
Losing 5 percent of body weight reduces liver fat. Losing 7 to 10 percent can reduce inflammation, and 10 percent or more may improve scarring.
Eat for your liver
Reduce sugar, sweet drinks, refined flour and fried food.
Eat more vegetables, pulses, fruits, nuts and whole grains.
Choose healthy fats such as olive, mustard or groundnut oil in moderation.
Limit or avoid alcohol.
Exercise
Aerobic activity and strength training both reduce liver fat, even without much weight loss. Aim for 150 minutes a week.
Medicines
Some diabetes medicines help the liver. GLP-1 medicines and pioglitazone may reduce liver fat and inflammation, and SGLT2 inhibitors may give modest benefits. Newer medicines for MASH are available in some countries. Your doctor will choose what suits you.
Control other risks
Manage blood pressure, cholesterol and sleep apnoea.
Surgery
Metabolic surgery can improve fatty liver in people with severe obesity.
When should you see a doctor?
See your doctor if your ultrasound shows fatty liver, your liver enzymes are high, you have diabetes and have never had a liver check, or you notice yellow eyes, swelling or black stools.
What to remember
Fatty liver is very common in type 2 diabetes.
Both are driven by insulin resistance and belly fat.
Most people have no symptoms, so screening matters.
Weight loss, diet, exercise and selected medicines help.
Untreated, it can progress to scarring and increase heart risk.
A fatty liver is a warning that can be reversed in its early stages. Acting now protects your liver, heart and kidneys. To get screened and plan treatment, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
Sources and further reading
NHLBI: Metabolic syndrome
NIDDK: Insulin resistance and prediabetes
Frequently asked questions
Why do people with diabetes get fatty liver?
Insulin resistance and belly fat cause the liver to store fat. High sugar and triglycerides add to it. Fatty liver then makes diabetes harder to control.
Can fatty liver be reversed?
Early fatty liver can improve or disappear with weight loss, healthy eating, exercise and good diabetes control. Scarring is harder to reverse, so early action is important.
Is fatty liver dangerous?
It can be. Over time, it may lead to inflammation, scarring and cirrhosis. It also raises the risk of heart disease. Early treatment reduces these risks.
Which test checks for liver scarring in fatty liver?
FIB-4 score and FibroScan are commonly used. Ultrasound shows fat but not scarring. Your doctor will advise the right test.
Which diabetes medicines help fatty liver?
GLP-1 medicines and pioglitazone may reduce liver fat, and SGLT2 inhibitors may help modestly. The choice depends on your overall health and goals.
Can I drink alcohol with fatty liver and diabetes?
It is best to avoid alcohol or keep it minimal. Alcohol can worsen liver injury and affect blood sugar. Ask your doctor for personal advice.
