faqs.q: What are the very first signs of type 2 diabetes?
faqs.a: Early signs often include increased thirst, frequent urination, tiredness and blurred vision. Some people notice slow-healing cuts or frequent infections. Many people have no symptoms, so testing is important if you have risk factors.

faqs.q: Can you have type 2 diabetes without symptoms?
faqs.a: Yes. Many people have no noticeable symptoms for years. Regular screening with fasting glucose or HbA1c helps detect diabetes early, especially for those with family history, excess weight or high blood pressure.

faqs.q: At what age should I get tested for diabetes?
faqs.a: Many guidelines suggest screening adults from around 35 years, or earlier for those with risk factors such as family history, obesity, PCOS or high blood pressure. Indians often develop diabetes earlier, so earlier testing is reasonable.

faqs.q: Which blood test is best for diagnosing diabetes?
faqs.a: Fasting glucose, HbA1c and the oral glucose tolerance test are all used. Each has strengths, and doctors often use more than one or repeat a test to confirm the diagnosis.

faqs.q: Are dark patches on the neck a sign of diabetes?
faqs.a: Dark, velvety patches in the neck or armpits, called acanthosis nigricans, often indicate insulin resistance. They are not diabetes themselves but are a reason to check blood sugar.

First Signs of Type 2 Diabetes You Should Not Ignore
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 2 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
Early signs of type 2 diabetes include increased thirst, frequent urination, tiredness, blurred vision, slow-healing cuts, frequent infections, tingling in the feet and unexplained weight changes. Many people have no symptoms at all, so adults with risk factors should get tested with fasting glucose or HbA1c even if they feel well.
Type 2 diabetes is a long-term condition in which blood sugar stays high because the body does not respond well to insulin and gradually makes less of it. It often develops slowly, and many people have no clear symptoms for years. Knowing the early signs helps you get tested and treated sooner.
What are the common early signs?
Increased thirst and frequent urination
High blood sugar draws water out of the body through urine, leading to more frequent urination, including at night, and constant thirst.
Tiredness
Cells cannot use glucose efficiently, leaving many people feeling tired or low on energy.
Blurred vision
Changing sugar levels can affect the eye's lens and cause blurred vision that comes and goes.
Slow-healing wounds and frequent infections
High sugar affects circulation and immunity, so cuts heal slowly and infections such as skin, gum, urinary or genital yeast infections become more common.
Tingling or numbness
Some people notice tingling, burning or numbness in the feet or hands, an early sign of nerve involvement.
Weight changes and hunger
Some people lose weight without trying or feel hungrier than usual.
Dark skin patches
Dark, velvety skin in the neck folds or armpits, called acanthosis nigricans, can signal insulin resistance.
Why do many people have no symptoms?
Blood sugar often rises gradually, and the body adjusts. People may notice symptoms only when sugar is quite high or complications begin. This is why screening matters.
Who should get tested?
Adults over about 30 to 35, especially with family history
People with overweight or obesity, particularly around the waist
People with high blood pressure or abnormal cholesterol
Women with previous gestational diabetes or PCOS
People with prediabetes
Those with an inactive lifestyle
South Asians, including Indians, tend to develop diabetes at a younger age and lower body weight, so earlier screening is often advised.
Which tests confirm diabetes?
Fasting plasma glucose
HbA1c, which reflects average sugar over about three months
Oral glucose tolerance test
Your doctor interprets results and often repeats a test to confirm.
When should you see a doctor?
See a doctor if you have any of the signs above or risk factors, even if you feel well. Seek urgent care for extreme thirst, vomiting, confusion, deep rapid breathing or drowsiness, which may indicate very high sugar levels.
A quick recap
Type 2 diabetes often develops silently.
Thirst, frequent urination and tiredness are common early signs.
Slow healing and frequent infections can be clues.
People with risk factors should get tested.
Simple blood tests confirm the diagnosis.
Early detection gives you the best chance to control diabetes and prevent complications. If you notice symptoms or have risk factors, a simple test can provide clarity. Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur, diagnoses and treats type 2 diabetes.
Sources and further reading
WHO: Diabetes fact sheet
NIDDK: What is diabetes
Frequently asked questions
What are the very first signs of type 2 diabetes?
Early signs often include increased thirst, frequent urination, tiredness and blurred vision. Some people notice slow-healing cuts or frequent infections. Many people have no symptoms, so testing is important if you have risk factors.
Can you have type 2 diabetes without symptoms?
Yes. Many people have no noticeable symptoms for years. Regular screening with fasting glucose or HbA1c helps detect diabetes early, especially for those with family history, excess weight or high blood pressure.
At what age should I get tested for diabetes?
Many guidelines suggest screening adults from around 35 years, or earlier for those with risk factors such as family history, obesity, PCOS or high blood pressure. Indians often develop diabetes earlier, so earlier testing is reasonable.
Which blood test is best for diagnosing diabetes?
Fasting glucose, HbA1c and the oral glucose tolerance test are all used. Each has strengths, and doctors often use more than one or repeat a test to confirm the diagnosis.
Are dark patches on the neck a sign of diabetes?
Dark, velvety patches in the neck or armpits, called acanthosis nigricans, often indicate insulin resistance. They are not diabetes themselves but are a reason to check blood sugar.

Fruits for Diabetes: Which, How Much and When
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 7 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
People with diabetes can eat most fruits in moderate portions, usually one small to medium fruit or about one cup of chopped fruit at a time. Good choices include guava, apple, pear, orange, papaya, berries and jamun. Eat fruit whole rather than as juice, pair it with protein or nuts, and limit very sweet fruits such as mango, chikoo and grapes to small portions.
A common myth is that people with diabetes must avoid fruit. In reality, whole fruits provide fibre, vitamins and antioxidants and can be part of a healthy diabetes diet. The key is choosing suitable fruits, controlling portions and timing them sensibly.
Why is whole fruit better than juice?
Whole fruit contains fibre that slows sugar absorption and keeps you full. Juice removes fibre and concentrates sugar, raising blood sugar quickly. Even fresh juice without added sugar is best avoided or limited.
Which fruits are good choices?
Lower to moderate impact fruits
Guava
Apple
Pear
Orange and sweet lime
Papaya
Berries such as strawberries
Jamun
Peach and plum
Fruits to eat in smaller portions
Mango
Banana, especially ripe
Chikoo (sapota)
Grapes
Custard apple
Pineapple
These are not forbidden but contain more sugar per portion.
Dried fruits
Raisins, dates and figs are concentrated sources of sugar. Small amounts may fit occasionally, but portions should be very small.
How much fruit is right?
Most people do well with one portion at a time and two to three portions a day, depending on their overall diet and sugar control. A portion is roughly one small apple, one orange, one guava or about a cup of papaya. Your doctor or dietitian can personalise this.
When is the best time to eat fruit?
As a mid-morning or evening snack
With a source of protein or healthy fat, such as a few nuts or curd
Not as a large dessert straight after a heavy carbohydrate meal
Avoid eating several fruits at once
Do fruit myths matter?
Fruit does not need to be eaten only on an empty stomach, and no single fruit cures diabetes. Balance and portion size matter most.
How can you check your response?
Checking blood sugar about two hours after eating fruit helps you understand how your body responds to different fruits.
A quick recap
People with diabetes can eat fruit.
Choose whole fruits over juice.
Guava, apple, orange, papaya and berries are good choices.
Limit very sweet fruits and dried fruits.
Pair fruit with protein or nuts and control portions.
Fruit can be a healthy, enjoyable part of a diabetes diet when chosen and portioned wisely. Personal monitoring helps you find what works for you. Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur guides patients on practical diabetes nutrition.
When to seek urgent care
Seek urgent care for vomiting, confusion, unusual drowsiness or symptoms of very high or very low sugar, especially if you take insulin or tablets that can cause low sugar.
Sources and further reading
WHO: Healthy diet
NIDDK: Diabetes diet, eating and physical activity
Frequently asked questions
Which fruits are best for diabetes?
Guava, apple, pear, orange, papaya, berries and jamun are good choices because they have fibre and a moderate effect on blood sugar. Portion size is still important.
Can diabetics eat mango?
Mango can be eaten occasionally in a small portion, such as a few slices, ideally with protein or nuts and not after a heavy meal. Monitor your sugar to see how you respond.
Is fruit juice okay for diabetes?
Fruit juice raises blood sugar quickly because it lacks fibre and concentrates sugar. Whole fruit is a much better choice. Limit or avoid juices.
How many fruits can a diabetic eat per day?
Many people do well with two to three portions spread through the day. Your doctor or dietitian can personalise this based on your diet and sugar control.
Can diabetics eat dates and dry fruits?
Dried fruits like dates and raisins are high in concentrated sugar. Very small portions may be eaten occasionally, but nuts such as almonds and walnuts are better daily snack choices.

faqs.q: What can I eat for breakfast with gestational diabetes?
faqs.a: Choose protein-rich options such as moong dal cheela, besan chilla, vegetable upma, eggs with whole-wheat toast or idli with sambar. Keep carbohydrate portions small, since morning sugars can be higher.

faqs.q: Can I eat rice with gestational diabetes?
faqs.a: Yes, in a small portion, such as half to one cup cooked, with dal, vegetables and protein. Brown rice or millets may be better. Check your sugar readings to see your response.

faqs.q: Which fruits are safe with gestational diabetes?
faqs.a: Guava, apple, papaya, pear, berries and orange in small portions, taken with nuts or curd. Avoid juices, and limit mango, grapes, banana and chikoo.

faqs.q: Is milk allowed in gestational diabetes?
faqs.a: Yes. Milk is a good source of calcium and protein. Have it without sugar, and count it as part of your carbohydrate intake. A glass at bedtime can help prevent night-time dips.

faqs.q: How many meals should I eat?
faqs.a: Three main meals and two to three snacks, spaced 2 to 3 hours apart, usually work well. Do not skip meals.

faqs.q: Can diet alone control gestational diabetes?

Gestational Diabetes Diet: Indian Foods and Meal Timing
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 19 October 2026 · 5 min read
Quick answer
A gestational diabetes diet includes three small meals and two to three snacks, with controlled portions of carbohydrates, plenty of vegetables, protein at each meal and healthy fats. Choose whole grains and pulses, limit sweets and refined foods, avoid fruit juices, and walk after meals. Do not skip meals or follow extreme diets. Ask your dietitian for a personal plan.
Food is the most powerful tool for controlling gestational diabetes. You do not need to give up Indian food. You need to adjust portions, balance your plate and space meals through the day.
What are the goals?
Keep sugars within your target range
Provide enough nutrition and calories for you and the baby
Prevent ketones, which can form if you skip meals or eat too little carbohydrate
Achieve healthy pregnancy weight gain
How should you build your plate?
Half the plate: Non-starchy vegetables such as spinach, gourd, beans, cabbage, cauliflower, tomatoes and salad.
One quarter: Protein such as dal, sprouts, paneer, eggs, fish, chicken, curd or tofu.
One quarter: Carbohydrates, preferably whole grains such as roti, jowar, bajra, ragi, brown rice or millets.
Add a small amount of healthy fat such as nuts, seeds or a teaspoon of ghee or oil.
What is a sample meal pattern?
Early morning
A glass of milk with no sugar, or a few soaked almonds.
Breakfast
Vegetable besan chilla, moong dal cheela, vegetable upma with extra vegetables, idli with sambar or whole-wheat toast with egg. Avoid white bread with jam, poha without vegetables and sweet cereals.
Mid-morning snack
A small fruit portion (such as guava or apple) with a few nuts, or roasted chana.
Lunch
One or two rotis or a small cup of cooked rice, dal, a large serving of vegetables, salad and curd.
Evening snack
Sprouts chaat, buttermilk, makhana or a handful of nuts.
Dinner
Similar to lunch but lighter: vegetable soup, roti with sabzi and dal or paneer.
Bedtime snack
A glass of milk or a small portion of curd with nuts. This prevents long overnight fasting.
Which foods should you limit?
Sweets, mithai, cakes and biscuits
Sugary drinks, packaged juices and soft drinks
White rice, maida products and large portions of potatoes
Fried snacks and fast food
Dry fruits in large amounts
Overripe or very sweet fruits like mango, grapes and banana in large portions
Fruit is allowed in measured portions. Eat it with protein or nuts, and not as juice.
What about timing?
Eat every 2 to 3 hours.
Do not skip breakfast.
Many women have higher sugars in the morning, so breakfast may need a lower carbohydrate portion.
Take a 10 to 15 minute walk after meals.
Space the last meal at least two hours before sleep.
How do you monitor?
Check your sugar fasting and one or two hours after meals, as your doctor advises. Targets are usually fasting below 95 mg/dL, one hour below 140 mg/dL and two hours below 120 mg/dL. Your doctor may set different targets. Keep a diary of foods and readings to identify which items raise your sugar.
Do you need supplements?
Continue prenatal vitamins, iron, calcium and folic acid as advised. Ask your doctor before starting any herbal or "sugar-control" products.
When should you see a doctor?
Contact your doctor if your readings are repeatedly above target, you feel very hungry or weak, you have ketones in the urine, you vomit often or you have reduced baby movements.
The quick version
Eat three meals and two to three snacks with balanced portions.
Fill half your plate with vegetables, add protein, and limit refined carbohydrates.
Avoid sweets, sugary drinks and juices.
Walk after meals and avoid skipping meals.
Monitor your sugar and review the diary with your doctor.
You can enjoy home food and still keep sugars steady. Small changes add up to a healthy pregnancy. For a personalised plan, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
Sources and further reading
WHO: Diabetes fact sheet
NIDDK: Gestational diabetes
Frequently asked questions
What can I eat for breakfast with gestational diabetes?
Choose protein-rich options such as moong dal cheela, besan chilla, vegetable upma, eggs with whole-wheat toast or idli with sambar. Keep carbohydrate portions small, since morning sugars can be higher.
Can I eat rice with gestational diabetes?
Yes, in a small portion, such as half to one cup cooked, with dal, vegetables and protein. Brown rice or millets may be better. Check your sugar readings to see your response.
Which fruits are safe with gestational diabetes?
Guava, apple, papaya, pear, berries and orange in small portions, taken with nuts or curd. Avoid juices, and limit mango, grapes, banana and chikoo.
Is milk allowed in gestational diabetes?
Yes. Milk is a good source of calcium and protein. Have it without sugar, and count it as part of your carbohydrate intake. A glass at bedtime can help prevent night-time dips.
How many meals should I eat?
Three main meals and two to three snacks, spaced 2 to 3 hours apart, usually work well. Do not skip meals.
Can diet alone control gestational diabetes?
For many women, yes, along with activity. If sugars stay above target despite good diet, your doctor may add insulin or medicines.

faqs.q: What blood sugar level is high in gestational diabetes?
faqs.a: Common treatment targets during pregnancy are fasting glucose below 95 mg/dL, 1-hour post-meal glucose below 140 mg/dL and 2-hour post-meal glucose below 120 mg/dL. These are treatment targets, not the same thresholds used to diagnose GDM. Your doctor may individualize the targets depending on your pregnancy and treatment.

faqs.q: When is the gestational diabetes test done?
faqs.a: GDM screening is commonly performed between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy. Women with previous GDM or other diabetes risk factors may be tested earlier. If an early test is normal, another test later in pregnancy may still be recommended.

faqs.q: Can gestational diabetes be controlled without insulin?
faqs.a: Yes, some women can keep their blood glucose within the desired range through appropriate nutrition, physical activity and regular monitoring. If glucose remains above target despite these measures, medication or insulin may be recommended.

faqs.q: Is insulin safe during pregnancy?
faqs.a: Insulin has an established role in treating diabetes during pregnancy and may be recommended when blood glucose cannot be controlled adequately through lifestyle measures. The type and dose need to be determined by the treating clinician. Insulin should not be started or changed without medical guidance.

faqs.q: Does gestational diabetes go away after delivery?
faqs.a: Blood glucose often improves after delivery because pregnancy-related insulin resistance falls once the placenta is delivered. However, women with previous GDM remain at increased risk of future Type 2 diabetes. That is why postpartum testing and continued screening are recommended.

faqs.q: When should I test for diabetes after gestational diabetes?
faqs.a: A 75-g oral glucose tolerance test is generally recommended around 4 to 12 weeks after delivery. If the result is normal, ongoing diabetes screening is still recommended at regular intervals because a history of GDM increases future Type 2 diabetes risk.

faqs.q: Can I eat rice if I have gestational diabetes?
faqs.a: Rice can often be included in a GDM meal plan. Portion size, the type of rice, what you eat with it and your individual glucose response all matter. A balanced meal containing vegetables, protein and an appropriate carbohydrate portion may be easier to manage than a large serving of rice alone.

faqs.q: Can gestational diabetes affect the baby?
faqs.a: Poorly controlled maternal blood glucose can increase the risk of excessive fetal growth and some complications after birth, including neonatal hypoglycaemia. This is why glucose monitoring, appropriate nutrition and antenatal assessment are important parts of GDM care.

Gestational Diabetes (GDM): Testing, Blood Sugar Targets, Diet, Insulin & After-Pregnancy Care
Gestational Diabetes
Gestational Diabetes (GDM): Testing, Blood Sugar Targets, Diet, Insulin & After-Pregnancy Care
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 18 October 2026 · Approximately 14 to 16 minutes
Quick answer
Gestational diabetes is diagnosed through blood glucose testing during pregnancy, even when there are no symptoms. Screening is commonly performed around 24 to 28 weeks, although women with certain risk factors may be tested earlier. Once GDM is diagnosed, treatment usually involves a combination of nutrition changes, pregnancy-appropriate physical activity and home blood glucose monitoring. Common treatment targets are fasting glucose below 95 mg/dL, 1-hour after meals below 140 mg/dL, or 2-hours after meals below 120 mg/dL. If glucose remains above the recommended range despite lifestyle measures, insulin may be required. After delivery, blood sugar often falls toward normal, but follow-up should not stop there. A postpartum diabetes test is recommended because a history of GDM increases the risk of developing Type 2 diabetes later in life.
Gestational diabetes mellitus, usually called GDM, is diabetes first diagnosed during pregnancy. It develops when the body cannot produce enough insulin to keep blood glucose at the desired level as pregnancy increases insulin resistance.
One of the frustrating things about GDM is that there may be no obvious warning signs. A woman can feel completely well and still have elevated blood sugar. That is why glucose testing during pregnancy is so important.
For many women, treatment starts with changes to food choices, meal portions and physical activity, along with regular blood sugar checks. Some will need medication or insulin as pregnancy progresses.
A diagnosis of GDM does not automatically mean that a woman will have diabetes for the rest of her life. Blood sugar often improves after delivery. There is, however, an important follow-up step: women who have had gestational diabetes have a higher future risk of Type 2 diabetes and should continue to be screened after pregnancy.
What is gestational diabetes?
Gestational diabetes is a form of high blood glucose that is first recognized during pregnancy.
During pregnancy, the placenta produces hormones that help support the baby's growth. Those same hormonal changes can make the mother's cells less responsive to insulin. This is known as insulin resistance.
The pancreas normally compensates by making more insulin. If it cannot keep up with the increased demand, glucose starts to build up in the bloodstream.
That is how GDM can develop in someone who did not have diabetes before becoming pregnant.
It is worth making a distinction here. Diabetes diagnosed early in pregnancy may sometimes represent previously undiagnosed Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes rather than typical gestational diabetes. This is one reason doctors pay attention to both the timing and the results of glucose testing.
What are the symptoms of gestational diabetes?
Most women with GDM do not notice any specific symptoms.
In some cases, high blood sugar can be associated with increased thirst, frequent urination, tiredness or blurred vision. The problem is that several of these symptoms can also occur during an otherwise normal pregnancy.
So symptoms alone cannot tell you whether you have gestational diabetes.
A blood glucose test is much more reliable than waiting for symptoms to appear.
When is gestational diabetes testing done?
GDM screening is commonly carried out during the second half of pregnancy.
For many women, testing takes place between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy. Earlier testing may be recommended when there is a higher risk of diabetes, such as a previous history of GDM or other metabolic risk factors.
If an early test is normal, the doctor may still recommend repeat testing later in pregnancy because insulin resistance can increase as pregnancy progresses.
This is especially relevant for women who have previously experienced gestational diabetes.
How is gestational diabetes diagnosed?
There is not just one testing method used worldwide. Different guidelines and healthcare systems use different approaches.
The oral glucose tolerance test
The oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) looks at how the body handles a measured amount of glucose.
With a commonly used 75-g OGTT, blood glucose may be measured while fasting and again after the glucose drink.
Under the one-step criteria commonly used internationally, GDM can be diagnosed when one or more of the following values meets the specified threshold:
Measurement
Threshold
Fasting glucose
92 mg/dL
1-hour glucose
180 mg/dL
2-hour glucose
153 mg/dL
The exact testing protocol used by your doctor may differ.
The DIPSI test used in India
The Diabetes in Pregnancy Study Group India (DIPSI) approach has also been used widely in India.
A woman receives 75 g of oral glucose and has her blood glucose checked two hours later. The test can be performed irrespective of when she last ate.
A 2-hour plasma glucose level of 140 mg/dL or higher is used as the diagnostic threshold in this approach.
Because different diagnostic systems use different thresholds and procedures, test results should always be interpreted according to the method that was actually used.
What are the blood sugar targets in gestational diabetes?
Once GDM has been diagnosed, monitoring generally focuses on fasting and after-meal blood glucose.
Common pregnancy targets are:
Blood glucose check
Common target
Fasting
Below 95 mg/dL
1 hour after a meal
Below 140 mg/dL
2 hours after a meal
Below 120 mg/dL
These are treatment targets rather than diagnostic criteria.
That distinction matters.
The number used to diagnose gestational diabetes is not necessarily the same number your doctor will use when monitoring treatment.
The aim is also not to drive glucose as low as possible. Pregnancy requires a careful balance between controlling high blood sugar and avoiding hypoglycaemia, particularly when insulin is being used.
Your doctor may also set an individualized monitoring schedule depending on your glucose pattern and treatment.
How do you check blood sugar at home during pregnancy?
Most women who need regular monitoring use a blood glucose meter.
Depending on the treatment plan, you may be asked to check:
Your fasting glucose in the morning
Glucose after breakfast
Glucose after lunch
Glucose after dinner
Additional readings when specifically advised
Try to record the readings consistently.
It can also be useful to note what you ate, when you ate, whether you exercised and when medication or insulin was taken. Over several days, this gives your doctor something more useful than a collection of isolated numbers.
For example, consistently high fasting readings suggest a different pattern from glucose that rises mainly after a particular meal.
Some pregnant women may also use continuous glucose monitoring (CGM). Whether this is useful depends on the type of diabetes, treatment and individual circumstances.
What should you eat if you have gestational diabetes?
A diagnosis of GDM does not mean you have to stop eating carbohydrates or follow an extremely restrictive diet.
Pregnancy still requires adequate nutrition.
The practical goal is to choose suitable carbohydrate sources, pay attention to portions and spread food intake appropriately throughout the day.
A balanced meal may include:
Vegetables
Protein-rich foods
Whole grains or other suitable carbohydrate sources
Pulses and legumes
Appropriate portions of fruit
Healthy fats
Suitable dairy foods
Adequate fluids
Carbohydrates have the most direct effect on blood glucose, so the quantity and timing of carbohydrate-containing foods are particularly relevant.
The ideal plan is not identical for every pregnant woman.
Calorie and nutritional requirements, weight, activity level, glucose readings, food preferences and the stage of pregnancy all need to be considered.
Can Indian foods be included in a gestational diabetes diet?
Yes.
Having GDM does not mean giving up familiar Indian meals.
The way a meal is put together often matters as much as the individual food itself. Portion size, carbohydrate quantity and the combination of vegetables and protein can all influence the post-meal glucose response.
For example, meals may include:
Roti with vegetables and a protein source
Dal with vegetables and an appropriate portion of rice
Paneer with vegetables and a suitable carbohydrate portion
Eggs with vegetables and whole-grain options
Unsweetened curd where appropriate
The important point is not to label individual foods as simply "good" or "bad."
A dietitian or diabetes clinician can help adapt your existing eating pattern instead of forcing you into a completely unfamiliar diet.
Which foods should be limited with gestational diabetes?
Foods and drinks containing a large amount of added sugar or rapidly absorbed carbohydrates can make blood glucose harder to control.
Examples include:
Sugary soft drinks
Sweetened beverages
Fruit juices
Mithai and other sweets
Cakes and pastries
Large portions of refined carbohydrates
Highly processed snack foods
That does not mean every carbohydrate-containing food needs to be removed.
Even nutritious foods can raise glucose when eaten in large quantities. Portion size and the overall meal pattern remain important.
Fruit is a good example. Whole fruit can often be included in a pregnancy diet, while fruit juice is much easier to consume quickly and contains less of the fibre found in whole fruit.
Can you eat rice during gestational diabetes?
Rice does not automatically have to be removed from the diet.
The more useful questions are how much rice you are eating, what type you are choosing and what you eat alongside it.
A moderate portion of rice served with vegetables, dal and an appropriate protein source is quite different from a large serving of rice eaten by itself.
Your own post-meal glucose readings can provide useful information about how your body responds.
The same idea applies to foods such as roti, poha, upma, idli and bread.
Rather than creating a long list of foods that are completely forbidden, the focus should be on portions, meal composition and individual response.
Does exercise help with gestational diabetes?
For women who have no medical reason to restrict activity, appropriate physical activity can be a useful part of GDM management.
Exercise can improve insulin sensitivity and may help reduce blood glucose, particularly after meals.
Walking is one simple option for many pregnant women. Other forms of pregnancy-appropriate exercise may also be suitable.
However, pregnancy is not the time to start an aggressive exercise programme without medical advice.
Women with bleeding, placenta-related complications, risk of premature labour or other pregnancy concerns should discuss physical activity with their obstetrician before exercising.
When is insulin needed for gestational diabetes?
Insulin may be recommended when blood glucose continues to exceed the desired pregnancy targets despite appropriate nutrition and physical activity.
This is an important point because some women feel that needing insulin means they have somehow failed to manage their diabetes.
It does not.
Pregnancy itself causes increasing insulin resistance. As pregnancy progresses, the body's insulin requirements can change considerably. In some women, lifestyle measures simply are not enough to overcome this physiological change.
Insulin may then be the safest way to bring glucose into the desired range.
Is insulin safe during pregnancy?
Insulin has a well-established role in the management of diabetes during pregnancy.
The type of insulin, timing and dose depend on the individual's glucose pattern and treatment plan.
Do not change an insulin dose yourself, even if a particular reading seems unusually high or low. Discuss the pattern with your treating doctor.
Does needing insulin mean the GDM is severe?
Not necessarily.
The need for insulin mainly tells us that the current glucose levels are not being controlled adequately with the measures already being used.
Some women need insulin for part or all of pregnancy and no longer require it once pregnancy-related insulin resistance falls after delivery.
Can metformin be used for gestational diabetes?
Metformin is used in some treatment pathways for GDM.
Its role varies between guidelines and clinical situations. In some cases, it may be considered when diet and physical activity do not achieve the desired glucose levels. In other situations, insulin may be preferred.
Metformin also crosses the placenta, so its use during pregnancy should be discussed carefully with the treating healthcare professional.
This is not a medicine to start or stop based on online information.
Your obstetrician or diabetes specialist can consider your glucose readings, gestational age, medical history and other pregnancy-related factors before choosing treatment.
What happens if gestational diabetes is not controlled?
Persistently high blood glucose during pregnancy can increase the risk of complications.
These can include:
Excessive fetal growth
Difficult delivery
Shoulder dystocia
High blood pressure or preeclampsia
Increased likelihood of induction or caesarean delivery in some situations
Low blood glucose in the newborn after birth
Other newborn complications
Having GDM does not mean these complications will definitely occur.
The purpose of monitoring and treatment is to reduce avoidable risks while keeping both mother and baby well.
Can gestational diabetes affect the baby?
It can.
Glucose crosses the placenta from the mother to the fetus. When maternal blood glucose remains high, the fetus can receive more glucose and respond by producing more insulin.
This can contribute to increased fetal growth.
After delivery, the mother's glucose supply stops suddenly, but the baby's insulin level may remain relatively high for a period. This is one reason newborns of mothers with diabetes may be monitored for low blood glucose.
Your maternity team may also monitor fetal growth and wellbeing throughout pregnancy depending on your individual circumstances.
Does gestational diabetes mean you need a caesarean section?
No.
A diagnosis of GDM does not automatically mean that a caesarean delivery will be necessary.
Delivery planning takes several factors into account, including:
Fetal growth
Glucose control
Blood pressure
Gestational age
Estimated fetal weight
Previous pregnancy history
Other maternal or fetal concerns
Whether medication or insulin is required
Your obstetrician will consider these factors together when discussing delivery.
What happens to blood sugar after delivery?
The hormonal changes of pregnancy begin to reverse after the placenta is delivered.
As a result, insulin resistance generally falls quickly. A woman who needed insulin during pregnancy may therefore require much less treatment, or may no longer need insulin.
That decision should still be made by the treating medical team.
For many women with GDM, blood glucose returns toward the normal range after delivery.
But there is another step that should not be overlooked: postpartum diabetes testing.
When should you test for diabetes after gestational diabetes?
The postpartum period provides an opportunity to find out whether blood glucose has returned to normal.
The American Diabetes Association recommends a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test 4 to 12 weeks after delivery for women with recent GDM.
Some Indian care pathways use a postpartum assessment around six weeks after delivery.
The exact timing should follow the plan given by your healthcare team.
Why is this test necessary?
Because the fact that blood sugar improves after pregnancy does not guarantee that glucose metabolism has completely returned to normal.
The postpartum test can identify:
Normal glucose regulation
Prediabetes
Diabetes
Finding prediabetes or diabetes early allows appropriate treatment and prevention strategies to begin.
Does gestational diabetes increase the risk of Type 2 diabetes?
Yes.
Women who have had GDM have a higher risk of developing Type 2 diabetes later compared with women who did not have GDM.
This does not mean that Type 2 diabetes is inevitable.
It does mean that regular screening is worth taking seriously.
The ADA recommends ongoing screening every 1 to 3 years after a history of GDM, depending on the individual's risk and previous test results.
Long-term care may include:
Regular diabetes screening
Regular physical activity
A balanced eating pattern
Maintaining a healthy weight where appropriate
Blood pressure monitoring
Cholesterol management
Planning ahead for future pregnancies
Can gestational diabetes happen again in another pregnancy?
Yes, it can.
A previous history of GDM is itself a risk factor for GDM in a future pregnancy.
If you have had gestational diabetes before, tell your obstetrician at the beginning of your next pregnancy.
Your doctor may recommend glucose testing earlier than usual. Even if that early test is normal, repeat testing later in pregnancy may still be needed.
This is one area where knowing your previous pregnancy history can make a real difference to antenatal planning.
Is breastfeeding beneficial after gestational diabetes?
Breastfeeding is generally encouraged when medically appropriate.
For women with a history of GDM, breastfeeding may also be associated with a lower future risk of Type 2 diabetes.
The postpartum period can be demanding, though. Nutrition should support recovery and milk production rather than being built around rapid weight loss.
If diabetes medication is required after delivery, the doctor should also consider whether the mother is breastfeeding when choosing treatment.
Common myths about gestational diabetes
"GDM happens because a woman eats too much sugar."
Not necessarily.
Pregnancy-related hormonal changes and increasing insulin resistance play a major role. Food choices are important for managing glucose, but GDM cannot simply be blamed on eating sugar.
"I have to stop eating carbohydrates completely."
No.
Carbohydrates remain an important source of energy during pregnancy. The focus is usually on choosing appropriate sources, controlling portions and spreading carbohydrate intake sensibly across meals.
"If i need insulin, i have failed."
Absolutely not.
Some women require insulin because their body's insulin requirements increase substantially during pregnancy. This can happen despite careful attention to diet and activity.
"GDM disappears after delivery, so i don't need another diabetes test."
This is a common misunderstanding.
Blood glucose often improves after delivery, but the future risk of Type 2 diabetes remains higher. Postpartum testing and continued screening are therefore important.
"Having GDM means my baby will definitely be very large."
Not necessarily.
Fetal growth depends on many factors. Good glucose management, appropriate antenatal care and monitoring can help the medical team identify concerns early.
When should you contact your doctor?
If your blood glucose readings are repeatedly above the targets given to you, contact your healthcare team rather than trying to adjust treatment yourself.
You should also seek urgent medical attention for serious symptoms such as:
Loss of consciousness
Severe confusion
Seizures
Severe weakness
Persistent vomiting with significant dehydration
Difficulty breathing
Chest pain
Severe hypoglycaemia
Sudden neurological symptoms
Pregnancy-specific warning signs also need prompt assessment. These include significant vaginal bleeding, severe abdominal pain or noticeably reduced fetal movement.
In short
Gestational diabetes is high blood glucose first recognized during pregnancy.
Many women have no obvious symptoms, making screening particularly important.
GDM testing is commonly performed around 24 to 28 weeks, with earlier assessment for women at higher risk.
Different diagnostic criteria are used around the world, so results should be interpreted according to the test method used.
Common treatment targets are fasting below 95 mg/dL, 1-hour post-meal below 140 mg/dL and 2-hour post-meal below 120 mg/dL.
Nutrition and pregnancy-appropriate activity form the foundation of management for many women.
Insulin may be necessary when glucose remains above target.
GDM does not automatically mean that a caesarean delivery is required.
Blood glucose often improves after childbirth, but postpartum testing remains important.
A history of GDM increases future Type 2 diabetes risk, making regular screening worthwhile.
Gestational diabetes can feel overwhelming when the diagnosis first appears on a pregnancy report. In practice, management is usually much more structured than it may initially seem.
The first step is understanding the diagnosis and knowing which glucose numbers your healthcare team wants you to aim for. From there, food choices, activity, home monitoring and treatment can be adjusted according to how your blood sugar behaves.
There may also be changes later in pregnancy. A woman who manages her GDM with lifestyle measures early on may eventually need insulin as insulin resistance increases. That is not a sign that she has done something wrong. It is simply one of the ways pregnancy can affect glucose metabolism.
And care should not stop at delivery.
The postpartum diabetes test and long-term screening are important because GDM can be an early warning sign of future metabolic problems. Taking that follow-up seriously gives women an opportunity to monitor their health well beyond pregnancy.
When to seek urgent care
In pregnancy, seek urgent care for vomiting, reduced fetal movements, severe headache, blurred vision, or symptoms of very high or very low sugar.

Frequently asked questions
What blood sugar level is high in gestational diabetes?
Common treatment targets during pregnancy are fasting glucose below 95 mg/dL, 1-hour post-meal glucose below 140 mg/dL and 2-hour post-meal glucose below 120 mg/dL. These are treatment targets, not the same thresholds used to diagnose GDM. Your doctor may individualize the targets depending on your pregnancy and treatment.
When is the gestational diabetes test done?
GDM screening is commonly performed between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy. Women with previous GDM or other diabetes risk factors may be tested earlier. If an early test is normal, another test later in pregnancy may still be recommended.
Can gestational diabetes be controlled without insulin?
Yes, some women can keep their blood glucose within the desired range through appropriate nutrition, physical activity and regular monitoring. If glucose remains above target despite these measures, medication or insulin may be recommended.
Is insulin safe during pregnancy?
Insulin has an established role in treating diabetes during pregnancy and may be recommended when blood glucose cannot be controlled adequately through lifestyle measures. The type and dose need to be determined by the treating clinician. Insulin should not be started or changed without medical guidance.
Does gestational diabetes go away after delivery?
Blood glucose often improves after delivery because pregnancy-related insulin resistance falls once the placenta is delivered. However, women with previous GDM remain at increased risk of future Type 2 diabetes. That is why postpartum testing and continued screening are recommended.
When should I test for diabetes after gestational diabetes?
A 75-g oral glucose tolerance test is generally recommended around 4 to 12 weeks after delivery. If the result is normal, ongoing diabetes screening is still recommended at regular intervals because a history of GDM increases future Type 2 diabetes risk.
Can I eat rice if I have gestational diabetes?
Rice can often be included in a GDM meal plan. Portion size, the type of rice, what you eat with it and your individual glucose response all matter. A balanced meal containing vegetables, protein and an appropriate carbohydrate portion may be easier to manage than a large serving of rice alone.
Can gestational diabetes affect the baby?
Poorly controlled maternal blood glucose can increase the risk of excessive fetal growth and some complications after birth, including neonatal hypoglycaemia. This is why glucose monitoring, appropriate nutrition and antenatal assessment are important parts of GDM care.

Gestational diabetes mellitus, usually called GDM, is diabetes first diagnosed during pregnancy. It develops when the body cannot produce enough insulin to keep blood glucose at the desired level as pregnancy increases insulin resistance.

One of the frustrating things about GDM is that there may be no obvious warning signs. A woman can feel completely well and still have elevated blood sugar. That is why glucose testing during pregnancy is so important.

For many women, treatment starts with changes to food choices, meal portions and physical activity, along with regular blood sugar checks. Some will need medication or insulin as pregnancy progresses.

A diagnosis of GDM does not automatically mean that a woman will have diabetes for the rest of her life. Blood sugar often improves after delivery. There is, however, an important follow-up step: women who have had gestational diabetes have a higher future risk of Type 2 diabetes and should continue to be screened after pregnancy.
Gestational diabetes is a form of high blood glucose that is first recognized during pregnancy.

During pregnancy, the placenta produces hormones that help support the baby's growth. Those same hormonal changes can make the mother's cells less responsive to insulin. This is known as insulin resistance.
The pancreas normally compensates by making more insulin. If it cannot keep up with the increased demand, glucose starts to build up in the bloodstream.
That is how GDM can develop in someone who did not have diabetes before becoming pregnant.

It is worth making a distinction here. Diabetes diagnosed early in pregnancy may sometimes represent previously undiagnosed Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes rather than typical gestational diabetes. This is one reason doctors pay attention to both the timing and the results of glucose testing.
Most women with GDM do not notice any specific symptoms.

In some cases, high blood sugar can be associated with increased thirst, frequent urination, tiredness or blurred vision. The problem is that several of these symptoms can also occur during an otherwise normal pregnancy.
So symptoms alone cannot tell you whether you have gestational diabetes.
A blood glucose test is much more reliable than waiting for symptoms to appear.
GDM screening is commonly carried out during the second half of pregnancy.

This is especially relevant for women who have previously experienced gestational diabetes.

Rice can often be included in a GDM meal plan. Portion size, the type of rice, what you eat with it and your individual glucose response all matter. A balanced meal containing vegetables, protein and an appropriate carbohydrate portion may be easier to manage than a large serving of rice alone.

Poorly controlled maternal blood glucose can increase the risk of excessive fetal growth and some complications after birth, including neonatal hypoglycaemia. This is why glucose monitoring, appropriate nutrition and antenatal assessment are important parts of GDM care.

pOnly: Gestational Diabetes
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
MD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 18 October 2026 · Approximately 14 to 16 minutes
Quick answer

Gestational diabetes is diagnosed through blood glucose testing during pregnancy, even when there are no symptoms. Screening is commonly performed around 24 to 28 weeks, although women with certain risk factors may be tested earlier. Once GDM is diagnosed, treatment usually involves a combination of nutrition changes, pregnancy-appropriate physical activity and home blood glucose monitoring. Common treatment targets are fasting glucose below 95 mg/dL, 1-hour after meals below 140 mg/dL, or 2-hours after meals below 120 mg/dL. If glucose remains above the recommended range despite lifestyle measures, insulin may be required. After delivery, blood sugar often falls toward normal, but follow-up should not stop there. A postpartum diabetes test is recommended because a history of GDM increases the risk of developing Type 2 diabetes later in life.

Gestational diabetes mellitus, usually called GDM, is diabetes first diagnosed during pregnancy. It develops when the body cannot produce enough insulin to keep blood glucose at the desired level as pregnancy increases insulin resistance.

One of the frustrating things about GDM is that there may be no obvious warning signs. A woman can feel completely well and still have elevated blood sugar. That is why glucose testing during pregnancy is so important.

For many women, treatment starts with changes to food choices, meal portions and physical activity, along with regular blood sugar checks. Some will need medication or insulin as pregnancy progresses.

A diagnosis of GDM does not automatically mean that a woman will have diabetes for the rest of her life. Blood sugar often improves after delivery. There is, however, an important follow-up step: women who have had gestational diabetes have a higher future risk of Type 2 diabetes and should continue to be screened after pregnancy.
Gestational diabetes is a form of high blood glucose that is first recognized during pregnancy.

During pregnancy, the placenta produces hormones that help support the baby's growth. Those same hormonal changes can make the mother's cells less responsive to insulin. This is known as insulin resistance.
The pancreas normally compensates by making more insulin. If it cannot keep up with the increased demand, glucose starts to build up in the bloodstream.
That is how GDM can develop in someone who did not have diabetes before becoming pregnant.

It is worth making a distinction here. Diabetes diagnosed early in pregnancy may sometimes represent previously undiagnosed Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes rather than typical gestational diabetes. This is one reason doctors pay attention to both the timing and the results of glucose testing.
Most women with GDM do not notice any specific symptoms.

In some cases, high blood sugar can be associated with increased thirst, frequent urination, tiredness or blurred vision. The problem is that several of these symptoms can also occur during an otherwise normal pregnancy.
So symptoms alone cannot tell you whether you have gestational diabetes.
A blood glucose test is much more reliable than waiting for symptoms to appear.
GDM screening is commonly carried out during the second half of pregnancy.

For many women, testing takes place between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy. Earlier testing may be recommended when there is a higher risk of diabetes, such as a previous history of GDM or other metabolic risk factors.
If an early test is normal, the doctor may still recommend repeat testing later in pregnancy because insulin resistance can increase as pregnancy progresses.
This is especially relevant for women who have previously experienced gestational diabetes.
There is not just one testing method used worldwide. Different guidelines and healthcare systems use different approaches.
The oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) looks at how the body handles a measured amount of glucose.
With a commonly used 75-g OGTT, blood glucose may be measured while fasting and again after the glucose drink.
Under the one-step criteria commonly used internationally, GDM can be diagnosed when one or more of the following values meets the specified threshold:
The exact testing protocol used by your doctor may differ.
The Diabetes in Pregnancy Study Group India (DIPSI) approach has also been used widely in India.
A woman receives 75 g of oral glucose and has her blood glucose checked two hours later. The test can be performed irrespective of when she last ate.
A 2-hour plasma glucose level of 140 mg/dL or higher is used as the diagnostic threshold in this approach.
Because different diagnostic systems use different thresholds and procedures, test results should always be interpreted according to the method that was actually used.
Once GDM has been diagnosed, monitoring generally focuses on fasting and after-meal blood glucose.
Common pregnancy targets are:
These are treatment targets rather than diagnostic criteria.
That distinction matters.
The number used to diagnose gestational diabetes is not necessarily the same number your doctor will use when monitoring treatment.
The aim is also not to drive glucose as low as possible. Pregnancy requires a careful balance between controlling high blood sugar and avoiding hypoglycaemia, particularly when insulin is being used.
Your doctor may also set an individualized monitoring schedule depending on your glucose pattern and treatment.
Most women who need regular monitoring use a blood glucose meter.
Depending on the treatment plan, you may be asked to check:
Try to record the readings consistently.

It can also be useful to note what you ate, when you ate, whether you exercised and when medication or insulin was taken. Over several days, this gives your doctor something more useful than a collection of isolated numbers.
For example, consistently high fasting readings suggest a different pattern from glucose that rises mainly after a particular meal.
Some pregnant women may also use continuous glucose monitoring (CGM). Whether this is useful depends on the type of diabetes, treatment and individual circumstances.
A diagnosis of GDM does not mean you have to stop eating carbohydrates or follow an extremely restrictive diet.
Pregnancy still requires adequate nutrition.
The practical goal is to choose suitable carbohydrate sources, pay attention to portions and spread food intake appropriately throughout the day.
A balanced meal may include:
Carbohydrates have the most direct effect on blood glucose, so the quantity and timing of carbohydrate-containing foods are particularly relevant.
The ideal plan is not identical for every pregnant woman.
Calorie and nutritional requirements, weight, activity level, glucose readings, food preferences and the stage of pregnancy all need to be considered.
Yes.
Having GDM does not mean giving up familiar Indian meals.

The way a meal is put together often matters as much as the individual food itself. Portion size, carbohydrate quantity and the combination of vegetables and protein can all influence the post-meal glucose response.
For example, meals may include:
The important point is not to label individual foods as simply "good" or "bad."
A dietitian or diabetes clinician can help adapt your existing eating pattern instead of forcing you into a completely unfamiliar diet.
Foods and drinks containing a large amount of added sugar or rapidly absorbed carbohydrates can make blood glucose harder to control.
Examples include:
That does not mean every carbohydrate-containing food needs to be removed.
Even nutritious foods can raise glucose when eaten in large quantities. Portion size and the overall meal pattern remain important.
Fruit is a good example. Whole fruit can often be included in a pregnancy diet, while fruit juice is much easier to consume quickly and contains less of the fibre found in whole fruit.
Rice does not automatically have to be removed from the diet.
The more useful questions are how much rice you are eating, what type you are choosing and what you eat alongside it.
A moderate portion of rice served with vegetables, dal and an appropriate protein source is quite different from a large serving of rice eaten by itself.
Your own post-meal glucose readings can provide useful information about how your body responds.
The same idea applies to foods such as roti, poha, upma, idli and bread.
Rather than creating a long list of foods that are completely forbidden, the focus should be on portions, meal composition and individual response.
For women who have no medical reason to restrict activity, appropriate physical activity can be a useful part of GDM management.
Exercise can improve insulin sensitivity and may help reduce blood glucose, particularly after meals.
Walking is one simple option for many pregnant women. Other forms of pregnancy-appropriate exercise may also be suitable.
However, pregnancy is not the time to start an aggressive exercise programme without medical advice.
Women with bleeding, placenta-related complications, risk of premature labour or other pregnancy concerns should discuss physical activity with their obstetrician before exercising.
Insulin may be recommended when blood glucose continues to exceed the desired pregnancy targets despite appropriate nutrition and physical activity.
This is an important point because some women feel that needing insulin means they have somehow failed to manage their diabetes.
It does not.

Pregnancy itself causes increasing insulin resistance. As pregnancy progresses, the body's insulin requirements can change considerably. In some women, lifestyle measures simply are not enough to overcome this physiological change.
Insulin may then be the safest way to bring glucose into the desired range.
Insulin has a well-established role in the management of diabetes during pregnancy.
The type of insulin, timing and dose depend on the individual's glucose pattern and treatment plan.
Do not change an insulin dose yourself, even if a particular reading seems unusually high or low. Discuss the pattern with your treating doctor.
Not necessarily.
The need for insulin mainly tells us that the current glucose levels are not being controlled adequately with the measures already being used.
Some women need insulin for part or all of pregnancy and no longer require it once pregnancy-related insulin resistance falls after delivery.
Metformin is used in some treatment pathways for GDM.

Its role varies between guidelines and clinical situations. In some cases, it may be considered when diet and physical activity do not achieve the desired glucose levels. In other situations, insulin may be preferred.
Metformin also crosses the placenta, so its use during pregnancy should be discussed carefully with the treating healthcare professional.
This is not a medicine to start or stop based on online information.
Your obstetrician or diabetes specialist can consider your glucose readings, gestational age, medical history and other pregnancy-related factors before choosing treatment.
Persistently high blood glucose during pregnancy can increase the risk of complications.
These can include:
Having GDM does not mean these complications will definitely occur.
The purpose of monitoring and treatment is to reduce avoidable risks while keeping both mother and baby well.
It can.
Glucose crosses the placenta from the mother to the fetus. When maternal blood glucose remains high, the fetus can receive more glucose and respond by producing more insulin.
This can contribute to increased fetal growth.

After delivery, the mother's glucose supply stops suddenly, but the baby's insulin level may remain relatively high for a period. This is one reason newborns of mothers with diabetes may be monitored for low blood glucose.
Your maternity team may also monitor fetal growth and wellbeing throughout pregnancy depending on your individual circumstances.
No.
A diagnosis of GDM does not automatically mean that a caesarean delivery will be necessary.
Delivery planning takes several factors into account, including:
Your obstetrician will consider these factors together when discussing delivery.
The hormonal changes of pregnancy begin to reverse after the placenta is delivered.
As a result, insulin resistance generally falls quickly. A woman who needed insulin during pregnancy may therefore require much less treatment, or may no longer need insulin.
That decision should still be made by the treating medical team.
For many women with GDM, blood glucose returns toward the normal range after delivery.
But there is another step that should not be overlooked: postpartum diabetes testing.
The postpartum period provides an opportunity to find out whether blood glucose has returned to normal.
The American Diabetes Association recommends a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test 4 to 12 weeks after delivery for women with recent GDM.
Some Indian care pathways use a postpartum assessment around six weeks after delivery.
The exact timing should follow the plan given by your healthcare team.
Why is this test necessary?
Because the fact that blood sugar improves after pregnancy does not guarantee that glucose metabolism has completely returned to normal.
The postpartum test can identify:
Finding prediabetes or diabetes early allows appropriate treatment and prevention strategies to begin.
Yes.
Women who have had GDM have a higher risk of developing Type 2 diabetes later compared with women who did not have GDM.
This does not mean that Type 2 diabetes is inevitable.
It does mean that regular screening is worth taking seriously.
The ADA recommends ongoing screening every 1 to 3 years after a history of GDM, depending on the individual's risk and previous test results.
Long-term care may include:
Yes, it can.
A previous history of GDM is itself a risk factor for GDM in a future pregnancy.
If you have had gestational diabetes before, tell your obstetrician at the beginning of your next pregnancy.
Your doctor may recommend glucose testing earlier than usual. Even if that early test is normal, repeat testing later in pregnancy may still be needed.
This is one area where knowing your previous pregnancy history can make a real difference to antenatal planning.
Breastfeeding is generally encouraged when medically appropriate.
For women with a history of GDM, breastfeeding may also be associated with a lower future risk of Type 2 diabetes.
The postpartum period can be demanding, though. Nutrition should support recovery and milk production rather than being built around rapid weight loss.
If diabetes medication is required after delivery, the doctor should also consider whether the mother is breastfeeding when choosing treatment.
Not necessarily.
Pregnancy-related hormonal changes and increasing insulin resistance play a major role. Food choices are important for managing glucose, but GDM cannot simply be blamed on eating sugar.
No.

Carbohydrates remain an important source of energy during pregnancy. The focus is usually on choosing appropriate sources, controlling portions and spreading carbohydrate intake sensibly across meals.
Absolutely not.
Some women require insulin because their body's insulin requirements increase substantially during pregnancy. This can happen despite careful attention to diet and activity.
This is a common misunderstanding.
Blood glucose often improves after delivery, but the future risk of Type 2 diabetes remains higher. Postpartum testing and continued screening are therefore important.
Not necessarily.
Fetal growth depends on many factors. Good glucose management, appropriate antenatal care and monitoring can help the medical team identify concerns early.
If your blood glucose readings are repeatedly above the targets given to you, contact your healthcare team rather than trying to adjust treatment yourself.
You should also seek urgent medical attention for serious symptoms such as:
Pregnancy-specific warning signs also need prompt assessment. These include significant vaginal bleeding, severe abdominal pain or noticeably reduced fetal movement.
Gestational diabetes can feel overwhelming when the diagnosis first appears on a pregnancy report. In practice, management is usually much more structured than it may initially seem.

The first step is understanding the diagnosis and knowing which glucose numbers your healthcare team wants you to aim for. From there, food choices, activity, home monitoring and treatment can be adjusted according to how your blood sugar behaves.

There may also be changes later in pregnancy. A woman who manages her GDM with lifestyle measures early on may eventually need insulin as insulin resistance increases. That is not a sign that she has done something wrong. It is simply one of the ways pregnancy can affect glucose metabolism.
And care should not stop at delivery.

The postpartum diabetes test and long-term screening are important because GDM can be an early warning sign of future metabolic problems. Taking that follow-up seriously gives women an opportunity to monitor their health well beyond pregnancy.
When to seek urgent care
In pregnancy, seek urgent care for vomiting, reduced fetal movements, severe headache, blurred vision, or symptoms of very high or very low sugar.

faqs.q: When is the gestational diabetes test done?
faqs.a: Usually between 24 and 28 weeks. In India, high-risk women may be tested in the first trimester too. Your doctor will advise the timing.

faqs.q: How does the glucose tolerance test work?
faqs.a: You fast, give a blood sample, drink a glucose solution, and have blood drawn again after one and two hours. The results show how your body handles sugar.

faqs.q: What are the normal values for the 75 g OGTT in pregnancy?
faqs.a: Fasting below 92, one hour below 180 and two hours below 153 mg/dL under IADPSG criteria. Your doctor may use slightly different criteria.

faqs.q: Can I eat before the glucose test?
faqs.a: Not for the fasting OGTT. You need to fast 8 to 14 hours and drink only water. Eat normally during the days before the test.

faqs.q: Is the glucose test safe for the baby?
faqs.a: Yes. The test is widely used and considered safe. The glucose load is similar to a sweet drink. Tell your doctor if you feel unwell.

faqs.q: What should I do if I fail the glucose test?
faqs.a: Do not panic. See a diabetologist and dietitian, learn to monitor your sugars and follow a plan. Most women control gestational diabetes with diet and activity.

Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 19 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
Most women are tested for gestational diabetes between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy using an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). In India, women are often tested early in pregnancy and again at 24 to 28 weeks if the first test is normal. The test involves a glucose drink and blood samples. Abnormal results lead to diet changes, monitoring and sometimes treatment.
Gestational diabetes is high blood sugar that first appears during pregnancy. It often has no symptoms, so testing is the only way to find it. Early detection protects both mother and baby. Here is what to expect.
Who should be tested?
In India, many guidelines advise testing all pregnant women, because the risk of diabetes is high. Early testing in the first trimester is advised for women who:
Are overweight or obese
Have a family history of diabetes
Had gestational diabetes in a previous pregnancy
Have PCOS
Have had a large baby before
Have high blood pressure
Are older than 30 to 35 years
When is the test done?
First visit or early pregnancy: Often for high-risk women, to detect pre-existing diabetes.
24 to 28 weeks: For all women with a normal early test.
Later in pregnancy: If symptoms or concerns arise, such as a large baby on scan.
What are the test options?
One-step OGTT
You fast overnight for at least 8 hours. A fasting blood sample is taken. You drink a solution containing 75 g of glucose. Blood samples are taken at one and two hours. This approach is commonly used in India and recommended by several international groups.
Two-step test
First, a 50 g glucose challenge is done without fasting, with one blood test at one hour. If high, a 100 g OGTT is done with fasting. This approach is used in some countries.
Your doctor will advise which one is used for you.
What are the diagnostic values?
For the common 75 g OGTT (IADPSG/WHO criteria), gestational diabetes is diagnosed if any one value is:
Fasting: 92 mg/dL or higher
At 1 hour: 180 mg/dL or higher
At 2 hours: 153 mg/dL or higher
Some Indian guidelines use a single 2-hour value of 140 mg/dL or higher after a 75 g glucose load. Your doctor will explain which criteria they follow.
How do you prepare?
Eat normally for the three days before, including adequate carbohydrates.
Fast for 8 to 14 hours as instructed, drinking water only.
Do not smoke or exercise heavily on the morning.
Tell the lab about any medicines or vomiting.
Remain seated and rest during the test.
Bring a snack for afterwards.
What if the drink makes you feel sick?
Some women feel nauseated after the sweet drink. Sip it slowly over five minutes. If you vomit, inform the staff. The test may need to be repeated.
What happens after an abnormal result?
You will be referred to a diabetologist and dietitian, and taught:
Home blood sugar monitoring
A healthy meal plan with measured carbohydrates
Safe physical activity such as walking
When medicines or insulin might be needed
Regular scans and checks track the baby's growth.
What if the result is normal?
You may still be at risk if you had symptoms or risk factors. Repeat testing at 24 to 28 weeks if the early test was normal, or if gestational diabetes is suspected later. Continue healthy habits.
When should you see a doctor?
Seek advice if you have excessive thirst, frequent urination, blurred vision, recurrent infections, a large baby on scan or excess amniotic fluid.
What to remember
Testing is done in early pregnancy for high-risk women and at 24 to 28 weeks for all.
The OGTT uses a glucose drink and blood samples.
One abnormal value may be enough for diagnosis under common criteria.
Prepare by fasting and eating normally in the days before.
Early diagnosis protects mother and baby.
A positive test is not a failure. It is an opportunity to protect your pregnancy with simple steps. For guidance, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
Sources and further reading
WHO: Diabetes fact sheet
NIDDK: Gestational diabetes
Frequently asked questions
When is the gestational diabetes test done?
Usually between 24 and 28 weeks. In India, high-risk women may be tested in the first trimester too. Your doctor will advise the timing.
How does the glucose tolerance test work?
You fast, give a blood sample, drink a glucose solution, and have blood drawn again after one and two hours. The results show how your body handles sugar.
What are the normal values for the 75 g OGTT in pregnancy?
Fasting below 92, one hour below 180 and two hours below 153 mg/dL under IADPSG criteria. Your doctor may use slightly different criteria.
Can I eat before the glucose test?
Not for the fasting OGTT. You need to fast 8 to 14 hours and drink only water. Eat normally during the days before the test.
Is the glucose test safe for the baby?
Yes. The test is widely used and considered safe. The glucose load is similar to a sweet drink. Tell your doctor if you feel unwell.
What should I do if I fail the glucose test?
Do not panic. See a diabetologist and dietitian, learn to monitor your sugars and follow a plan. Most women control gestational diabetes with diet and activity.
