GIP stands for glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide. It is another hormone involved in the body's response to food.
This comparison does not mean that one medicine should automatically be chosen over the other.
The appropriate choice can depend on diabetes control, weight, cardiovascular and kidney health, other medicines, adverse-effect concerns, access, cost and the patient's treatment priorities.
No.

Some medicines in this group are used to treat Type 2 diabetes. Certain medicines also have approved indications for chronic weight management in people who do not have diabetes but meet the relevant medical criteria.
That distinction is worth understanding.

A person does not need to have diabetes simply because they are being considered for a GLP-1-based medicine for obesity. At the same time, having obesity does not automatically mean that medication is necessary.
Doctors generally look at the overall picture, including:
The aim is to treat the person's health condition, rather than simply chase a number on the weighing scale.
There is no single group of patients who automatically "needs" a GLP-1 medicine.
Instead, doctors may consider these medicines in several situations.
A person with Type 2 diabetes may be considered for a GLP-1-based medicine when blood glucose remains above the individual's treatment target or when the existing treatment plan needs to be changed.
The decision does not depend on HbA1c alone.
The doctor also considers the person's weight, other medical conditions, current medicines and the risks and benefits of available treatment options.
This is an important situation because diabetes and excess weight frequently occur together.
For these patients, a treatment that can help with both glucose control and weight may be useful.
The 2026 ADA Standards of Care place considerable emphasis on selecting glucose-lowering treatments with beneficial effects on weight for people with Type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity.
Obesity is a chronic medical condition. Diet and physical activity remain central to treatment, but they are not always enough on their own for every person.
For patients who meet the appropriate criteria, prescription medication can be one part of a longer-term weight-management plan.

The decision should take into account health risks associated with obesity, previous attempts at weight management, potential benefits and adverse effects, and whether the patient can realistically continue treatment.
Some GLP-1-based medicines have demonstrated cardiovascular benefits in specific groups of people with Type 2 diabetes.
Certain medicines may also have a role in people with diabetes and chronic kidney disease, depending on the clinical situation.

This is an area where treatment selection becomes particularly individual. A person with diabetes may need a medicine partly because of cardiovascular or kidney considerations, even when weight loss is not the main goal.
These medicines are not appropriate for everybody.
Before prescribing one, a doctor may need to consider a history of:
The exact contraindications and warnings vary between products, so the prescribing information for the particular medicine matters.
This is also why buying or using a prescription medicine simply because someone else has had a good experience with it can be unsafe.
Not necessarily.
Metformin and GLP-1-based medicines work in different ways, and they can sometimes be used together.
For some patients, a GLP-1 medicine may become an important part of treatment. For others, metformin may remain appropriate, either alone or alongside another medicine.
The same principle applies to insulin.
They do not automatically replace insulin.
Some people with Type 2 diabetes continue to require insulin because their pancreas does not produce enough insulin or because of the severity and duration of their diabetes.

A GLP-1 medicine may sometimes be added to an insulin-based treatment plan. If this happens, the overall medication regimen may need adjustment because blood glucose can change and the risk of hypoglycaemia can be affected.
Insulin should never be stopped or reduced without medical advice.
Starting treatment should involve more than simply deciding which injection to use.
A doctor may first review:
Blood glucose: HbA1c, fasting glucose, home glucose readings or other relevant information can help establish the current level of diabetes control.
Weight and metabolic health: Weight, BMI and sometimes waist circumference provide useful context. Blood pressure and cholesterol may also be reviewed.
Kidney function: Kidney health can influence overall diabetes treatment decisions.
Heart health: A history of cardiovascular disease or cardiovascular risk factors may influence medicine selection.
Digestive symptoms: Existing gastrointestinal problems are relevant because GLP-1-based medicines can affect stomach emptying and cause gastrointestinal side effects.
Current medication: The doctor needs to know about diabetes medicines, insulin and other prescription or non-prescription treatments.
Pregnancy: Pregnancy status and pregnancy plans need to be discussed when relevant.
Treatment goals: The reason for treatment matters. Someone primarily concerned about glucose control may have different priorities from someone being treated mainly for obesity.

This assessment is especially relevant in metabolic health, where diabetes, obesity, blood pressure, cholesterol and cardiovascular risk can overlap. Niramay Clinics describes its clinical focus around diabetes, obesity, metabolic disease, preventive cardiology and prevention of diabetes complications.
Most GLP-1-based medicines are introduced gradually.
A lower starting dose is commonly used, followed by stepwise increases according to the specific product's prescribing information and the patient's response.
Why start slowly?
One reason is tolerability. Nausea and other digestive symptoms can be more noticeable when treatment begins or when the dose is increased.

The correct dose is not simply the highest dose a person can tolerate. Treatment needs to be adjusted according to the medicine, its approved indication, response and the patient's clinical circumstances.
A separate supporting article in the Niramay content cluster is planned specifically around how GLP-1 treatment is started, including titration and the first few weeks of treatment.
Digestive symptoms are among the most commonly reported side effects.
These can include:
For some people, these symptoms settle as the body becomes accustomed to treatment. For others, they may persist or become troublesome.
Eating smaller meals, eating slowly and avoiding foods that clearly worsen symptoms may help some people. But persistent symptoms should not simply be ignored.
Contact your healthcare professional if vomiting continues, you cannot maintain adequate fluid intake, abdominal pain is significant or symptoms are interfering with normal daily activities.
Severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, marked dehydration or other concerning symptoms warrant prompt medical assessment.
On their own, GLP-1-based medicines generally have a relatively low risk of causing hypoglycaemia because their effect on insulin secretion is linked to blood glucose.
That does not mean the risk is always absent.
The situation can change when a GLP-1 medicine is combined with insulin or certain medicines that increase insulin release.
A patient may therefore need changes to the wider diabetes treatment plan when a GLP-1 medicine is introduced.
Symptoms of low blood sugar can include:
Anyone using diabetes medication should know how to recognise hypoglycaemia and what their doctor has advised them to do if it occurs.
Weight-loss medicines should not be used during pregnancy.

Pregnancy requires a different approach to managing blood glucose and weight. If someone is pregnant, planning pregnancy or could become pregnant, this should be discussed with the treating doctor before starting or continuing medication.
Some GLP-1-based medicines carry specific pregnancy warnings, and certain medicines need to be stopped well before a planned pregnancy.
This is not a decision to make independently. Speak with your doctor about the appropriate timing and alternatives.
They can be used as part of long-term treatment when medically appropriate.
This is particularly relevant to obesity. Obesity is a chronic condition, so stopping treatment simply because a certain weight has been reached may not always be the end of the treatment plan.
Weight regain can occur after obesity medication is stopped.

That does not mean the medicine has "failed". It reflects the fact that appetite regulation, energy balance and metabolic disease involve biological processes that can persist after treatment is discontinued.
Patients considering these medicines should therefore ask about the longer-term plan before starting:
GLP-1 treatment does not make lifestyle management irrelevant.
In fact, many patients benefit from using medication and lifestyle changes together.
A sensible plan may include:
For someone with obesity or Type 2 diabetes, preserving muscle while losing excess body fat can also matter. The treatment plan should therefore look beyond the weighing scale.
There is no universal answer to this question.

Semaglutide and tirzepatide have different mechanisms and are used under different product indications. Their effects, dosing schedules, tolerability and other practical considerations can also differ.
The choice depends on what the patient is being treated for and what matters most clinically.
For example, the relevant question may be:
A consultation should therefore focus on fit, not simply on which medicine is generating the most attention online.
If you are considering a GLP-1 medicine, take a few practical questions to your appointment.
You could ask:
These questions can make the consultation much more useful and help you understand why a particular treatment has been selected.
Most side effects from GLP-1 medicines are not emergencies, but certain symptoms should not be ignored.
Seek prompt medical assessment for symptoms such as:
The appropriate response depends on the symptoms and the person's overall medical condition.
Not quite.
Some medicines in this group are used to treat Type 2 diabetes, while specific products also have approved indications for chronic weight management.
Their effects involve glucose regulation, appetite and other metabolic processes.
Medication does not replace nutrition, physical activity, sleep or other aspects of metabolic care.
The two approaches can work alongside each other.
No.
Diabetes treatment is individual. A GLP-1 medicine may be useful for one patient and unnecessary or unsuitable for another.
They do not.
Obesity is a chronic condition, and weight can return after treatment is stopped. Long-term management is often part of successful obesity care.
This is not a safe assumption.
Different medicines have different indications, contraindications and dosing requirements. Your own medical history matters.
GLP-1 medicines have added an important option to the treatment of Type 2 diabetes and obesity. Their effects go beyond simply lowering the number on a glucose meter or weighing scale.
For the right patient, they may help improve glucose control, reduce appetite and support weight management. But the right medicine, dose and treatment duration are different from person to person.

That is why a good GLP-1 consultation is about more than choosing a popular medicine. It should look at the person's diabetes, weight, cardiovascular and kidney health, current medication, possible side effects, treatment goals and ability to continue treatment over time.
If you are considering a GLP-1 medicine, the safest starting point is a proper medical assessment rather than self-treatment.

faqs.q: How long do GLP-1 side effects last?
faqs.a: Stomach side effects usually appear in the first weeks or after a dose increase and improve over days to weeks. If they last longer or are severe, talk to your doctor about adjusting the dose.

faqs.q: What should I eat when I feel nauseated on a GLP-1?
faqs.a: Try small portions of light food such as curd rice, toast, banana, khichdi or plain biscuits. Avoid fried, oily and sweet items. Sip fluids slowly through the day.

faqs.q: Can GLP-1 medicines cause constipation?
faqs.a: Yes. Slow stomach and gut movement can cause constipation. Drink water, add fibre gradually, stay active and speak to your doctor if it continues. A stool softener may be advised.

faqs.q: Do GLP-1 injections cause pancreatitis?
faqs.a: Pancreatitis is a rare but serious risk. Severe, persistent upper abdominal pain, sometimes spreading to the back with vomiting, needs urgent medical attention. Stop the medicine and call your doctor.

faqs.q: Can I take anti-nausea medicine with GLP-1?
faqs.a: Your doctor may prescribe a suitable anti-nausea medicine. Do not self-medicate, especially if you have other conditions or take other medicines.

faqs.q: Should I stop my GLP-1 medicine if I get side effects?
faqs.a: Do not stop on your own. Mild effects often improve. Your doctor may pause or reduce the dose, or change the plan. Stop and seek urgent help if you have severe abdominal pain or allergic signs.

GLP-1 Side Effects: Nausea, Constipation and Fixes
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 8 October 2026 · 5 min read
Quick answer
The most common side effects of GLP-1 medicines are nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, constipation, bloating and reduced appetite. They are most likely when starting or increasing the dose and usually improve within days to weeks. Eating smaller meals, avoiding fatty food, drinking fluids and increasing the dose slowly can help. Severe stomach pain or persistent vomiting needs urgent medical care.
GLP-1 medicines are effective, but many people feel some stomach upset when they start. This is common, usually mild and often settles with time and small changes in eating habits. Knowing what to expect helps you stay on treatment safely.
Why do these medicines cause stomach symptoms?
GLP-1 medicines slow the emptying of the stomach and act on appetite centres in the brain. Food stays in the stomach longer, so you feel full sooner. This is part of how they work, but it can cause nausea, bloating and reflux, especially with large or fatty meals.
What are the common side effects?
Nausea
Vomiting
Diarrhoea
Constipation
Stomach pain or cramps
Burping, bloating and acid reflux
Tiredness and dizziness
Mild redness or itching at the injection site
How can you manage nausea and vomiting?
Eat small, frequent meals instead of large ones.
Stop eating when you feel full.
Avoid fried, oily and very sweet food.
Eat slowly and sit upright for a while after meals.
Avoid lying down right after eating.
Sip water or buttermilk through the day.
Try ginger tea or dry snacks like plain biscuits or toast when nauseated.
Avoid alcohol and strong smells that trigger nausea.
Ask your doctor about anti-nausea medicine if needed.
How can you manage constipation?
Drink enough water, 2 to 3 litres a day unless advised otherwise.
Add fibre slowly: vegetables, fruits, oats, pulses and whole grains.
Walk daily.
Ask your doctor about a mild stool softener or fibre supplement.
How can you manage diarrhoea?
Drink oral rehydration solution or fluids.
Eat light food such as curd rice, banana or khichdi.
Avoid oily, spicy foods and excess caffeine.
Inform your doctor if it lasts more than two days.
How does the dose affect side effects?
Doctors usually start with a low dose and increase every few weeks. This gives the body time to adjust. If side effects are strong, the dose may be held or reduced for a while. Do not increase the dose faster than advised.
What about serious side effects?
Rare but important problems include:
Pancreatitis: Severe, persistent stomach pain that may spread to the back, often with vomiting.
Gallbladder problems: Pain in the upper right abdomen, fever or yellow eyes. Rapid weight loss raises the risk of gallstones.
Dehydration and kidney strain: From repeated vomiting or diarrhoea.
Low blood sugar: More likely when combined with insulin or sulfonylurea tablets.
Allergic reactions: Swelling, rash or difficulty breathing.
Thyroid concerns: A lump in the neck, hoarseness or trouble swallowing. These medicines are not advised in people with certain thyroid cancer histories.
Eye changes: Sudden vision changes, especially in people with diabetic eye disease.
When should you see a doctor urgently?
Seek medical care at once for severe or constant stomach pain, repeated vomiting, inability to drink fluids, signs of dehydration, yellowing of the skin or eyes, swelling of the face or throat, or a fast heartbeat with dizziness.
A quick recap
Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and constipation are the most common side effects.
They are usually mild and settle with time.
Small meals, fluids, fibre and slow dose increases help.
Severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting or allergic signs need urgent care.
Never stop or change doses without speaking to your doctor.
Most people tolerate GLP-1 medicines well when they are started slowly and supported with simple food changes. Speak up early if something feels wrong. For safe supervision and dose planning, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.

Frequently asked questions
How long do GLP-1 side effects last?
Stomach side effects usually appear in the first weeks or after a dose increase and improve over days to weeks. If they last longer or are severe, talk to your doctor about adjusting the dose.
What should I eat when I feel nauseated on a GLP-1?
Try small portions of light food such as curd rice, toast, banana, khichdi or plain biscuits. Avoid fried, oily and sweet items. Sip fluids slowly through the day.
Can GLP-1 medicines cause constipation?
Yes. Slow stomach and gut movement can cause constipation. Drink water, add fibre gradually, stay active and speak to your doctor if it continues. A stool softener may be advised.
Do GLP-1 injections cause pancreatitis?
Pancreatitis is a rare but serious risk. Severe, persistent upper abdominal pain, sometimes spreading to the back with vomiting, needs urgent medical attention. Stop the medicine and call your doctor.
Can I take anti-nausea medicine with GLP-1?
Your doctor may prescribe a suitable anti-nausea medicine. Do not self-medicate, especially if you have other conditions or take other medicines.
Should I stop my GLP-1 medicine if I get side effects?
Do not stop on your own. Mild effects often improve. Your doctor may pause or reduce the dose, or change the plan. Stop and seek urgent help if you have severe abdominal pain or allergic signs.

faqs.a: Typically below 150 mg/dL, though your doctor will interpret it for you.

faqs.a: Excess calories and sugar often matter more than dietary fat alone.

faqs.q: Does alcohol raise triglycerides?
faqs.a: Yes, even moderate drinking can raise them in some people.

faqs.q: Can triglycerides be lowered quickly?
faqs.a: Diet and activity can lower them within weeks.

faqs.a: Your doctor will advise whether fasting is needed.

faqs.a: Yes, they are closely related.

High Triglycerides, Diabetes and Obesity: What Is the Link?
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 21 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
Insulin resistance, excess body fat, high sugar intake, refined carbohydrates, alcohol and uncontrolled diabetes can all raise triglycerides. Very high levels can cause pancreatitis, and moderately high levels raise heart risk. Weight loss, diet changes, activity, good diabetes control and sometimes medicines bring them down.
Triglycerides are a type of fat in the blood. High levels often go hand in hand with diabetes and excess weight.
Why triglycerides rise
Insulin resistance increases fat production in the liver
Excess calories, especially from sugar and refined carbohydrates
Alcohol
Poorly controlled diabetes
Certain medicines and conditions
Genetic tendencies
Why it matters
Higher risk of heart disease
Often accompanies low HDL and fatty liver
Very high levels can trigger acute pancreatitis
How to lower triglycerides
Diet
Reduce sweets, sugary drinks and refined flour
Limit fried and processed foods
Choose fish, nuts, vegetables and whole grains
Limit or avoid alcohol
Lifestyle
Lose weight
Exercise regularly
Medical
Better blood sugar control
Medicines when levels remain high
Testing
A fasting blood test measures triglycerides along with cholesterol. Your doctor will advise how often to repeat it.
The quick version
Diabetes and obesity raise triglycerides.
Sugar, refined carbs and alcohol worsen them.
Weight loss and diet changes help a lot.
Control of diabetes matters.
Very high levels need urgent care.
Triglycerides respond well to lifestyle change. For guidance, you can consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
When to seek urgent care
Seek urgent care for chest pain, breathlessness, confusion, vomiting, or symptoms of very high or very low sugar.
Sources and further reading
NHLBI: Metabolic syndrome
NIDDK: Insulin resistance and prediabetes
Frequently asked questions
What is a normal triglyceride level?
Typically below 150 mg/dL, though your doctor will interpret it for you.
Does eating fat raise triglycerides?
Excess calories and sugar often matter more than dietary fat alone.
Does alcohol raise triglycerides?
Yes, even moderate drinking can raise them in some people.
Can triglycerides be lowered quickly?
Diet and activity can lower them within weeks.
Do I need a fasting test?
Your doctor will advise whether fasting is needed.
Are triglycerides linked to fatty liver?
Yes, they are closely related.

Quick answer

Insulin resistance, excess body fat, high sugar intake, refined carbohydrates, alcohol and uncontrolled diabetes can all raise triglycerides. Very high levels can cause pancreatitis, and moderately high levels raise heart risk. Weight loss, diet changes, activity, good diabetes control and sometimes medicines bring them down.
Triglycerides are a type of fat in the blood. High levels often go hand in hand with diabetes and excess weight.
A fasting blood test measures triglycerides along with cholesterol. Your doctor will advise how often to repeat it.
Triglycerides respond well to lifestyle change. For guidance, you can consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.

faqs.q: Who discovered GLP-1?
faqs.a: Several scientists contributed. In the 1980s, researchers studying the glucagon gene identified GLP-1 and showed that it stimulates insulin release. Later work turned this knowledge into medicines.

faqs.q: What does the Gila monster have to do with GLP-1 medicines?
faqs.a: A hormone in the saliva of the Gila monster, called exendin-4, resembles GLP-1 but lasts longer. It led to the first GLP-1 medicine for diabetes, exenatide.

faqs.q: When were GLP-1 medicines first approved?
faqs.a: The first GLP-1 medicine for type 2 diabetes was approved in the mid-2000s. Longer-acting and weekly versions followed, and weight-management doses came later.

faqs.q: How is semaglutide different from natural GLP-1?
faqs.a: Semaglutide is modified to resist breakdown and stay in the body for about a week, while natural GLP-1 lasts only minutes. This allows weekly dosing.

faqs.q: Why were GLP-1 medicines first used for diabetes?
faqs.a: Because they lower blood sugar by increasing insulin release when sugar is high. Their effect on appetite and weight was noticed later, leading to trials for obesity.

faqs.q: What is the difference between GLP-1 and GIP?
faqs.a: Both are gut hormones that help release insulin after eating. Tirzepatide acts on both, which may explain its stronger effect on weight and blood sugar in studies.

The Surprising History of GLP-1 Drugs
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 10 October 2026 · 5 min read
Quick answer
GLP-1 stands for glucagon-like peptide-1, a hormone made in the gut after eating. Scientists discovered it in the 1980s and found it helps the pancreas release insulin. Because the natural hormone breaks down in minutes, researchers created longer-acting versions, including one inspired by a hormone in the saliva of the Gila monster lizard. This led to modern medicines such as semaglutide and tirzepatide.
GLP-1 medicines are now in the headlines for diabetes and weight loss. But they did not appear overnight. Their story spans several decades and began with curious scientists studying how the gut talks to the pancreas.
How was the gut-pancreas link found?
In the 1960s, researchers noticed that sugar taken by mouth caused a larger insulin release than the same sugar given through a vein. This difference was called the incretin effect. It suggested that hormones from the gut signal the pancreas to release insulin when food arrives.
How was GLP-1 discovered?
In the 1980s, scientists studying the gene for glucagon found a related fragment, which they named glucagon-like peptide-1. They showed that this hormone, made by gut cells, strongly stimulates insulin release when blood sugar is high. It also reduces glucagon, slows stomach emptying and lowers appetite.
What was the problem with the natural hormone?
Natural GLP-1 is broken down by an enzyme in the blood within a couple of minutes. A medicine based on it could not work for long. This led researchers to look for ways to make a stable version.
Where did the gila monster come in?
In the early 1990s, researchers studying the saliva of the Gila monster, a venomous lizard from North America, found a hormone called exendin-4. It was similar to human GLP-1 but resisted breakdown. This led to the first GLP-1 medicine for diabetes, exenatide, approved in the mid-2000s. It was taken as an injection twice a day.
How did the medicines improve?
Longer-acting versions
Scientists redesigned the molecule so that it lasted longer in the body. This allowed once-daily injections, and later once-weekly injections.
Semaglutide
Semaglutide was designed with a fatty-acid side chain that binds to proteins in the blood, protecting it from breakdown and extending its action. It is available as a weekly injection and as a daily tablet.
Weight-loss discovery
Doctors noticed that people on GLP-1 medicines lost weight, which led to trials in people with obesity. Higher doses were studied specifically for weight management and showed significant results.
Dual agonists
Tirzepatide acts on two gut hormones, GLP-1 and GIP, and showed even greater effects in some trials.
What did researchers learn along the way?
GLP-1 medicines lower blood sugar with a low risk of hypoglycaemia on their own.
Some reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke in people with diabetes and heart disease.
They can protect the kidneys in certain patients.
They affect appetite centres in the brain.
Why does this history matter?
Knowing the story shows that these medicines are the result of decades of careful research and not a passing fad. It also explains why they are used under medical supervision and why newer versions keep appearing.
When should you see a doctor?
If you are considering a GLP-1 medicine for diabetes or weight, speak to a diabetologist first to check whether it is suitable and safe for you.
A quick recap
GLP-1 is a gut hormone that helps control blood sugar and appetite.
Scientists found it in the 1980s, and its short life in the body was a problem.
A hormone in Gila monster saliva inspired the first long-acting version.
Semaglutide and tirzepatide are the result of decades of improvement.
These medicines should be started only with medical guidance.
The path from a lizard's saliva to modern medicine shows how patient science can change lives. To learn whether this class of medicines is right for you, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.

Frequently asked questions
Who discovered GLP-1?
Several scientists contributed. In the 1980s, researchers studying the glucagon gene identified GLP-1 and showed that it stimulates insulin release. Later work turned this knowledge into medicines.
What does the Gila monster have to do with GLP-1 medicines?
A hormone in the saliva of the Gila monster, called exendin-4, resembles GLP-1 but lasts longer. It led to the first GLP-1 medicine for diabetes, exenatide.
When were GLP-1 medicines first approved?
The first GLP-1 medicine for type 2 diabetes was approved in the mid-2000s. Longer-acting and weekly versions followed, and weight-management doses came later.
How is semaglutide different from natural GLP-1?
Semaglutide is modified to resist breakdown and stay in the body for about a week, while natural GLP-1 lasts only minutes. This allows weekly dosing.
Why were GLP-1 medicines first used for diabetes?
Because they lower blood sugar by increasing insulin release when sugar is high. Their effect on appetite and weight was noticed later, leading to trials for obesity.
What is the difference between GLP-1 and GIP?
Both are gut hormones that help release insulin after eating. Tirzepatide acts on both, which may explain its stronger effect on weight and blood sugar in studies.

pOnly: Technology and Evolution of GLP-1
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
MD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 10 October 2026 · 5 min read
Quick answer

GLP-1 stands for glucagon-like peptide-1, a hormone made in the gut after eating. Scientists discovered it in the 1980s and found it helps the pancreas release insulin. Because the natural hormone breaks down in minutes, researchers created longer-acting versions, including one inspired by a hormone in the saliva of the Gila monster lizard. This led to modern medicines such as semaglutide and tirzepatide.

GLP-1 medicines are now in the headlines for diabetes and weight loss. But they did not appear overnight. Their story spans several decades and began with curious scientists studying how the gut talks to the pancreas.

In the 1960s, researchers noticed that sugar taken by mouth caused a larger insulin release than the same sugar given through a vein. This difference was called the incretin effect. It suggested that hormones from the gut signal the pancreas to release insulin when food arrives.

In the 1980s, scientists studying the gene for glucagon found a related fragment, which they named glucagon-like peptide-1. They showed that this hormone, made by gut cells, strongly stimulates insulin release when blood sugar is high. It also reduces glucagon, slows stomach emptying and lowers appetite.
Natural GLP-1 is broken down by an enzyme in the blood within a couple of minutes. A medicine based on it could not work for long. This led researchers to look for ways to make a stable version.

In the early 1990s, researchers studying the saliva of the Gila monster, a venomous lizard from North America, found a hormone called exendin-4. It was similar to human GLP-1 but resisted breakdown. This led to the first GLP-1 medicine for diabetes, exenatide, approved in the mid-2000s. It was taken as an injection twice a day.
Scientists redesigned the molecule so that it lasted longer in the body. This allowed once-daily injections, and later once-weekly injections.

Semaglutide was designed with a fatty-acid side chain that binds to proteins in the blood, protecting it from breakdown and extending its action. It is available as a weekly injection and as a daily tablet.
Doctors noticed that people on GLP-1 medicines lost weight, which led to trials in people with obesity. Higher doses were studied specifically for weight management and showed significant results.
Tirzepatide acts on two gut hormones, GLP-1 and GIP, and showed even greater effects in some trials.

Knowing the story shows that these medicines are the result of decades of careful research and not a passing fad. It also explains why they are used under medical supervision and why newer versions keep appearing.
If you are considering a GLP-1 medicine for diabetes or weight, speak to a diabetologist first to check whether it is suitable and safe for you.

The path from a lizard's saliva to modern medicine shows how patient science can change lives. To learn whether this class of medicines is right for you, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.

faqs.q: Does a GLP-1 pen injection hurt?
faqs.a: Most people feel only a light prick or nothing, because the needle is very thin and short. Rotating sites and using a new needle each time help reduce discomfort.

faqs.q: How does a GLP-1 pen measure the dose?
faqs.a: A dial or preset mechanism moves a plunger a fixed distance. Some pens have clicks for each unit, while others are preset for a specific weekly dose. Always follow the instructions for your pen.

faqs.q: Can I reuse the needle on my pen?
faqs.a: No. Needles should be used once. Reuse can cause pain, infection, a blocked needle and inaccurate dosing.

faqs.q: How do I store a GLP-1 pen?
faqs.a: Store unused pens in the refrigerator, away from the freezer compartment. Follow the label for how long an in-use pen can be kept at room temperature. Avoid heat and direct sunlight.

faqs.q: Can I travel with a GLP-1 pen?
faqs.a: Yes. Use an insulated pouch, keep it away from heat, and carry it in hand baggage, not checked luggage. Keep a prescription copy for airport security.

faqs.q: What if my pen is not delivering the dose?
faqs.a: Check the needle and cap, and look for leakage. Do not repeat the injection on your own. Contact your doctor, nurse or the manufacturer for guidance.

How GLP-1 Injection Pens Work: The Technology
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 10 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
A GLP-1 pen is a pre-filled or cartridge-based device that holds the medicine and delivers a precise dose through a very fine needle when you dial the dose and press the button. The pen uses a dial or preset click system to measure the dose, a spring or mechanical plunger to push the medicine, and a thin needle that is attached for each use.
The idea of a weekly injection worries many people at first. In reality, modern pens are small, simple and designed to make dosing easy. A look at how they work can take away much of the fear.
Why use a pen instead of a syringe?
The dose is measured by the device, which reduces errors.
The needle is very thin, so injections are less painful.
The pen is portable and discreet.
Dose adjustment is simple.
It suits people with poor eyesight or limited dexterity.
It reduces the fear of handling vials and syringes.
What are the parts of a pen?
The body or cartridge holder
It holds a sealed cartridge containing the medicine.
The dose selector
A dial, or a click mechanism, sets the dose. In some pens, each click equals a measured amount. Others have preset doses for weekly use.
The dose window
It shows the dose you have selected.
The injection button
Pressing it delivers the dose. A counter or click tells you when it is complete.
The needle
A tiny disposable needle is screwed or clicked on before each use. It is usually 4 to 6 mm long and very thin, which makes most injections feel like a light prick.
The cap
It protects the pen and the needle.
How does the dose get delivered?
When you set the dose, the pen's internal mechanism moves a plunger a set distance. When you press the button, the plunger pushes the medicine from the cartridge through the needle into the fat layer under the skin. The medicine is then absorbed slowly into the blood. This slow release is part of why weekly dosing is possible.
How has pen design improved?
Thinner and shorter needles, reducing pain
Pens with audible clicks to confirm the dose
Pens that hide the needle, helpful for needle-fearful people
Pre-set weekly doses, reducing mistakes
Dose counters and memory features in some devices
Smaller, lighter bodies for easier carrying
How should pens be stored?
Keep unopened pens in the refrigerator, not in the freezer.
Follow the label for how long an in-use pen can stay at room temperature.
Protect from direct sunlight and heat.
Do not use a pen if the medicine looks cloudy, discoloured or has particles, unless the label says it should look that way.
Never share pens with others, even with a new needle.
What mistakes should you avoid?
Reusing needles
Not priming when the instructions say to
Injecting into the same spot every week
Not holding the button long enough
Using an expired pen
Storing in a hot vehicle or a freezer
When should you see a doctor?
Contact your doctor or nurse if the pen jams, the dose does not seem to go in, you see leakage, or you have swelling, redness or a lump at the injection site that does not settle.
A quick recap
GLP-1 pens deliver a measured dose through a very fine needle.
Dial, plunger and button work together for accuracy.
Modern pens are designed for comfort and easy use.
Correct storage and rotation of sites are important.
Ask your doctor or nurse to show you the technique.
Pen technology has made injections far less intimidating. With a short demonstration, most people become comfortable within a week or two. For help learning the technique, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
Sources and further reading
NIDDK: Prescription medicines for overweight and obesity
WHO: Diabetes fact sheet
Frequently asked questions
Does a GLP-1 pen injection hurt?
Most people feel only a light prick or nothing, because the needle is very thin and short. Rotating sites and using a new needle each time help reduce discomfort.
How does a GLP-1 pen measure the dose?
A dial or preset mechanism moves a plunger a fixed distance. Some pens have clicks for each unit, while others are preset for a specific weekly dose. Always follow the instructions for your pen.
Can I reuse the needle on my pen?
No. Needles should be used once. Reuse can cause pain, infection, a blocked needle and inaccurate dosing.
How do I store a GLP-1 pen?
Store unused pens in the refrigerator, away from the freezer compartment. Follow the label for how long an in-use pen can be kept at room temperature. Avoid heat and direct sunlight.
Can I travel with a GLP-1 pen?
Yes. Use an insulated pouch, keep it away from heat, and carry it in hand baggage, not checked luggage. Keep a prescription copy for airport security.
What if my pen is not delivering the dose?
Check the needle and cap, and look for leakage. Do not repeat the injection on your own. Contact your doctor, nurse or the manufacturer for guidance.

pOnly: Technology and Evolution of GLP-1
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
MD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 10 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer

A GLP-1 pen is a pre-filled or cartridge-based device that holds the medicine and delivers a precise dose through a very fine needle when you dial the dose and press the button. The pen uses a dial or preset click system to measure the dose, a spring or mechanical plunger to push the medicine, and a thin needle that is attached for each use.
The idea of a weekly injection worries many people at first. In reality, modern pens are small, simple and designed to make dosing easy. A look at how they work can take away much of the fear.
It holds a sealed cartridge containing the medicine.
A dial, or a click mechanism, sets the dose. In some pens, each click equals a measured amount. Others have preset doses for weekly use.
It shows the dose you have selected.
Pressing it delivers the dose. A counter or click tells you when it is complete.
A tiny disposable needle is screwed or clicked on before each use. It is usually 4 to 6 mm long and very thin, which makes most injections feel like a light prick.
It protects the pen and the needle.

When you set the dose, the pen's internal mechanism moves a plunger a set distance. When you press the button, the plunger pushes the medicine from the cartridge through the needle into the fat layer under the skin. The medicine is then absorbed slowly into the blood. This slow release is part of why weekly dosing is possible.
Contact your doctor or nurse if the pen jams, the dose does not seem to go in, you see leakage, or you have swelling, redness or a lump at the injection site that does not settle.

Pen technology has made injections far less intimidating. With a short demonstration, most people become comfortable within a week or two. For help learning the technique, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.

faqs.q: Where is the best place to inject a GLP-1 medicine?
faqs.a: The abdomen, thigh or back of the upper arm. The abdomen, away from the navel, is common and easy. Rotate sites each week.

faqs.q: Can I inject GLP-1 at any time of day?
faqs.a: Weekly injections can be taken at any time of day, as long as it is the same day each week. Daily injections should follow the timing your doctor advises.

faqs.q: Should GLP-1 injections be taken with food?
faqs.a: Injections can be taken with or without food. Tablets, however, must be taken on an empty stomach with a sip of water and 30 minutes before food.

faqs.q: Can I store my GLP-1 pen at room temperature?
faqs.a: Unopened pens go in the refrigerator. In-use pens may be kept at room temperature for a limited time as stated on the label. Avoid heat and sunlight.

faqs.q: What if the injection site bleeds or bruises?
faqs.a: Minor bleeding or bruising is common. Press lightly with cotton. It should settle in a few days. Rotate sites and see a doctor if it is large or painful.

faqs.q: How do I dispose of used needles?
faqs.a: Place them in a sharps container or a hard plastic bottle with a secure cap and hand it to a hospital or clinic for disposal. Do not throw loose needles in household waste.

How Are GLP-1 Medicines Given? Technique and Storage
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 14 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
GLP-1 injections are given under the skin of the abdomen, thigh or upper arm, usually once a week. Use a new needle each time, rotate sites, inject at the same time each week, and store unused pens in the refrigerator. Always follow the instructions for your specific pen and ask your nurse or doctor to demonstrate the first injection.
Most GLP-1 medicines for diabetes and weight management are given as an injection under the skin. The needle is tiny, and the technique is easy to learn. Doing it correctly helps the medicine work well and keeps you comfortable.
How often are they given?
Weekly injections: Semaglutide and tirzepatide for diabetes and weight are given once a week, on the same day.
Daily injections: Some GLP-1 medicines are taken daily.
Tablets: Oral semaglutide is taken once daily on an empty stomach.
Your doctor will tell you which schedule applies.
Where can you inject?
Abdomen: At least 5 cm away from the navel. It is a common, easy site.
Front or outer thigh: Good for self-injection.
Back of the upper arm: Easier if someone else gives the injection.
Rotate within the same area, moving at least 2 to 3 cm from the previous spot. Avoid scars, bruises, moles, lumpy areas or places where the skin is hard.
What are the steps?
Wash your hands. Gather the pen, a new needle and an alcohol swab.
Check the pen. Read the label, the expiry date and the colour and clarity of the medicine.
Attach a new needle. Remove the paper tab, screw or click it on, and remove both caps.
Prime if needed. Some pens need a small test dose. Follow your pen's instructions.
Dial the dose. Check the dose window to be sure it is correct.
Clean the skin. Let it dry.
Insert the needle. Insert straight in. You can gently pinch the skin if you have little fat.
Press the button. Hold it down and count slowly as instructed, often up to 6 to 10.
Remove the needle. Do not rub hard. A small drop of blood is normal.
Dispose of the needle safely. Use a sharps container or a hard plastic bottle. Replace the pen cap.
How should you store GLP-1 pens?
Store unopened pens in the refrigerator, away from the freezer section.
Never use a pen that has frozen.
In-use pens may be kept at room temperature or in the fridge for a limited number of days, as stated on your pen's label.
Keep away from sunlight, heat and car dashboards.
Carry pens in an insulated pouch when travelling, in hand luggage.
Do not share pens.
What if you miss a dose?
For weekly injections, follow the label. Many instructions say to take a missed dose if it is within a few days of the due date, otherwise skip it and take the next dose on the usual day. Do not take two doses close together. When unsure, call your doctor.
What common problems occur?
Bruising or small bleed: Normal, press lightly with cotton.
Redness or itching: Often mild. Rotate sites.
Lumps under the skin: From repeated injections in one place. Change sites.
Leakage: Hold the pen in place for the full count.
Pain: Use a new needle, let the pen reach room temperature before injecting, if the label allowsd and relax the muscles.
When should you see a doctor?
See a doctor if you have swelling, spreading redness, pus, fever, a hard painful lump, a pen that is not working or if you are unsure about your dose. Seek urgent care for allergic reactions like swelling of the face or trouble breathing.
The quick version
Most GLP-1 medicines are injected under the skin once a week.
Rotate sites and use a new needle each time.
Store pens in the refrigerator and protect them from heat.
Follow the label if you miss a dose.
Ask for a demonstration at the start.
With a little practice, injecting becomes routine. Good technique makes treatment easier and safer. For hands-on guidance, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
Sources and further reading
NIDDK: Prescription medicines for overweight and obesity
WHO: Diabetes fact sheet
Frequently asked questions
Where is the best place to inject a GLP-1 medicine?
The abdomen, thigh or back of the upper arm. The abdomen, away from the navel, is common and easy. Rotate sites each week.
Can I inject GLP-1 at any time of day?
Weekly injections can be taken at any time of day, as long as it is the same day each week. Daily injections should follow the timing your doctor advises.
Should GLP-1 injections be taken with food?
Injections can be taken with or without food. Tablets, however, must be taken on an empty stomach with a sip of water and 30 minutes before food.
Can I store my GLP-1 pen at room temperature?
Unopened pens go in the refrigerator. In-use pens may be kept at room temperature for a limited time as stated on the label. Avoid heat and sunlight.
What if the injection site bleeds or bruises?
Minor bleeding or bruising is common. Press lightly with cotton. It should settle in a few days. Rotate sites and see a doctor if it is large or painful.
How do I dispose of used needles?
Place them in a sharps container or a hard plastic bottle with a secure cap and hand it to a hospital or clinic for disposal. Do not throw loose needles in household waste.

Quick answer

GLP-1 injections are given under the skin of the abdomen, thigh or upper arm, usually once a week. Use a new needle each time, rotate sites, inject at the same time each week, and store unused pens in the refrigerator. Always follow the instructions for your specific pen and ask your nurse or doctor to demonstrate the first injection.

Most GLP-1 medicines for diabetes and weight management are given as an injection under the skin. The needle is tiny, and the technique is easy to learn. Doing it correctly helps the medicine work well and keeps you comfortable.
Your doctor will tell you which schedule applies.
Rotate within the same area, moving at least 2 to 3 cm from the previous spot. Avoid scars, bruises, moles, lumpy areas or places where the skin is hard.

For weekly injections, follow the label. Many instructions say to take a missed dose if it is within a few days of the due date, otherwise skip it and take the next dose on the usual day. Do not take two doses close together. When unsure, call your doctor.

See a doctor if you have swelling, spreading redness, pus, fever, a hard painful lump, a pen that is not working or if you are unsure about your dose. Seek urgent care for allergic reactions like swelling of the face or trouble breathing.

faqs.q: What should I eat when I start a GLP-1 medicine?
faqs.a: Small, protein-rich meals with vegetables and whole grains are best. Avoid oily, fried and very sweet foods. Eat slowly and stop when full.

faqs.q: What if I miss a weekly dose?
faqs.a: Follow the instructions for your medicine. Many allow taking the missed dose within a few days. If it is much later, skip it and continue as scheduled. Ask your doctor if unsure.

faqs.q: Will I need to adjust my other diabetes medicines?
faqs.a: Possibly. Insulin and sulfonylureas may need to be lowered to prevent low blood sugar. Your doctor will guide changes. Do not adjust them yourself.

How Is GLP-1 Treatment Started? Dose and First Weeks
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 14 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
GLP-1 treatment starts with a medical assessment, followed by a low starting dose that is increased in steps every few weeks. This slow increase, called titration, helps the body adjust and reduces nausea and other side effects. Most people reach the working dose within about 2 to 4 months. Regular follow-up lets the doctor adjust the dose, check side effects and support diet and activity.
Starting a new injection can feel daunting. Knowing what the first weeks look like helps you feel prepared. This guide explains how treatment usually begins, why the dose goes up slowly and what to expect.
Step 1: the medical assessment
Before the first dose, your doctor will:
Review your medical history and family history
Check for conditions where these medicines are unsafe
Review all your current medicines
Measure weight, BMI, waist and blood pressure
Order blood tests, such as HbA1c, kidney and liver tests
Check eyes if you have diabetes
Discuss goals, expected results, side effects and costs
Step 2: choosing the medicine and form
The medicine, brand, pen and form (injection or tablet) are chosen based on your condition, goals and availability. Your doctor will teach you or a family member how to use the pen.
Step 3: starting low
The first dose is a small starting dose. It is not meant to give the full effect. Its job is to let your gut and brain get used to the medicine.
Step 4: slow dose increase (Titration)
Most schedules increase the dose every 4 weeks, depending on the medicine. For example, weekly injections often start at the lowest dose for four weeks, then step up. The exact schedule depends on the product. Your doctor will follow the approved plan for your medicine.
The dose may be:
Increased if you tolerate it well and need more effect
Held at the same level if side effects are present
Reduced if side effects are troublesome
You do not need to reach the highest dose to benefit.
What do the first weeks feel like?
Reduced appetite and feeling full sooner
Mild nausea, burping or bloating
Loose stools or constipation
Fatigue in some people
Slow weight change at first, with more visible loss after a few months
Lower blood sugar readings in people with diabetes
How can you make the first weeks easier?
Eat small, slow meals and stop when full.
Avoid heavy, oily and very sweet foods.
Drink enough water.
Keep protein in every meal.
Do not lie down right after meals.
Inject on the same day each week.
Keep a simple diary of dose, symptoms, weight and sugar readings.
What about other diabetes medicines?
If you take insulin or a sulfonylurea (such as glimepiride), your doctor may reduce these doses to avoid low blood sugar as the GLP-1 medicine works. Never adjust them on your own.
What follow-up should you expect?
A review within 2 to 4 weeks
Dose reviews at each step
Blood tests after a few months
Support from a dietitian or exercise guide
Regular weight, waist and blood sugar tracking
What if you miss a dose?
For weekly injections, instructions usually allow a missed dose to be taken within a few days of the due date. If it is much later, skip it and continue on schedule. Follow the instructions for your specific medicine, and ask your doctor if unsure.
When should you see a doctor urgently?
Contact your doctor if you have severe or persistent stomach pain, repeated vomiting, unable to drink fluids, signs of dehydration, severe low sugar symptoms or allergic signs.
The quick version
Treatment starts with a careful assessment.
The dose starts low and is increased slowly every few weeks.
Mild stomach effects are common early on and usually settle.
Diet habits and follow-up make the first weeks easier.
Other diabetes medicines may need adjustment.
A slow start makes treatment easier to stick with. With good support, most people settle into their treatment in a few weeks. To begin safely, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
Sources and further reading
NIDDK: Prescription medicines for overweight and obesity
WHO: Diabetes fact sheet
Frequently asked questions
Why is the GLP-1 dose increased slowly?
A slow increase gives the digestive system and brain time to adjust, reducing nausea, vomiting and other side effects. It improves tolerance and helps people stay on treatment.
How long does it take to reach the full dose?
Often 2 to 4 months or longer, depending on the medicine and your tolerance. Not everyone needs the highest dose, and your doctor decides the target for you.
When will I start losing weight on a GLP-1?
Many notice reduced appetite within the first weeks, with weight loss becoming clearer after the dose rises over a few months. Results vary.
What should I eat when I start a GLP-1 medicine?
Small, protein-rich meals with vegetables and whole grains are best. Avoid oily, fried and very sweet foods. Eat slowly and stop when full.
What if I miss a weekly dose?
Follow the instructions for your medicine. Many allow taking the missed dose within a few days. If it is much later, skip it and continue as scheduled. Ask your doctor if unsure.
Will I need to adjust my other diabetes medicines?
Possibly. Insulin and sulfonylureas may need to be lowered to prevent low blood sugar. Your doctor will guide changes. Do not adjust them yourself.

Follow the instructions for your medicine. Many allow taking the missed dose within a few days. If it is much later, skip it and continue as scheduled. Ask your doctor if unsure.
Possibly. Insulin and sulfonylureas may need to be lowered to prevent low blood sugar. Your doctor will guide changes. Do not adjust them yourself.

Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
MD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 14 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer

GLP-1 treatment starts with a medical assessment, followed by a low starting dose that is increased in steps every few weeks. This slow increase, called titration, helps the body adjust and reduces nausea and other side effects. Most people reach the working dose within about 2 to 4 months. Regular follow-up lets the doctor adjust the dose, check side effects and support diet and activity.

Starting a new injection can feel daunting. Knowing what the first weeks look like helps you feel prepared. This guide explains how treatment usually begins, why the dose goes up slowly and what to expect.
Before the first dose, your doctor will:
The medicine, brand, pen and form (injection or tablet) are chosen based on your condition, goals and availability. Your doctor will teach you or a family member how to use the pen.
The first dose is a small starting dose. It is not meant to give the full effect. Its job is to let your gut and brain get used to the medicine.

Most schedules increase the dose every 4 weeks, depending on the medicine. For example, weekly injections often start at the lowest dose for four weeks, then step up. The exact schedule depends on the product. Your doctor will follow the approved plan for your medicine.
The dose may be:
You do not need to reach the highest dose to benefit.
If you take insulin or a sulfonylurea (such as glimepiride), your doctor may reduce these doses to avoid low blood sugar as the GLP-1 medicine works. Never adjust them on your own.

For weekly injections, instructions usually allow a missed dose to be taken within a few days of the due date. If it is much later, skip it and continue on schedule. Follow the instructions for your specific medicine, and ask your doctor if unsure.
When should you see a doctor urgently?
Contact your doctor if you have severe or persistent stomach pain, repeated vomiting, unable to drink fluids, signs of dehydration, severe low sugar symptoms or allergic signs.

A slow start makes treatment easier to stick with. With good support, most people settle into their treatment in a few weeks. To begin safely, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.

How Much Weight Can You Lose on GLP-1 Medicines?
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 8 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
In clinical studies, people taking GLP-1 medicines for weight management lost on average about 5 to 15 percent of their body weight over several months to a year, depending on the medicine, dose and lifestyle. People with type 2 diabetes usually lose somewhat less. Results vary widely, and weight is often regained if treatment stops.
Social media is full of dramatic before-and-after photos. Real results are meaningful but more gradual, and they differ from person to person. Knowing what is realistic helps you set goals and avoid disappointment.
What do studies show?
Large trials have shown that:
Semaglutide at higher weight-management doses led to average weight loss in the range of about 15 percent over roughly a year and a half in people without diabetes.
Tirzepatide at higher doses showed average losses of about 15 to 20 percent or more in some studies.
In people with type 2 diabetes, average weight loss is usually lower, often around 5 to 10 percent.
Lower doses used mainly for blood sugar control give smaller weight changes.
These are averages. Some people lose less, and a few lose more.
How long does it take?
First 4 to 8 weeks: The dose is gradually increased. Weight loss is often slow at first.
3 to 6 months: Most visible weight loss begins as the dose approaches the target.
6 to 12 months: Weight loss usually peaks, then levels off.
After a year: Weight usually stabilises while treatment continues.
What else improves besides weight?
Blood sugar and HbA1c
Blood pressure
Waist size and belly fat
Fatty liver markers
Cholesterol and triglycerides
Sleep apnoea and joint pain in some people
For some medicines, heart and kidney benefits in selected patients
What affects your results?
The medicine and dose: Different molecules and strengths produce different results.
Your starting weight: People with higher body weight often lose more kilograms, although the percentage may be similar.
Diabetes status: Weight loss is often smaller in people with diabetes.
Diet and activity: Protein-rich meals, fibre and regular activity improve results and protect muscle.
Sleep and stress: Poor sleep and high stress can slow progress.
Side effects: Severe nausea may limit the dose.
Consistency: Missing doses reduces results.
Other medicines: Some medicines for diabetes, mood or epilepsy can cause weight gain.
Do you lose only fat?
Some of the weight lost can be muscle. To protect it, eat enough protein, do strength exercises two to three times a week and avoid crash diets. A dietitian can help with a personalised plan.
What if you do not lose weight?
A small number of people respond poorly. Your doctor will check your dose, adherence, diet, sleep, other medicines and conditions such as thyroid disease or Cushing's syndrome. Sometimes a different medicine or approach is better.
How should you set goals?
Aim for gradual loss of around 0.5 to 1 kg a week at most, after the initial phase.
Set the first goal at about 5 percent of body weight.
Track waist size, energy and blood sugar, not just the scale.
Review progress with your doctor every few weeks to months.
When should you see a doctor?
See your doctor if you lose weight very fast, feel weak or dizzy, have severe stomach pain, cannot eat or drink, or notice signs of dehydration.
Points to keep
Average weight loss with GLP-1 medicines ranges from about 5 to 15 percent or more, depending on the medicine and dose.
People with diabetes usually lose less.
Most weight loss occurs over 6 to 12 months.
Protein, strength training and sleep protect results and muscle.
Treatment is a long-term plan, not a quick fix.
GLP-1 medicines are a powerful tool, but they work best together with food, movement and follow-up. Realistic goals keep you motivated and safe. For a personalised plan, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
Sources and further reading
NIDDK: Prescription medicines for overweight and obesity
WHO: Diabetes fact sheet
Frequently asked questions
How much weight can I lose with semaglutide?
At weight-management doses, studies show average loss of about 15 percent of body weight over around a year and a half, though individuals vary. In type 2 diabetes the average is lower. Your result depends on dose, diet and consistency.
How much weight can I lose with tirzepatide?
At higher doses, studies show average weight loss of about 15 to 20 percent or more in people without diabetes. In people with diabetes, it is usually less. Individual results vary.
How fast will I lose weight on a GLP-1 medicine?
Most people lose weight slowly at first, as the dose increases over weeks. Noticeable loss usually appears after a few months and peaks at about 6 to 12 months.
Can I lose weight without exercise on GLP-1?
You may, but it is not ideal. Without strength exercise and enough protein, more of the weight lost can be muscle. Activity also improves blood sugar, mood and long-term maintenance.
Why am I not losing weight on a GLP-1 medicine?
Possible reasons include a low dose, missed doses, high-calorie liquids, poor sleep, other medicines or medical conditions. Review your habits and dose with your doctor before changing anything.
Will I regain weight after stopping?
Many people regain a significant part of the weight when they stop, because appetite returns. A maintenance plan with your doctor helps reduce this risk.

faqs.a: Contact your doctor, as treatment may need adjusting.

How Often Should You Check Blood Sugar and HbA1c?
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 2 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
HbA1c is usually checked every three months when control is changing and every six months when it is stable. Home blood sugar testing may range from several times a day for people on insulin to a few times a week for those on tablets with stable control. Your doctor will set a schedule for you.
Testing shows how well your plan is working. The right frequency depends on your treatment, your control and your doctor's advice.
HbA1c testing
Every three months if treatment has changed or sugar is not at target
Every six months if control is stable
No fasting needed
Home blood sugar testing
On insulin
Often before meals and at bedtime, and when symptoms occur.
On tablets only
Often fasting and after meals a few days a week, as advised.
Newly diagnosed or changing treatment
More frequent testing for a period.
Useful times to test
Fasting, before breakfast
Two hours after a main meal
Before bed
When you feel unwell or have symptoms of low or high sugar
Keep a record
Write readings in a notebook or app with notes on meals and activity. Bring it to your visits.
Other regular checks
Blood pressure and cholesterol
Kidney tests
Eye and foot examinations
In short
HbA1c is checked every three to six months.
Home testing depends on treatment.
Test at useful times, not randomly.
Keep a record.
Follow your doctor's plan.
Testing is only useful when the results guide action. For a monitoring plan, you can consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
When to seek urgent care
Seek urgent care for extreme thirst with vomiting, confusion, deep rapid breathing, unusual drowsiness, or signs of very low sugar such as sweating, shaking and confusion.
Sources and further reading
WHO: Diabetes fact sheet
NIDDK: What is diabetes
Frequently asked questions
Do I need to test daily if I take only tablets?
Not always. Your doctor will advise how often.
Why is my HbA1c high when my fasting sugar is normal?
Post-meal sugars may be high. Testing after meals can help.
Can I test at any time?
Yes, but readings are most useful at set times.
Is a glucometer accurate?
Reasonably, if used correctly. Lab tests are the reference.
Should I test when I feel unwell?
Yes, illness can raise sugar.
What if my readings are always high?
Contact your doctor, as treatment may need adjusting.

faqs.q: How often should I check HbA1c with prediabetes?
faqs.a: Most people should check at least once a year. Testing every three to six months may be helpful if results are close to the diabetes range or you are making lifestyle changes.

faqs.q: Do I need a home glucometer for prediabetes?
faqs.a: Routine home monitoring is usually not necessary. Lab tests such as HbA1c and fasting glucose are the main tools. Your doctor may suggest occasional home checks in some situations.

faqs.q: Which test is best for monitoring prediabetes?
faqs.a: HbA1c and fasting glucose are both commonly used. Using the same test each time makes comparison easier. Your doctor may also use an oral glucose tolerance test in some cases.

faqs.q: What other tests are needed with prediabetes?
faqs.a: Blood pressure, cholesterol, triglycerides, weight, waist circumference and sometimes liver and kidney tests help assess overall metabolic and heart risk.

faqs.q: What if my test moves into the diabetes range?
faqs.a: Your doctor will usually confirm with a repeat test and then discuss treatment, which may include lifestyle changes and medicines. Early treatment helps prevent complications.

How Often to Test for Diabetes With Prediabetes
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 3 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
People with prediabetes are generally advised to test at least once a year with HbA1c or fasting glucose. Testing every three to six months can be useful while making lifestyle changes or if results are close to the diabetes range. Doctors may also check blood pressure, cholesterol, kidney function and weight.
If you have been told you have prediabetes, regular testing is important. It shows whether your lifestyle changes are working and catches diabetes early if it develops. Testing frequency depends on your results and risk factors.
Why is regular testing important?
Prediabetes can progress silently to type 2 diabetes
Early diagnosis allows early treatment and fewer complications
Test results show whether diet, exercise and weight loss are helping
Regular checks keep motivation high
Which tests are used?
HbA1c
Shows average blood sugar over about three months and does not require fasting.
Fasting plasma glucose
Measures blood sugar after an overnight fast.
Oral glucose tolerance test
Measures sugar before and two hours after a glucose drink. It can detect problems not seen on fasting tests and is sometimes used in high-risk people.
Using the same test each time helps compare results.
How often should you test?
At least once a year for most people with prediabetes
Every three to six months if your HbA1c is close to 6.5 percent, if you are actively making changes, or if your doctor recommends closer monitoring
More frequently if you develop symptoms such as excessive thirst, frequent urination or unexplained weight loss
What other checks matter?
Prediabetes often comes with other risk factors. Doctors may check:
Blood pressure
Cholesterol and triglycerides
Weight, BMI and waist circumference
Liver function and fatty liver risk
Kidney function in some people
Should you check sugar at home?
Routine home glucose monitoring is not usually necessary for prediabetes. Your doctor may suggest occasional checks in specific situations, but lab HbA1c or fasting glucose remain the main tests.
What do changes in results mean?
Falling into the normal range: keep up healthy habits and continue annual checks
Staying in the prediabetes range: review diet, activity and weight goals
Rising toward or into the diabetes range: your doctor will confirm and discuss treatment
What to remember
Test at least once a year with prediabetes.
Test more often if results are high or you are making changes.
HbA1c and fasting glucose are the main tests.
Check blood pressure, cholesterol and weight too.
Regular testing supports early action.
Regular testing turns prediabetes into an opportunity to stay ahead of diabetes. Your doctor can set the right schedule for you. Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur monitors patients with prediabetes and helps them stay on track.
When to seek urgent care
Seek urgent care for extreme thirst with vomiting, confusion, deep rapid breathing or unusual drowsiness, which can signal very high sugar.
Sources and further reading
ADA: Prediabetes
NIDDK: Preventing type 2 diabetes
Frequently asked questions
How often should I check HbA1c with prediabetes?
Most people should check at least once a year. Testing every three to six months may be helpful if results are close to the diabetes range or you are making lifestyle changes.
Do I need a home glucometer for prediabetes?
Routine home monitoring is usually not necessary. Lab tests such as HbA1c and fasting glucose are the main tools. Your doctor may suggest occasional home checks in some situations.
Which test is best for monitoring prediabetes?
HbA1c and fasting glucose are both commonly used. Using the same test each time makes comparison easier. Your doctor may also use an oral glucose tolerance test in some cases.
What other tests are needed with prediabetes?
Blood pressure, cholesterol, triglycerides, weight, waist circumference and sometimes liver and kidney tests help assess overall metabolic and heart risk.
What if my test moves into the diabetes range?
Your doctor will usually confirm with a repeat test and then discuss treatment, which may include lifestyle changes and medicines. Early treatment helps prevent complications.

faqs.q: What is an AGP report?
faqs.a: The Ambulatory Glucose Profile is a standard one-page CGM report. It shows time in range, average glucose, variability and a graph of a typical day built from about 14 days of data.

faqs.q: What is a good GMI?
faqs.a: The GMI is an estimated HbA1c from CGM data. A GMI near 7 percent corresponds to an average glucose of around 154 mg/dL. Targets vary by person, so ask your doctor.

faqs.q: What does a wide band on the AGP mean?
faqs.a: It means your glucose varies a lot at that time of day. A narrower band suggests steadier control. Wide bands often signal inconsistent meals, activity or medicine timing.

faqs.q: Why does my CGM average differ from my HbA1c?
faqs.a: CGM reflects only the days you wore the sensor, while HbA1c covers about three months. Individual differences in red blood cell life can also cause gaps. Both are useful.

faqs.q: How many days of CGM data are needed?
faqs.a: At least 14 days, with the sensor worn for 70 percent or more of that time, gives a reliable picture of your patterns.

faqs.q: What is the dawn phenomenon on a CGM?
faqs.a: It is a natural early-morning rise in glucose caused by hormones such as cortisol and growth hormone. It is common in diabetes. If it is high, your doctor may adjust treatment.

How to Read a CGM Report: AGP and Glucose Patterns
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 17 October 2026 · 5 min read
Quick answer
A CGM report usually shows the Ambulatory Glucose Profile (AGP), a graph that combines your readings over 14 days into one typical day. Key numbers are time in range, time above and below range, average glucose, the glucose management indicator (GMI) and variability. Look for patterns: when sugars rise, when they fall, and how steady the line is. Review them with your doctor.
After wearing a continuous glucose monitor for two weeks, you receive a report full of charts and numbers. It can look overwhelming. In truth, only a few parts matter, and learning them helps you see what is happening with your diabetes.
What is the AGP?
The AGP is a standard report format used worldwide. It includes:
A summary of key metrics
A bar showing time in each range
A graph of a typical day, built from 14 days of data
Daily graphs for each day
What are the key metrics?
Time in range (TIR)
The percentage of time your glucose stays between 70 and 180 mg/dL. The common goal is above 70 percent.
Time above range (TAR)
The percentage of time above 180 mg/dL, with a separate figure for above 250 mg/dL. Lower is better.
Time below range (TBR)
The percentage of time below 70 mg/dL, and below 54 mg/dL. These should be as low as possible, ideally less than 4 percent and less than 1 percent.
Average glucose
The mean of all readings. It is similar to HbA1c but covers only the wearing period.
Glucose management indicator (GMI)
An estimated HbA1c calculated from the CGM average. It may differ from your lab HbA1c.
Glucose variability (CV)
The coefficient of variation shows how much your glucose swings. A value of 36 percent or lower suggests stable sugars.
Sensor use
The report should show that you wore the sensor for at least 70 percent of the 14 days. Otherwise, the data may not represent your usual pattern.
How do you read the AGP graph?
The graph has a central line, the median glucose, and shaded bands around it.
Median line (50th percentile): Your typical glucose at each time of day.
Dark band (25th to 75th percentile): Where half of your readings fall.
Light band (5th to 95th percentile): Where most readings fall. A wide band means large swings.
Target range lines: Usually at 70 and 180 mg/dL.
A flat, narrow band within the target range is the ideal picture.
What patterns should you look for?
Post-meal peaks: A rise after breakfast, lunch or dinner. This suggests food portions or timing need review.
Early morning rise: Sometimes called the dawn phenomenon. It happens due to morning hormones.
Night-time lows: Dips below 70 mg/dL during sleep need urgent review of medicines.
Daytime lows before meals: May be a sign of medicine timing problems.
High overnight plateau: May be due to a heavy dinner or insufficient medicine.
Wide swings: Suggest inconsistent meals, activity or medicine timing.
How do you use the report?
Check sensor wear and time in range first.
Look at time below range. Fix low readings before high ones.
Look for patterns that repeat across several days.
Compare with your food, activity, sleep and medicine diary.
Pick one or two changes to try, such as a smaller dinner or a post-meal walk.
Review again after the next sensor.
What mistakes should you avoid?
Reacting to a single reading rather than patterns
Changing medicine doses without your doctor
Ignoring low readings that occur at night
Comparing your numbers with someone else's
When should you see a doctor?
Contact your doctor if you see frequent lows, long periods above 250 mg/dL, sudden changes from your usual pattern or if the numbers confuse you.
A quick recap
The AGP combines 14 days of CGM data into one typical day.
Focus on time in range, time below range and variability.
Look for repeated patterns, not single readings.
Fix lows first, then address highs.
Review the report with your doctor and plan small changes.
A CGM report is a map, and your doctor helps you read it. Small, steady changes based on real patterns improve control and safety. To review your report, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
Sources and further reading
NIDDK: Continuous glucose monitoring
WHO: Diabetes fact sheet
Frequently asked questions
What is an AGP report?
The Ambulatory Glucose Profile is a standard one-page CGM report. It shows time in range, average glucose, variability and a graph of a typical day built from about 14 days of data.
What is a good GMI?
The GMI is an estimated HbA1c from CGM data. A GMI near 7 percent corresponds to an average glucose of around 154 mg/dL. Targets vary by person, so ask your doctor.
What does a wide band on the AGP mean?
It means your glucose varies a lot at that time of day. A narrower band suggests steadier control. Wide bands often signal inconsistent meals, activity or medicine timing.
Why does my CGM average differ from my HbA1c?
CGM reflects only the days you wore the sensor, while HbA1c covers about three months. Individual differences in red blood cell life can also cause gaps. Both are useful.
How many days of CGM data are needed?
At least 14 days, with the sensor worn for 70 percent or more of that time, gives a reliable picture of your patterns.
What is the dawn phenomenon on a CGM?
It is a natural early-morning rise in glucose caused by hormones such as cortisol and growth hormone. It is common in diabetes. If it is high, your doctor may adjust treatment.
