faqs.q: Is there a GLP-1 tablet for diabetes?
faqs.a: Yes. Oral semaglutide is an approved GLP-1 tablet for type 2 diabetes in several countries. Availability and brands in India should be confirmed with your doctor and pharmacy.

faqs.q: How do I take an oral GLP-1 tablet?
faqs.a: Take it on an empty stomach in the morning with a small sip of water, swallow it whole, and wait about 30 minutes before eating, drinking or taking other medicines.

faqs.q: Are GLP-1 tablets as effective as injections?
faqs.a: Studies show that tablets lower blood sugar and weight, but results can differ from injections, partly because absorption is variable. The best choice depends on your goals and routine.

faqs.q: Can I take a GLP-1 tablet if I fear needles?
faqs.a: Possibly. Many needle-fearful people prefer tablets. Talk to your doctor to check if it suits your condition and whether you can follow the dosing rules.

faqs.q: Will pills replace weight-loss injections?
faqs.a: Not completely, at least for now. Pills will add options, and newer oral medicines may be easier to take. Injections remain widely used, especially when strong effects are needed.

faqs.q: What are the side effects of GLP-1 tablets?
faqs.a: They are similar to injections: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, constipation and stomach discomfort, mostly in the first weeks. Report severe pain or allergic symptoms right away.

Oral GLP-1 Tablets: Are Pills Replacing Injections?
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 10 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
Oral GLP-1 tablets exist and are being developed further. The first approved tablet uses semaglutide with an absorption enhancer so that it can pass through the stomach lining. It must be taken on an empty stomach with a small amount of water. Pills may suit people who fear needles, but they are not a complete replacement yet, and injections remain common.
Many people dislike injections. When news spread that GLP-1 medicines are also available as tablets, hope grew that needles might soon be unnecessary. The truth is more nuanced. Pills are an important step forward, but they work a little differently from injections.

Studies show that tablets lower blood sugar and weight, but results can differ from injections, partly because absorption is variable. The best choice depends on your goals and routine.

Possibly. Many needle-fearful people prefer tablets. Talk to your doctor to check if it suits your condition and whether you can follow the dosing rules.

Not completely, at least for now. Pills will add options, and newer oral medicines may be easier to take. Injections remain widely used, especially when strong effects are needed.

They are similar to injections: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, constipation and stomach discomfort, mostly in the first weeks. Report severe pain or allergic symptoms right away.

faqs.q: What foods should I avoid with prediabetes?
faqs.a: Limit sugary drinks, sweets, maida-based bakery foods, fried snacks, large portions of white rice and processed foods. These raise blood sugar quickly. You do not need to avoid all carbohydrates, but choose whole grains and control portions.

faqs.q: Can I eat rice if I have prediabetes?
faqs.a: Yes, in controlled portions. Combine rice with dal, vegetables and protein, and consider mixing with millets or choosing brown rice. Keeping rice to about a quarter of your plate helps.

faqs.q: Which roti is best for prediabetes?
faqs.a: Whole wheat, jowar, bajra or ragi rotis are better choices than maida rotis because they contain more fibre. Portion size still matters.

faqs.q: Are fruits allowed in prediabetes?
faqs.a: Yes. Whole fruits such as guava, apple, papaya, orange and berries are good in moderate portions. Avoid fruit juices and limit very sweet fruits in large amounts.

faqs.q: Do I need a special diabetic diet for prediabetes?
faqs.a: No special foods are needed. A balanced Indian diet with portion control, more vegetables and protein, whole grains and fewer sweets and refined foods is effective. A dietitian can personalise it.

Prediabetes Diet: What to Eat in an Indian Diet
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 4 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
For prediabetes, fill half your plate with vegetables, a quarter with protein such as dal, paneer, eggs, fish or chicken, and a quarter with whole grains or millets. Limit sugary drinks, sweets, refined flour (maida) products, fried snacks and large portions of white rice. Eat regular meals, include fibre and watch portion sizes.
A prediabetes diet is an eating pattern that helps bring blood sugar back toward normal and lowers the risk of type 2 diabetes. It does not require special foods or giving up home-cooked Indian meals. It focuses on balance, portions and smarter choices.
Why does diet matter in prediabetes?
Carbohydrates have the biggest impact on blood sugar. Refined carbohydrates and sugar raise blood sugar quickly, while fibre, protein and healthy fats slow absorption. Better food choices also support weight loss, which improves insulin sensitivity.
What should you eat more of?
Vegetables
Leafy greens, gourds, beans, cauliflower, cabbage, okra and salads add fibre and nutrients with few calories.
Whole grains and millets
Jowar, bajra, ragi, broken wheat, brown rice and whole wheat atta digest more slowly than refined grains.
Pulses and legumes
Dal, rajma, chana, moong and sprouts provide protein and fibre.
Protein
Paneer, curd, eggs, fish, chicken and tofu help with fullness and steadier sugar.
Healthy fats in moderation
Nuts, seeds and small amounts of cooking oil such as mustard or groundnut oil.
Whole fruits
Choose whole fruits like guava, apple, papaya or orange in moderate portions rather than juices.
What should you limit?
Sugary drinks, packaged juices and sweetened tea or coffee
Sweets, mithai and desserts
Maida-based foods like white bread, biscuits, bakery items and noodles
Large portions of white rice and potatoes
Fried snacks such as samosas, pakoras and chips
Processed and packaged foods high in sugar or salt
How do you build a balanced plate?
Use the plate method:
Half: non-starchy vegetables and salad
Quarter: protein such as dal, paneer, fish or chicken
Quarter: whole grain roti, millet bhakri or a controlled portion of rice
What are simple swaps?
White rice to mixed rice with vegetables or millet
Maida roti to whole wheat or jowar roti
Fruit juice to whole fruit
Fried snacks to roasted chana or sprouts chaat
Sweetened tea to unsweetened or less sugar
Does meal timing matter?
Regular meals help prevent overeating and large sugar spikes. Avoid long gaps followed by heavy meals. A short walk after meals can help lower post-meal sugar.
A quick recap
You can keep Indian food while managing prediabetes.
Use the plate method for balance.
Choose whole grains, pulses, vegetables and protein.
Limit sugar, maida, fried foods and large rice portions.
Regular meals and walks after meals help.
Small, sustainable food changes can bring prediabetes back toward normal. A personalised plan works better than strict diets. Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur helps patients build practical Indian meal plans for prediabetes and diabetes.
When to seek urgent care
Seek urgent care for extreme thirst with vomiting, confusion, deep rapid breathing or unusual drowsiness, which can signal very high sugar.
Sources and further reading
ADA: Prediabetes
NIDDK: Preventing type 2 diabetes
Frequently asked questions
What foods should I avoid with prediabetes?
Limit sugary drinks, sweets, maida-based bakery foods, fried snacks, large portions of white rice and processed foods. These raise blood sugar quickly. You do not need to avoid all carbohydrates, but choose whole grains and control portions.
Can I eat rice if I have prediabetes?
Yes, in controlled portions. Combine rice with dal, vegetables and protein, and consider mixing with millets or choosing brown rice. Keeping rice to about a quarter of your plate helps.
Which roti is best for prediabetes?
Whole wheat, jowar, bajra or ragi rotis are better choices than maida rotis because they contain more fibre. Portion size still matters.
Are fruits allowed in prediabetes?
Yes. Whole fruits such as guava, apple, papaya, orange and berries are good in moderate portions. Avoid fruit juices and limit very sweet fruits in large amounts.
Do I need a special diabetic diet for prediabetes?
No special foods are needed. A balanced Indian diet with portion control, more vegetables and protein, whole grains and fewer sweets and refined foods is effective. A dietitian can personalise it.

faqs.q: What HbA1c level is considered prediabetes?
faqs.a: An HbA1c of 5.7% to 6.4% falls within the prediabetes range for non-pregnant adults. An HbA1c of 6.5% or higher is within the diabetes range, although a diabetes diagnosis generally requires appropriate confirmation when there is no unequivocal hyperglycaemia.

faqs.q: Can prediabetes go away?
faqs.a: Prediabetes can improve, and some people return to a blood glucose range below the prediabetes threshold. Improvements may occur with changes in physical activity, eating habits, weight management when appropriate and treatment of other metabolic risk factors. Continued monitoring is still important because glucose levels can rise again.

faqs.q: Does prediabetes always cause symptoms?
faqs.a: No. Prediabetes commonly has no clear symptoms. A person may feel completely well while having an elevated HbA1c or fasting glucose level. This is why blood testing is important for people who have relevant diabetes risk factors.

faqs.q: Can I eat rice if I have prediabetes?
faqs.a: Rice does not automatically need to be eliminated. The amount, type of rice, meal composition and overall eating pattern matter. Combining a sensible carbohydrate portion with vegetables, protein and other nutrient-rich foods can be more practical than completely avoiding traditional staples.

faqs.q: How much exercise should I do if I have prediabetes?
faqs.a: For many adults at high risk of diabetes, structured prevention programs aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity per week. The appropriate amount and intensity depend on your age, fitness, medical conditions and current activity level.

faqs.q: Can prediabetes become Type 2 diabetes?
faqs.a: Yes, prediabetes increases the risk of developing Type 2 diabetes, but progression is not inevitable. Risk varies between individuals. Lifestyle changes, appropriate weight management, regular physical activity and medical follow-up can help reduce the risk.

faqs.q: Do people with prediabetes need medicine?
faqs.a: Not everyone does. Lifestyle intervention is central to prevention. Medication such as metformin may be considered for selected people at particularly high risk, depending on factors such as age, BMI, glucose levels, HbA1c and previous gestational diabetes.

faqs.q: How often should HbA1c be checked with prediabetes?
faqs.a: The ADA recommends testing people with prediabetes at least annually, although the appropriate interval can vary according to individual risk and previous results. Your doctor may recommend more frequent monitoring when there is a reason to do so.

Prediabetes: HbA1c, Blood Sugar Levels, Symptoms & How to Prevent Type 2 Diabetes
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 3 October 2026 · 12 to 15 minutes
Quick answer
Prediabetes is generally diagnosed when an HbA1c is 5.7% to 6.4%, fasting plasma glucose is 100 to 125 mg/dL, or the 2-hour glucose during a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test is 140 to 199 mg/dL. It usually does not cause clear symptoms. Prevention focuses on improving food quality, increasing physical activity, addressing excess weight when present, and following an appropriate monitoring plan.
Prediabetes means that your blood glucose is higher than the normal range, but it has not yet reached the level used to diagnose diabetes. The important part is that prediabetes often causes no obvious symptoms. A person can feel completely well and still have an abnormal HbA1c or blood glucose result.
That is why finding prediabetes is useful. It gives you an opportunity to look at your blood sugar, weight, food habits, physical activity and other risk factors before Type 2 diabetes develops.

What is prediabetes?
Prediabetes is a state in which blood glucose levels are above the usual healthy range but below the diagnostic threshold for diabetes.
It is often associated with insulin resistance. In simple terms, insulin is a hormone that helps glucose move from the bloodstream into cells. When the body's tissues become less responsive to insulin, the pancreas has to produce more insulin to maintain normal glucose levels.
Over time, this compensation may become less effective, and blood glucose begins to rise.
Prediabetes is therefore not simply a slightly abnormal blood test. It can be a sign that the body's glucose-regulation system is under increasing metabolic stress.
At the same time, a diagnosis of prediabetes should not be viewed as a prediction that you will definitely develop diabetes. Risk varies from person to person.
What HbA1c level means you have prediabetes?
An HbA1c of 5.7% to 6.4% falls within the prediabetes range.
HbA1c is different from a single blood glucose reading. It reflects your average blood glucose exposure over roughly the previous two to three months.
For example, someone may have a fasting glucose that looks acceptable on one morning but still have an elevated HbA1c. Conversely, an isolated high glucose result does not automatically tell the whole story.
How to understand the HbA1c number
Below 5.7%: generally below the prediabetes range
5.7% to 6.4%: prediabetes range
6.5% or higher: diabetes range
A result close to a diagnostic threshold may require appropriate confirmation and clinical interpretation. In people without unequivocal hyperglycaemia, diabetes generally requires confirmation with repeat testing or another abnormal diagnostic test.
Your HbA1c should therefore be interpreted in context rather than treated as a number that tells you everything about your health.
What blood sugar level is considered prediabetes?
Prediabetes can be identified using more than one glucose test.
Fasting blood sugar
A fasting glucose of 100 to 125 mg/dL is in the prediabetes range.
The test is usually performed after an appropriate period without eating, as instructed by the laboratory or clinician.
Two-hour glucose test
During a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test, a 2-hour glucose value of 140 to 199 mg/dL falls in the prediabetes range.
Why can different tests give different results?
HbA1c and glucose tests measure different aspects of glucose metabolism. It is therefore possible for someone to have a result in the prediabetes range on one test and a different result on another.
Rather than trying to interpret each number independently, discuss the overall pattern with your doctor.
Does prediabetes have symptoms?
Often, no.
This is one of the reasons prediabetes can go unnoticed.
Some people may report symptoms such as tiredness or increased hunger, but these symptoms are not specific enough to diagnose prediabetes. Many people discover the condition only after a routine blood test.
This is also why waiting for symptoms is not a reliable way to decide whether you should be tested.
If you have risk factors for diabetes, periodic screening can identify changes before symptoms become apparent.
Why does prediabetes happen?
There is rarely one single cause.
Prediabetes can develop through a combination of genetic, metabolic and lifestyle factors. Insulin resistance is an important part of the process for many people.
Factors that can increase risk include:
Excess body weight, particularly abdominal fat
Low physical activity
A family history of Type 2 diabetes
Increasing age
Previous gestational diabetes
High blood pressure
Abnormal cholesterol or triglyceride levels
Conditions associated with insulin resistance
Certain medications or medical conditions
Not everyone with prediabetes has the same combination of risk factors.
Who is at higher risk of prediabetes?
You may have a higher risk if diabetes runs in your family or if you have several metabolic risk factors.
It is worth discussing screening with a doctor if you have:
A parent or sibling with Type 2 diabetes
Overweight or obesity
High blood pressure
Abnormal cholesterol levels
A history of gestational diabetes
Limited physical activity
Previous abnormal blood glucose results
Other conditions associated with insulin resistance
Risk assessment should not be based on body weight alone.
Why is prediabetes important for Indians?
South Asian populations can develop Type 2 diabetes and metabolic abnormalities at lower levels of body weight than might be expected from conventional assumptions based only on obesity.
That makes metabolic risk particularly relevant when assessing an Indian patient.
Someone who does not consider themselves overweight can still have insulin resistance, abdominal fat, abnormal lipids or elevated blood glucose.
This is one reason routine screening should be based on the individual's overall risk profile rather than appearance alone.
How is prediabetes diagnosed?
Prediabetes is diagnosed through blood testing.
Common tests include:
HbA1c
This measures glycated haemoglobin and provides an estimate of average blood glucose over the preceding few months.
Fasting plasma glucose
This measures blood glucose after fasting.
Oral glucose tolerance test
This involves measuring glucose before and after consuming a standard glucose drink.
A doctor may choose one test or more than one depending on the person's circumstances.
It is also important to understand that one abnormal result does not always tell the complete story. The test used, laboratory conditions, symptoms, medical history and whether confirmation is required all matter.
What should you do after being diagnosed with prediabetes?
The first step is not panic.
The diagnosis is an opportunity to identify the factors contributing to your blood glucose level and decide what needs to change.
A useful medical assessment may include looking at:
HbA1c and glucose readings
Blood pressure
Weight and waist measurements
Lipid profile
Family history
Physical activity
Eating patterns
Sleep and other lifestyle factors
Other conditions associated with metabolic risk
From there, your doctor can help decide how frequently you need monitoring and whether lifestyle intervention alone is appropriate or whether additional treatment should be considered.
Can prediabetes be prevented from becoming Type 2 diabetes?
In many people, the risk can be reduced substantially.
The strongest approach is usually not one dramatic change. It is a collection of manageable changes that can be maintained over time.
For adults with overweight or obesity who are at high risk, the 2026 ADA Standards recommend a structured lifestyle approach that aims for around 5 to 7% weight loss, where appropriate, together with at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity per week.
That does not mean everyone with prediabetes needs to lose weight.
If you are already at a healthy weight, the focus may instead be on food quality, activity, sleep, muscle strength and other metabolic risk factors.
What should you eat if you have prediabetes?
There is no single food plan that works for every person with prediabetes.
The goal is to build a pattern of eating that supports blood glucose control and is realistic enough to follow over the long term.
For many people, this means giving more space to:
Non-starchy vegetables
Whole fruits
Pulses and legumes
Whole grains
Nuts and seeds
Lean protein sources
Appropriate portions of dairy or alternatives
At the same time, it is useful to reduce frequent intake of:
Sugary drinks
Sweets and desserts
Refined grains
Highly processed foods
Foods that are very high in calories but low in nutritional value
The ADA emphasizes overall dietary quality and individualized nutrition rather than a single universal diet.
Do you have to stop eating rice or roti?
Not necessarily.
For an Indian household, completely removing staple foods may not be practical or necessary. Portion size, preparation, the type of carbohydrate, protein, vegetables and the overall meal pattern all matter.
A plate containing a large portion of rice with very little protein or vegetables is different from a balanced meal containing a more moderate carbohydrate portion alongside vegetables and protein.
The right approach depends on your overall health, glucose levels, dietary habits and goals.
How does exercise help with prediabetes?
Regular physical activity helps the body use glucose more effectively.
You do not need to begin with an intense workout routine.
Walking, cycling, swimming, resistance training and other activities can all have a place in a prevention plan.
A practical target for many adults is at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity each week, provided there is no medical reason to restrict exercise. Resistance training can also be useful.
Breaking up long periods of sitting is another simple habit worth considering.
The important point is consistency. A realistic routine performed regularly is usually more useful than an ambitious exercise plan that lasts only a few weeks.
Does weight loss help prediabetes?
If you have overweight or obesity, even a moderate amount of weight loss can improve glucose metabolism and other cardiometabolic risk factors.
For people at high risk, a target of approximately 5 to 7% reduction in body weight is used in structured diabetes-prevention approaches.
For example, a person weighing 80 kg would reach 5% weight loss after losing about 4 kg.
But the number on the scale is not the only outcome that matters.
Changes in waist circumference, blood glucose, blood pressure, fitness and metabolic health can also be clinically meaningful.
And if your weight is already in a healthy range, deliberately losing weight may not be appropriate. Prevention should be individualized.
Is medicine ever used for prediabetes?
Lifestyle intervention is an important part of prediabetes management, but medication may be considered for selected people at particularly high risk.
For example, the ADA notes that metformin may be considered in certain high-risk adults, including some younger adults with obesity, higher glucose or HbA1c levels, or a history of gestational diabetes.
That does not mean everyone with prediabetes should take metformin.
The decision depends on the individual's risk profile, medical history, laboratory results and other factors.
Do not start, stop or change diabetes medication based solely on information found online.
How often should you test for diabetes if you have prediabetes?
People with prediabetes generally need regular follow-up rather than a one-time test.
The ADA recommends annual testing for people with prediabetes, although your doctor may recommend a different interval depending on your individual risk and previous results.
Follow-up is useful because blood glucose can change over time.
A repeat HbA1c may show improvement, stability or progression. The result should be considered alongside your weight, lifestyle, medications and other health measurements.
What happens if prediabetes is ignored?
Prediabetes does not automatically become diabetes.
But it is associated with an increased risk of developing Type 2 diabetes, particularly when several risk factors are present.
It may also occur alongside other cardiometabolic problems such as high blood pressure, abnormal cholesterol and excess abdominal fat.
The purpose of identifying prediabetes is therefore not to label someone as "almost diabetic." It is to identify an opportunity for prevention and risk reduction.

Common myths about prediabetes
Myth 1: "prediabetes means i already have diabetes."
No. Prediabetes and diabetes have different diagnostic ranges. However, prediabetes is a meaningful warning sign that deserves attention.
Myth 2: "if i feel fine, my sugar must be normal."
Not necessarily. Prediabetes frequently has no noticeable symptoms.
Myth 3: "i need to stop eating carbohydrates completely."
No. Carbohydrates can be part of a healthy diet. Portion size, food quality and the overall meal pattern are more important than simply banning an entire food group.
Myth 4: "only people with obesity get prediabetes."
No. Body weight is only one part of metabolic risk.
Myth 5: "once i have prediabetes, diabetes is unavoidable."
No. Risk is increased, but progression is not inevitable. Lifestyle changes and appropriate medical follow-up can help reduce risk.
Myth 6: "one normal sugar test means i do not need another test."
Not always. Different tests provide different information, and your future screening schedule should depend on your overall risk.
When should you see a doctor about prediabetes?
Consider a medical evaluation if:
Your HbA1c is in the prediabetes range.
Your fasting glucose is repeatedly elevated.
You have several diabetes risk factors.
Diabetes runs strongly in your family.
You have previously had gestational diabetes.
You have unexplained changes in weight or metabolic health.
You have already been told that your blood sugar is abnormal and need a prevention plan.
If you develop symptoms such as marked thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss, significant weakness, vomiting, confusion or other concerning symptoms, seek medical assessment rather than assuming they are simply due to prediabetes.
What to remember
Prediabetes means blood glucose is higher than normal but below the diabetes range.
HbA1c of 5.7 to 6.4% is in the prediabetes range.
Prediabetes often causes no obvious symptoms.
Family history, excess weight, inactivity and other metabolic risk factors can increase risk.
You do not necessarily need to eliminate rice, roti or carbohydrates completely.
Regular physical activity is an important part of prevention.
If overweight or obesity is present, even moderate weight loss may improve metabolic health.
Some high-risk people may benefit from medication such as metformin under medical supervision.
Regular follow-up helps identify whether blood glucose is improving, remaining stable or progressing.
A prediabetes diagnosis is worth taking seriously, but it does not need to become a source of constant worry.
For many people, this is the stage at which relatively practical changes can make a meaningful difference. The focus should be on understanding why the blood glucose is elevated, identifying the risk factors that can be changed, and creating a plan that fits everyday life.
You do not need to overhaul everything overnight.
A sustainable eating pattern, regular movement, appropriate weight management when needed and periodic blood tests can form the foundation of diabetes prevention.
If your HbA1c or blood glucose has recently come back abnormal, discussing the result with a doctor can help you understand what it means in the context of your overall health.

Frequently asked questions
What HbA1c level is considered prediabetes?
An HbA1c of 5.7% to 6.4% falls within the prediabetes range for non-pregnant adults. An HbA1c of 6.5% or higher is within the diabetes range, although a diabetes diagnosis generally requires appropriate confirmation when there is no unequivocal hyperglycaemia.
Can prediabetes go away?
Prediabetes can improve, and some people return to a blood glucose range below the prediabetes threshold. Improvements may occur with changes in physical activity, eating habits, weight management when appropriate and treatment of other metabolic risk factors. Continued monitoring is still important because glucose levels can rise again.
Does prediabetes always cause symptoms?
No. Prediabetes commonly has no clear symptoms. A person may feel completely well while having an elevated HbA1c or fasting glucose level. This is why blood testing is important for people who have relevant diabetes risk factors.
Can I eat rice if I have prediabetes?
Rice does not automatically need to be eliminated. The amount, type of rice, meal composition and overall eating pattern matter. Combining a sensible carbohydrate portion with vegetables, protein and other nutrient-rich foods can be more practical than completely avoiding traditional staples.
How much exercise should I do if I have prediabetes?
For many adults at high risk of diabetes, structured prevention programs aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity per week. The appropriate amount and intensity depend on your age, fitness, medical conditions and current activity level.
Can prediabetes become Type 2 diabetes?
Yes, prediabetes increases the risk of developing Type 2 diabetes, but progression is not inevitable. Risk varies between individuals. Lifestyle changes, appropriate weight management, regular physical activity and medical follow-up can help reduce the risk.
Do people with prediabetes need medicine?
Not everyone does. Lifestyle intervention is central to prevention. Medication such as metformin may be considered for selected people at particularly high risk, depending on factors such as age, BMI, glucose levels, HbA1c and previous gestational diabetes.
How often should HbA1c be checked with prediabetes?
The ADA recommends testing people with prediabetes at least annually, although the appropriate interval can vary according to individual risk and previous results. Your doctor may recommend more frequent monitoring when there is a reason to do so.

Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
MD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 3 October 2026 · 12 to 15 minutes
Quick answer

Prediabetes is generally diagnosed when an HbA1c is 5.7% to 6.4%, fasting plasma glucose is 100 to 125 mg/dL, or the 2-hour glucose during a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test is 140 to 199 mg/dL. It usually does not cause clear symptoms. Prevention focuses on improving food quality, increasing physical activity, addressing excess weight when present, and following an appropriate monitoring plan.

Prediabetes means that your blood glucose is higher than the normal range, but it has not yet reached the level used to diagnose diabetes. The important part is that prediabetes often causes no obvious symptoms. A person can feel completely well and still have an abnormal HbA1c or blood glucose result.
That is why finding prediabetes is useful. It gives you an opportunity to look at your blood sugar, weight, food habits, physical activity and other risk factors before Type 2 diabetes develops.
Prediabetes does not mean that diabetes is inevitable. For many people, timely lifestyle changes and appropriate medical follow-up can substantially lower the risk of progression.
These ranges apply to non-pregnant adults; pregnancy uses different diagnostic criteria.
Prediabetes is a state in which blood glucose levels are above the usual healthy range but below the diagnostic threshold for diabetes.

It is often associated with insulin resistance. In simple terms, insulin is a hormone that helps glucose move from the bloodstream into cells. When the body's tissues become less responsive to insulin, the pancreas has to produce more insulin to maintain normal glucose levels.
Over time, this compensation may become less effective, and blood glucose begins to rise.
Prediabetes is therefore not simply a slightly abnormal blood test. It can be a sign that the body's glucose-regulation system is under increasing metabolic stress.
At the same time, a diagnosis of prediabetes should not be viewed as a prediction that you will definitely develop diabetes. Risk varies from person to person.
An HbA1c of 5.7% to 6.4% falls within the prediabetes range.
HbA1c is different from a single blood glucose reading. It reflects your average blood glucose exposure over roughly the previous two to three months.

For example, someone may have a fasting glucose that looks acceptable on one morning but still have an elevated HbA1c. Conversely, an isolated high glucose result does not automatically tell the whole story.

A result close to a diagnostic threshold may require appropriate confirmation and clinical interpretation. In people without unequivocal hyperglycaemia, diabetes generally requires confirmation with repeat testing or another abnormal diagnostic test.
Your HbA1c should therefore be interpreted in context rather than treated as a number that tells you everything about your health.
Prediabetes can be identified using more than one glucose test.
A fasting glucose of 100 to 125 mg/dL is in the prediabetes range.
The test is usually performed after an appropriate period without eating, as instructed by the laboratory or clinician.
During a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test, a 2-hour glucose value of 140 to 199 mg/dL falls in the prediabetes range.
HbA1c and glucose tests measure different aspects of glucose metabolism. It is therefore possible for someone to have a result in the prediabetes range on one test and a different result on another.
Rather than trying to interpret each number independently, discuss the overall pattern with your doctor.
Often, no.
This is one of the reasons prediabetes can go unnoticed.

Some people may report symptoms such as tiredness or increased hunger, but these symptoms are not specific enough to diagnose prediabetes. Many people discover the condition only after a routine blood test.
This is also why waiting for symptoms is not a reliable way to decide whether you should be tested.
If you have risk factors for diabetes, periodic screening can identify changes before symptoms become apparent.
There is rarely one single cause.
Prediabetes can develop through a combination of genetic, metabolic and lifestyle factors. Insulin resistance is an important part of the process for many people.
Factors that can increase risk include:
Not everyone with prediabetes has the same combination of risk factors.
You may have a higher risk if diabetes runs in your family or if you have several metabolic risk factors.
It is worth discussing screening with a doctor if you have:
Risk assessment should not be based on body weight alone.
South Asian populations can develop Type 2 diabetes and metabolic abnormalities at lower levels of body weight than might be expected from conventional assumptions based only on obesity.
That makes metabolic risk particularly relevant when assessing an Indian patient.
Someone who does not consider themselves overweight can still have insulin resistance, abdominal fat, abnormal lipids or elevated blood glucose.
This is one reason routine screening should be based on the individual's overall risk profile rather than appearance alone.
Prediabetes is diagnosed through blood testing.
Common tests include:
This measures glycated haemoglobin and provides an estimate of average blood glucose over the preceding few months.
This measures blood glucose after fasting.
This involves measuring glucose before and after consuming a standard glucose drink.
A doctor may choose one test or more than one depending on the person's circumstances.

It is also important to understand that one abnormal result does not always tell the complete story. The test used, laboratory conditions, symptoms, medical history and whether confirmation is required all matter.
The first step is not panic.
The diagnosis is an opportunity to identify the factors contributing to your blood glucose level and decide what needs to change.
A useful medical assessment may include looking at:
From there, your doctor can help decide how frequently you need monitoring and whether lifestyle intervention alone is appropriate or whether additional treatment should be considered.
In many people, the risk can be reduced substantially.
The strongest approach is usually not one dramatic change. It is a collection of manageable changes that can be maintained over time.

For adults with overweight or obesity who are at high risk, the 2026 ADA Standards recommend a structured lifestyle approach that aims for around 5 to 7% weight loss, where appropriate, together with at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity per week.
That does not mean everyone with prediabetes needs to lose weight.
If you are already at a healthy weight, the focus may instead be on food quality, activity, sleep, muscle strength and other metabolic risk factors.
There is no single food plan that works for every person with prediabetes.
The goal is to build a pattern of eating that supports blood glucose control and is realistic enough to follow over the long term.

At the same time, it is useful to reduce frequent intake of:
The ADA emphasizes overall dietary quality and individualized nutrition rather than a single universal diet.
Not necessarily.

For an Indian household, completely removing staple foods may not be practical or necessary. Portion size, preparation, the type of carbohydrate, protein, vegetables and the overall meal pattern all matter.
A plate containing a large portion of rice with very little protein or vegetables is different from a balanced meal containing a more moderate carbohydrate portion alongside vegetables and protein.
The right approach depends on your overall health, glucose levels, dietary habits and goals.
Regular physical activity helps the body use glucose more effectively.
You do not need to begin with an intense workout routine.
Walking, cycling, swimming, resistance training and other activities can all have a place in a prevention plan.

A practical target for many adults is at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity each week, provided there is no medical reason to restrict exercise. Resistance training can also be useful.
Breaking up long periods of sitting is another simple habit worth considering.
The important point is consistency. A realistic routine performed regularly is usually more useful than an ambitious exercise plan that lasts only a few weeks.
If you have overweight or obesity, even a moderate amount of weight loss can improve glucose metabolism and other cardiometabolic risk factors.
For people at high risk, a target of approximately 5 to 7% reduction in body weight is used in structured diabetes-prevention approaches.
For example, a person weighing 80 kg would reach 5% weight loss after losing about 4 kg.
But the number on the scale is not the only outcome that matters.
Changes in waist circumference, blood glucose, blood pressure, fitness and metabolic health can also be clinically meaningful.
And if your weight is already in a healthy range, deliberately losing weight may not be appropriate. Prevention should be individualized.
Lifestyle intervention is an important part of prediabetes management, but medication may be considered for selected people at particularly high risk.

For example, the ADA notes that metformin may be considered in certain high-risk adults, including some younger adults with obesity, higher glucose or HbA1c levels, or a history of gestational diabetes.
That does not mean everyone with prediabetes should take metformin.
The decision depends on the individual's risk profile, medical history, laboratory results and other factors.
Do not start, stop or change diabetes medication based solely on information found online.
People with prediabetes generally need regular follow-up rather than a one-time test.
The ADA recommends annual testing for people with prediabetes, although your doctor may recommend a different interval depending on your individual risk and previous results.
Follow-up is useful because blood glucose can change over time.
A repeat HbA1c may show improvement, stability or progression. The result should be considered alongside your weight, lifestyle, medications and other health measurements.
Prediabetes does not automatically become diabetes.
But it is associated with an increased risk of developing Type 2 diabetes, particularly when several risk factors are present.
It may also occur alongside other cardiometabolic problems such as high blood pressure, abnormal cholesterol and excess abdominal fat.
The purpose of identifying prediabetes is therefore not to label someone as "almost diabetic." It is to identify an opportunity for prevention and risk reduction.
The diagnostic thresholds above are based on current ADA criteria for non-pregnant adults.
No. Prediabetes and diabetes have different diagnostic ranges. However, prediabetes is a meaningful warning sign that deserves attention.
Not necessarily. Prediabetes frequently has no noticeable symptoms.
No. Carbohydrates can be part of a healthy diet. Portion size, food quality and the overall meal pattern are more important than simply banning an entire food group.
No. Body weight is only one part of metabolic risk.
No. Risk is increased, but progression is not inevitable. Lifestyle changes and appropriate medical follow-up can help reduce risk.
Not always. Different tests provide different information, and your future screening schedule should depend on your overall risk.
Consider a medical evaluation if:

If you develop symptoms such as marked thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss, significant weakness, vomiting, confusion or other concerning symptoms, seek medical assessment rather than assuming they are simply due to prediabetes.
A prediabetes diagnosis is worth taking seriously, but it does not need to become a source of constant worry.

For many people, this is the stage at which relatively practical changes can make a meaningful difference. The focus should be on understanding why the blood glucose is elevated, identifying the risk factors that can be changed, and creating a plan that fits everyday life.
You do not need to overhaul everything overnight.
A sustainable eating pattern, regular movement, appropriate weight management when needed and periodic blood tests can form the foundation of diabetes prevention.
If your HbA1c or blood glucose has recently come back abnormal, discussing the result with a doctor can help you understand what it means in the context of your overall health.

faqs.q: What HbA1c level is prediabetes?
faqs.a: An HbA1c between 5.7 and 6.4 percent is generally considered prediabetes. Below 5.7 percent is normal, and 6.5 percent or higher suggests diabetes when confirmed.

faqs.q: Is HbA1c 6.0 serious?
faqs.a: An HbA1c of 6.0 percent is in the prediabetes range and indicates higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes. It is a strong signal to start lifestyle changes and regular monitoring.

faqs.q: Can HbA1c be wrong?
faqs.a: HbA1c can be less accurate in anaemia, haemoglobin variants, pregnancy, recent blood loss or kidney disease. Your doctor may use other tests in these situations.

faqs.q: How quickly can HbA1c improve?
faqs.a: Because HbA1c reflects about three months of sugar levels, changes usually show after around three months of consistent lifestyle changes. Some improvement may be visible sooner.

faqs.q: Do I need medicine for prediabetes?
faqs.a: Most people start with lifestyle changes. Doctors may consider metformin for some high-risk individuals. Discuss your situation with your doctor.

Prediabetes HbA1c: What the Number Means
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 4 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
HbA1c below 5.7 percent is generally considered normal, 5.7 to 6.4 percent indicates prediabetes, and 6.5 percent or higher on repeated testing suggests diabetes. A prediabetes result is a signal to act now with weight management, physical activity and healthier eating, plus regular follow-up testing.
HbA1c, also called glycated haemoglobin or A1C, is a blood test that shows your average blood sugar over the past two to three months. It is one of the main tests used to detect prediabetes and diabetes. Understanding your HbA1c helps you act early to prevent type 2 diabetes.
What does HbA1c measure?
Glucose in the blood attaches to haemoglobin in red blood cells. Because red cells live about three months, the percentage of haemoglobin with glucose attached reflects average sugar levels over that time. Unlike a single sugar reading, HbA1c is not affected by what you ate that morning.
How do you read your result?
Below 5.7 percent: normal range
5.7 to 6.4 percent: prediabetes
6.5 percent or above: diabetes, usually confirmed with a repeat test or another test
Within the prediabetes range, a higher number such as 6.2 to 6.4 percent suggests a greater risk of progressing to diabetes, so prompt action is especially important.
What can affect HbA1c accuracy?
HbA1c may be less reliable in people with:
Anaemia or iron deficiency
Haemoglobin variants such as thalassaemia trait or sickle cell trait
Recent blood loss or transfusion
Pregnancy
Advanced kidney or liver disease
In these situations, doctors may use fasting glucose or a glucose tolerance test instead.
What should you do if HbA1c shows prediabetes?
Lose excess weight
Losing about 5 to 7 percent of body weight can lower the risk of progressing to diabetes.
Be active
Aim for about 150 minutes of moderate activity each week, such as brisk walking, plus strength training.
Improve eating habits
Reduce refined carbohydrates, sugary drinks and sweets. Add vegetables, pulses, protein and whole grains.
Sleep and stress
Good sleep and stress management support better sugar control.
Medicines
In some high-risk people, doctors may consider metformin.
How often should you retest?
People with prediabetes are usually retested at least once a year, and sometimes every three to six months while making changes. Your doctor will guide timing.
The quick version
HbA1c shows average sugar over about three months.
5.7 to 6.4 percent indicates prediabetes.
Some conditions can affect accuracy.
Weight loss, activity and diet changes lower risk.
Retest regularly to track progress.
A prediabetes HbA1c is a valuable early warning, not a diagnosis of diabetes. Acting now can bring your numbers back toward normal. Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur helps patients interpret results and plan prevention.
When to seek urgent care
Seek urgent care for extreme thirst with vomiting, confusion, deep rapid breathing or unusual drowsiness, which can signal very high sugar.
Sources and further reading
ADA: Prediabetes
NIDDK: Preventing type 2 diabetes
Frequently asked questions
What HbA1c level is prediabetes?
An HbA1c between 5.7 and 6.4 percent is generally considered prediabetes. Below 5.7 percent is normal, and 6.5 percent or higher suggests diabetes when confirmed.
Is HbA1c 6.0 serious?
An HbA1c of 6.0 percent is in the prediabetes range and indicates higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes. It is a strong signal to start lifestyle changes and regular monitoring.
Can HbA1c be wrong?
HbA1c can be less accurate in anaemia, haemoglobin variants, pregnancy, recent blood loss or kidney disease. Your doctor may use other tests in these situations.
How quickly can HbA1c improve?
Because HbA1c reflects about three months of sugar levels, changes usually show after around three months of consistent lifestyle changes. Some improvement may be visible sooner.
Do I need medicine for prediabetes?
Most people start with lifestyle changes. Doctors may consider metformin for some high-risk individuals. Discuss your situation with your doctor.

faqs.q: How much weight should I lose to reverse prediabetes?
faqs.a: Losing about 5 to 7 percent of body weight can significantly reduce diabetes risk and often improves blood sugar. For an 80 kg person, this means about 4 to 6 kg. Your doctor can set a personal target.

faqs.q: Does losing belly fat help prediabetes?
faqs.a: Yes. Abdominal fat is strongly linked to insulin resistance. Reducing waist size through diet and exercise improves how the body uses insulin and lowers blood sugar.

faqs.q: How fast should I lose weight with prediabetes?
faqs.a: A gradual rate of about 0.5 to 1 kg per week is generally safe and easier to maintain. Rapid loss without supervision may cause muscle loss and weight regain.

faqs.q: Can I reverse prediabetes without losing weight?
faqs.a: Exercise and diet changes can improve blood sugar even with small weight changes, but weight loss usually gives the strongest benefit for people with excess weight.

faqs.q: What if I cannot lose weight despite trying?
faqs.a: Conditions such as thyroid problems, PCOS, stress or certain medicines can affect weight. Speak with your doctor, who may check for these and discuss additional support options.

Prediabetes and Weight Loss: How Much Helps?
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 4 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
Losing about 5 to 7 percent of your body weight, combined with regular physical activity, can significantly lower the risk of prediabetes progressing to type 2 diabetes. For someone weighing 80 kg, that means about 4 to 6 kg. Reducing waist size matters too, because fat around the abdomen is closely linked to insulin resistance.
Weight loss is one of the most effective ways to reverse prediabetes and prevent type 2 diabetes. You do not need to reach an ideal weight to benefit. Modest, steady weight loss can make a meaningful difference to how your body handles sugar.
Why does weight affect blood sugar?
Excess body fat, especially around the abdomen and inside the liver, makes cells less responsive to insulin. The pancreas then has to work harder to keep sugar in range. Over time, it may not keep up, and blood sugar rises. Losing weight reduces this fat and improves insulin sensitivity.
Why is waist size important?
Abdominal fat is more harmful than fat elsewhere. Many Indians have higher abdominal fat at a lower body weight. Waist circumference above about 90 cm in men and 80 cm in women is often used as a marker of higher risk in Asian populations. Reducing waist size improves metabolic health.
What is a realistic target?
Aim for 5 to 7 percent of body weight over several months
Lose weight gradually, often around 0.5 to 1 kg per week
Focus on sustainable habits rather than quick results
Maintain the loss over the long term
How can you lose weight safely?
Eat balanced meals
Fill half the plate with vegetables, add protein, choose whole grains and control portions of rice and rotis.
Cut liquid sugars
Avoid sugary drinks, juices and sweetened tea or coffee.
Increase activity
Aim for about 150 minutes of moderate activity per week plus strength training twice weekly.
Sleep and stress
Poor sleep and stress increase appetite and cravings.
Track progress
Weigh yourself weekly and measure your waist monthly.
Should you try crash diets?
Very low-calorie diets without supervision can cause nutrient deficiencies, muscle loss and weight regain. Some structured low-calorie programmes are used under medical supervision. Discuss options with your doctor.
What if weight loss is difficult?
Hormonal conditions such as hypothyroidism or PCOS, certain medicines and stress can make weight loss harder. Your doctor can check for these and may consider medicines that support weight loss in selected people.
A quick recap
Losing 5 to 7 percent of body weight lowers diabetes risk.
Abdominal fat is closely linked to insulin resistance.
Aim for gradual, sustainable weight loss.
Combine diet changes with regular activity.
Get medical help if weight loss is hard.
You do not need dramatic weight loss to protect yourself from diabetes. Small, steady changes add up. Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur supports patients with practical weight and prediabetes plans.
When to seek urgent care
Seek urgent care for extreme thirst with vomiting, confusion, deep rapid breathing or unusual drowsiness, which can signal very high sugar.

NIDDK: Preventing type 2 diabetes
Frequently asked questions

Losing about 5 to 7 percent of body weight can significantly reduce diabetes risk and often improves blood sugar. For an 80 kg person, this means about 4 to 6 kg. Your doctor can set a personal target.
Does losing belly fat help prediabetes?
Yes. Abdominal fat is strongly linked to insulin resistance. Reducing waist size through diet and exercise improves how the body uses insulin and lowers blood sugar.
How fast should I lose weight with prediabetes?
A gradual rate of about 0.5 to 1 kg per week is generally safe and easier to maintain. Rapid loss without supervision may cause muscle loss and weight regain.
Can I reverse prediabetes without losing weight?
Exercise and diet changes can improve blood sugar even with small weight changes, but weight loss usually gives the strongest benefit for people with excess weight.
What if I cannot lose weight despite trying?
Conditions such as thyroid problems, PCOS, stress or certain medicines can affect weight. Speak with your doctor, who may check for these and discuss additional support options.

pOnly: Prediabetes
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
MD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 4 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer

Losing about 5 to 7 percent of your body weight, combined with regular physical activity, can significantly lower the risk of prediabetes progressing to type 2 diabetes. For someone weighing 80 kg, that means about 4 to 6 kg. Reducing waist size matters too, because fat around the abdomen is closely linked to insulin resistance.

Weight loss is one of the most effective ways to reverse prediabetes and prevent type 2 diabetes. You do not need to reach an ideal weight to benefit. Modest, steady weight loss can make a meaningful difference to how your body handles sugar.

Excess body fat, especially around the abdomen and inside the liver, makes cells less responsive to insulin. The pancreas then has to work harder to keep sugar in range. Over time, it may not keep up, and blood sugar rises. Losing weight reduces this fat and improves insulin sensitivity.

Abdominal fat is more harmful than fat elsewhere. Many Indians have higher abdominal fat at a lower body weight. Waist circumference above about 90 cm in men and 80 cm in women is often used as a marker of higher risk in Asian populations. Reducing waist size improves metabolic health.
Fill half the plate with vegetables, add protein, choose whole grains and control portions of rice and rotis.
Avoid sugary drinks, juices and sweetened tea or coffee.
Aim for about 150 minutes of moderate activity per week plus strength training twice weekly.
Poor sleep and stress increase appetite and cravings.
Weigh yourself weekly and measure your waist monthly.

Very low-calorie diets without supervision can cause nutrient deficiencies, muscle loss and weight regain. Some structured low-calorie programmes are used under medical supervision. Discuss options with your doctor.

Hormonal conditions such as hypothyroidism or PCOS, certain medicines and stress can make weight loss harder. Your doctor can check for these and may consider medicines that support weight loss in selected people.

You do not need dramatic weight loss to protect yourself from diabetes. Small, steady changes add up. Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur supports patients with practical weight and prediabetes plans.
When to seek urgent care
Seek urgent care for extreme thirst with vomiting, confusion, deep rapid breathing or unusual drowsiness, which can signal very high sugar.

Preparing Your Child, and Yourself, for Adolescence
Parenting
Preparing Your Child, and Yourself, for Adolescence
Written by Dr. Prajakta A. Kaduskar, Child and adolescent specialist, Nagpur
Dr. Prajakta A. KaduskarMBBS, DCH, PGDAP, MA (Clinical Psychology)
Published 8 July 2026 · Updated 2 October 2026 · 6 min
In brief
Behaviour is learned, which means it can be changed.
Childhood is the best time to build habits that carry a child through adolescence.
Parents need courage, patience and practice, and consistency matters more than perfection.
Today's preparation shapes tomorrow
A child's nature is their own, but behaviour is learned. A well-behaved child is not a matter of luck. And if children learn behaviour, they can also learn to change it.
Children are often seen as a measure of their parents, and families feel judged by their children's behaviour and results. Think of how people choose apples, holding each one to the light and checking for blemishes. In the same way, we want our children to be perfect: happy, respectful, well behaved, motivated and independent. The goals are shared by almost every parent. Reaching them takes effort that starts in early childhood.
Why parenting feels harder today
Many of us were brought up with strict discipline at school and at home. Today, with smaller families, most children are deeply loved and sometimes over-indulged at home, while still facing discipline at school. Parents ask: why don't the old methods work any more?
Part of the answer is that childhood itself has become harder:
Children feel constant pressure from friends, school, media and sometimes parents.
Working parents often come home tired, and patience runs short. Single parenting brings its own stresses.
A generation ago, families in the same neighbourhood shared similar rules. Today every family has its own standards, and children see many versions of right and wrong.
Childhood often passes smoothly. Then adolescence arrives, and expectations change suddenly. In school, children get labelled as "high scorers" or "low scorers", "good" or "bad", sometimes simply because of the friends they keep. A teenager who feels labelled may become stubborn, and as parents and teachers tighten discipline, a cycle of misbehaviour can set in. This is why it helps to prepare, both ourselves and our children, well before adolescence begins.
Love does not always light the way
A young child's mind is more flexible than a teenager's, so childhood is the time to shape behaviour. Every parent can make three promises:
Courage. Be open to new ideas. If what you are doing works, keep doing it. If it does not, have the courage to try something different.
Patience. Change takes time. We are used to instant results, from quick photos to instant meals, and expect behaviour to change overnight. A few days is not long enough to judge a new approach; some take weeks.
Practice. Every parent must practise, including me. My child does not care that I look after other children's health. At home, I am a mother, and I get tested just like every other parent. There is no magic wand.
What helps change behaviour
Reward what you want to see, and calmly ignore minor misbehaviour. Children repeat behaviour that gets rewarded and drop behaviour that gets no attention.
Be consistent. Rewarding a behaviour one day and punishing it the next confuses children.
Know what is normal for each age. This helps you tell ordinary phases from real problems.
Avoid physical punishment. It is less effective, and harmful. Stories and examples that show good behaviour being valued teach lessons that last.
Build good habits early: tidiness, personal hygiene, an organised study space. Habits are not inherited; children copy what they see every day, so sometimes parents need to change their own habits first.
Teach them to handle success and failure. Studies, competition, achievement and disappointment are part of life. Learning to face them calmly brings lasting happiness.
Model healthy routines at home: regular meals, physical activity, sensible screen time and sleep. Watch programmes together when you can, talk about what you see, and explain the difference between fantasy and real life.
Praise often, when it is deserved, and correct mistakes privately, never in front of others.
Keep a simple behaviour diary for children who find change hard. It helps you see gradual progress and stay patient.
Keep going
The years when children need us most pass quickly. Most children come through them well, despite bumps along the way. Parents who persevere, with courage, patience and practice, give their children the best start to adolescence.

Building Self-Esteem in Teenagers with Disabilities
Written by Dr. Prajakta A. Kaduskar, Child and adolescent specialist, Nagpur
Dr. Prajakta A. KaduskarMBBS, DCH, PGDAP, MA (Clinical Psychology)
Published 8 July 2026 · Updated 2 October 2026 · 6 min
In brief
Self-esteem is how we feel about ourselves, and it shapes how we act.
Teenagers with disabilities have the same hopes as other teenagers; barriers in their surroundings often hold them back more than the disability itself.
Families, schools and health professionals can all help remove those barriers.
What self-esteem looks like
Self-esteem is how we feel about ourselves, and our behaviour reflects it. It is one of the foundations of happiness and success.
A young person with healthy self-esteem is more likely to:
act independently and take responsibility
take pride in what they achieve
cope with frustration
try new tasks and challenges
handle both positive and negative emotions
help others
A young person with low self-esteem may:
avoid trying new things
feel unloved or unwanted
blame others for their own difficulties
seem indifferent, or pretend not to care
become upset easily when things go wrong
put down their own talents
be easily influenced by others
Adolescence and disability
Adolescence is a time of big physical, emotional and social change. For most young people, when their needs are met, it can be a fairly smooth path to adulthood: further study or work, new relationships and a clearer sense of who they are. When a physical, sensory, learning or developmental disability is part of the picture, building self-esteem needs extra attention.
Teenagers with disabilities want what all teenagers want: happiness, meaningful work, close relationships, independence, and to be believed in and accepted. What often stands in the way is not the disability itself, but prejudice, missing opportunities to learn skills, and practical or financial barriers.
These challenges show up in three areas of life:
External: education, work and independent living
Interpersonal: friendships and relationships
Personal: self-image and the risk of social isolation
Teenagers with disabilities are more likely to have fewer friends and fewer chances to join in activities, and to spend leisure time alone. Over time this can lead to loneliness and a lower sense of being accepted.
Where help begins: the family
Help starts at home, with parents, and the young person, accepting the disability as a different way of being able rather than a lack of ability. Seek help from a health professional whenever it is needed.
A good approach is family-centred and respectful. Teenagers should:
lead decisions about the type and amount of support they receive, and
be treated with respect at every step.
Rather than trying to "fix" young people so they fit society's expectations, we should work on removing the barriers around them: educating others, changing attitudes, improving physical access in schools and public places, and building links with community support such as transport, volunteers and care services.
Tips for teenagers
Focus on what you can do. Everyone has strengths and limitations. Acknowledge your disability, and build on your abilities.
Avoid unfair comparisons. Compare like with like. A young athlete with a locomotor disability may not play in the Olympics, but can compete in the Paralympics.
Set realistic goals. If reading takes you longer, allow the extra time and reward yourself for persevering.
Don't over-generalise. Not being able to do one thing does not make you a failure. Do not tie your self-worth to a single skill or event.
Drop unfair "should" statements. "I should finish this exam in 50 minutes like everyone else" may not be fair. Accommodations such as extra time exist so that everyone can show what they know.
Appreciate all of yourself. List your strengths, including how you cope with your disability. Those coping skills are strengths too.
Tips for parents: fair, firm and friendly
Discipline works best when it is fair, firm and friendly. When your teenager faces a problem:
Clarify it together. Ask questions that help them describe what they see, hear and feel, and what needs to change.
Brainstorm options. There is usually more than one solution; suggest some if they have none.
Let them choose, after thinking through the consequences. The best choice solves the problem and leaves them feeling good about themselves.
Review the result together. What worked, what did not, and why. This builds better decisions next time.
Remember
Teenagers with disabilities are teenagers first. Like everyone, they want to be happy. They may not reach every goal, but it matters that they try and that they understand the obstacles they face. Families, schools and health professionals can help them build the confidence to live full lives.
If you are concerned about your teenager's confidence, mood or social life, Blooming Buds can help with assessment, counselling and guidance for the family.

Semaglutide vs Tirzepatide: Which One Might Suit You?
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 15 October 2026 · 5 min read
Quick answer
Semaglutide activates the GLP-1 receptor. Tirzepatide activates both GLP-1 and GIP receptors. In head-to-head studies, tirzepatide generally lowered HbA1c and body weight more than semaglutide, while semaglutide has strong evidence for heart protection and is also available as a tablet. Which one suits you depends on your condition, side effects, cost and availability, so a doctor should decide.
Semaglutide and tirzepatide are often mentioned together. Both are weekly injections that lower blood sugar and body weight. They are not the same, and the right choice depends on your health, goals, tolerance and cost.
How do they work?
Semaglutide
It copies the gut hormone GLP-1. It helps the pancreas release insulin when blood sugar is high, lowers glucagon, slows stomach emptying and reduces appetite.
Tirzepatide
It copies both GLP-1 and GIP, another gut hormone. The added GIP action may improve insulin response and fat metabolism, and may contribute to its stronger effects on weight and blood sugar in studies.
How are they given?
Both are given once a week as an injection under the skin.
Doses are started low and increased every few weeks.
Semaglutide also comes as a daily tablet.
What do studies show?
Feature
Semaglutide
Tirzepatide
Receptors
GLP-1
GLP-1 and GIP
Blood sugar lowering
Strong
Often stronger in head-to-head studies
Average weight loss
Significant
Often greater in studies
Heart benefit
Proven in people with diabetes and heart disease
Studies ongoing and emerging
Forms
Weekly injection and daily tablet
Weekly injection
Side effects
Mainly stomach-related
Mainly stomach-related
These are averages from clinical trials. Individual results differ.
Semaglutide may be preferred if
You have established heart disease and your doctor wants a medicine with proven heart protection
You prefer or need a tablet option
Cost or availability favours it
You tolerate it well and are meeting your goals
Tirzepatide may be preferred if
You need larger weight loss
Your HbA1c is well above target
You have not responded enough to other GLP-1 medicines
Your doctor judges it suitable for your condition
Do they have different side effects?
Both commonly cause nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, constipation and reduced appetite, especially when the dose is increased. Rare risks include pancreatitis, gallbladder problems and dehydration. Neither is advised in people with a personal or family history of certain thyroid cancers (medullary thyroid carcinoma) or MEN2 syndrome, in pregnancy, or in those with a history of pancreatitis without specialist advice.
What about cost and availability?
Prices and brands in India are changing. Ask your doctor and pharmacy for current details. Do not switch brands or medicines without medical advice.
Can you switch from one to the other?
Yes, a doctor may switch you based on response and tolerance. The new medicine is started at a suitable dose, not the same dose number.
When should you see a doctor?
See a diabetologist before starting either medicine. Report severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, signs of dehydration or allergic reactions right away.
Points to keep
Semaglutide acts on GLP-1. Tirzepatide acts on GLP-1 and GIP.
Tirzepatide often shows greater weight and sugar lowering in studies.
Semaglutide has strong heart evidence and a tablet form.
Side effects are similar and mostly stomach-related.
The choice should be individual and doctor-guided.
There is no single winner for everyone. The best medicine is the one that is safe for you, effective and sustainable. To find your best option, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.

Is tirzepatide better than semaglutide?
In several head-to-head studies, tirzepatide lowered HbA1c and weight more than semaglutide. But semaglutide has strong heart-protection data. The better option depends on your needs and tolerance.
Can I switch from semaglutide to tirzepatide?
Yes, under a doctor's guidance. The doctor will choose a starting dose and adjust it gradually. Do not switch on your own.
Do both cause similar side effects?
Yes. Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and constipation are the most common. They are usually mild and improve with time. Serious side effects are rare.
Is semaglutide available as a tablet?
Yes, oral semaglutide is available in some countries for type 2 diabetes. Tirzepatide is given as an injection. Check availability in India with your doctor.
Which one is better for weight loss?
On average, tirzepatide shows greater weight loss in trials. Individual response varies. Your doctor will weigh benefits, risks and cost.
Which one is more affordable?
Prices change and depend on brand and dose. Ask your doctor and pharmacy for current prices before deciding.

Smart Love: Parenting Teenagers with Connection, Not Control
Written by Dr. Prajakta A. Kaduskar, Child and adolescent specialist, Nagpur
Dr. Prajakta A. KaduskarMBBS, DCH, PGDAP, MA (Clinical Psychology)
Published 8 July 2026 · Updated 2 October 2026 · 7 min
In brief
Three things matter most in the parent and teen relationship: connection, monitoring and psychological autonomy.
Discipline works best when rules are agreed in advance and enforced calmly.
Watch for signs that stress is affecting your teenager, and ask for help early.
Parenting teens: still a challenge
Adolescence is the move from childhood to adulthood. Parenting a teenager means guiding a young person towards independence, passing on values, and helping them handle friendships and relationships. Every child is different, and even the same parents face new challenges with each child.
All parents want a happy, successful child, yet there is little agreement on how to get there. We often try to teach teenagers to obey without question. What they need more is to learn to disagree openly and respectfully, and to ask for guidance when they are unsure rather than acting on impulse.
The three pillars: connection, monitoring and autonomy
1. Connection. A warm, steady and loving relationship is the background against which everything else happens. Teenagers who feel connected to their parents are more likely to be confident and cooperative with others.
2. Monitoring. Knowing where your teenager is, who their friends are and what they are doing matters. Within a warm relationship, this comes across as caring rather than intrusive.
3. Psychological autonomy. Encourage your teenager to think independently and express their own ideas. Listen to their feelings and show love without conditions. The opposite, psychological control, means changing the subject, personal criticism, withdrawing affection or making a child feel guilty for thinking differently. It pushes teenagers into their shell.
These three sound simple, but turning them into daily habits is hard, especially with a teenager whose favourite lines are "You just don't understand" and "Leave me alone". Separating from parents is a normal part of adolescence, and friends matter more each year. Even so, nothing replaces the parent and teen relationship. Spending relaxed time together, through hobbies, sport, a shared meal or a walk, keeps you connected and helps you stay aware of what is happening in their life.
Discipline: shaping a bright future
Discipline is unpleasant for everyone, but a relationship built on warmth can withstand it. Teenagers rarely admit it, yet firm boundaries reassure them.
Set rules together, in advance. Involve your teenager in setting family rules and agreeing the consequences before a rule is broken.
Stay calm. When a rule is broken, enforce the agreed consequence without treating it as a personal attack. This avoids power struggles.
Separate discipline from control. Help your child make sense of the world by offering explanations, but also listen respectfully to their view of their own experience. Trying to control how a teenager thinks rarely changes what they do, and often makes them withdraw.
When stress becomes too much
Teenagers today face pressure from studies, exams, friends, social media and family expectations. Most feel stressed when a situation seems difficult or threatening and they do not have the tools to cope. Some become overloaded, which can show up as anxiety, withdrawal, anger, physical complaints, or unhealthy coping such as substance use.
How parents can help:
Notice when stress is affecting sleep, appetite, mood, behaviour or studies.
Listen carefully, without rushing to advise or judge.
Encourage sport, hobbies and time with supportive friends.
Learn simple stress-management techniques together.
Seek help from an adolescent health professional early.
In an emergency
If your teenager talks about hopelessness, self-harm or suicide, take it seriously and get help the same day. Call 112 in an emergency, or Tele-MANAS, the Government of India's free 24-hour mental health helpline, on 14416 or 1-800-891-4416.
"Smart love"
The book Smart Love by Martha Heineman Pieper and William J. Pieper offers a compassionate approach to parenting, from newborns to teenagers. Its central idea is that a child's inner happiness is the foundation of good behaviour. In our own words, the ideas I find most useful for parents are:
A child is a child. See the world through your child's eyes, and accept immaturity instead of fighting it.
Build optimism. Help your child face obstacles honestly, without frightening them into pessimism.
Nurture inner happiness. Lasting contentment comes from within, not from outside rewards.
Be the example. Children learn from how we treat them. Constant criticism teaches them to expect unhappiness.
Happy children behave better. Good behaviour grows from feeling secure and valued more than from constant correction.
Give time, not only "quality time". Being present regularly matters.
Attention builds independence. Loving attention does not spoil children; it gives them the security to become independent.
Find the middle ground. You need not choose between being a pushover and being strict.
Trust yourself. Your parenting instincts are usually sound; listen to both your head and your heart.
In short
Parents who focus on guiding their teenager, rather than controlling them, tend to have more success and far less conflict. Give your teenager love, time, clear boundaries and the freedom to think for themselves, and you may find you enjoy watching them grow into an independent young adult.
Reference: Pieper, M. H. and Pieper, W. J. Smart Love: The Compassionate Alternative to Discipline That Will Make You a Better Parent and Your Child a Better Person.
