pOnly: Type 2 Diabetes
MD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 1 October 2026 · 15 min

Type 2 diabetes rarely begins with one dramatic symptom. For many people, blood sugar rises gradually, sometimes for years, without causing anything that feels obviously wrong. Others notice increased thirst, frequent urination, unusual tiredness or changes in their weight and only then decide to get tested.
That is one reason diabetes can be easy to overlook in its early stages.

Type 2 diabetes develops when the body becomes less responsive to insulin and, over time, the pancreas may not be able to produce enough insulin to keep blood glucose within a healthy range. The condition is common, but the way it develops and the treatment a person needs can vary considerably.
Managing it is not simply a matter of avoiding sugar.

Food choices, physical activity, body weight, sleep, medications, blood pressure, cholesterol, kidney health and cardiovascular risk can all form part of diabetes care. For some people, lifestyle changes make a substantial difference. Others need one or more medicines, and some eventually require insulin.

The aim is not to chase a single “perfect” blood sugar reading. Good diabetes care means keeping glucose in an appropriate range while also reducing the risk of problems involving the heart, kidneys, eyes, nerves and feet.
Type 2 diabetes is a long-term metabolic condition in which blood glucose becomes persistently elevated.

The main problem usually involves insulin resistance. Insulin is a hormone that helps glucose move from the bloodstream into cells, where it can be used for energy. When the body's cells respond poorly to insulin, the pancreas has to work harder to maintain normal glucose levels.
For a period of time, the pancreas may compensate by producing more insulin. Eventually, however, insulin production may no longer be enough to overcome the body's insulin resistance.
Blood glucose then begins to rise.
This process is not identical in everyone. Genetics, excess body fat, physical inactivity, age, family history and other metabolic factors can contribute to the development of Type 2 diabetes.
Some people have clear symptoms. Others have none.
Common symptoms include:
The difficulty is that several of these symptoms are nonspecific. Tiredness, for example, can have many causes.
That is why symptoms alone cannot establish whether someone has diabetes. A blood test is needed for diagnosis.
Yes.
This is one of the reasons routine testing matters, particularly for people who have risk factors for diabetes.
Someone can have elevated blood glucose and feel completely normal. By the time symptoms become noticeable, blood sugar may already have been elevated for some time.
If you have a strong family history of diabetes, excess weight, high blood pressure, abnormal cholesterol or other risk factors, speak with a doctor about whether you should be tested.
Diabetes is diagnosed using specific blood glucose or HbA1c criteria.
The commonly used diagnostic thresholds include:

An abnormal result does not always mean that the diagnosis can be made immediately, particularly when a person has no obvious symptoms. In many situations, the result needs to be confirmed with repeat testing or another diagnostic test.
The exact test used can depend on the person's circumstances.
HbA1c is one of the most useful tests in diabetes care.
Unlike a glucose test that tells you the blood sugar level at one particular point in time, HbA1c provides an indication of average blood glucose exposure over roughly the previous three months.
It does not require fasting.
For diagnosis, an HbA1c of 6.5% or above falls within the diabetes range. An HbA1c between 5.7% and 6.4% is generally classified as prediabetes.
But HbA1c should not be interpreted in isolation.

Certain conditions affecting red blood cells, haemoglobin, blood loss or other medical factors can affect how reliable the result is. If the HbA1c does not appear to fit the clinical picture, your doctor may recommend another form of testing.
There is no single HbA1c target that is appropriate for every person.

For many adults with diabetes, a target around 7% or lower may be appropriate, but the goal should be individualized. Age, duration of diabetes, other medical conditions, medications, risk of hypoglycaemia and the person's overall treatment situation all matter.
Lower is not automatically better if achieving a very low glucose level creates significant risk.
The target should therefore be discussed with the treating doctor rather than copied from someone else's diabetes plan.
Both measurements can provide useful information, but they answer slightly different questions.
Fasting blood glucose is measured after a period without food, usually after at least eight hours of fasting when used for diagnostic testing.
Post-meal glucose looks at how blood sugar behaves after eating. Depending on when it is measured, it can help identify glucose rises that may not be obvious from a fasting reading alone.
A person may have a reasonable fasting glucose but still experience substantial rises after meals.
That is why diabetes management sometimes involves looking at patterns rather than focusing on one number.
There is rarely one single cause.
Several factors can contribute, including:
Having one or more risk factors does not mean that diabetes is inevitable.
Likewise, someone without an obvious risk factor can still develop the condition.
Treatment is usually built around several parts rather than one intervention.
Depending on the individual, management may include:
The plan can change over time.

A person who needs medication today may require a different combination later. Conversely, someone whose diabetes is initially well controlled through lifestyle changes may eventually need medication as the disease progresses.
That does not mean treatment has “failed.” Type 2 diabetes is a chronic condition, and its treatment often needs to evolve.
A diabetes-friendly diet does not have to mean giving up every food you enjoy.
For many Indian households, the practical questions are much more specific:
Can I eat roti?
What about rice?
Are fruits allowed?
What should I have for breakfast?
Can I eat sweets occasionally?
The answer usually comes down to portion size, carbohydrate quantity and quality, overall diet, meal pattern and individual treatment needs.
A useful starting point is to build meals around vegetables, appropriate protein sources, high-fibre foods and controlled portions of carbohydrate-containing foods.
Foods such as whole grains, pulses, vegetables, nuts and seeds can often fit into a balanced eating pattern.
Sugary drinks, frequent sweets and highly processed foods are generally less helpful for blood glucose management.
But there is no universal “diabetes food list” that works equally well for everyone.
Your diet should take into account your blood glucose pattern, weight goals, medications, activity level, food preferences and other health conditions.
Yes.
Physical activity can improve insulin sensitivity and help the body use glucose more effectively. It can also support weight management and cardiovascular health.
The right exercise plan depends on the person's age, fitness level, complications and other medical conditions.
For someone who has been inactive for a long time, starting with manageable activity and gradually increasing it may be more realistic than suddenly attempting intense workouts.
Walking, resistance training and other forms of aerobic activity can all have a role.
If you have diabetes-related complications or significant cardiovascular problems, discuss an exercise plan with your doctor before starting strenuous activity.
Lifestyle changes are an important part of diabetes management, but they are not always sufficient on their own.
Depending on the person's glucose levels, cardiovascular and kidney health, body weight, risk of hypoglycaemia and other factors, a doctor may consider medicines such as:
These medicines work in different ways.
Some improve insulin sensitivity. Some increase glucose loss through the urine. Others influence insulin secretion, appetite or glucose regulation.

The choice is not simply about which medicine lowers blood sugar the most. Doctors also consider side effects, kidney function, cardiovascular disease, weight, cost, hypoglycaemia risk and other individual factors.
A medicine that is suitable for one patient may not be appropriate for another.
No.
Some people with Type 2 diabetes can manage their blood glucose without insulin, particularly during earlier stages of the disease.
Others may need insulin temporarily or permanently.

Insulin can become necessary when the pancreas is no longer producing enough insulin, when glucose levels are markedly elevated, during certain illnesses or situations, or when other treatment approaches are insufficient.
Needing insulin is not a sign that someone has done something wrong.
It is simply one of the treatment options available when the body requires additional insulin support.
There is no single monitoring schedule for every person with Type 2 diabetes.
Someone taking insulin may need to monitor more frequently than someone whose diabetes is controlled with lifestyle measures or certain non-insulin medicines.
Some patients may also benefit from continuous glucose monitoring (CGM), depending on their treatment and clinical circumstances.
HbA1c is another part of follow-up and is commonly checked at regular intervals, with the frequency determined by the person's treatment plan and level of glucose control.
The useful question is not simply, “How many times should I check my sugar?”
It is:
What information do we need from monitoring to make the next treatment decision?
Persistently high blood glucose can affect blood vessels and nerves over time.
Important complications include:
Diabetes can damage the small blood vessels supplying the retina. Regular eye examinations can help detect changes before vision is seriously affected.
Diabetes is an important cause of chronic kidney disease. Blood and urine tests can help assess kidney function and detect early changes.
Diabetic neuropathy may cause burning, tingling, numbness or altered sensation, particularly in the feet.
Reduced sensation and poor circulation can make seemingly minor foot injuries more serious. Regular foot checks are therefore an important part of diabetes care.
Diabetes is associated with increased cardiovascular risk. Blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking status, weight and other risk factors therefore deserve attention alongside glucose.
The purpose of regular screening is not to create anxiety. It is to identify problems early enough to act on them.
A diabetes follow-up appointment may involve more than checking blood glucose.
Depending on the individual, regular care may include:
The exact schedule varies according to the person's age, diabetes duration, treatment and existing complications.
This question needs careful wording.
Some people with Type 2 diabetes can achieve remission, particularly after substantial and sustained weight loss or other major metabolic changes.
Remission is not the same thing as saying that diabetes has been permanently cured.
Blood glucose can rise again, particularly if weight is regained or the underlying metabolic problems return.
For that reason, even someone whose glucose levels have returned to the non-diabetes range should continue appropriate follow-up.
This is a common situation and does not necessarily mean the medication is ineffective.
Blood glucose can be influenced by:
Rather than increasing or stopping medication independently, persistent high readings should be discussed with the treating doctor.
Sometimes the issue is the medication itself. Sometimes the treatment is appropriate but needs adjustment because the person's metabolic situation has changed.
Consider seeking specialist diabetes care if:
Early specialist input can also be useful when several metabolic risk factors are present together.
When is high blood sugar an emergency?
Very high or very low glucose can sometimes become an emergency.
Seek urgent medical attention if diabetes is accompanied by symptoms such as:
People taking glucose-lowering medicines should also know the warning signs of hypoglycaemia, particularly sweating, shaking, hunger, dizziness, confusion or unusual behaviour.
Emergency symptoms should not be managed by adjusting medication at home without appropriate medical advice.
It is easy to think of diabetes management as a daily battle with a glucose meter.
In practice, it is broader than that.

Good management means understanding your condition, knowing your treatment, monitoring when monitoring is useful, staying physically active, eating in a sustainable way and attending recommended follow-ups.
It also means looking beyond blood sugar.
Blood pressure, cholesterol, kidney health, eye health, weight, cardiovascular risk and foot health are all relevant.
There will also be days when the numbers are not perfect.
The goal is not perfection. The goal is sustained management that reduces the risk of complications while fitting realistically into everyday life.
Type 2 diabetes is manageable, but it needs more than occasional blood sugar checks.
The earlier the condition is identified and the more consistently it is followed, the more opportunities there are to address glucose levels and other cardiovascular and metabolic risk factors.

Treatment may involve food and exercise changes, medication, insulin, glucose monitoring or a combination of these. The right approach depends on the individual rather than a standard plan copied from someone else.

If your blood sugar or HbA1c is repeatedly elevated, or you have been diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes and are unsure what to do next, a consultation with a diabetes specialist can help clarify the diagnosis, treatment options and follow-up plan.

How Much Weight Loss Can Improve Type 2 Diabetes?
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 12 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
Even a modest loss of around 5 percent of body weight can improve blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol. Greater and sustained weight loss improves control further, and in some people, especially soon after diagnosis, it can lead to remission. The right pace and plan should be set with your doctor.
In type 2 diabetes, excess body fat makes the body less responsive to insulin. Losing weight can reverse part of that problem.
Why weight loss helps
Reduces fat in the liver and pancreas
Improves insulin sensitivity
Lowers blood pressure and cholesterol
May reduce the dose or number of medicines
What different amounts may do
Modest loss: better sugar and blood pressure
Larger loss: bigger improvement and, for some, remission
Maintaining the loss matters as much as achieving it
Safe ways to lose weight
Portion control and fewer refined carbohydrates
More vegetables, pulses and protein
Regular activity, including strength work
Good sleep
Medical support when needed, including medicines or procedures
Adjust medicines
As weight falls, sugar may drop. Doses of insulin and some tablets may need reducing to avoid low sugar. Do not change them yourself.
Keep the weight off
Continue healthy habits
Weigh yourself regularly
Keep follow-up visits
What to remember
Modest weight loss helps.
More loss can bring greater benefit.
Medicines may need adjusting.
Sustained habits keep results.
Medical support is available.
Every kilogram counts. For a weight and diabetes plan, you can consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
When to seek urgent care
Seek urgent care for chest pain, breathlessness, confusion, vomiting, or symptoms of very high or very low sugar.
Sources and further reading
WHO: Obesity and overweight
NIDDK: Health risks of overweight and obesity
Frequently asked questions
Can weight loss reverse diabetes?
In some people, especially early in the disease, it can lead to remission.
How fast should I lose weight?
Gradual loss is safer and easier to maintain.
Do I stop my medicines when I lose weight?
Only your doctor should change doses.
What if I cannot lose weight?
Speak to your doctor about other options.
Does belly fat matter?
Yes, abdominal fat is closely linked to insulin resistance.
Is exercise enough?
It helps, but combining with diet works better.

faqs.a: Some doctors use lower doses to maintain results, but the best approach depends on the person and the medicine. It should be decided with your doctor.

What Happens When You Stop a GLP-1 Medicine?
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 9 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
When GLP-1 medicines are stopped, appetite usually returns and a large portion of lost weight is often regained over the next months. Blood sugar may also rise in people with diabetes. The medicine controls appetite while you take it, but it does not permanently reset the body. A planned, doctor-guided approach, with lifestyle support, can reduce regain.
Many people start a GLP-1 medicine and lose weight, then wonder what happens when they stop. The honest answer is that for most people, appetite and weight tend to return. Understanding why helps you plan, instead of being surprised.
Why does weight come back?
Obesity is a chronic condition. The body defends its higher weight with hormones that increase hunger and reduce fullness. GLP-1 medicines lower these signals. Once the medicine leaves the body, hunger signals return to their previous levels. Studies that followed people after stopping have shown that, on average, most of the weight lost was regained within about a year.
What else changes after stopping?
Appetite and cravings: Often return within weeks.
Blood sugar: In type 2 diabetes, HbA1c may rise again.
Blood pressure and cholesterol: Improvements may fade as weight returns.
Fatty liver and sleep apnoea: May worsen if weight returns.
Side effects: Nausea and stomach symptoms stop.
Does everyone regain?
Not everyone. People who build strong habits during treatment, such as regular exercise, protein-rich meals, good sleep and mindful eating, tend to keep more of the benefit. Some people maintain with a lower dose. Others may restart later.
How can you plan to stop safely?
Talk to your doctor first
Do not stop suddenly without advice, especially if you have diabetes and take other medicines. Your doctor may adjust other medicines to avoid high sugar.
Taper or reduce the dose
In some cases, doctors lower the dose in steps, rather than stopping at once, though evidence for the best approach is still developing.
Build habits during treatment
Keep protein at every meal.
Do strength exercises two to three times a week.
Walk daily.
Sleep seven to eight hours.
Learn portion sizes and mindful eating.
Limit sweet drinks and ultra-processed snacks.
Monitor after stopping
Weigh yourself weekly and check your waist. For diabetes, monitor sugar levels and have an HbA1c test in about three months. Early action on small regain is easier than a big regain.
Consider long-term options
Some people stay on a lower maintenance dose. Others use different medicines, or consider metabolic surgery if severe obesity returns. Your doctor can discuss these.
When might you stop?
You have reached your goal and have a maintenance plan
Side effects are not tolerable
A medical condition makes it unsafe
You are planning pregnancy
You cannot afford to continue
Always plan this with your doctor.
When should you see a doctor?
See your doctor if you notice rapid weight regain, high sugar readings, increased thirst or urination, or return of symptoms such as snoring or knee pain after you stop.
In short
Appetite and weight usually return after stopping a GLP-1 medicine.
Blood sugar may rise again in type 2 diabetes.
Habits built during treatment help keep results.
Do not stop suddenly without medical advice.
Plan maintenance, monitoring and next steps with your doctor.
GLP-1 medicines work best as part of a long-term plan, not a short course. If you are thinking of stopping, plan early so that your hard-won progress is protected. For guidance, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
Sources and further reading
NIDDK: Prescription medicines for overweight and obesity
WHO: Diabetes fact sheet
Frequently asked questions
Will I regain weight after stopping GLP-1 injections?
Many people do. Studies show that on average a large share of lost weight returns within a year, because appetite signals go back to their earlier levels. Lifestyle habits and maintenance plans can reduce regain.
Can I stop a GLP-1 medicine suddenly?
It is not harmful in the way some medicines are, but sudden stopping can lead to quick return of appetite and high blood sugar in diabetes. Talk to your doctor before stopping.
How long after stopping does hunger return?
Many people notice increased appetite within a few weeks as the medicine leaves the body. The timing varies with the medicine and dose.
Can I keep my weight off after stopping?
Some can, especially with strong habits such as strength training, protein-rich meals, good sleep and regular follow-up. Others need a lower maintenance dose or a different treatment.
Will my diabetes come back if I stop?
If you have type 2 diabetes, blood sugar often rises again after stopping, since the underlying condition remains. Your doctor may adjust other medicines to keep control.
Is a lower maintenance dose possible?
Some doctors use lower doses to maintain results, but the best approach depends on the person and the medicine. It should be decided with your doctor.

Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
MD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 9 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer

When GLP-1 medicines are stopped, appetite usually returns and a large portion of lost weight is often regained over the next months. Blood sugar may also rise in people with diabetes. The medicine controls appetite while you take it, but it does not permanently reset the body. A planned, doctor-guided approach, with lifestyle support, can reduce regain.

Many people start a GLP-1 medicine and lose weight, then wonder what happens when they stop. The honest answer is that for most people, appetite and weight tend to return. Understanding why helps you plan, instead of being surprised.

Obesity is a chronic condition. The body defends its higher weight with hormones that increase hunger and reduce fullness. GLP-1 medicines lower these signals. Once the medicine leaves the body, hunger signals return to their previous levels. Studies that followed people after stopping have shown that, on average, most of the weight lost was regained within about a year.

Not everyone. People who build strong habits during treatment, such as regular exercise, protein-rich meals, good sleep and mindful eating, tend to keep more of the benefit. Some people maintain with a lower dose. Others may restart later.
Do not stop suddenly without advice, especially if you have diabetes and take other medicines. Your doctor may adjust other medicines to avoid high sugar.
In some cases, doctors lower the dose in steps, rather than stopping at once, though evidence for the best approach is still developing.
Weigh yourself weekly and check your waist. For diabetes, monitor sugar levels and have an HbA1c test in about three months. Early action on small regain is easier than a big regain.
Some people stay on a lower maintenance dose. Others use different medicines, or consider metabolic surgery if severe obesity returns. Your doctor can discuss these.
Always plan this with your doctor.
See your doctor if you notice rapid weight regain, high sugar readings, increased thirst or urination, or return of symptoms such as snoring or knee pain after you stop.

GLP-1 medicines work best as part of a long-term plan, not a short course. If you are thinking of stopping, plan early so that your hard-won progress is protected. For guidance, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.

What Is Diabesity? Understanding Diabetes and Obesity Together
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 12 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
Excess body fat, especially around the abdomen, causes insulin resistance, which can lead to type 2 diabetes. Diabetes and some of its medicines can in turn make weight gain easier. Managing both through food, activity, sleep, suitable medicines and sometimes surgery can improve sugar, weight and overall health.
"Diabesity" is an informal term for diabetes that occurs alongside obesity. The two conditions feed each other, so treating them together works best.
How the two are linked
Fat cells release substances that reduce insulin action
The pancreas works harder and may tire over time
High insulin levels promote fat storage
Some diabetes medicines can add weight
Why south asians need extra care
People of South Asian origin may develop diabetes at lower body weights and with more abdominal fat, so waist size matters.
Health risks
Heart disease and high blood pressure
Fatty liver
Sleep apnoea
Joint problems
Kidney and eye complications
Managing both together
Balanced diet with portion control
Regular physical activity
Good sleep
Medicines that help both sugar and weight, chosen by your doctor
Metabolic surgery for selected people with significant obesity
Set realistic goals
Steady weight loss and improving blood sugar are goals worth celebrating, even without a "perfect" weight.
In short
Diabetes and obesity are closely linked.
Waist size matters, especially for South Asians.
Treating both gives better results.
Medicines and surgery are options.
Realistic goals sustain progress.
You can improve both conditions together. For a combined plan, you can consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
When to seek urgent care
Seek urgent care for chest pain, breathlessness, confusion, vomiting, or symptoms of very high or very low sugar.
Sources and further reading
WHO: Obesity and overweight
NIDDK: Health risks of overweight and obesity
Frequently asked questions
Is diabesity a medical diagnosis?
No, it is an informal term describing the overlap.
Can I have diabetes without being overweight?
Yes, especially in South Asians.
Does losing weight help diabetes?
Yes, it often improves control.
Do all diabetes medicines cause weight gain?
No. Some are weight-neutral and some help weight loss.
Is surgery an option?
For selected people with obesity and diabetes, yes.
Where should I start?
With a medical assessment and a realistic plan.

What Is Insulin Resistance? Symptoms and Causes
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 13 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
Insulin resistance means the body's cells do not respond well to insulin, the hormone that moves sugar from the blood into the cells. The pancreas makes more insulin to compensate. Over time, it can no longer keep up, and blood sugar rises. It is closely linked to excess belly fat, inactivity, poor sleep and family history, and it can improve with weight loss, exercise and healthy eating.
Insulin resistance is one of the most common hidden problems in modern life. It can be present for many years before blood sugar rises to the diabetes range. Spotting it early gives you the best chance to prevent diabetes and other health problems.
What does insulin do?
After a meal, blood sugar rises. Insulin acts like a key, unlocking the cells of the muscles, liver and fat so that sugar can enter and be used for energy. This keeps blood sugar in a healthy range.
What goes wrong in insulin resistance?
The cells become "deaf" to insulin. Sugar stays in the blood, so the pancreas releases extra insulin. High insulin levels cause weight gain, particularly around the belly, and make the resistance worse. Over the years, the pancreas may fail to keep up, leading to prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.
What are the symptoms?
Many people have no symptoms. Signs that may suggest it include:
A large waist (for Indians, more than about 90 cm in men and 80 cm in women)
Dark, velvety skin patches on the neck, armpits or groin (acanthosis nigricans)
Skin tags
Tiredness, especially after meals
Increased hunger and sugar cravings
Difficulty losing weight
Irregular periods or acne in women with PCOS
Fatty liver on ultrasound
High blood pressure, triglycerides or low HDL cholesterol
How is it diagnosed?
There is no single routine test. Doctors look at the pattern: waist size, BMI, blood pressure, fasting blood sugar, HbA1c, lipid profile and sometimes fasting insulin levels. A diagnosis of prediabetes or metabolic syndrome often signals insulin resistance.
How can you improve it?
Move more
Aim for at least 150 minutes of brisk activity a week and add strength training twice a week. Muscle uses sugar and improves insulin response.
Eat well
Choose whole grains, pulses, vegetables and nuts.
Reduce sweets, sugary drinks, white bread and fried snacks.
Fill half your plate with vegetables, and include protein at each meal.
Lose excess weight
Even a loss of 5 to 10 percent of body weight can improve insulin sensitivity.
Sleep and stress
Aim for seven to eight hours of sleep. Treat sleep apnoea if present. Manage stress with walking, yoga or meditation.
Medicines
Metformin and other medicines may help in selected people, such as those with prediabetes at high risk, PCOS or type 2 diabetes. GLP-1 medicines can help in people with obesity.
When should you see a doctor?
Get tested if you have a large waist, a family history of diabetes, skin changes, PCOS, high blood pressure or cholesterol, or fatty liver. Early testing can prevent progression.
In short
Insulin resistance means cells respond poorly to insulin.
It often comes with belly fat, inactivity and poor sleep.
Many people have no symptoms, but signs include dark skin patches and a large waist.
Exercise, healthy eating and weight loss can improve it.
Early testing helps prevent type 2 diabetes.
Insulin resistance is a warning, not a sentence. Acting early gives you a lot of control. For a personal assessment, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
Sources and further reading
WHO: Obesity and overweight
NIDDK: Health risks of overweight and obesity
Frequently asked questions
What is insulin resistance in simple words?
It is when the body's cells do not respond well to insulin, so sugar stays in the blood and the pancreas has to make more insulin. Over time, this can lead to prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.
What are the early signs of insulin resistance?
A large waist, dark skin patches on the neck or armpits, skin tags, tiredness after meals, strong cravings and difficulty losing weight can be signs. Many people have no symptoms.
Can insulin resistance be reversed?
It can often be improved significantly through weight loss, exercise, better sleep and healthy eating. Early action gives the best results.
How is insulin resistance tested?
Doctors use waist size, BMI, blood pressure, blood sugar, HbA1c and lipid levels. Fasting insulin may be checked in some cases. Diagnosis considers the whole picture.
Does insulin resistance only happen in overweight people?
No. People with normal weight can have it, especially South Asians with belly fat, PCOS or a family history of diabetes. Waist size matters more than weight alone.
Which foods worsen insulin resistance?
Sugary drinks, sweets, refined flour products, fried snacks and large portions of white rice can worsen it. Choose whole foods, pulses, vegetables and protein instead.

faqs.a: No, but it greatly raises the risk of developing it.

faqs.q: Can it be reversed?
faqs.a: Many people improve with weight loss and healthier habits.

faqs.q: Do I need medicines?
faqs.a: Some people do for blood pressure, sugar or cholesterol.

faqs.q: Does it cause symptoms?
faqs.a: Usually not, apart from signs such as a larger waist.

faqs.q: Can thin people have it?
faqs.a: Yes. Some people with a normal weight still have the risk factors.

faqs.q: How often should I be checked?
faqs.a: Your doctor will advise based on your risk.

What Is Metabolic Syndrome? 5 Risk Factors Explained
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 22 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
Metabolic syndrome is usually diagnosed when a person has at least three of five risk factors: a large waist, high blood pressure, high blood sugar, high triglycerides and low HDL cholesterol. Lifestyle changes, such as weight loss, activity and a healthier diet, can improve all of them.
Metabolic syndrome is not a single disease. It is a group of related problems that often appear together and increase the risk of type 2 diabetes, heart disease and stroke.
The five risk factors
1. large waist
Excess fat around the abdomen. Cut-offs are lower for South Asians than for many other groups.
2. high blood pressure
Blood pressure above the target range, or treatment for it.
3. high blood sugar
Raised fasting sugar or treatment for diabetes.
4. high triglycerides
Raised levels of this blood fat.
5. low HDL cholesterol
Low levels of the "good" cholesterol.
Why it matters
Together these factors raise the risk of diabetes, heart attack, stroke and fatty liver.
How it is diagnosed
Measurements of waist, blood pressure and blood tests for sugar and lipids. Your doctor interprets them together.
How to reduce the risk
Lose excess weight, especially abdominal fat
Exercise regularly
Eat more vegetables, whole grains and pulses
Cut sugar, refined carbohydrates and fried foods
Stop smoking and limit alcohol
Treat blood pressure, sugar and cholesterol as advised
Points to keep
Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of risk factors.
Three of five make the diagnosis.
It raises diabetes and heart risk.
Lifestyle change helps all components.
Early action matters.
Catching it early gives you time to act. For an assessment, you can consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
When to seek urgent care
Seek urgent care for chest pain, breathlessness, confusion, vomiting, or symptoms of very high or very low sugar.
Sources and further reading
NHLBI: Metabolic syndrome
NIDDK: Insulin resistance and prediabetes
Frequently asked questions
Is metabolic syndrome the same as diabetes?
No, but it greatly raises the risk of developing it.
Can it be reversed?
Many people improve with weight loss and healthier habits.
Do I need medicines?
Some people do for blood pressure, sugar or cholesterol.
Does it cause symptoms?
Usually not, apart from signs such as a larger waist.
Can thin people have it?
Yes. Some people with a normal weight still have the risk factors.
How often should I be checked?
Your doctor will advise based on your risk.

faqs.q: What is a good time in range for diabetes?
faqs.a: For most adults, more than 70 percent of the time between 70 and 180 mg/dL, less than 4 percent below 70 mg/dL and less than 25 percent above 180 mg/dL. Targets differ for older adults and in pregnancy.

faqs.q: Is time in range better than HbA1c?
faqs.a: They are complementary. HbA1c shows average glucose over three months, while TIR shows daily swings and lows. Doctors use both together.

faqs.q: What is the time in range target in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The target range is tighter, about 63 to 140 mg/dL, with a goal of more than 70 percent of the time within it. Your pregnancy team will set your specific goals.

faqs.q: How many days of CGM data are needed to calculate TIR?
faqs.a: About 14 days, with the sensor worn for at least 70 percent of that time, gives a reliable estimate.

faqs.q: Can type 2 diabetes patients track time in range?
faqs.a: Yes, with a CGM. It helps those on insulin and also those trying to understand the effect of food and activity on their sugar.

faqs.q: How do I increase my time in range?
faqs.a: Balanced meals, post-meal walks, regular medicines, good sleep and review of your patterns with your doctor can all raise TIR.

Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 17 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
Time in range (TIR) is the percentage of time during a day that your glucose stays within a target range, usually 70 to 180 mg/dL, as measured by a continuous glucose monitor (CGM). For most adults with diabetes, the goal is more than 70 percent of the time in range (about 17 hours a day), less than 4 percent below 70 mg/dL and less than 25 percent above 180 mg/dL.
HbA1c tells you your average blood sugar over three months. But two people with the same HbA1c can have very different days, one steady and the other swinging up and down. Time in range shows this difference.
Why was TIR introduced?
HbA1c is an average. It does not show how high or low your sugar goes, or how often. A person with frequent highs and lows can have a "normal" average. TIR captures this variation and is closely linked to complications, along with HbA1c.
What are the standard ranges?
International consensus targets for most adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes:

Targets differ for older adults, people at high risk of low sugar and pregnancy. In pregnancy, the usual range is tighter, about 63 to 140 mg/dL.
How does TIR relate to HbA1c?
A TIR of about 70 percent roughly matches an HbA1c of around 7 percent. Each 10 percent change in TIR corresponds to about 0.5 percent change in HbA1c. But HbA1c and TIR are not interchangeable. TIR adds detail about daily swings and low sugar.
How is TIR measured?
You need a CGM. The device records glucose every few minutes. The software calculates TIR for the last 14 days, as long as the sensor was worn at least 70 percent of the time. Your report will show the percentage in each range.
How can you improve your TIR?
Food
Choose balanced meals with fibre, protein and fewer refined carbohydrates.
Watch portion sizes of rice, roti and sweets.
Eat meals at regular times.
Activity
A 10 to 15 minute walk after meals can reduce post-meal peaks. Regular exercise improves insulin sensitivity.
Medicines
Take medicines as prescribed. Your doctor may adjust doses or change medicines based on your CGM patterns.
Sleep and stress
Poor sleep and stress raise sugar. Aim for regular sleep and relaxation.
Learn your patterns
Look for repeated highs after a particular meal, early morning rises or night-time lows. Small adjustments to those moments can add up.
Is TIR useful without a CGM?
TIR needs continuous data. But the idea of aiming for steady sugar, rather than only a good average, is valuable for everyone.
When should you see a doctor?
See your doctor if your time in range is less than your target, if your time below 70 mg/dL is more than 4 percent, or if you have night-time lows or symptoms of hypoglycaemia.
A quick recap
TIR is the percentage of time your sugar is within 70 to 180 mg/dL.
The common goal is more than 70 percent TIR with minimal low sugar.
TIR complements HbA1c by showing daily variation.
It requires a CGM.
Food, activity, sleep and medicine adjustments improve it.
Time in range turns your glucose graph into a simple, useful goal. Even small improvements in TIR are linked to better outcomes. To use CGM data effectively, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.

NIDDK: Continuous glucose monitoring
WHO: Diabetes fact sheet
Frequently asked questions
What is a good time in range for diabetes?
For most adults, more than 70 percent of the time between 70 and 180 mg/dL, less than 4 percent below 70 mg/dL and less than 25 percent above 180 mg/dL. Targets differ for older adults and in pregnancy.
Is time in range better than HbA1c?
They are complementary. HbA1c shows average glucose over three months, while TIR shows daily swings and lows. Doctors use both together.
What is the time in range target in pregnancy?
The target range is tighter, about 63 to 140 mg/dL, with a goal of more than 70 percent of the time within it. Your pregnancy team will set your specific goals.
How many days of CGM data are needed to calculate TIR?
About 14 days, with the sensor worn for at least 70 percent of that time, gives a reliable estimate.
Can type 2 diabetes patients track time in range?
Yes, with a CGM. It helps those on insulin and also those trying to understand the effect of food and activity on their sugar.
How do I increase my time in range?
Balanced meals, post-meal walks, regular medicines, good sleep and review of your patterns with your doctor can all raise TIR.

faqs.q: When do doctors start insulin in gestational diabetes?
faqs.a: When sugars remain above target after one to two weeks of diet and activity, when readings are very high at diagnosis, or when scans show excess growth of the baby.

faqs.q: Is insulin safe for my baby?
faqs.a: Yes. Insulin does not cross the placenta significantly and has a long safety record. Good sugar control with insulin lowers risks for the baby.

faqs.q: Will I need insulin for the rest of my life?
faqs.a: Usually not. Most women stop insulin after delivery. You will have a sugar test after birth and again at six to twelve weeks to see whether diabetes continues.

faqs.q: Can I take tablets instead of insulin?
faqs.a: Some doctors use metformin or other tablets. They cross the placenta to some extent, and guidelines vary. Discuss the options with your doctor.

faqs.q: How many times a day is insulin taken?
faqs.a: It depends on your readings. Some women need one dose at bedtime for fasting sugars, others need doses before meals. Your doctor will tailor it.

faqs.q: What should I do if I have low blood sugar?
faqs.a: Take 15 g of fast sugar such as glucose tablets or half a cup of juice, recheck in 15 minutes and have a snack. Inform your doctor so the dose can be adjusted.

When Is Insulin Needed in Gestational Diabetes?
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 19 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
Insulin is needed in gestational diabetes when blood sugars stay above target despite 1 to 2 weeks of proper diet and activity, or when sugars are very high at diagnosis. Insulin does not cross the placenta in significant amounts and is considered safe for the baby. Roughly one in three women with gestational diabetes may need medicine, and many can stop after delivery.
Many women feel anxious when told they may need insulin in pregnancy. It can feel like a setback. In reality, insulin is a safe and effective way to protect you and your baby when diet and activity are not enough.
What are the blood sugar targets?
Targets are usually:
Fasting: below 95 mg/dL
1 hour after meals: below 140 mg/dL
2 hours after meals: below 120 mg/dL
Your doctor may adjust them. If more than a few readings in a week are above target despite good diet and activity, treatment is stepped up.
When do doctors start insulin?
Persistently high readings: Fasting or post-meal sugars remain above target after one to two weeks of lifestyle changes.
Very high sugar at diagnosis: For example, a fasting value well above the normal range.
Signs of excess growth: A baby measuring large on scan, especially with a large abdomen, or excess amniotic fluid.
Ketones despite adequate diet: Which suggests the need for better control.
Pre-existing diabetes: Diagnosed in early pregnancy.
Why is insulin preferred?
It does not cross the placenta in meaningful amounts.
It is effective at lowering sugars in pregnancy.
The dose can be adjusted easily.
It has a long safety record.
What about tablets?
Metformin is used in some centres, and sometimes glibenclamide. These cross the placenta to some extent, and long-term effects on children are still being studied. Guidelines differ by country, and the decision is individual. Your doctor will explain the pros and cons.
How is insulin given?
Small injections with a pen and a very fine needle, usually into the abdomen or thigh.
Basal insulin (long-acting): At bedtime or morning, to control fasting sugars.
Rapid-acting insulin: Before meals, to control post-meal peaks.
Doses start low and are adjusted every few days based on your sugar diary.
What are the risks?
The main risk is low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia). Symptoms include shakiness, sweating, hunger, headache and palpitations. Treat with fast sugar such as glucose or fruit juice, then a snack, and inform your doctor. Weight gain can also occur, but it is usually modest.
Is insulin safe for the baby?
Yes. Good sugar control reduces the risks of a very large baby, birth injury, early delivery, newborn low sugar and breathing problems. Not using insulin when it is needed carries greater risk than using it.
Will you need insulin after delivery?
In most women with gestational diabetes, insulin is stopped right after delivery, as the placental hormones that cause insulin resistance disappear. Your sugar is checked after birth and again at six to twelve weeks to find out whether diabetes persists.
How can you reduce the chance of needing insulin?
Follow the meal plan and do not skip meals.
Walk for 10 to 15 minutes after meals.
Monitor your sugar as advised.
Manage sleep and stress.
Keep appointments.
Even with perfect habits, some women need insulin because of their hormones. It is not a failure.
When should you see a doctor?
Contact your doctor if readings are above target, you feel faint or sweaty, you have repeated lows, you vomit often or you notice decreased baby movements.
Points to keep
Insulin is added when diet and activity do not keep sugars in range.
It is safe for the baby and effective.
Dose adjustments are based on your sugar diary.
Watch for low blood sugar and know how to treat it.
Insulin is usually stopped after delivery.
Needing insulin does not mean you did something wrong. It means your body needs extra help during pregnancy. For caring, personalised guidance, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
Sources and further reading
WHO: Diabetes fact sheet
NIDDK: Gestational diabetes
Frequently asked questions
When do doctors start insulin in gestational diabetes?
When sugars remain above target after one to two weeks of diet and activity, when readings are very high at diagnosis, or when scans show excess growth of the baby.
Is insulin safe for my baby?
Yes. Insulin does not cross the placenta significantly and has a long safety record. Good sugar control with insulin lowers risks for the baby.
Will I need insulin for the rest of my life?
Usually not. Most women stop insulin after delivery. You will have a sugar test after birth and again at six to twelve weeks to see whether diabetes continues.
Can I take tablets instead of insulin?
Some doctors use metformin or other tablets. They cross the placenta to some extent, and guidelines vary. Discuss the options with your doctor.
How many times a day is insulin taken?
It depends on your readings. Some women need one dose at bedtime for fasting sugars, others need doses before meals. Your doctor will tailor it.
What should I do if I have low blood sugar?
Take 15 g of fast sugar such as glucose tablets or half a cup of juice, recheck in 15 minutes and have a snack. Inform your doctor so the dose can be adjusted.

When Should You See a Diabetologist?
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 2 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
See a diabetologist when diabetes is newly diagnosed, blood sugar is not controlled despite treatment, you need insulin or injectable medicines, you have complications, you are pregnant or planning pregnancy, or you have frequent low sugar episodes. Regular specialist review is also useful once a year even when control is good.
A diabetologist is a doctor who specialises in diabetes and related conditions. Not everyone needs one at first, but certain situations make specialist care valuable.
Situations that call for a specialist
Newly diagnosed diabetes, to set the right plan
HbA1c above target despite medicines
Starting or adjusting insulin
Frequent hypoglycaemia
Diabetes with kidney, eye, nerve or heart complications
Pregnancy or planning pregnancy
Diabetes in a young person or suspected type 1 diabetes
Considering newer medicines or glucose monitors
Diabetes with obesity or other metabolic problems
What a diabetologist offers
Detailed assessment and tailored treatment
Guidance on food, activity and monitoring
Screening for complications
Experience with newer medicines and technology
How to prepare
Bring recent reports and medicines
Bring glucose readings
Write down your questions
Working with your family doctor
Specialist and family doctor care can work together for continuity.
The quick version
Specialist care helps at diagnosis and when control slips.
Insulin, complications and pregnancy need expert input.
Yearly review is valuable.
Bring records to the visit.
Team care gives the best results.
Good diabetes care is often a team effort. For specialist guidance, you can consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
When to seek urgent care
Seek urgent care for extreme thirst with vomiting, confusion, deep rapid breathing, unusual drowsiness, or signs of very low sugar such as sweating, shaking and confusion.
Sources and further reading
WHO: Diabetes fact sheet
NIDDK: What is diabetes
Frequently asked questions
Do I need a diabetologist if my sugar is controlled?
An annual review can still be helpful.
What is the difference between a diabetologist and an endocrinologist?
A diabetologist focuses on diabetes, while an endocrinologist treats hormone disorders more broadly.
Can I see one only for a second opinion?
Yes, that is common and reasonable.
What tests will they ask for?
Typically HbA1c, kidney and lipid tests, and eye and foot checks.
Will I always need insulin?
Not necessarily. Your doctor will explain your options.
How often should I visit?
Often every three to six months, or as advised.

faqs.q: Who should not take semaglutide or tirzepatide?
faqs.a: People with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN2, those with a serious allergy to the medicine, and pregnant or breastfeeding women. Others need special caution.

faqs.q: Can I take a GLP-1 medicine if I had pancreatitis?
faqs.a: Usually this needs specialist advice, and many doctors avoid it. The risk depends on the cause and timing of the earlier episode.

faqs.q: Is it safe to take GLP-1 medicines when planning pregnancy?
faqs.a: They are not recommended in pregnancy. Plan with your doctor to stop them in advance and switch to safer options for blood sugar and weight control.

faqs.q: Can people with type 1 diabetes use GLP-1 medicines?
faqs.a: They are not standard for type 1 diabetes and do not replace insulin. Any use should be under specialist supervision.

faqs.q: Do GLP-1 medicines affect surgery or anaesthesia?
faqs.a: They slow stomach emptying, which may raise the risk of food remaining in the stomach during anaesthesia. Tell your surgeon and anaesthetist so they can advise you on pausing.

faqs.q: Can older adults use GLP-1 medicines?
faqs.a: Many can, but frail or underweight older adults need care, since weight loss may include muscle. Doses and goals should be individualised.

Who Should Not Take GLP-1 Medicines?
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 15 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
GLP-1 medicines should not be used by people with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN2 syndrome, by those who have had a serious allergic reaction to them, and during pregnancy or breastfeeding. They need special caution in people with a history of pancreatitis, gallbladder disease, severe stomach or bowel problems, kidney disease, diabetic eye disease and type 1 diabetes. Always get a medical assessment first.
GLP-1 medicines help many people with diabetes and obesity. But they are not right for everyone. Some people should avoid them completely, and others need extra care. This guide explains who and why, so you can have an informed talk with your doctor.
Medullary thyroid cancer or mEN2
These medicines carry a warning about thyroid C-cell tumours seen in animal studies. They are not advised for people with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or the genetic condition MEN2.
Serious allergy
Anyone who has had a severe allergic reaction to a GLP-1 medicine or its ingredients should not take it.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding
They are not recommended during pregnancy or while breastfeeding. Women planning pregnancy are usually advised to stop the medicine well before trying to conceive. Ask your doctor how long.
Who needs extra caution?
History of pancreatitis
GLP-1 medicines have been linked to pancreatitis. People who have had it need specialist advice, and many doctors avoid these medicines.
Gallstones or gallbladder disease
Rapid weight loss and these medicines can raise the risk of gallstones and gallbladder inflammation.
Severe stomach or bowel disease
Gastroparesis (very slow stomach emptying), severe reflux or bowel obstruction can worsen with slowed digestion.
Kidney disease
Vomiting and dehydration can strain the kidneys. Dose adjustments or close monitoring may be needed.
Diabetic retinopathy
In people with advanced eye disease, rapid improvement in blood sugar has been linked with temporary worsening of retinopathy in some studies. An eye check is advised before and during treatment.
Type 1 diabetes
These medicines are not standard treatment for type 1 diabetes, and they do not replace insulin.
Eating disorders
People with a history of anorexia, bulimia or binge eating need careful assessment. Appetite-reducing medicines can worsen such conditions.
Low body weight or frailty
Older adults who are frail or underweight may lose muscle and become weaker.
Other medicines
People on insulin or sulfonylureas have a higher risk of low blood sugar, and doses may need adjustment. Some oral medicines may be absorbed differently as stomach emptying slows.
Planned surgery
Because of slowed stomach emptying, anaesthetists may ask you to pause the medicine before surgery or sedation. Tell your surgeon and anaesthetist.
Is weight loss without obesity safe?
These medicines are meant for people with diabetes, obesity (or overweight with weight-related disease). Using them for small cosmetic weight loss is not recommended, and risks may outweigh benefits.
What checks should you expect before starting?
Your medical and family history
A list of all your medicines
Weight, BMI and waist
Blood tests for HbA1c, kidney, liver and sometimes lipid levels
Eye examination if you have diabetes
Pregnancy plans
A discussion about expectations, cost and follow-up
When should you see a doctor?
Always consult a diabetologist before starting. Contact your doctor at once if, during treatment, you have severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, a neck lump, hoarseness, trouble swallowing, vision changes or signs of an allergy.
The quick version
Avoid GLP-1 medicines if you have a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN2, or a serious allergy.
Do not use them in pregnancy or breastfeeding.
Take extra caution with pancreatitis, gallbladder disease, severe stomach problems, kidney disease and eye disease.
Always have a medical assessment first.
Tell all doctors you are using one, especially before surgery.
Knowing who should not take these medicines keeps treatment safe. A careful check before starting protects you from avoidable harm. To find out if you are a suitable candidate, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
Sources and further reading
NIDDK: Prescription medicines for overweight and obesity
WHO: Diabetes fact sheet
Frequently asked questions
Who should not take semaglutide or tirzepatide?
People with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN2, those with a serious allergy to the medicine, and pregnant or breastfeeding women. Others need special caution.
Can I take a GLP-1 medicine if I had pancreatitis?
Usually this needs specialist advice, and many doctors avoid it. The risk depends on the cause and timing of the earlier episode.
Is it safe to take GLP-1 medicines when planning pregnancy?
They are not recommended in pregnancy. Plan with your doctor to stop them in advance and switch to safer options for blood sugar and weight control.
Can people with type 1 diabetes use GLP-1 medicines?
They are not standard for type 1 diabetes and do not replace insulin. Any use should be under specialist supervision.
Do GLP-1 medicines affect surgery or anaesthesia?
They slow stomach emptying, which may raise the risk of food remaining in the stomach during anaesthesia. Tell your surgeon and anaesthetist so they can advise you on pausing.
Can older adults use GLP-1 medicines?
Many can, but frail or underweight older adults need care, since weight loss may include muscle. Doses and goals should be individualised.

Many can, but frail or underweight older adults need care, since weight loss may include muscle. Doses and goals should be individualised.

pOnly: GLP-1 Medicines
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
MD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 15 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer

GLP-1 medicines should not be used by people with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN2 syndrome, by those who have had a serious allergic reaction to them, and during pregnancy or breastfeeding. They need special caution in people with a history of pancreatitis, gallbladder disease, severe stomach or bowel problems, kidney disease, diabetic eye disease and type 1 diabetes. Always get a medical assessment first.

GLP-1 medicines help many people with diabetes and obesity. But they are not right for everyone. Some people should avoid them completely, and others need extra care. This guide explains who and why, so you can have an informed talk with your doctor.

These medicines carry a warning about thyroid C-cell tumours seen in animal studies. They are not advised for people with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or the genetic condition MEN2.
Anyone who has had a severe allergic reaction to a GLP-1 medicine or its ingredients should not take it.
They are not recommended during pregnancy or while breastfeeding. Women planning pregnancy are usually advised to stop the medicine well before trying to conceive. Ask your doctor how long.
GLP-1 medicines have been linked to pancreatitis. People who have had it need specialist advice, and many doctors avoid these medicines.
Rapid weight loss and these medicines can raise the risk of gallstones and gallbladder inflammation.
Gastroparesis (very slow stomach emptying), severe reflux or bowel obstruction can worsen with slowed digestion.
Vomiting and dehydration can strain the kidneys. Dose adjustments or close monitoring may be needed.
In people with advanced eye disease, rapid improvement in blood sugar has been linked with temporary worsening of retinopathy in some studies. An eye check is advised before and during treatment.
These medicines are not standard treatment for type 1 diabetes, and they do not replace insulin.
People with a history of anorexia, bulimia or binge eating need careful assessment. Appetite-reducing medicines can worsen such conditions.
Older adults who are frail or underweight may lose muscle and become weaker.
People on insulin or sulfonylureas have a higher risk of low blood sugar, and doses may need adjustment. Some oral medicines may be absorbed differently as stomach emptying slows.
Because of slowed stomach emptying, anaesthetists may ask you to pause the medicine before surgery or sedation. Tell your surgeon and anaesthetist.
These medicines are meant for people with diabetes, obesity (or overweight with weight-related disease). Using them for small cosmetic weight loss is not recommended, and risks may outweigh benefits.

Always consult a diabetologist before starting. Contact your doctor at once if, during treatment, you have severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, a neck lump, hoarseness, trouble swallowing, vision changes or signs of an allergy.

Knowing who should not take these medicines keeps treatment safe. A careful check before starting protects you from avoidable harm. To find out if you are a suitable candidate, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.

faqs.a: Because they produce significant weight loss and improve blood sugar and other health markers. Social media, celebrity stories and growing awareness of obesity as a medical condition also boosted interest.

faqs.q: Are GLP-1 medicines just for weight loss?
faqs.a: No. They were first used for type 2 diabetes and may also help the heart, kidneys and liver in selected patients. Weight management is one of several uses.

faqs.q: Is the GLP-1 trend a fad?
faqs.a: The science behind them is solid, and they are likely to remain important. But hype can lead to misuse. Decisions should rest on medical advice, not social media.

faqs.q: Are GLP-1 drugs safe for everyone?
faqs.a: No. They are not suitable for people with certain thyroid cancers, pancreatitis, pregnancy plans and some other conditions. Your doctor will check your history before prescribing.

faqs.q: Can I buy GLP-1 medicines online?
faqs.a: You should not buy them from unverified websites. Fake or unsafe products exist. Use a prescription and a licensed pharmacy.

faqs.q: Do I need a GLP-1 medicine to lose weight?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Many people lose weight through diet, activity and sleep. A medicine is considered if you have obesity or weight-related disease and need more help, after discussion with a doctor.

Why Did GLP-1 Medicines Become a Global Trend?
Technology and Evolution of GLP-1
Why Did GLP-1 Medicines Become a Global Trend?
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 11 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
GLP-1 medicines became a global trend because clinical trials showed large, reliable weight loss and health benefits in people with obesity and diabetes, because obesity affects hundreds of millions of people, because celebrities and social media amplified the results, and because new brands, doses and competition made the medicines more visible. A trend is not a reason to start a medicine. Suitability should be decided by a doctor.
A few years ago, few people outside diabetes clinics had heard of GLP-1. Today, the term appears in news, social media and family conversations. What changed so fast, and what should you take from it?
What changed in the science?
Earlier weight-loss medicines gave modest results and had safety concerns.
Higher-dose GLP-1 medicines showed average weight loss many times greater in trials.
Studies showed benefits for the heart, kidneys, liver and sleep apnoea in selected patients.
Tirzepatide raised expectations further.
Obesity began to be seen as a chronic disease, not a failure of willpower.
Why is obesity such a big problem?
Obesity raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, heart disease, fatty liver, joint problems and some cancers. In India, many people develop diabetes at lower body weights, and belly fat is common. Few effective long-term options existed before, so the arrival of strong medicines drew attention.
How did social media and celebrities play a part?
Dramatic before-and-after stories spread quickly online. Public figures spoke about using these medicines. This created strong demand and curiosity, but also myths, misuse and unrealistic expectations. Many posts do not show side effects, regain after stopping or the supervision behind the results.
What role did the market play?
Companies invested heavily in research and marketing.
Supply shortages in some countries drew headlines.
New brands and local manufacturing increased visibility, and in India prices began to fall.
Insurance, employers and governments started discussing coverage.
Investors tracked the sector as one of the biggest in medicine.
What is different in India?
India has a very large number of people with diabetes and obesity risk. Cost, access and cultural attitudes to weight shape the conversation. With more brands entering the market, interest is high. At the same time, concerns about unsupervised use, counterfeit products and online sales have grown.
What should you be careful about?
Trend-driven decisions without medical advice
Buying injectables from unverified websites or sellers
Expecting a quick, permanent fix
Ignoring diet, exercise and sleep
Using medicines for small cosmetic weight loss when risks may outweigh benefits
Who should seriously consider them?
People with type 2 diabetes, especially with obesity, heart or kidney disease, and people with obesity and weight-related health problems may benefit most. A doctor can assess your health and risks.
When should you see a doctor?
If you are considering a GLP-1 medicine, see a diabetologist for a proper assessment. Do not start on someone else's advice or from an online source.
What to remember
GLP-1 medicines grew popular because of strong trial results and a huge need.
Social media and celebrity stories fuelled demand.
More brands and falling prices have increased access in India.
Trend does not mean suitability. Medical advice is essential.
Lifestyle remains the foundation.
It is good that obesity and diabetes are finally being taken seriously. Use the buzz as a reason to speak with a doctor, not as a shortcut. To get honest, personalised advice, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
Sources and further reading
NIDDK: Prescription medicines for overweight and obesity
WHO: Diabetes fact sheet
Frequently asked questions
Why are GLP-1 drugs so popular?
Because they produce significant weight loss and improve blood sugar and other health markers. Social media, celebrity stories and growing awareness of obesity as a medical condition also boosted interest.
Are GLP-1 medicines just for weight loss?
No. They were first used for type 2 diabetes and may also help the heart, kidneys and liver in selected patients. Weight management is one of several uses.
Is the GLP-1 trend a fad?
The science behind them is solid, and they are likely to remain important. But hype can lead to misuse. Decisions should rest on medical advice, not social media.
Are GLP-1 drugs safe for everyone?
No. They are not suitable for people with certain thyroid cancers, pancreatitis, pregnancy plans and some other conditions. Your doctor will check your history before prescribing.
Can I buy GLP-1 medicines online?
You should not buy them from unverified websites. Fake or unsafe products exist. Use a prescription and a licensed pharmacy.
Do I need a GLP-1 medicine to lose weight?
Not necessarily. Many people lose weight through diet, activity and sleep. A medicine is considered if you have obesity or weight-related disease and need more help, after discussion with a doctor.

No. They are not suitable for people with certain thyroid cancers, pancreatitis, pregnancy plans and some other conditions. Your doctor will check your history before prescribing.
You should not buy them from unverified websites. Fake or unsafe products exist. Use a prescription and a licensed pharmacy.
Not necessarily. Many people lose weight through diet, activity and sleep. A medicine is considered if you have obesity or weight-related disease and need more help, after discussion with a doctor.

pOnly: Technology and Evolution of GLP-1
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
MD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 11 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer

GLP-1 medicines became a global trend because clinical trials showed large, reliable weight loss and health benefits in people with obesity and diabetes, because obesity affects hundreds of millions of people, because celebrities and social media amplified the results, and because new brands, doses and competition made the medicines more visible. A trend is not a reason to start a medicine. Suitability should be decided by a doctor.

A few years ago, few people outside diabetes clinics had heard of GLP-1. Today, the term appears in news, social media and family conversations. What changed so fast, and what should you take from it?

Obesity raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, heart disease, fatty liver, joint problems and some cancers. In India, many people develop diabetes at lower body weights, and belly fat is common. Few effective long-term options existed before, so the arrival of strong medicines drew attention.

Dramatic before-and-after stories spread quickly online. Public figures spoke about using these medicines. This created strong demand and curiosity, but also myths, misuse and unrealistic expectations. Many posts do not show side effects, regain after stopping or the supervision behind the results.

India has a very large number of people with diabetes and obesity risk. Cost, access and cultural attitudes to weight shape the conversation. With more brands entering the market, interest is high. At the same time, concerns about unsupervised use, counterfeit products and online sales have grown.
People with type 2 diabetes, especially with obesity, heart or kidney disease, and people with obesity and weight-related health problems may benefit most. A doctor can assess your health and risks.
If you are considering a GLP-1 medicine, see a diabetologist for a proper assessment. Do not start on someone else's advice or from an online source.

It is good that obesity and diabetes are finally being taken seriously. Use the buzz as a reason to speak with a doctor, not as a shortcut. To get honest, personalised advice, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.

faqs.q: Why can't I lose weight with type 2 diabetes?
faqs.a: High insulin levels, insulin resistance, hormones, certain medicines, poor sleep and stress can make it harder. A structured plan and medicine review often help.

faqs.q: Does insulin make you gain weight?
faqs.a: It can, because insulin promotes fat storage and some people eat more to prevent low sugar. Careful dose adjustment, diet, exercise and sometimes adding other medicines can limit gain.

faqs.q: Which diabetes medicines help with weight loss?
faqs.a: Metformin may be weight-neutral or lead to slight loss. SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 medicines can help reduce weight. Your doctor will choose based on your health.

faqs.q: How much weight should I aim to lose?
faqs.a: Start with 5 percent of your body weight, then aim for 10 percent or more if appropriate. Even a modest loss improves blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol.

faqs.q: Is exercise enough to lose weight in diabetes?
faqs.a: Exercise helps blood sugar and fitness, but weight loss usually needs diet changes too. Combine regular activity with healthy eating and good sleep.

faqs.q: Can diabetes go into remission with weight loss?
faqs.a: In some people, substantial weight loss, especially early in the disease, can lead to remission. It needs medical follow-up because diabetes can return if weight comes back.

Why Is Weight Loss So Hard With Type 2 Diabetes?
Written by Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, Diabetologist, Nagpur
Dr. Ajay V. KaduskarMD (Medicine), PGDHSc (Diabetology), FEACD (The Netherlands)
Published 13 October 2026 · 4 min read
Quick answer
Weight loss is harder in type 2 diabetes because of insulin resistance, high insulin levels that encourage fat storage, stronger hunger signals, some diabetes medicines that cause weight gain, poor sleep and stress, and a body that defends its weight. The right combination of food, activity, sleep, medicine adjustments and, when needed, weight-loss medicines can overcome these barriers.
If you have type 2 diabetes and find that weight does not budge despite effort, you are not alone, and you are not lazy. Diabetes, its medicines and the hormones involved can all work against weight loss. Knowing why helps you choose smarter strategies.
What makes it harder?
1. insulin resistance and high insulin levels
When cells resist insulin, the body makes more of it. High insulin promotes fat storage, especially around the belly, and makes fat harder to burn.
2. hunger and fullness hormones
Obesity and diabetes can change hormones such as leptin, ghrelin and GLP-1. Hunger rises, fullness fades, and cravings increase.
3. medicines that raise weight
Insulin, sulfonylureas (such as glimepiride) and pioglitazone can cause weight gain. Some medicines for blood pressure, depression, epilepsy or steroids can also add weight. Never stop them on your own. Ask your doctor about alternatives.
4. fear of low blood sugar
Some people eat extra snacks to avoid hypoglycaemia, which adds calories.
5. poor sleep and stress
Short sleep and stress increase appetite and cortisol, which favours belly fat.
6. reduced muscle and activity
Fatigue, joint pain, neuropathy or foot problems can limit exercise. Less muscle lowers the metabolic rate.
7. other conditions
Thyroid disease, PCOS, sleep apnoea and depression may make weight loss harder.
8. crash diets and yo-yo cycles
Extreme dieting leads to muscle loss, slower metabolism and rebound weight gain.
What actually helps?
Food
Eat balanced plates: half vegetables, a quarter protein, a quarter whole grains.
Reduce sweets, sugary drinks, fried food and refined flour.
Eat protein at each meal to protect muscle and control hunger.
Eat slowly, and avoid skipping meals.
Keep a food diary for two weeks to find hidden calories.
Movement
Walk after meals for 10 to 15 minutes.
Aim for 150 minutes or more of weekly exercise.
Add resistance training twice or thrice a week.
Reduce long sitting.
Sleep and stress
Prioritise seven to eight hours of sleep, treat sleep apnoea and find ways to relax.
Medicine review
Ask your doctor whether your diabetes medicines can be changed to ones that help weight, such as metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 medicines.
Medical and surgical options
GLP-1 medicines, other weight-loss medicines and metabolic surgery can be considered in suitable patients with obesity.
How much weight loss is worth aiming for?
Even 5 percent can improve blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol. Ten percent or more can improve blood sugar dramatically, and in some cases lead to remission of diabetes.
What should you avoid?
Crash diets and fasting without medical advice
Skipping medicines
Weight-loss supplements and unverified products
Comparing yourself with others
When should you see a doctor?
See a diabetologist if you are gaining weight despite effort, if your sugars are not controlled, or if you plan major dietary changes while taking insulin or tablets that can cause low sugar.
The quick version
Insulin resistance, hormones, medicines, sleep and stress can make weight loss harder in type 2 diabetes.
It is a biological issue, not a lack of willpower.
Balanced eating, activity, sleep and medicine review help.
Weight-loss medicines or surgery can be options.
Even 5 percent weight loss brings benefits.
Be kind to yourself and focus on steady, sustainable changes. The right team and plan can make a big difference. For a personalised weight and diabetes plan, consult Dr. Ajay V. Kaduskar, a diabetologist at Niramay Clinics in Nagpur.
Sources and further reading
WHO: Obesity and overweight
NIDDK: Health risks of overweight and obesity
Frequently asked questions
Why can't I lose weight with type 2 diabetes?
High insulin levels, insulin resistance, hormones, certain medicines, poor sleep and stress can make it harder. A structured plan and medicine review often help.
Does insulin make you gain weight?
It can, because insulin promotes fat storage and some people eat more to prevent low sugar. Careful dose adjustment, diet, exercise and sometimes adding other medicines can limit gain.
Which diabetes medicines help with weight loss?
Metformin may be weight-neutral or lead to slight loss. SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 medicines can help reduce weight. Your doctor will choose based on your health.
How much weight should I aim to lose?
Start with 5 percent of your body weight, then aim for 10 percent or more if appropriate. Even a modest loss improves blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol.
Is exercise enough to lose weight in diabetes?
Exercise helps blood sugar and fitness, but weight loss usually needs diet changes too. Combine regular activity with healthy eating and good sleep.
Can diabetes go into remission with weight loss?
In some people, substantial weight loss, especially early in the disease, can lead to remission. It needs medical follow-up because diabetes can return if weight comes back.

Quick answer

Weight loss is harder in type 2 diabetes because of insulin resistance, high insulin levels that encourage fat storage, stronger hunger signals, some diabetes medicines that cause weight gain, poor sleep and stress, and a body that defends its weight. The right combination of food, activity, sleep, medicine adjustments and, when needed, weight-loss medicines can overcome these barriers.

If you have type 2 diabetes and find that weight does not budge despite effort, you are not alone, and you are not lazy. Diabetes, its medicines and the hormones involved can all work against weight loss. Knowing why helps you choose smarter strategies.
When cells resist insulin, the body makes more of it. High insulin promotes fat storage, especially around the belly, and makes fat harder to burn.
Obesity and diabetes can change hormones such as leptin, ghrelin and GLP-1. Hunger rises, fullness fades, and cravings increase.

Insulin, sulfonylureas (such as glimepiride) and pioglitazone can cause weight gain. Some medicines for blood pressure, depression, epilepsy or steroids can also add weight. Never stop them on your own. Ask your doctor about alternatives.
Some people eat extra snacks to avoid hypoglycaemia, which adds calories.
Short sleep and stress increase appetite and cortisol, which favours belly fat.
Fatigue, joint pain, neuropathy or foot problems can limit exercise. Less muscle lowers the metabolic rate.
Thyroid disease, PCOS, sleep apnoea and depression may make weight loss harder.
Extreme dieting leads to muscle loss, slower metabolism and rebound weight gain.
Prioritise seven to eight hours of sleep, treat sleep apnoea and find ways to relax.
Ask your doctor whether your diabetes medicines can be changed to ones that help weight, such as metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 medicines.
GLP-1 medicines, other weight-loss medicines and metabolic surgery can be considered in suitable patients with obesity.
Even 5 percent can improve blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol. Ten percent or more can improve blood sugar dramatically, and in some cases lead to remission of diabetes.
See a diabetologist if you are gaining weight despite effort, if your sugars are not controlled, or if you plan major dietary changes while taking insulin or tablets that can cause low sugar.
